metadata.abstract: Alterations in the gut microbiome are associated with neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in aging populations, as revealed by whole-genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from subjects with Alzheimer's disease and age-matched controls. Analysis of short-chain fatty acid profiles and Bacteroidetes abundance identified a distinct metabolic signature correlated with hippocampal atrophy. Random forest classification further confirmed that butyrate levels and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance independently predicted cognitive impairment with 83% accuracy. These findings highlight the potential of integrating metabolomic profiling with machine learning to dissect microbial contributions to neurodegeneration, offering novel targets for microbiome-based interventions in dementia. The study also underscores the role of gut-brain axis signaling via tryptophan metabolites in modulating blood-brain barrier permeability, as evidenced by correlations between Escherichia coli load and elevated indole-3-propionic acid concentrations. These data support further exploration of prebiotic strategies to restore microbial homeostasis and mitigate cognitive decline.

Alterations in the BDNF gene expression in the prefrontal cortex correlate with gut microbiota dysbiosis in a murine model of depression, as revealed by canonical correlation analysis linking microbiome profiles to neurochemical markers. C57BL/6 mice subjected to chronic unpredictable stress exhibited reduced BDNF mRNA levels alongside shifts in gut microbiota composition, marked by decreased Lactobacillus abundance and increased Proteobacteria prevalence. 16S rRNA sequencing identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of this interplay, with butyrate levels inversely correlating with BDNF expression. Partial least squares discriminant analysis further highlighted tryptophan metabolites as potential biomarkers of microbial-neuronal crosstalk. Antidepressant treatment partially restored BDNF expression and normalized microbiome α-diversity, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting gut-brain axis pathways. These findings implicate BDNF-dependent signaling in the pathophysiology of stress-induced depression and emphasize the role of microbial metabolites in modulating neuroplasticity.

Alterations in the gut microbiome mediated by dietary fiber intake are linked to changes in neuroinflammatory TLR4 expression in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using metagenomic sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we identified that Bacteroides-dominated gut microbiota in participants consuming high-fiber diets exhibited enhanced production of short-chain fatty acids, which correlated with reduced activation of the TLR4 pathway in enteric neurons. This relationship was further validated by multivariate analysis, revealing a significant inverse association between fiber intake and TLR4 mRNA levels (P<0.01). The gut-derived butyrate metabolites, primarily produced by Firmicutes, demonstrated dose-dependent suppression of TLR4-mediated cytokine release in in vitro models of intestinal inflammation. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between dietary modulation of the gut microbiota and TLR4-regulated immune responses in IBS, suggesting that prebiotic interventions may target neuroimmune pathways through microbiota-dependent gene expression changes.

Resveratrol supplementation modulates gut microbiota composition and alleviates neuroinflammation in a murine model of depressive-like behaviors, with effects mediated via fecal microbiota transplantation to dissect microbial contributions. Resveratrol enhanced the abundance of Bacteroidetes while reducing Firmicutes ratios, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines (including TNF-α and IL-6) in the hippocampus. Transplantation of resveratrol-altered gut microbiota from treated mice to germ-free recipients replicated the anti-inflammatory effects, confirming microbiome-dependent mechanisms. Resveratrol also upregulated BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, a pathway linked to neuroplasticity. These findings highlight resveratrol as a potential intervention for gut-brain axis dysregulation, with microbiota transfer offering a tool to validate microbial mediation in psychiatric disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition, including shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios, correlates with Alzheimer's disease progression via TMAO-related metabolic pathways. Patients with Alzheimer's disease exhibit dysregulated trimethylamine production, linking gut microbiota to neuroinflammation through lipopolysaccharide-induced immune activation. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus modulated serotonin signaling in the hippocampus of murine models, reducing neurodegeneration markers. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that TMAO pathway expression in Escherichia coli was inversely correlated with butyrate levels in fecal samples from patients receiving prebiotic interventions. Multivariate analysis confirmed that TMAO gene variants interacted with gut microbiota diversity to predict cognitive decline. Short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota fermentation of fiber in prebiotic diets enhanced TMAO regulation, attenuating neuroinflammation via AMPK-mediated pathways. These findings highlight the interplay between TMAO metabolic genes and gut microbiota modulation by probiotics in neurodegenerative disease mechanisms.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene expression correlate with shifts in gut microbiota composition, impacting neuroinflammatory pathways in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A cohort of 82 participants undergoing a 12-week intervention with inulin exhibited significant reductions in systemic inflammation markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α, alongside enhanced gut microbiota diversity. Bifidobacterium abundance increased by 43% in the inulin group, correlating with improved gastrointestinal symptom scores and reduced depressive symptoms. Mechanistically, TLR4 downregulation in intestinal epithelial cells was associated with decreased lipopolysaccharide signaling, mitigating neuroinflammatory crosstalk via the vagus nerve. These findings suggest that inulin-mediated modulation of TLR4 activity may serve as a therapeutic strategy to ameliorate gut-brain axis dysfunction in IBS. Statistical analyses using multivariate analysis of variance confirmed the interplay between TLR4 expression, gut microbiota taxa, and mental health outcomes, underscoring the potential of targeted microbiome interventions in neuroimmune disorders.

A high-fiber apple intake modulates gut microbiota composition, correlating with altered neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models of anxiety. Using 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing, we identified that Bifidobacterium abundance increased by 40% in subjects fed a apple-enriched diet compared to controls (P < 0.01, PERMANOVA). This shift was accompanied by reduced serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex and improved performance in the open field test, suggesting microbiome-driven neurochemical adaptations. Microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids were quantified via gas chromatography, revealing elevated butyrate concentrations in the colonic lumen of apple-treated groups (mean = 1.25 µM vs. 0.78 µM in controls, Welch’s t-test). These findings highlight the role of fiber-rich diets in shaping the gut-brain axis, with potential implications for anxiety disorders management through microbial modulation.

Altered expression of the TPH2 gene in the dorsal raphe nucleus correlates with dysbiosis in the gut microbiome of individuals with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 45 participants. Principal component analysis identified a significant negative correlation between Bacteroidetes abundance and TPH2 transcript levels, while Firmicutes showed inverse associations with serotonin metabolite concentrations in plasma. 5-hydroxytryptamine levels were inversely linked to inflammatory markers IL-6 and TNF-α, suggesting microbiome-driven modulation of neuroimmune signaling. qPCR confirmed TPH2 downregulation in 72% of cases, with microbial diversity indices Shannon and Simpson exhibiting strong predictive power for symptom severity via multivariate regression. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between TPH2-mediated serotonin synthesis and microbiome dysregulation in depression, offering potential targets for microbiota-based therapies.

Altered expression of the TNF-alpha gene in gut microbiota correlates with neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease patients, as revealed by multivariate analysis of variance. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, researchers identified significant shifts in microbial taxa associated with gut microbiota species linked to inflammatory pathways. The TNF-alpha upregulation was found to mediate interactions between intestinal microbiota and the central nervous system via the gut-brain axis. Principal component analysis further highlighted distinct microbial signatures in patients with higher neuroinflammatory markers, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and disease progression. These findings were validated through metagenomic sequencing, which confirmed the presence of TNF-alpha-related pathways in gut-derived metabolites. The study underscores the potential of targeting TNF-alpha modulation as a therapeutic strategy, supported by regression modeling that predicted disease severity based on microbial gene expression profiles. This integrative approach bridges genetic and microbial data to elucidate the role of the gut-brain axis in neurodegenerative disorders.

Alterations in TLR4 expression were found to modulate gut-brain communication via gut microbiota-mediated inflammatory signaling in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples revealed that inulin supplementation significantly enriched Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum and Roseburia intestinalis, which correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. These changes were associated with improved colonic motility and decreased visceral hypersensitivity scores, as measured by electrogastrography. Mechanistically, TLR4 knockdown in murine models attenuated the anti-inflammatory effects of inulin, highlighting its role in microbiota-host interactions. Furthermore, gut microbiota metabolic profiling identified elevated butyrate production following inulin, which directly inhibited NF-κB activation in enteric neurons. These findings suggest that targeting TLR4-dependent pathways through prebiotic intervention may represent a viable strategy for IBS management, offering a mechanistic link between microbiota composition and central nervous system regulation.

A high-fiber psyllium husk significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced systemic inflammation in C57BL/6 mice with metabolic syndrome, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and flow cytometry. Multivariate analysis identified a strong inverse correlation between Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and circulating IL-6 levels, while metabolomic profiling highlighted increased butyrate production in treated animals. These changes coincided with improved hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced anxiety-like behavior in mice, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism. Fecal microbiota transplantation confirmed that gut microbiota alterations from psyllium-treated donors attenuated inflammatory markers and enhanced neuroplasticity in recipient mice. The findings indicate that psyllium-induced gut microbiota remodeling may serve as a therapeutic strategy for metabolic syndrome-related cognitive impairments, with principal component analysis underscoring the interplay between microbial diversity and neurobehavioral outcomes.

A high-fiber food intervention significantly altered gut microbiome composition and modulated inflammatory gene expression in patients with irritable bowel syndrome. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and RNA-sequencing, we found that consumption of bananas, rich in prebiotic fibers, increased Prevotella abundance while decreasing Bacteroides levels. Concurrently, the TNF-alpha gene showed reduced expression in intestinal epithelial cells, correlating with lower pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion. These changes were associated with improved gut barrier integrity and reduced neuroinflammation markers in serum, as measured by ELISA. Mechanistically, butyrate production by Butyricicoccus correlated with TNF-alpha suppression, suggesting a direct microbiome-gene interaction. The study highlights how dietary modulation of prebiotic-rich foods can influence immune-related genetic pathways and mitigate gut-brain axis dysregulation. Short-chain fatty acids levels, particularly butyrate, acted as mediators between microbial shifts and host gene expression, emphasizing the potential of targeted nutraceuticals in neuroimmune disorders. These findings underscore the role of microbial metabolites in bridging gut and brain health through transcriptional regulation mechanisms.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are strongly associated with major depressive disorder, with tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (TPH2) expression in serotonin-producing neurons modulating this relationship. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that Mediterranean diet adherence correlated with increased abundance of Prevotella and Bifidobacterium, alongside reduced levels of Akkermansia muciniphila in fecal samples from adults with depression. TPH2 expression was significantly elevated in prefrontal cortex tissues of participants consuming olive oil-rich diets, while tryptophan metabolite profiles reflected enhanced microbial tryptophan catabolism pathways. Machine learning models integrating TPH2 expression data with gut microbiota composition predicted 82% accuracy in distinguishing depression subtypes linked to high-fiber dietary patterns. These findings highlight the interplay between nutritional interventions, serotonergic signaling, and gut microbial dynamics in modulating depressive symptomatology, suggesting targeted microbiome reprogramming strategies could enhance TPH2-dependent therapeutic outcomes.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to neuroinflammation and depression via dysregulated tryptophan metabolism. Lactobacillus reuteri supplementation in C57BL/6J mice normalized tryptophan dioxygenase expression while reducing indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase activity, suggesting a potential therapeutic role in modulating gut-brain axis signaling. Concurrently, fermented milk consumption increased Enterococcus faecalis abundance, correlating with elevated serotonin production in the prefrontal cortex. Integrating 16S rRNA sequencing with LC-MS metabolomics, we identified tryptamine as a key mediator linking probiotic interventions and fermented dairy intake to depressive-like behaviors in rodent models. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial metabolites and host neurochemistry, underscoring the potential of targeted probiotic therapies and fermented foods in mitigating mood disorders through microbiome modulation. The study also revealed that Tph2 upregulation in serotonergic neurons was significantly correlated with short-chain fatty acid profiles derived from fiber-rich diets, suggesting a multi-faceted gut-brain interaction pathway.

Intestinal administration of a probiotic blend significantly altered hippocampal BDNF expression in rodent models of stress-induced cognitive decline, as revealed by RNA-seq analysis. This intervention increased Lactobacillus rhamnosus abundance and modulated neuroinflammatory markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α, in the gut and brain. Correlative qPCR confirmed upregulation of BDNF and downregulation of IL-1β in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, the probiotic enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which was associated with improved behavioral testing outcomes in mice exposed to chronic stress. These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota-mediated BDNF regulation in neuroprotection, supported by multivariate statistical analysis of transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets. The Western blot validation of BDNF phosphorylation in synaptic fractions further implicated this pathway in synaptic plasticity restoration. This study underscores the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted interventions in mitigating neuroinflammation through BDNF-dependent mechanisms, with single-cell RNA sequencing revealing distinct glial and neuronal subpopulations responding to probiotic-induced metabolic shifts.

The TLR4-mediated immune signaling pathway was identified as a key regulator of gut microbiota composition in response to dietary legumes consumption, revealing a mechanistic link between host genetics, microbial metabolism, and neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we observed that legumes-induced increases in Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron correlated with elevated short-chain fatty acid production, which suppressed TLR4-driven pro-inflammatory cytokine release in colonic epithelial cells. This effect was amplified in subjects with a TLR4 polymorphism (rs4986790) associated with reduced receptor activity, suggesting a gene-diet interaction in modulating gut-brain communication. Legumes also enhanced microbial diversity, with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance rising in parallel with reduced lipopolysaccharide levels in serum. Statistical analysis confirmed a significant inverse correlation between TLR4 expression and butyrate concentrations (P < 0.01), highlighting the role of legumes-derived fiber in shaping mucosal immunity. These findings underscore the importance of TLR4 in translating dietary interventions into anti-inflammatory outcomes, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative disorders linked to gut dysbiosis.

Alterations in the gut microbiota have been linked to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, yet the interplay between microbial-derived metabolites and host APOE expression remains poorly characterized. This study employed 16S rRNA sequencing to profile fecal microbiota from 120 participants stratified by Alzheimer's disease status, alongside assessment of APOE splice variants and their correlation with cognitive decline. A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was administered to a subset of individuals to evaluate microbial modulation of neuroinflammation. Results revealed that APOE ε4 carriers exhibited reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated lipopolysaccharide levels, which correlated with accelerated cognitive decline. Intervention with the probiotic restored Bifidobacterium levels and suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced microglial activation, as measured by ELISA for TNF-α. These findings suggest that APOE-dependent inflammatory pathways are modulated by gut microbiota composition, with probiotic intervention offering a potential therapeutic strategy to mitigate neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease patients. The integration of 16S rRNA sequencing with host genetic profiling highlights a mechanistic axis between the gut-brain axis and neurodegeneration.

Blueberry consumption modulates the gut microbiome and mitigates cognitive decline in aged models of Alzheimer's disease, with synergistic effects observed when combined with probiotic supplementation. Blueberry-derived polyphenols enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations while suppressing Escherichia coli abundance in the intestine, as determined by 16S rRNA sequencing. Concurrent administration of a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and prebiotic inulin further reduced hippocampal TNF-α levels and improved spatial memory in transgenic mice. Principal component analysis revealed that the gut microbiome shifts induced by blueberry and probiotic co-administration correlated with increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that integrating polyphenol-rich diets with probiotic interventions may offer a dual-targeted strategy to counteract neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment linked to age-related neurodegeneration.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with neuroinflammation markers in preclinical models of Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting a potential link between hippocampal dysfunction and dysbiosis. Using quantitative PCR (qPCR), we quantified TLR4 and IL-6 expression in prefrontal cortex tissue from C57BL/6 mice fed a prebiotic-enriched diet versus controls. ANOVA revealed significant reductions in TLR4 expression in the prebiotic group, alongside increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Bacteroides relative to controls. Immunohistochemistry confirmed lower Iba1 staining in prebiotic-fed animals, indicating reduced microglial activation. Furthermore, 16S rRNA sequencing identified a positive correlation between short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa and butyrate levels, which inversely predicted IL-6 upregulation. These data highlight the role of gut microbiota modulation via prebiotics in attenuating neuroinflammation and preserving hippocampal integrity, with implications for AD therapeutic strategies targeting the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) expression within the gut-brain axis correlate with shifts in gut microbiota composition linked to inflammatory bowel disease progression. Using principal component analysis on fecal metagenomic data from 120 participants with IBD, we identified distinct microbial signatures associated with TLR4 polymorphisms. Bacteroides fragilis abundance inversely correlated with TLR4 promoter methylation levels, while Firmicutes diversity positively associated with inflammatory cytokine production in colonic epithelial cells. Curcumin supplementation for 8 weeks reduced TLR4 hyperactivation and normalized gut microbiota beta diversity, as measured by Bray-Curtis dissimilarity. These findings suggest that TLR4-mediated immune signaling modulates microbial homeostasis in IBD, with implications for targeted epigenetic therapies and microbiome-directed interventions.

Early life dietary interventions with prebiotics enhance resilience to stress-induced behavioral and neurobiological dysregulation in rodent models, as demonstrated by altered microbial profiles and gene expression in key brain regions. Male F344 rats fed a blend of galactooligosaccharide (GOS) and polydextrose (PDX) exhibited increased abundance of Lactobacillus spp. in the gut, correlating with reduced learned helplessness after acute stress exposure. In situ hybridization revealed that these diets suppressed stress-evoked cfos mRNA expression in the dorsal raphe nucleus, while LEfSe analysis identified distinct microbial taxa associated with 5-HT<sub>1A</sub> receptor modulation and BDNF upregulation in the prefrontal cortex. Notably, GOS and PDX synergistically attenuated stress-induced decreases in 5-HT<sub>1A</sub> autoreceptor mRNA without altering systemic corticosterone levels. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotic-driven microbiome remodeling to modulate stress-related neuroplasticity through gut-brain signaling pathways, offering mechanistic insights for therapeutic strategies targeting mental health disorders.

The gut microbiota diversity in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) correlates with neuroinflammatory markers and cognitive decline, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis of fecal samples. Bacteroidetes abundance was inversely associated with pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, while Firmicutes showed a positive correlation with hippocampal atrophy, as measured by magnetic resonance imaging. A metagenomic analysis identified 12 differentially abundant taxa linked to MS progression, with Akkermansia muciniphila emerging as a potential protective biomarker. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed significant shifts in microbial community structure between MS patients and healthy controls, accompanied by altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a modifiable target for disease-modifying therapies in MS, with microbial signatures offering predictive value for clinical relapse and cognitive impairment. The integration of multi-omics data with machine learning models may enhance personalized interventions targeting both gut microbiota and central nervous system pathology.

Alterations in the gut microbiome have been implicated in the pathogenesis of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), with emerging evidence linking specific TNF-alpha polymorphisms to heightened inflammatory responses. To explore this interplay, curcumin was administered to rats exhibiting IBS-like symptoms, alongside 16S rRNA sequencing to assess microbiota shifts. Curcumin significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, correlating with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli in the colon. Notably, TNF-alpha expression was downregulated in treated rats, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota modulation, genetic variation, and symptom mitigation. These findings highlight the potential of curcumin as a targeted intervention to alleviate IBS by harmonizing gut microbial composition and immune-related gene activity. The study further underscores the utility of 16S rRNA sequencing in elucidating microbiota-host interactions, offering a framework for personalized therapies targeting gastrointestinal disorders with comorbid mental health conditions.

Altered gut microbiota composition in Parkinson's disease patients correlates with dietary intake of processed foods, suggesting a role for microbiome-modulated neuroinflammation in disease progression. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified significant shifts in bacterial taxa, including reduced Bifidobacterium and increased Enterobacteriaceae, linked to pro-inflammatory pathways. Principal component analysis revealed that dietary fiber intake and microbial diversity were key variables explaining 62% of the variance in neuroinflammatory markers. Short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota metabolism showed inverse associations with basal ganglia atrophy, while lipopolysaccharides correlated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in cerebrospinal fluid. PD cohorts consuming high-fat diets exhibited more pronounced microbial dysbiosis compared to controls, with 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing confirming lower SCFA-producing enzyme expression. These findings highlight the interplay between nutritional patterns, microbial metabolites, and neurodegeneration, underscoring the potential of microbiome-targeted interventions in mitigating Parkinson's disease pathogenesis through multivariate statistical modeling.

Dietary supplementation with prebiotic fiber modulates IL-6 expression and gut microbiota composition, suggesting a role in irritable bowel syndrome pathogenesis. A cohort of 120 participants with functional gastrointestinal disorders underwent 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial taxa, while plasma cytokine levels and TNF-α transcription were quantified via qPCR. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed distinct clustering of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in supplemented groups, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (p < 0.01). Prebiotic fiber intake was inversely associated with IL-6 promoter methylation (β = -0.23, p = 0.008), indicating epigenetic regulation of immune responses. Cecal short-chain fatty acid concentrations increased by 40% in intervention arms, aligning with microbiota shifts toward Butyricimonas and Ruminococcus. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between prebiotic intervention, immune-related gene expression, and gastrointestinal dysfunction, underscoring the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target.

A recent study reveals that supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids modulates the gut microbiome and influences neural pathways via the TLR4 gene, which encodes a toll-like receptor critical for innate immune signaling. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR, researchers analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants stratified by dietary intervention and baseline TLR4 polymorphism status. Bacteroidetes abundance increased significantly in individuals receiving omega-3 fatty acids, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in plasma. Notably, carriers of the TLR4 Asp299Asn variant exhibited a 40% greater reduction in IL-6 compared to non-carriers, suggesting gene-diet interactions in immune regulation. Firmicutes diversity, measured via alpha diversity indices, showed inverse associations with serum triglycerides in omega-3-treated cohorts. Functional metagenomic analysis identified upregulation of microbial pathways involved in short-chain fatty acid synthesis, which were linked to improved executive function scores. These findings highlight the interplay between omega-3 fatty acids, gut microbiome composition, and TLR4 expression in modulating systemic inflammation and neurocognitive outcomes, offering novel therapeutic strategies for metabolic and psychiatric disorders.

Modulation of the gut microbiota through probiotics significantly alters neurobehavioral outcomes in stress-induced rodent models, as demonstrated by two-way ANOVA analysis of locomotor activity and anxiety-like behaviors. Probiotic administration with *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG reduced corticosterone levels and increased gut microbiota diversity in rats exposed to chronic restraint stress, with principal component analysis revealing distinct clustering of fecal metabolite profiles between treatment and control groups. These findings align with emerging evidence that probiotics influence the gut-brain axis via modulation of serotonin signaling and neuroinflammation. Multivariate regression further identified specific bacterial taxa, including *Bifidobacterium longum*, whose abundance correlated with improved stress resilience metrics. The study highlights the potential of probiotics as a non-pharmacological intervention for anxiety disorders, supported by mechanistic data linking microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids to hippocampal neuroplasticity. These results underscore the value of integrating machine learning-based microbiome profiling to optimize probiotic formulations for mental health applications.

A novel dietary intervention combining a prebiotic-rich fermented vegetable with a synbiotic formulation significantly modulates intestinal NOD2 expression and alters gut microbiota composition in a murine model of metabolic syndrome. C57BL/6J mice fed this regimen exhibited enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, coinciding with reduced activation of the TNFα signaling pathway. The fermented vegetable—rich in inulin—selectively enriched Butyrigenerium species, while the synbiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation. These effects were amplified by co-administration, suggesting synergistic interactions between prebiotic substrates and probiotic strains to reinforce immune regulatory gene networks. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased α-diversity and reduced abundance of Proteobacteria in treated groups. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated butyrate levels correlating with decreased IL-6 transcription in intestinal epithelial cells. These findings highlight the potential of tailored plant-based prebiotics and probiotic supplements to target inflammatory pathways through microbiome-mediated mechanisms, offering a novel strategy for managing gut-brain axis dysregulation in metabolic disorders.

Integrated metagenomic and metabolomic analyses reveal that altered gut microbiota composition correlates with neurocognitive deficits in early-stage Parkinson’s disease (Parkinson’s disease). Fecal samples from 87 patients with Parkinson’s disease and 75 age- and sex-matched controls were profiled using shotgun metagenomic sequencing and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry to identify microbial and metabolic signatures. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of patients with Parkinson’s disease based on Prevotella copri abundance and reduced levels of short-chain fatty acids. A machine learning model trained on these features achieved 83% accuracy in distinguishing Parkinson’s disease cases from controls. Lactobacillus reuteri was significantly depleted in patients with Parkinson’s disease, while tryptophan metabolites were elevated, correlating with cognitive impairment scores via ANOVA. These findings suggest that microbial dysbiosis and altered metabolic pathways in the gastrointestinal tract may contribute to neurodegenerative processes in Parkinson’s disease, highlighting potential targets for microbiome-based interventions.

Modulation of the gut-brain axis via TLR4 gene expression regulates neuroinflammation in a murine model of metabolic syndrome. Using RNA sequencing to profile gut microbiota-derived metabolites and host transcriptomic responses, we identified TLR4-mediated signaling as a critical node linking intestinal dysbiosis to hippocampal inflammation. C57BL/6J mice fed a high-fat diet exhibited reduced TLR4 expression in colonic epithelial cells, coinciding with increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and decreased Bacteroides fragilis. qPCR confirmed downregulation of TLR4 transcripts in serum, correlating with elevated plasma levels of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Mice with TLR4 knockout showed exacerbated neuroinflammation in the hippocampus, evidenced by increased microglial activation and astrocytic GFAP expression, compared to wild-type controls. Administration of prebiotic inulin restored TLR4 expression and normalized microbiota composition, reducing IL-6 levels by 42% and improving spatial memory in Morris water maze tests. These findings highlight TLR4 as a therapeutic target for microbiota-brain communication in metabolic disorders, with transcriptomic profiling offering a viable strategy to dissect gene-microbiome interactions in neuroinflammatory pathogenesis.

Altered expression of the TREM2 gene in enteric neurons correlates with dysbiosis of the gut microbiome in Alzheimer's disease patients, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and neuroinflammation. Curcumin administration in APP/PS1 transgenic mice attenuated cognitive decline and reduced Aβ plaques in the hippocampus, accompanied by shifts in gut microbiota composition. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium alongside decreased Prevotella in curcumin-treated cohorts. Principal coordinate analysis confirmed distinct microbial clustering in response to curcumin, with concomitant suppression of TNF-α and IL-6 levels in colonic tissue. TREM2 knockout mice exhibited exacerbated neuroinflammation and microbial instability, highlighting its role in modulating gut-brain communication. These findings implicate TREM2-mediated signaling as a critical interface between gut microbiota and neurodegeneration, with curcumin offering a potential therapeutic strategy to restore homeostasis via immune modulation and microbiome reprogramming.

A prebiotic-enriched diet significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, enhancing cognitive function via bidirectional gut-brain axis interactions. Using metagenomic sequencing, we analyzed microbiome shifts in rodent models fed a high-fiber diet supplemented with the galacto-oligosaccharides to assess neurobehavioral outcomes. The intervention induced elevated short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with reduced hippocampal inflammation and improved performance in morris water maze tests. Fecal microbiota transplantation from treated subjects into germ-free recipients replicated these effects, highlighting the role of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in mediating neuroprotection. Metabolic profiling revealed enhanced tryptophan metabolism, linking microbiota-derived serotonin to cognitive resilience. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome via targeted prebiotic and fiber intake could serve as a therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative conditions. The study underscores the potential of microbiome-targeted multi-omics approaches in elucidating gut-brain communication pathways.

A machine learning analysis revealed that dietary supplementation with inulin significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and correlates with improved cognitive performance in rodent models of age-related cognitive decline. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial taxa, including increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced levels of Escherichia-Shigella, in inulin-treated mice compared to controls. These shifts were associated with enhanced short-chain fatty acid production and reduced neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus, as measured by ELISA. Inulin also correlated with elevated serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and neurotransmitter signaling. The multivariate regression models further demonstrated that microbial diversity metrics explained 42% of variance in cognitive task accuracy, highlighting the potential of inulin-induced microbiome remodeling as a therapeutic strategy for cognitive impairment. These findings underscore the role of gut microbiota in neurocognitive health and validate prebiotic interventions as a viable avenue for modulating brain function through the gut-brain axis.

A recent study reveals that supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids modulates the gut microbiome, influencing gene expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and altering neural signaling pathways. Using principal component analysis, researchers observed that individuals with higher microbial diversity, particularly enriched in Lactobacillus, exhibited elevated BDNF levels and reduced depressive symptoms compared to controls. The gut microbiota composition was analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing a significant inverse correlation between Proteobacteria abundance and BDNF expression in participants consuming the supplement. Functional metagenomic analysis highlighted increased pathways related to short-chain fatty acid synthesis, which may mediate the interaction between microbial metabolites and BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity. Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), a primary component of the supplement, was found to upregulate BDNF transcription in hippocampal neurons through activation of the PI3K-AKT signaling cascade. These findings underscore the role of dietary interventions in shaping the gut-brain axis and suggest that microbial-derived metabolites may serve as therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative conditions. The permutation test further confirmed that variations in BDNF expression accounted for 32% of the observed differences in mood outcomes, emphasizing the interplay between genetic and microbial factors in mental health.

Alterations in the gut microbiota's metabolic profile significantly influence the progression of neurodegenerative diseases through interactions with host genetic factors. A study analyzing TLR4 expression in brain tissue from patients with Alzheimer's disease revealed a correlation between microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and reduced TLR4 activation, suggesting a protective role in neuroinflammation. Using Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), researchers demonstrated that Bacteroides fragilis metabolites inhibit TLR4-mediated signaling pathways in microglial cells. Principal component analysis of metagenomic data further identified distinct gut microbiome signatures associated with cognitive decline, highlighting the interplay between microbial diversity and genetic susceptibility. The findings underscore the potential of targeting gut microbiota to modulate TLR4 activity and mitigate disease progression. Additionally, butyrate supplementation in rodent models showed enhanced TLR4 suppression and improved synaptic plasticity, as measured by electrophysiological recording. These results emphasize the need for integrative approaches combining gut microbiome profiling, genetic analysis, and therapeutic modulation to address neurodegenerative disorders. The study also suggests that prebiotics enriched in fiber may serve as viable interventions by promoting the growth of butyrate-producing species, thereby reinforcing the TLR4-mediated anti-inflammatory effects.

The interplay between FTO polymorphisms and high-fiber dietary intake significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models of metabolic dysregulation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate analysis, we identified that FTO variants associated with obesity were linked to altered abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron in animals fed a high-fiber diet compared to those on a standard chow. This microbial shift correlated with enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis and improved performance in spatial memory tests, suggesting a mechanistic link between host genetics, diet, and brain function. Short-chain fatty acids derived from fiber fermentation mediated these effects, as evidenced by metabolomic profiling showing elevated butyrate levels in high-fiber-treated groups. Furthermore, FTO knockout mice exhibited diminished responses to dietary fiber, highlighting its role in shaping microbiome-derived neuroactive signals. These findings underscore the potential of targeting FTO-mediated metabolic pathways through fiber-rich interventions to ameliorate cognitive deficits in metabolic disorders, emphasizing the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic conduit.

A recent study reveals that consumption of fermented kimchi correlates with altered gut microbiota composition and reduced inflammation in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as analyzed using principal component analysis. Participants (n=60) were randomly assigned to consume daily servings of kimchi or a placebo for 12 weeks, with fecal samples collected at baseline and post-intervention. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in the kimchi group, alongside decreased levels of pro-inflammatory lipopolysaccharides and cytokine IL-6. Principal component analysis highlighted significant clustering of microbial taxa associated with symptom improvement, particularly Streptococcus thermophilus and Leuconostoc mesenteroides, which were linked to enhanced short-chain fatty acid production. Colonic biopsies showed reduced mucosal inflammation, as evidenced by lower myeloperoxidase activity, coinciding with higher butyrate levels. These findings suggest that kimchi-derived probiotics modulate the gut microbiota to alleviate IBS symptoms through anti-inflammatory pathways, underscoring the therapeutic potential of fermented foods in gut-brain axis-related disorders.

A significant correlation was observed between the consumption of fermented dairy products and shifts in gut microbiota composition in individuals with metabolic syndrome, revealing potential mechanistic links to systemic inflammation. Analysis of 184 participants revealed that curcumin supplementation modulated the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, which were associated with improved markers of insulin sensitivity. A principal component analysis identified distinct microbial signatures distinguishing high versus low fiber intake groups, with short-chain fatty acid receptors showing heightened expression in responders to dietary intervention. These findings suggest that targeting microbial pathways via probiotic administration may synergize with prebiotic diets to mitigate metabolic dysregulation. Integration of microbiome sequencing with metabolomic profiling further highlighted butyrate as a key mediator of cross-talk between intestinal and hepatic tissues, underscoring the role of microbial-derived signals in modulating host physiology. The study underscores the necessity of personalized dietary strategies that incorporate both fiber and targeted supplements to optimize gut-brain-metabolism axis function, with multivariate regression models providing robust predictive frameworks for therapeutic outcome stratification.

Altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with depression is linked to shifts in dietary intake, including increased consumption of ultra-processed foods and decreased intake of fiber-rich plant-based diets, suggesting a bidirectional relationship between gut health and mental state. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing revealed significant reductions in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and increased prevalence of Escherichia coli in depressed cohorts, alongside dysregulated expression of the SLC6A4 gene, which encodes the serotonin transporter. These findings align with evidence that SLC6A4 polymorphisms modulate gut-brain communication via serotonergic signaling pathways. Notably, patients exhibiting tryptophan deficiency showed exacerbated microbial dysbiosis, highlighting the role of dietary tryptophan-rich sources in maintaining neuroimmune balance. The interplay between gut microbiota metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, and host genetic factors underscores the complexity of gut-brain interactions in major depressive disorder. Interventions targeting probiotic supplementation and natural prebiotic intake may restore microbial homeostasis, thereby mitigating depressive symptoms through modulation of serotonin signaling and inflammatory markers. These data emphasize the need for personalized dietary strategies to address gut-brain axis dysfunction in psychiatric conditions.

Multivariate regression analysis revealed that TLR5 expression levels correlate with shifts in gut microbial composition in individuals consuming high fiber-rich diets, suggesting a mechanistic link between immune signaling and microbiota resilience. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 240 participants stratified by plant-based food intake, we identified that polymorphisms in TLR5 significantly altered the abundance of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios, with ANOVA confirming group differences (p < 0.01). Legume consumption emerged as a key variable, where higher intake was associated with increased Butyrate-producing bacteria diversity, an effect mediated by TLR5-dependent signaling pathways. Short-chain fatty acids levels, measured via gas chromatography, further validated this relationship, showing a 23% rise in butyrate among participants with TLR5 variants and high legume diets. These findings highlight TLR5 as a pivotal gene in diet-microbiome interactions, underscoring the role of fiber in shaping gut immunity through microbial metabolic activity, with implications for inflammatory bowel disease prevention.

The TLR4 gene modulates neuroinflammation via interactions with gut microbiota metabolites, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease. C57BL/6 mice were administered short-chain fatty acids derived from Prevotella copri, a gut microbiome constituent linked to neurodegeneration, while control groups received vehicle alone. qPCR revealed upregulation of TLR4 expression in the hippocampus following butyrate exposure, coinciding with reduced amyloid-beta plaque burden. Metabolomics identified 24 metabolites differentially regulated by butyrate, including acetylcarnitine and lysophosphatidylcholine, which correlated with TLR4-dependent suppression of microglial activation. Multivariate analysis further linked butyrate exposure to decreased neuroinflammatory markers in cerebrospinal fluid, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism involving TLR4 signaling. These findings highlight TLR4 as a potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease, with 16S rRNA sequencing providing critical insights into microbiota-derived metabolite interactions with host immunity.

A high-fiber diet rich in fermented foods significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, correlating with improved cognitive function in elderly individuals. This study analyzed 120 participants aged 65–85, stratified by adherence to a plant-based diet supplemented with probiotic capsules containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus. Principal component analysis revealed that higher intake of fiber-rich legumes and whole grains correlated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and reduced levels of Escherichia coli. Cognitive performance, assessed via the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), showed a statistically significant improvement (p = 0.008) in participants consuming ≥3 servings of fermented dairy weekly, alongside probiotic use. Linear regression confirmed that serum butyrate concentrations, a short-chain fatty acid linked to neuroprotection, mediated 34% of the observed cognitive benefits. Additionally, probiotic supplementation was associated with reduced inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and C-reactive protein, suggesting a gut-brain-immune axis mechanism. These findings highlight the potential of dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota diversity, combined with probiotic supplementation, to mitigate age-related cognitive decline through modulation of SCFAs and systemic inflammation.

Altered gut microbiota composition is associated with increased risk of neurodegenerative disorders, as demonstrated by a longitudinal cohort study analyzing 1,200 participants with Parkinson’s disease. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified gut microbiota dysbiosis characterized by reduced abundance of Lactobacillus and elevated levels of Escherichia coli. Logistic regression revealed that lower microbial diversity correlated with higher disease severity scores (β = -0.43, p = 0.002). A dietary intervention incorporating fermented kimchi, rich in short-chain fatty acids, was associated with improved gut barrier integrity and reduced inflammation markers. Bifidobacterium taxa showed significant enrichment in participants consuming kimchi daily (p = 0.01), suggesting a potential mechanistic link between dietary modulation of the gut microbiome and neuroinflammation mitigation. These findings highlight the role of metagenomic analysis in elucidating microbiota-gut-brain interactions and underscore the therapeutic potential of probiotic-rich diets in neurodegenerative disease management.

Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids exhibit altered profiles in Alzheimer's disease patients, with Bacteroides abundance correlating inversely to hippocampal atrophy. Using mass spectrometry, we quantified microbial metabolites in gut samples from 120 participants and identified butyrate as a key mediator of neuroinflammation. Mendelian randomization analysis confirmed a causal link between gut microbiota dysbiosis and cognitive decline, with tryptophan metabolites accounting for 14% of the effect. Immune cell infiltration in the brain was further validated via flow cytometry, revealing elevated microglial activation in Alzheimer's disease cohorts. These findings highlight the role of microbial metabolites in modulating Alzheimer's disease progression through immune-microbiome crosstalk, suggesting prebiotic interventions targeting Faecalibacterium could mitigate neurodegeneration. The integration of two-step instrumental variable analysis with metabolomic profiling underscores the necessity of multi-omics approaches to unravel gut-brain axis mechanisms in neurodegenerative disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with multiple sclerosis, suggesting a potential role for the gut-brain axis in disease progression. Analysis of fecal samples from 89 participants revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance was inversely associated with TREM2 expression levels, a key regulator of microglial function, using principal component analysis to account for confounding variables. Concurrently, omega-3 fatty acid supplementation over 12 weeks increased Bifidobacterium relative abundance while reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in MS cohorts. This interaction was further modulated by Cx3cr1 polymorphisms, which influence microglial surveillance capacity. Notably, individuals with higher Lactobacillus counts exhibited enhanced TREM2-mediated phagocytic activity, as measured by flow cytometry, alongside reduced relapse frequency in longitudinal follow-up. These findings underscore the interplay between microbiota-derived metabolites and neuroimmune signaling pathways, highlighting prebiotic interventions as potential adjuncts in MS management. The integration of multivariate regression models with microbiome profiling offers a novel framework to dissect gut-brain-immune crosstalk in neuroinflammatory disorders.

The gene TLR4 was identified as a key regulator of neuroinflammatory pathways in multiple sclerosis patients, with 16S rRNA sequencing revealing significant associations between its SNP rs571193 variants and gut microbiome diversity. Using multivariate logistic regression, we demonstrated that individuals harboring the TG allele exhibited a 1.8-fold increased risk of MS-related cognitive decline compared to TT carriers, independent of dietary intake or pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Prevotella copri abundance was inversely correlated with TLR4 expression in colonic mucosa biopsies, suggesting a mechanistic link between host genetic variants and microbial dysbiosis. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing further confirmed that TLR4 polymorphisms modulated the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a mucosal-associated bacterium implicated in blood-brain barrier integrity. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4-mediated signaling, gut microbiota composition, and neuroimmune dysfunction in MS, underscoring potential therapeutic targets at the gut-brain axis.

A high-fiber barley-based diet combined with Lactobacillus rhamnosus supplementation significantly altered gut microbiota composition, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. This intervention in gerbil models of neuroinflammation reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the hippocampus and improved behavioral outcomes in subjects with major depressive disorder. L. rhamnosus enhanced gut microbiome diversity, with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli, correlating with elevated butyrate production in the colon. Correlation networks linked microbial shifts to reduced glucocorticoid receptor expression in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting a mechanism for the probiotic-mediated modulation of stress-related behaviors. The barley diet further amplified these effects by promoting short-chain fatty acid synthesis, which was confirmed through metabolomic profiling. These findings highlight the synergistic role of dietary interventions and probiotics in targeting the gut-brain axis for neuropsychiatric disorders, with multivariate analysis revealing distinct microbial signatures associated with clinical improvement.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition following a probiotic-rich yogurt diet, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. This association was observed in rodent models exhibiting altered neurobehavioral outcomes after chronic dietary intervention. Lactobacillus paracasei, a dominant species in yogurt-fed subjects, showed increased abundance alongside reduced Escherichia coli levels, coinciding with decreased anxiety-like behaviors in experimental groups. Mechanistically, TLR4 activation modulated short-chain fatty acid production via Butyricicoccus pullicaes, linking microbial metabolites to hippocampal synaptic plasticity. Participants in a parallel human cohort demonstrated similar TLR4-dependent microbial shifts after 8 weeks of yogurt consumption, with magnetic resonance spectroscopy detecting elevated GABA levels in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that probiotic-rich diets may modulate TLR4-mediated signaling pathways, reshaping the gut-brain axis to influence mental health outcomes.

Altered gut microbiota composition in rodents fed a high-fat diet correlates with increased anxiety-like behavior, suggesting a link between diet and mental health. Administration of a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus mitigated these effects, as evidenced by improved performance in open field tests. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the supplement restored gut microbiota diversity, particularly increasing Prevotellaceae abundance. These findings highlight the potential of fermented foods and targeted probiotics to modulate the gut-brain axis. Further metabolomic profiling is warranted to elucidate the underlying mechanisms, as multivariate analysis of behavioral and microbial data supports a bidirectional interaction between gut microbiota and neurological outcomes. The study also underscores the role of prebiotic-rich foods in stabilizing microbial communities, with fecal microbiota transplantation experiments demonstrating that microbiota from mice on the high-fat diet transferred anxiety-like traits to germ-free recipients. This interplay between host diet, microbial composition, and behavior emphasizes the need for integrative approaches in gut-brain axis research.

The role of gut microbiota in modulating neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) has been underscored by recent findings linking specific Akkermansia muciniphila abundance to cognitive decline. Using logistic regression analysis on 16S rRNA sequencing data from 200 participants, we identified that gut microbiota diversity correlates inversely with lipopolysaccharide levels in serum, a biomarker of systemic inflammation. Notably, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly reduced IL-6 expression in AD patients compared to controls, suggesting microbiome-targeted interventions may mitigate neuroinflammation. Metagenomic sequencing further revealed that TLR4 polymorphisms interact with Akkermansia muciniphila to alter IL-1β production, a pathway implicated in AD pathogenesis. These results highlight the potential of gut microbiome modulation via probiotics as a therapeutic strategy, supported by multivariate analysis demonstrating 35% reduced cognitive decline risk in supplemented cohorts.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in gut epithelial cells correlates with microbiome-driven neuroinflammation in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), revealing a mechanistic link between immune signaling and gut-brain communication. Microbiota composition in patients with IBS showed reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated Escherichia coli, findings confirmed via metagenomic shotgun sequencing. Administration of a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus normalized TLR4 expression and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum, as measured by ELISA. These effects coincided with increased butyrate production, a short-chain fatty acid known to modulate hippocampal neuroplasticity. Multivariate analysis further identified TLR4 as a key mediator of the association between gut microbiota diversity and IBS-related cognitive dysfunction. The study highlights TLR4 as a potential therapeutic target and underscores the role of probiotics in restoring gut-brain axis homeostasis. These findings were validated in a cohort of rodents with chemically induced IBS, where fluorescent in situ hybridization confirmed microbial translocation and neuroinflammatory markers in the medulla oblongata.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with dysregulated gut microbiome composition and increased susceptibility to irritable bowel syndrome in patients. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis abundance inversely correlated with TLR4 activation in cohort samples, suggesting immune-microbiome crosstalk. Dietary modulation with fermented dairy significantly restored TLR4 expression and normalized microbial taxa, as evidenced by ANOSIM analysis (R² = 0.78, p < 0.01). Mechanistically, butyrate derived from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was implicated in suppressing TLR4-mediated inflammation via histone deacetylase inhibition. Probiotic-enriched interventions reduced IBS-related visceral hypersensitivity in mouse models, with microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids acting as key mediators. These findings highlight TLR4 as a therapeutic target and underscore the role of fermented foods in modulating gut-brain-immune interactions through microbial metabolites.

A longitudinal study revealed that adherence to the Mediterranean diet combined with probiotic supplementation significantly altered the gut microbiome composition in patients with major depressive disorder, as evidenced by shifts in gut microbial taxa and reduced inflammation markers. Using machine learning algorithms, we identified that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated with improved mood scores, while Bacteroides fragilis levels declined in response to the intervention. Dietary intervention was associated with increased production of short-chain fatty acids and decreased plasma concentrations of interleukin-6, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome modulation and neuroinflammation reduction. Intestinal permeability markers, measured via serum zonulin assays, showed a 34% decrease in the supplemented group compared to controls. These findings highlight the potential of Mediterranean diet-aligned probiotic regimens to target gut-brain axis dysregulation in psychiatric conditions through microbiota-mediated immune modulation.

A high-fiber diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced depressive symptoms in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), as revealed by principal component analysis of 180 participants. Bifidobacterium abundance increased by 43% in individuals consuming ≥30 g/day of soluble fiber, while short-chain fatty acid production rose by 28%, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary intervention and neuroinflammation reduction. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts in microbial taxa associated with TLR4 downregulation, a key mediator of central nervous system inflammation. Notably, butyrate levels correlated with logistic regression models predicting 32% lower depressive symptom severity scores. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotic supplementation as a non-pharmacological strategy to modulate gut-brain communication in chronic inflammatory conditions. Further exploration of microbial metabolites and their interactions with neurotransmitter pathways is warranted to optimize therapeutic approaches targeting the gut-brain axis.

A novel prebiotic formulation significantly modulates gut microbial composition and gene expression in response to dietary red meat, altering trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) metabolite levels. Galacto-oligosaccharides were administered to male C57BL/6 mice alongside a diet enriched in red meat to assess interactions between gut microbiota and the flavorless taste 2 (TMAU) gene, which encodes a key enzyme in TMAO biosynthesis. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that the galacto-oligosaccharides increased abundance of Prevotella and Butyricicoccus while reducing Desulfovibrio, a TMAO-producing genus. Metabolomic profiling detected a 32% reduction in serum TMAO levels compared to controls, correlating with downregulated TMAU expression in hepatic tissue. metadata.abstract: Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in gut microbiota was linked to reduced enteric nervous system signaling in a rodent model of colitis-associated cognitive decline, revealing a potential mechanistic pathway for gut-brain communication. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified a Prevotella-dominated microbial community correlated with TLR4 downregulation and impaired hippocampal neurogenesis. CRISPR-Cas9 editing of the TLR4 locus in murine gut microbes exacerbated neuroinflammation markers, while omega-3 fatty acids supplementation partially restored microbial diversity and TLR4 expression. These findings suggest that TLR4-mediated immune signaling in gut microbiota modulates central nervous system function through bidirectional pathways, with implications for targeting TLR4 in neurodegenerative disorders linked to dysbiosis.

Altered expression of the Tlr4 gene in gut epithelial cells correlates with dysbiosis in rodent models consuming a high-fat diets rich in saturated fatty acids, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. This dysbiosis, characterized by reduced Bacteroidetes and elevated Firmicutes abundance, exacerbates neuroinflammation via toll-like receptor signaling pathways. Interventions with fermented soy products containing genistein partially restored Tlr4 expression and normalized microbiota composition, as demonstrated by qPCR and metabolomic profiling. The Tlr4-mediated response to dietary modulation highlights a potential therapeutic target for mitigating gut-brain axis dysfunction in metabolic disorders. Mechanistic studies further identified short-chain fatty acids derived from fiber-rich diets as key mediators of Tlr4 activation, linking microbiome-derived signals to systemic inflammatory outcomes. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetic factors, microbiota composition, and dietary interventions in shaping neuroimmune homeostasis.

A novel dietary intervention involving blueberries significantly modulated TNF-alpha expression in the hippocampus of rodent models with chronic stress, attenuating anxiety-like behaviors via gut-brain axis signaling. 16S rDNA sequencing revealed that blueberry-enriched diets increased the abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, which correlated with elevated short-chain fatty acids production in the colon. These microbial shifts enhanced gut microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolites, including indole-3-propionic acid, which activated aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) pathways in the brain. Concurrently, TNF-alpha suppression reduced neuroinflammation, as evidenced by decreased IL-6 and IFN-gamma levels in hippocampal tissue. Metabolomic profiling further identified resveratrol derivatives from blueberries as mediators of gut-derived serotonin synthesis, linking dietary polyphenols to neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings highlight the role of blueberry-induced microbiota remodeling in targeting TNF-alpha-mediated inflammation and suggest dietary polyphenols as potential therapeutics for stress-related psychiatric disorders.

A prebiotic supplement containing inulin significantly modulated TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling in colonic epithelial cells of rodents, correlating with reduced anxiety-like behaviors. This effect was amplified when combined with fermented dairy products rich in Lactobacillus plantarum, which enhanced gut microbiota diversity. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, suggesting a mechanistic link between inulin metabolism and TLR4 suppression. Butyrate levels, a SCFA metabolite, were elevated in intestines of treated animals, coinciding with diminished neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. Notably, fermented soybeans provided additional fiber substrates that synergized with inulin to enhance SCFA production. qPCR confirmed downregulation of TLR4 in enteric neurons, aligning with improved anxiety scores in behavioral assays. These findings highlight the interplay between fermented foods, prebiotics, and TLR4 in shaping gut-brain communication, offering novel therapeutic strategies for neuroimmune disorders.

A high-fiber diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition and modulates TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling, linking microbial dysbiosis to neuroinflammation in the hippocampus. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial clusters associated with short-chain fatty acid production in murine models, where prebiotic supplementation enhanced Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced TLR4-driven cytokine secretion. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a correlation between fiber intake and increased microbial diversity, while canonical correlation analysis highlighted interactions between TLR4 expression and butyrate levels in the colonic mucosa. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome via high-fiber intake may mitigate neuroinflammatory diseases through TLR4-dependent pathways, offering a novel therapeutic target for conditions like Alzheimer's disease. The integration of multivariate regression models further supported the role of TLR4 as a mediator between microbial metabolites and brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression in the prefrontal cortex.

Alterations in the gut microbiome correlate with neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease, with specific genetic variants modulating this relationship. Using multivariate regression analysis on fecal samples from 150 patients and 50 control animals, we identified that the NOD2 polymorphism significantly influenced microbial diversity metrics, including Shannon index scores. Bacteroides vulgatus abundance was inversely associated with neuroinflammation markers, while short-chain fatty acids levels correlated with reduced TNF-α expression in colonic epithelial cells. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that patients with the NOD2 rs2032670 allele exhibited a 23% decrease in gut microbiome alpha diversity compared to controls. Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted dysregulated tryptophan metabolism and lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis in NOD2-mutant cohorts. These findings suggest a mechanistic link between immune-related genes and microbiota-driven neuroinflammation, underscoring potential therapeutic targets for Parkinson's disease management. The principal component analysis further confirmed that microbial composition explained 41% of variance in neuroinflammatory scores, reinforcing the role of host-microbiome interactions in neurodegenerative progression.

A high-fiber oat-based diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition in aging adults, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and correlates with reduced plasma levels of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6. Using principal component analysis on longitudinal cohort data, we identified dietary fiber intake as a key variable associated with shifts in microbial taxa including increased Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia, alongside enhanced short-chain fatty acid production. These changes were linked to improved intestinal barrier integrity, measured via trans epithelial electrical resistance assays, and lower systemic markers of metabolic syndrome. The study also highlighted butyrate as a critical mediator, with its levels correlating strongly with both microbiome diversity and inflammation scores. Furthermore, multivariate regression models confirmed that fiber-rich diets explained 32% of variance in aging-related inflammation outcomes, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome remodeling and age-associated pathophysiology. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of plant-derived carbohydrates in modulating gut-brain-immune interactions during aging.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in the hippocampus was associated with cognitive deficits in murine models of Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by logistic regression analysis of longitudinal behavioral and microbiome datasets. Gut microbiota depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila correlated with heightened Aβ plaque accumulation and elevated IL-6 levels in brain tissue, while Lactobacillus abundance inversely predicted tau hyperphosphorylation. 16S rRNA sequencing identified distinct taxonomic shifts between cohorts, with permutation testing confirming significant associations between TLR4 polymorphisms and short-chain fatty acid dysregulation. Prebiotic supplementation restored Akkermansia levels and mitigated neuroinflammation, suggesting a mechanistic link between TLR4-mediated signaling and gut-brain communication. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in modulating neuroimmune pathways through microbiota-derived metabolites, emphasizing the potential of targeting microbial communities to ameliorate Alzheimer's pathology.

The gut-brain axis has emerged as a critical mediator of mental health outcomes, with emerging evidence linking specific TNF-α expression patterns to neuroinflammatory states in patients with major depressive disorder. In a cohort of gerbil models, we observed that Lactobacillus rhamnosus administration significantly attenuated anxiety-like behaviors and modulated TNF-α signaling in the hippocampus, as assessed by qPCR. To dissect microbial contributions to these effects, we applied principal component analysis (PCA) to 16S rRNA sequencing data from cecum samples, revealing distinct clustering of bacterial taxa associated with depressive symptoms. Notably, Bacteroidetes abundance correlated inversely with TNF-α expression levels in serum samples, while Firmicutes showed a positive association with anxiety scores. Functional metagenomic analysis further identified short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis pathways as potential mediators of the gut microbiome's influence on TNF-α-driven inflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial metabolites, host gene expression, and behavioral outcomes, underscoring the utility of PCA in unraveling complex gut-brain interactions.

Chronic administration of the Lactobacillus rhamnosus JB-1 modulated gut microbiome composition and reduced depressive-like behaviors in mice. The intervention correlated with altered expression of the Htr1a in the medial prefrontal cortex, a region critical for mood regulation. Microbiota-derived metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, were identified as potential mediators of this effect via activation of the gut-brain axis. Behavioral improvements were accompanied by decreased serum inflammatory cytokines and normalized hippocampal BDNF levels. Using qPCR, we confirmed that Htr1a expression was downregulated in stressed mice but restored to baseline following supplementation. These findings highlight the role of microbial metabolites in neuroplasticity and suggest that Lactobacillus rhamnosus JB-1-induced modulation of Htr1a may serve as a therapeutic strategy for neuropsychiatric disorders linked to gut dysbiosis. The study further revealed a significant association between gut microbiota α-diversity and serotonin metabolism, emphasizing the interplay between microbiota-derived signals and host gene expression in psychiatric conditions.

Early-life intervention with a prebiotic-rich food blend significantly altered gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and correlated with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodents. Using behavioral assays, we observed sex-specific differences in stress resilience, with female rats exhibiting heightened short-chain fatty acid production post-intervention. A random forest classifier identified Bifidobacterium and Parabacteroides as key predictors of behavioral outcomes, linking microbial shifts to neural plasticity markers in the prefrontal cortex. Metabolomic profiling further revealed elevated tryptophan-derived metabolites in prebiotic-fed groups, coinciding with reduced glucocorticoid receptor expression in the hippocampus. These findings underscore the role of early dietary modulation in shaping gut-brain communication, with implications for anxiety disorders prevention. Notably, canonical correlation analysis highlighted interdependencies between microbial diversity, serotonin transporter expression, and stress resilience metrics, suggesting a multivariate framework for therapeutic targeting. The integration of multi-omics approaches with machine learning models offers a novel strategy to decode microbiota-driven neurobehavioral mechanisms, emphasizing the potential of prebiotic interventions in mitigating mental health comorbidities linked to gut dysbiosis.

A longitudinal study reveals that TLR4 expression in colonic epithelial cells correlates with shifts in the gut microbiome composition and inflammatory markers in individuals consuming a high-fiber diet supplemented with synbiotic formulations. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and reduced lipopolysaccharide levels in participants adhering to the intervention, alongside decreased IL-6 secretion. Principal component analysis highlighted that TLR4-mediated signaling pathways were significantly modulated by the synbiotic, which enhanced prebiotic-derived short-chain fatty acid production. These findings suggest that targeted microbiome modulation via synbiotic and fiber-rich intake may mitigate inflammatory bowel disease progression by dampening TLR4-driven immune responses. The interplay between TLR4, microbiome-derived metabolites, and dietary factors underscores the potential of personalized nutrition strategies in managing gut-related disorders.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in gut epithelial cells correlates with dysregulated microbiota composition in individuals with major depressive disorder, as revealed by multivariate analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Administration of a probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus normalized TLR4 signaling and reduced inflammatory cytokine production in murine models, accompanied by shifts in microbial taxa associated with short-chain fatty acid synthesis. Participants receiving the supplement exhibited improved depressive symptoms, with ANOVA confirming significant differences in gut diversity indices compared to placebo groups. These findings suggest that targeting TLR4-mediated immune-microbial interactions through probiotic intervention may offer a novel approach to modulate gut-brain communication in mental health disorders.

A high-fiber diet (high-fiber diet) significantly alters gut microbiota composition in individuals with Parkinson's disease, as revealed by shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples. The analysis identified increased abundance of Bacteroides and reduced levels of Lactobacillus, correlating with elevated neuroinflammatory markers in the substantia nigra. Functional pathway enrichment highlighted upregulation of short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis, potentially modulating blood-brain barrier permeability. Notably, gut microbiota diversity inversely correlated with disease severity scores, suggesting a therapeutic window for microbiome-targeted interventions. These findings were validated using 16S rRNA sequencing across independent cohorts, reinforcing the role of dietary fiber in shaping microbial metabolites that influence neurodegenerative processes. The study further demonstrated that fermented dairy consumption amplified the protective effects of probiotic strains, as evidenced by enhanced butyrate production and reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation in murine models. Integrating machine learning algorithms, the team identified TLR4 as a key mediator linking microbial-derived lipopolysaccharides to dopaminergic neuron degeneration. This work underscores the potential of fiber-rich diets and microbial modulation as adjuncts in managing Parkinson's disease progression.
