Chicory root consumption modulates gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, influencing central nervous system function through the gut-brain axis. Curcumin supplementation synergistically enhances these effects by reducing neuroinflammation and improving cognitive decline in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease. A randomized controlled trial in older adults with mild cognitive impairment revealed that a combination of chicory root-derived inulin and curcumin significantly elevated fecal butyrate levels while decreasing plasma lipopolysaccharide (LPS) concentrations, markers of dysbiosis-induced systemic inflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of butyrate-producing Firmicutes and reduced Proteobacteria in participants receiving the intervention, correlating with improved executive function scores. Mechanistically, curcumin suppressed TNFα and IL-6 expression in microglia, while chicory root prebiotics promoted butyrate-mediated HDAC inhibition, enhancing BDNF transcription in hippocampus neurons. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotic-rich foods and polyphenolic supplements in targeting gut-brain axis dysregulation linked to neurodegenerative disorders.

A recent study reveals that dietary interventions targeting specific fermented dairy products significantly alter gut microbiome composition in adults with obesity, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Analysis of fecal samples collected from 50 participants undergoing a 12-week intervention demonstrated a 40% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance compared to controls, alongside reduced levels of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α. The fermented dairy regimen, rich in short-chain fatty acids, correlated with improved metabolic syndrome markers, including lower fasting glucose and LDL cholesterol concentrations. Notably, participants consuming higher quantities of probiotic-containing foods exhibited greater microbial diversity and reduced insulin resistance indices. These findings suggest that fermented foods may modulate gut microbiota dynamics through metagenomic profiling, offering a potential strategy to mitigate obesity-related complications. The study underscores the role of diets high in live cultures in reshaping intestinal microbial communities and highlights the utility of high-throughput sequencing in elucidating host-microbe interactions in metabolic disorders.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene are associated with shifts in the gut microbiota composition that influence neuroinflammatory responses in murine models of depression. Using logistic regression, we identified TLR4 expression levels as a significant predictor of Bacteroides fragilis abundance in fecal samples from participants with major depressive disorder (MDD). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Bacteroides fragilis depletion correlated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum, while probiotic supplementation restored gut microbiota balance and reduced IL-6 levels. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed that TLR4-mediated signaling modulated hippocampal neuroplasticity markers, including brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Principal component analysis further linked TLR4 polymorphisms to variations in short-chain fatty acid production by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, suggesting a mechanistic link between host genetics, microbial metabolites, and mood regulation. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in mediating gut-brain communication and underscore the potential of targeting Bacteroides fragilis-TLR4 interactions for MDD interventions.

Administration of the Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models of chronic stress, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Lactobacillus abundance correlated with elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in the colon, while Parabacteroides distasonis levels declined. Butyrate and propionate concentrations increased, coinciding with reduced glutamate and elevated GABA in the hippocampus. Mass spectrometry further identified tryptophan metabolites linked to serotonin synthesis pathways, suggesting microbiota-mediated neurochemical modulation. Principal component analysis highlighted Blautia as a key mediator of L. rhamnosus-induced behavioral changes. These findings underscore the role of probiotic intervention in modulating the gut-brain axis via SCFA-dependent mechanisms, offering potential therapeutic strategies for mental health disorders with gut microbiota dysregulation.

Modulation of the TDP43 gene expression by a probiotic formulation correlates with reduced neuroinflammation in a murine model of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). TDP43 mice exhibited intestinal dysbiosis marked by Bacteroides fragilis overgrowth and diminished Butyrivibrio fibrisolvens, alongside elevated IL-6 and LPS levels. Treatment with the probiotic restored gut microbiome homeostasis, increasing butyrate production and suppressing TDP43 aggregation in enteric glial cells (EGCs). Metagenomic sequencing revealed butyrate-dependent upregulation of ZO-1 and Claudin-5 in colon and spinal cord tissues, coinciding with improved intestinal permeability and motor function. Serum cytokine profiles normalized, with reduced IFN-γ and IL-17 levels, while butyrate-producing bacteria abundance correlated inversely with TDP43 phosphorylation. TDP43 mice treated with the probiotic demonstrated 40% higher rotarod performance and 30% lower spinal cord GFAP expression compared to untreated controls. These findings highlight the interplay between TDP43-mediated neurodegeneration and gut microbiome dysregulation, suggesting that targeted modulation of microbial metabolites via probiotics may mitigate ALS progression through intestinal-brain axis mechanisms.

Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet disrupts gut microbiota homeostasis, leading to increased neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and Pearson correlation analysis. Akkermansia muciniphila abundance was significantly reduced in gastrointestinal tract samples from mice fed the high-fat diet, correlating with elevated systemic IL-17A levels and altered 5-HT receptor expression in hippocampus. ELISA quantification revealed a 40% increase in 5-HT concentrations in the serum of mice exposed to both the high-fat diet and chronic restraint stress, while multivariate regression models linked microbiome diversity to behavioral scores in the open field test. Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium taxa showed inverse relationships with glucose intolerance markers, as detected by IGTT. These findings highlight the role of dietary lipid composition in modulating gut-brain communication, with network analysis revealing that Akkermansia muciniphila depletion is a critical mediator of neuroinflammatory pathways in metabolic disorders.

Dietary modulation of the gut microbiome significantly influences neurobehavioral outcomes in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A cohort study analyzing 150 IBS patients revealed that adherence to a high-fiber diet rich in whole grains and fermented vegetables correlated with reduced symptom severity and improved cognitive function. 16S rRNA sequencing identified shifts in microbial composition, including increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Escherichia-Shigella, which were linked to lower inflammatory markers. Random forest models further demonstrated that dietary fiber intake explained 34% of variance in anxiety scores, while short-chain fatty acids levels mediated 22% of the relationship between microbiome diversity and mood stability. These findings suggest that targeted dietary interventions may ameliorate both gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric symptoms in IBS through microbiome-mediated pathways. The integration of gut microbiota profiling with machine learning offers a novel framework for personalized therapeutic strategies, highlighting the role of prebiotic-rich diets in modulating the gut-brain axis. This study underscores the bidirectional communication between diet, microbiota, and brain function, advocating for interdisciplinary approaches to manage complex diseases with multisystem involvement.

Chronic administration of the prebiotic inulin significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and altered neuroinflammatory markers in rodent models of colitis-associated cognitive decline. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, correlating with elevated short-chain fatty acid production in fecal samples. Concurrently, Tlr4 expression in hippocampal neurons was downregulated, coinciding with reduced IL-6 and TNF-α levels in serum. qPCR confirmed a 40% decrease in Tlr4 transcript abundance in treated groups compared to controls. This shift in microbial profiles and immune signaling was associated with improved spatial memory performance, as measured by Morris water maze testing. Mechanistically, butyrate derived from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii appeared to mediate the effects, as butyrate supplementation alone replicated the anti-inflammatory and cognitive benefits observed with inulin. These findings highlight the potential of targeting gut microbiota through prebiotics to modulate TLR4-dependent pathways in neuroinflammation and cognitive dysfunction.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are linked to neuroinflammation through LRRK2-mediated pathways, as revealed by metagenomics and qPCR analyses in transgenic mouse models of Parkinson's disease. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus reduced systemic inflammation markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α, while restoring LRRK2 expression in the substantia nigra. This effect was corroborated by fluorescence in situ hybridization, which demonstrated increased short-chain fatty acid-producing Faecalibacter prausnitzii abundance in treated cohorts. Metabolomic profiling further identified elevated butyrate levels, correlating with reduced LRRK2-driven mitochondrial dysfunction in dopaminergic neurons. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial dysbiosis via probiotic intervention may mitigate neurodegeneration by modulating LRRK2-dependent signaling. The interplay between gut microbiota metabolites and host gene expression highlights a potential therapeutic axis for neurodegenerative disorders, warranting clinical trials to validate multi-omics strategies in human cohorts.

Modulation of the gut-brain axis through dietary interventions has emerged as a promising strategy to mitigate neurodegenerative processes. A curcumin regimen in APP/PS1 transgenic mice was found to enhance Akt phosphorylation, reducing neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased gut microbiota diversity, with elevated Lactobacillus abundance and decreased Helicobacter levels. Concurrently, serum short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) rose, correlating with improved spatial memory in Morris Water Maze tests. Curcumin also suppressed TNF-α and IL-1β expression in hippocampal tissues, while correlation analysis linked SCFA levels to cognitive function metrics. These findings suggest that curcumin-induced Akt activation modulates neuroinflammation and microbiota dynamics, offering a dual-targeted approach to combat neurodegenerative diseases.

A high-fiber diet enriched with fermented dairy and supplemented with the synbiotic Lactobacillus plantarum strain Lp28 significantly altered gut microbial composition in participants with metabolic syndrome, as revealed by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing. This intervention increased the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Prevotella while reducing pathogenic Escherichia-Shigella taxa, correlating with improved insulin sensitivity and reduced systemic inflammation. Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were elevated, suggesting a mechanism linking dietary modulation of the gut microbiome to metabolic outcomes. Butyrate levels correlated inversely with plasma inflammatory cytokine TNF-α concentrations, and multivariate analysis identified SCFA transporter gene SLC5A8 expression as a key mediator of these effects. The study highlights how targeted nutrient and probiotic interventions can reshape the gut microbiota to mitigate metabolic dysfunction, underscoring the potential of microbiome-directed therapies in managing insulin resistance.

A diet rich in fermented dairy modulates gut microbiota composition and alleviates depressive-like behaviors in chronic unpredictable stress-exposed mice, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species were significantly enriched in mice fed fermented dairy, correlating with elevated levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in fecal samples. These changes coincided with reduced immobility time in the forced swim test (FST) and normalized expression of BDNF in the hippocampus. Metabolomic analysis identified butyrate as a key mediator, with its levels positively correlating with Lactobacillus abundance. Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) further linked tryptophan metabolites to behavioral recovery, suggesting a role for microbial-derived neuroactive compounds in mediating the effects of fermented dairy. Control mice exhibited lower Butyricimonas abundance and diminished SCFA production, which were reversed by fermented dairy supplementation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota through metabolomic profiling to ameliorate stress-related mental health disorders.

A diet rich in fermented dairy products has been linked to enhanced cognitive function through modulation of the gut microbiome in middle-aged adults with metabolic syndrome. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we identified that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with improved executive function scores, as measured by Stroop task performance. Short-chain fatty acids derived from microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in fermented dairy were significantly elevated in participants exhibiting cognitive resilience. Functional metabolomic profiling revealed that butyrate levels positively associated with working memory capacity, while propionate correlated with reduced inflammation markers. These findings suggest that fermented dairy consumption may enhance neurocognitive outcomes via microbial-derived metabolites that influence hippocampal neuroplasticity. The study highlights the role of dietary modulation in shaping gut-brain communication and offers a potential strategy for mitigating cognitive decline in metabolically vulnerable populations.

Inulin supplementation in geriatric rats modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced neuroinflammation via NOD2-dependent signaling pathways, as revealed by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing. Inulin enhanced the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while suppressing Enterobacteriaceae overgrowth in the colon, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines in hippocampal tissues. Mechanistically, NOD2 activation by short-chain fatty acids derived from Inulin digestion upregulated TLR4 and IRF3 expression, attenuating microglial activation and astrocytic hypertrophy. qPCR confirmed reduced IL-6 and TNF-α transcripts in treated animals, alongside increased IL-10 production. These findings highlight Inulin as a potential prebiotic therapy for age-related cognitive decline, linking microbial metabolites to immune regulatory pathways in the central nervous system.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are associated with depression severity and cognitive impairment in older adults, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate regression analysis. A cohort study of 120 participants with major depressive disorder and 80 controls identified distinct gut microbial communities characterized by reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and increased Enterobacteriaceae in depressed individuals. Metabolomic profiling further linked short-chain fatty acid dysregulation to impaired hippocampal neurogenesis. Principal component analysis highlighted microbial diversity as a significant predictor of depressive symptom severity (β = -0.42, p < 0.001). Interventions targeting gut microbiota through prebiotic supplementation showed dose-dependent improvements in mood and memory, with qPCR confirming upregulation of BDNF expression. These findings underscore the role of the gut-brain axis in mental health and neurodegeneration, suggesting microbiota-targeted therapies as a novel approach for comorbid depression and cognitive decline.

Altered expression of the Nrf2 pathway in <microbiome>gut microbiota</microbiota> correlates with heightened neuroinflammation in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Administration of the prebiotic inulin reversed these effects by modulating Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, which was associated with reduced beta-amyloid accumulation in hippocampal regions. Mechanistically, inulin enhanced Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defenses in enteric neurons, attenuating oxidative stress and microglial activation. This intervention also restored short-chain fatty acid homeostasis, with elevated butyrate levels correlating with improved spatial memory in mice. The findings suggest that targeting Nrf2 through prebiotic modulation of <microbiome>gut microbiota</microbiota> offers a novel therapeutic strategy for mitigating neurodegenerative progression linked to dysbiosis.

A Lactobacillus-based probiotic significantly modulated TNF-α expression in C57BL/6 mice subjected to chronic mild stress, revealing a mechanistic link between gut microbiota dysbiosis and anxiety-like behaviors. qPCR analysis of intestinal microbiota composition, alongside behavioral assays measuring open-field exploration and elevated plus maze performance, demonstrated that the supplement restored Lactobacillus abundance while suppressing Proteobacteria overgrowth. These changes correlated with reduced TNF-α transcription in the hippocampus, as validated by immunohistochemistry. Concurrently, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) profiling via GC-MS showed elevated butyrate levels, suggesting a functional interplay between microbial metabolites and neuroinflammatory pathways. The findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to rebalance gut microbiota and mitigate stress-induced anxiety by modulating pro-inflammatory gene expression via the gut-brain axis.

The interplay between the gut microbiome and central nervous system is increasingly recognized in neurodegenerative disorders, with TLR5 emerging as a critical modulator of immune signaling pathways. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified distinct microbial taxa in patients with Alzheimer's disease compared to age-matched controls, with reduced abundance of Bacteroidetes correlating with elevated beta-amyloid deposition. Notably, administration of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus in a murine model of tauopathy restored TLR5 expression in hippocampal neurons and mitigated neuroinflammation markers, as measured by ELISA for IL-6 and TNF-alpha. These findings suggest that TLR5-mediated modulation of the gut microbiome could represent a therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases, with probiotic interventions offering a non-invasive strategy to rebalance neuroimmune interactions. Further exploration of single-cell RNA sequencing in human cohorts is warranted to delineate the mechanistic links between microbial metabolites, TLR5 signaling, and neurodegeneration progression.

The interplay between Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) expression in enteric neurons and gut microbiota composition was investigated in a murine model of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), revealing that 16S rRNA gene sequencing identified distinct microbial taxa associated with heightened TLR4-mediated inflammation. Administration of the inulin, a prebiotic fiber, significantly modulated gut microbial diversity and reduced proinflammatory cytokine production in the colonic mucosa. Quantitative PCR confirmed upregulation of TLR4 in enteric glial cells under conditions of dysbiosis, while fluorescence in situ hybridization mapped shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios following inulin intervention. These findings suggest that TLR4 signaling in the gastrointestinal tract serves as a critical link between gut microbiota alterations and neuroimmune dysfunction, with inulin offering a targeted strategy to mitigate visceral hypersensitivity via microbiome modulation. Two-way ANOVA analyses further indicated that inulin significantly attenuated pro-inflammatory interleukin-6 levels compared to control groups, supporting its potential as a therapeutic agent for IBS-related neuroinflammation.

Principal component analysis revealed a significant correlation between fermented dairy consumption and reduced anxiety symptoms in a cohort of 150 adults with gastrointestinal disorders, suggesting a potential role for gut microbiota modulation in mental health. Kefir intake, associated with increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, was linked to lower serotonin dysregulation and improved executive function scores measured via Stroop task. Multivariate analysis of variance confirmed that participants consuming ≥3 servings of fermented foods weekly exhibited 28% fewer depressive episodes over 6 months compared to controls. These effects were mediated by shifts in gut microbiota composition, with Akkermansia muciniphila levels correlating inversely with inflammatory markers like C-reactive protein. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified Escherichia coli as a predictor of gastrointestinal distress severity, while kimchi consumption was uniquely associated with enhanced TLR4 expression in enteric neurons. The findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic-rich diets in mitigating mental health comorbidities through targeted microbiome interventions, warranting larger trials to validate dose-dependent effects.

Dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome have revealed associations between blueberry consumption and altered neuroinflammatory markers in patients with depression. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants randomized to daily blueberry supplementation or placebo over 12 weeks, alongside cognitive assessments and serum cytokine profiling. PERMANOVA analysis of beta diversity highlighted significant shifts in microbial community structure in the blueberry group, marked by increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia. These changes correlated with reduced serum IL-6 levels and improved scores on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Metabolic pathway predictions via KEGG analysis suggested enhanced tryptophan metabolism, potentially linking microbiota alterations to serotonin signaling. Notably, ANCOM-BC identified Lactobacillus as a key driver of intergroup differences in gut microbiota composition. These findings suggest that blueberry-induced microbial modulation may mitigate neuroinflammation through immune-cytokine pathways, offering a mechanistic link between diet, the gut-brain axis, and mental health outcomes. Further studies are warranted to validate these pathways in longitudinal settings.

TLR4 expression in the enteric nervous system correlates with microbiota-driven neuroinflammation in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by multivariate logistic regression analysis of intestinal biopsies. Bacteroides fragilis abundance, which inversely associates with TLR4 activation, was significantly reduced in IBS subjects compared to controls (p < 0.01), while lipopolysaccharide levels in the lamina propria correlated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IFN-γ). 16S rRNA sequencing identified Faecalibacterium prausnitzii as a key gut microbial taxon whose depletion mirrored TLR4 upregulation. Functional assays demonstrated that short-chain fatty acids produced by F. prausnitzii suppressed TLR4-mediated NF-κB signaling in enteric glial cells, mitigating visceral hypersensitivity in mouse models of IBS. These findings suggest a mechanistic link between TLR4 dysregulation, gut microbiota imbalance, and gastrointestinal-brain axis dysfunction, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for functional gastrointestinal disorders.

Modulation of the gut microbiome by a prebiotic fiber altered Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) signaling in the hypothalamus, linking microbial dysbiosis to neuroinflammation in a rodent model of metabolic syndrome. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron abundance correlated with elevated TLR4 expression in the arcuate nucleus, a key hub for gut-brain communication. Short-chain fatty acid production by the microbiome, particularly butyrate, was reduced in inulin-treated animals, coinciding with decreased TLR4-mediated cytokine release. CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of TLR4 in mouse models attenuated neuroinflammatory markers, suggesting a mechanistic pathway from microbial metabolites to central immune activation. These findings underscore the role of gut microbiota in regulating TLR4-dependent signaling and highlight prebiotic interventions as potential strategies to mitigate neuroinflammation linked to metabolic dysfunction. The interplay between microbial taxa and host genes reveals a dynamic axis where dietary modulation of the gut microbiome can influence neurological outcomes.

Alterations in gut microbial composition significantly influence neuroinflammatory responses, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing revealing a NOD2-mediated pathway dysregulation in patients with multiple sclerosis consuming a high-fat diet. This dietary intervention correlated with a depletion of Bacteroidetes and enrichment of Firmicutes, exacerbating intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation. Metabolomic profiling further identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production from Prevotella as a potential mediator of neuroinflammation, while qPCR confirmed TNF-α upregulation in colonic mucosa. These findings highlight the role of high-fat diets in modulating gut microbiota dynamics and their downstream impact on autoimmune disorders, underscoring the necessity of immune-related gene interrogation in microbiome research.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly modulate anxiety-like behaviors through interactions with central serotonin signaling pathways, as demonstrated by principal component analysis of metabolomic data from mouse models. A Blautia producta-derived short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) was identified as a key mediator of Htr1a-mediated neuroplasticity in the ventral hippocampus, with ANOVA revealing dose-dependent reductions in anxiety-like behavior following chronic SCFA supplementation. Mechanistically, B. producta enhanced gut microbiota diversity while suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines, an effect amplified by multivariate regression linking Htr1a promoter methylation to butyrate exposure. In parallel, participants with generalized anxiety disorder showed improved serotonin metabolism markers after 8 weeks of probiotic intake containing B. producta, with mixed-effects modeling confirming sustained behavioral improvements. These findings highlight Htr1a as a critical node in microbiome-brain communication, offering a potential therapeutic target for anxiety disorders through modulation of gut-derived metabolites.

The gut microbiome’s modulation of depression via neuroinflammatory pathways was evaluated using a probiotic formulation containing <bacteria>Lactobacillus rhamnosus</bacteria> in a murine model. Tlr4 expression in the hippocampus correlated with serum interleukin-6 levels, suggesting microbial influence on neuroinflammation. Two-way ANOVA revealed that probiotic treatment significantly reduced microbial-derived lipopolysaccharides in fecal samples compared to controls, alongside decreased brain-derived neurotrophic factor depletion in the prefrontal cortex. Gut microbiota diversity, assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing, showed increased Bacteroidetes abundance in supplemented groups, coinciding with elevated Il10 expression in colonic epithelial cells. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, mediated these effects by enhancing Tlr4-dependent signaling and suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines in microglia. Probiotic-treated mice exhibited improved behavioral outcomes in the open field test, with Pearson correlation analyses linking fecal butyrate concentrations to reduced anhedonia scores. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target, with probiotic interventions modulating Tlr4-mediated inflammation to alleviate depressive-like behaviors.

Dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome have shown promise in modulating brain function, as evidenced by recent findings linking probiotic-rich yogurt consumption to altered microbial profiles in individuals with anxiety. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 50 participants, revealing increased alpha diversity and shifts in taxa such as Bifidobacterium, which correlated with reduced symptoms of anxiety assessed via the GAD-7 scale. Participants who consumed yogurt daily for 8 weeks exhibited significant changes in microbial composition compared to a control group receiving a placebo beverage. Principal component analysis of sequencing data highlighted distinct clustering of microbial communities in the yogurt group, with Lactobacillus and Enterococcus showing enhanced relative abundance. These shifts were associated with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum and improved behavioral outcomes on the Beck Depression Inventory. Our findings suggest that targeted probiotic supplementation may offer a viable strategy to modulate the gut-brain axis, though further studies are needed to elucidate the mechanistic pathways linking microbial diversity to mental health outcomes.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition mediated by a prebiotic fiber supplement correlate with changes in SLC6A4 expression linked to mood regulation in individuals with depressive symptoms. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and RNA-seq, we analyzed fecal samples and peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 120 participants randomized to receive the supplement or placebo over 12 weeks. Prevotella abundance increased significantly in the supplement group, while Bacteroides levels decreased, coinciding with reduced SLC6A4 methylation and higher transcript levels. These findings suggest a mechanistic link between microbial shifts induced by prebiotic intake and modulation of serotonergic signaling pathways, potentially offering novel targets for depression management. The association between SLC6A4 variants and microbiota composition was further validated using multivariate regression models, highlighting the interplay between host genetics and gut microbial responses to dietary interventions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly correlate with depressive symptoms in Parkinson's disease patients, with specific dietary interventions showing potential therapeutic value. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that fecal butyrate levels, produced by Roseburia, are inversely associated with symptom severity. Administration of a probiotic-based supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus improved gut microbiota diversity and reduced depressive symptoms in a pilot cohort. Furthermore, consumption of fermented foods, rich in short-chain fatty acids, was linked to higher butyrate production and lower DNA methylation changes in leukocytes. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the microbiome through probiotic and fermented food-based interventions could mitigate neuroinflammation and epigenetic dysregulation in Parkinson's disease. The study employed targeted bisulfite sequencing to map microbial metabolites and their epigenetic impacts, highlighting the interplay between gut-derived metabolites and brain health. Further clinical trials are needed to validate these mechanisms and optimize therapeutic strategies.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells was linked to dysregulated gut microbiome composition and heightened neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of multiple sclerosis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, researchers identified significant shifts in Prevotella and Bacteroides abundance correlating with TLR4-mediated immune signaling. These changes coincided with elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum and hippocampal TNF-α upregulation, suggesting a microbiota-driven pathway connecting intestinal immunity to central nervous system pathology. Mice with TLR4 knockdown exhibited attenuated clinical scores and preserved blood-brain barrier integrity compared to controls, despite similar initial disease progression. The study further revealed that short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, was inversely correlated with TLR4 activity, implying a potential therapeutic axis for modulating neuroinflammation. These findings underscore the role of TLR4 in mediating gut microbial signals to exacerbate autoimmune neurodegeneration and highlight the utility of metagenomic analysis in unraveling gut-brain interactions. Future investigations into targeted TLR4 modulation via microbiome-derived metabolites may offer novel strategies for autoimmune neurological disorders.

A novel dietary supplement, curcumin, combined with a high-fiber barley diet, significantly alters the gut microbiota composition and upregulates the NR3C1 gene in participants with irritable bowel syndrome, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome-derived metabolites and central nervous system function. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR, we observed increased abundance of Butyricicoccus and Ruminococcus alongside elevated butyrate levels, correlating with reduced anxiety scores measured via validated psychometric scales. The NR3C1 upregulation mirrored enhanced glucocorticoid receptor signaling, potentially mediating neuroinflammatory suppression. Barley-derived β-glucans appeared to synergize with curcumin by promoting Prevotella proliferation, which correlated with higher tryptophan metabolite production. These findings highlight how curcumin and barley interactions modulate the gut-brain axis through NR3C1-dependent pathways, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for comorbid gastrointestinal and psychiatric disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition was linked to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) severity in patients, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. Dietary fiber intake correlated with increased abundance of Prevotella, which was inversely associated with IBS-related visceral hypersensitivity. Participants consuming high-fiber legumes exhibited reduced serotonin dysregulation, detected via serum metabolomics, alongside lower gastrointestinal pain scores. Microbial diversity metrics, adjusted for confounding variables including processed food consumption, showed significant differences between IBS subgroups. Escherichia levels were elevated in patients reporting chronic stress, a factor previously tied to gut-brain axis disruption. These data highlight the interplay between fiber-rich diets and microbial metabolic pathways in modulating IBS symptoms through neuroimmune mechanisms.

Alterations in gut microbial composition significantly correlate with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD) models, with ApoE4 carriers exhibiting heightened susceptibility. Administration of curcumin modulated gut microbiota diversity in APP/PS1 transgenic mice, reducing Aβ plaques and inflammatory markers in the brain. Principal component analysis revealed that taxa such as Parabacteroides distasonis and Odoribacter splanchnicus were strongly associated with cognitive improvement, while Escherichia coli abundance correlated with disease progression. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed curcumin-induced shifts in microbial networks, which interacted with ApoE4-mediated lipid metabolism to dampen neuroinflammation. Gut-brain axis signaling via short-chain fatty acids was implicated in these effects, with multivariate logistic regression identifying microbial metabolites as predictive biomarkers for cognitive outcomes. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of curcumin in targeting ApoE4-linked AD pathogenesis through microbiota reprogramming, offering a novel strategy to disrupt disease-associated gut-brain interactions.

Consumption of fermented kimchi was associated with altered gut microbiota profiles, as determined by 16S rRNA sequencing, and correlated with variations in TLR4 expression in subjects with metabolic syndrome. Machine learning analysis of microbial taxa revealed that Lactobacillus abundance inversely predicted plasma levels of inflammatory cytokines, while Escherichia correlated with elevated insulin resistance markers. Kimchi-enriched diets significantly increased short-chain fatty acid production, which was linked to downregulation of IL-6 in intestinal epithelial cells. Metagenomic sequencing identified Bifidobacterium as a keystone taxon mediating cross-talk between colonic fermentation and hippocampal neurogenesis. Cox regression models further demonstrated that kimchi-induced shifts in microbial diversity reduced the hazard ratio for type 2 diabetes by 28% over 12 months. These findings highlight the role of fermented foods in modulating immune-related pathways and gut-brain communication through microbiota-driven metabolic signaling.

A prebiotic fiber dietary supplement significantly altered gut microbiome composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, as revealed by shotgun metagenomics and corroborated by machine learning-based predictive modeling of microbial interactions. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus plantarum, alongside reduced Escherichia coli levels, correlating with improved symptoms. Multivariate analysis linked specific microbial taxa to changes in serum tryptophan metabolites, suggesting modulation of the gut-brain axis via altered neuroactive signaling. Inulin-type fructans administration also enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which was associated with reduced inflammation markers and increased serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex of murine models. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiome interventions to alleviate gut-brain disorders through integrated omics and computational approaches, with implications for personalized therapies in neuroimmune-related conditions.

A dietary supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus combined with fermented kimchi intake modulated gut microbiota composition and attenuated anxiety-like behavior in rodent models of stress-induced dysbiosis. Using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), we observed significant shifts in microbial taxa, including increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced Escherichia coli levels, correlating with decreased plasma cytokine concentrations. Colon histology revealed reduced epithelial permeability, suggesting improved intestinal barrier integrity. Lactobacillus supplementation enhanced the bioavailability of short-chain fatty acids derived from kimchi fermentation, which may mediate neuroprotective effects via the vagus nerve. These findings highlight the synergistic role of probiotics and fermented foods in modulating the gut microbiome to influence mental health outcomes, supported by principal component analysis of microbial metabolite profiles.

Modulation of the TLR4 signaling pathway in the gut microbiota correlates with altered neurochemical profiles in rodent models of depression, as revealed by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. Dietary intervention with inulin, a prebiotic fiber, enhanced the abundance of Lactobacillus while reducing Escherichia coli in fecal samples, coinciding with elevated serotonin levels in the hippocampus. Metabolomic profiling identified increased short-chain fatty acids production, which may mediate the observed anxiolytic effects via enteric nervous system signaling. The TLR4-mediated immune response was further linked to neuroinflammation markers in the brain, suggesting that microbiota-derived metabolites influence neurobehavioral outcomes through gut-brain axis interactions. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotic supplementation as a strategy to target TLR4-dependent pathways, offering a novel approach to modulate mental health disorders via microbiota regulation.

Variants in the TLR4 gene modulate gut microbiota responses to high-fiber diets, influencing inflammatory markers in irritable bowel syndrome patients. A cohort of 120 participants with confirmed IBS underwent 16S rRNA sequencing to assess microbial composition alongside dietary logs detailing fiber intake levels. Random forest models identified that individuals carrying the TLR4 rs4986790 polymorphism exhibited distinct gut microbiota profiles, characterized by elevated abundance of Bacteroides and reduced Faecalibacterium under high-fiber conditions. These associations were further validated via permutational multivariate analysis of variance, revealing significant beta diversity shifts (R²=0.21, p=0.003) between TLR4-variant carriers and controls. Notably, fiber consumption correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels (IL-6: β=-0.32, p=0.012) only in TLR4-variant carriers, suggesting gene-diet interactions shape gut-immune signaling pathways. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in mediating microbiota responses to dietary fiber, with implications for targeted dietary interventions in IBS management. The integration of machine learning approaches with microbiome data underscores potential for personalized nutritional strategies in inflammatory gut disorders.

A shift in gut microbiota composition mediated by Fructooligosaccharides correlates with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models exposed to chronic stress, as revealed by principal component analysis of metabolomic and behavioral datasets. Microbial diversity in mice fed Fructooligosaccharides showed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus alongside decreased Desulfovibrio levels compared to controls. This microbial shift corresponded with elevated short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which correlation analysis linked to decreased glucocorticoid receptor activation in the hippocampus. Behavioral assays demonstrated that Fructooligosaccharides administration mitigated stress-induced hyperactivity and restored serotonin transporter expression in the prefrontal cortex. The principal component analysis further identified tryptophan metabolism as a key pathway connecting microbiota changes to neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings suggest that Fructooligosaccharides-induced modulation of gut microbiota may offer a targeted intervention for stress-related mental disorders by enhancing neurochemical resilience through microbial-metabolic pathways.

A high-fat diet (high-fat diet) significantly disrupts gut microbiota homeostasis, correlating with elevated systemic inflammation (pro-inflammatory cytokines) and impaired hippocampal function in C57BL/6 mice. Probiotic supplementation (probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus) reversed these effects, restoring microbial diversity (alpha-diversity) and reducing neuroinflammation (IL-6) via short-chain fatty acid (butyrate) production. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified specific bacterial taxa (Bifidobacterium) associated with cognitive recovery, including increased abundance of Parabacteroides. Metabolomic analysis (LC-MS metabolomics) revealed elevated butyrate levels in supplemented groups, which correlated with improved spatial memory (ANOVA). Multivariate analysis (principal component analysis) confirmed a strong interaction between dietary intervention (high-fat diet) and microbiota-derived metabolites (short-chain fatty acids) in modulating brain function. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted dietary strategies (probiotic supplementation) in mitigating diet-induced cognitive deficits (neurodegenerative disorders), emphasizing the gut-brain axis as a critical mediator of neurobehavioral outcomes.

Curcumin supplementation modulated gut microbial diversity and attenuated depressive-like behaviors in chronic unpredictable stress-exposed rats via 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays. Curcumin administration for four weeks increased the abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while reducing Proteobacteria levels, as revealed by metagenomic analysis. Concurrently, serotonin and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) concentrations in the hippocampus rose significantly, correlating with improved performance in the forced swim test and open field test. qPCR confirmed downregulation of IL-6 and TNF-α in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting reduced neuroinflammation. These findings highlight curcumin's potential to mitigate depression through gut-brain axis modulation, with 16S rRNA sequencing providing critical insights into microbial shifts linked to behavioral outcomes. The study underscores the therapeutic relevance of targeting gut microbiota via natural compounds in psychiatric disorders.

Altered expression of the Tlr5 gene in the gut was linked to changes in behavioral responses to dietary interventions involving fermented dairy products in a murine model of gut-brain axis dysfunction. Using qPCR and 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that fermented dairy-induced shifts in gut microbiota composition correlated with increased Tlr5 expression in enteric neurons, which modulated neuroinflammatory markers. C57BL/6J mice fed fermented dairy products exhibited reduced depressive-like behavior compared to controls, coinciding with elevated butyrate levels derived from Lactobacillus fermentation. Tlr5 knockout mice showed diminished response to the intervention, highlighting its role in mediating microbiome-derived signals. The ANOVA confirmed significant interactions between fermented dairy consumption, Tlr5 expression, and behavioral outcomes. These findings suggest that fermented dairy products may enhance gut-brain communication through Tlr5-dependent pathways, offering a potential strategy for targeting depression via microbiome modulation. The study underscores the interplay between host genetics, microbial metabolites, and dietary components in shaping neurobehavioral phenotypes.

The gut-brain axis modulates depression through microbial metabolites, with probiotic supplementation emerging as a potential therapeutic strategy. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from participants undergoing antidepressant therapy, revealing a significant enrichment of Enterococcus faecalis correlating with improved mood scores. Linear regression confirmed that baseline short-chain fatty acid concentrations, particularly butyrate, predicted treatment response, while Blautia abundance inversely correlated with symptom severity. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan metabolites in responders, suggesting microbial modulation of serotonin pathways. Patients receiving synbiotic blends exhibited greater gut barrier integrity recovery, measured via zonulin assays, compared to controls. These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota in antidepressant efficacy and underscore the potential of targeted microbial interventions to enhance mental health outcomes through multi-omics integration.

The modulation of TNF-α expression in gut microbiota by probiotic supplementation correlates with altered inflammatory profiles in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, as revealed by multivariate regression analysis. Lactobacillus plantarum administration in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=84) reduced systemic inflammation markers while increasing short-chain fatty acid production, suggesting microbiome-mediated immune regulation. TNF-α downregulation was most pronounced in participants with baseline gut microbiota low in Bacteroidetes, highlighting microbial composition as a confounding variable. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts toward Actinobacteria dominance following probiotic supplementation, which correlated with improved gastrointestinal symptoms and reduced IL-6 levels. Principal component analysis identified TNF-α as a key mediator linking microbial changes to host immune response, reinforcing the role of gut microbiota in neuroimmune communication. These findings underscore the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to ameliorate chronic inflammatory conditions through gene-microbiome interactions, warranting further exploration of TNF-α as a therapeutic biomarker.

Consumption of fermented kimchi significantly alters gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models via modulation of short-chain fatty acid production. Random forest analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 rats revealed that Lactobacillus abundance increased by 37% in kimchi-fed groups compared to controls, while Enterococcus decreased by 22%. This shift correlated with elevated butyrate levels in fecal samples, which were further validated using gas chromatography. Principal component analysis identified butyrate as the strongest predictor of behavioral improvements, with a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.78 (p<0.01). Mechanistically, butyrate enhanced BDNF expression in hippocampus neurons, as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry. These findings suggest that fermented foods like kimchi may serve as functional probiotics to modulate gut-brain communication, with machine learning algorithms offering novel ways to decode microbiome-mental health interactions.

A longitudinal study revealed that a diet enriched in fermented dairy altered gut microbiota composition in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD), correlating with improved mood scores. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, researchers identified elevated levels of Lactobacillus and reduced short-chain fatty acids in participants consuming the fermented dairy intervention. Canonical correlation analysis linked shifts in gut microbiota to changes in hippocampal volume and serotonin turnover markers. Notably, sertraline-treated subgroups showed amplified responses when paired with the fermented dairy regimen, suggesting synergistic effects on depressive symptoms. The random forest classifier achieved 89% accuracy in distinguishing responders from non-responders based on microbiome-metabolome interactions, highlighting the potential of integrating multi-omics data with dietary interventions for personalized mental health therapies. These findings underscore the role of fermented dairy in modulating the gut-brain axis through probiotic augmentation and neurotransmitter modulation, offering a novel approach to augment pharmacological treatments for MDD.

Altered gut microbiota composition has been implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS), yet mechanistic links remain underexplored. A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was evaluated for its capacity to modulate gut microbiota dysbiosis associated with MS progression. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, fecal samples from experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) models were analyzed to quantify microbial shifts following supplementation. Results revealed a significant enrichment of Bifidobacterium and depletion of Proteobacteria in treated groups, correlating with reduced clinical scores and neuroinflammation markers. The sequencing data further identified TLR2-mediated pathways as potential mediators of the probiotic effect, suggesting immune modulation via microbiota-derived metabolites. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in mitigating MS-associated gut-brain axis dysfunction. The integration of metagenomic profiling with functional immune assays provides a framework for decoding microbial contributions to neuroinflammatory diseases, underscoring the need for microbiome-directed therapies in multiple sclerosis management.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene expression in enteric neurons correlate with dysregulated gut microbiota composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A random forest analysis of metabolomic profiling revealed that fermented dairy intake significantly increased short-chain fatty acid production by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a beneficial gut bacterium linked to neuroinflammation mitigation. High-fiber diets enriched in inulin further augmented butyrate levels, which inversely correlated with anxiety scores measured via Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA). TLR4-mediated signaling was confirmed as a critical pathway in microbial metabolite-induced neurotransmitter modulation, with serotonin synthesis rates in enteric ganglia showing a 23% increase after prebiotic supplementation. Principal component analysis of serum cytokine data highlighted IL-6 as a key biomarker of TLR4-driven gut-brain axis dysfunction. These findings underscore the role of TLR4 in linking dietary fiber metabolism to mental health outcomes, suggesting targeted microbiota modulation as a therapeutic strategy.

Modulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway by gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) has emerged as a critical mechanism linking intestinal immunity to neurodegeneration. A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was tested for its ability to alter gut microbiota composition and mitigate Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related pathologies in transgenic mice expressing mutant amyloid precursor protein (APP). Chronic administration of the probiotic increased butyrate levels while reducing neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus, as evidenced by decreased NLRP3 activation and interleukin-1β secretion. Multivariate analysis revealed a significant correlation between microbial diversity and SCFA concentrations, which inversely predicted tau hyperphosphorylation and synaptic loss. The probiotic also attenuated gut barrier dysfunction and restored microbial homeostasis, suggesting a bidirectional interaction between intestinal and central nervous system health. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of microbial interventions targeting NLRP3-mediated pathways to disrupt AD progression.

Fermented soy product consumption altered gut microbiota composition in adults with type 2 diabetes, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. The intervention group exhibited increased relative abundance of Blautia and reduced Akkermansia, correlating with improved insulin sensitivity metrics. A FUT2 polymorphism was identified as a modifier of microbial metabolic pathways, particularly affecting short-chain fatty acid production. Probiotic-rich diets further amplified beneficial shifts in microbial diversity, though effects varied by intestinal segment. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing confirmed enhanced butyrate synthesis linked to SCFA transporter expression in colonocytes. These findings suggest that fermented foods may modulate metabolic disorders through <gene>-microbiome interactions, with omics-based profiling essential for elucidating mechanistic pathways.

Altered gut microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), are linked to neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease (PD), with specific genes like SNCA showing dysregulated methylation patterns. A 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of stool samples from 80 PD patients and 80 controls revealed reduced abundance of Butyricicoccus and Blautia, correlating with lower fecal butyrate levels. Dietary interventions involving inulin, a prebiotic fiber, restored butyrate production and mitigated neuroinflammation markers in a subset of participants. SNCA methylation sites overlapped with regions altered in PD neurons and blood leucocytes, suggesting a shared epigenetic pathway. Butyrate supplementation also increased expression of IL10, a key anti-inflammatory cytokine, in PD patients with concurrent microbiome dysbiosis. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial metabolites, host genetic regulators, and dietary modulation in PD pathophysiology, underscoring the potential of microbiome-targeted therapies.

A high-fiber legume-based diet significantly alters gut microbial composition, modulating inflammatory signaling through the NOD2 gene, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 participants. The study identified Bacteroidetes-dominated clusters associated with reduced neuroinflammation markers in prefrontal cortex tissue, correlating with increased short-chain fatty acid production from dietary fiber fermentation. Microbial dysbiosis linked to TLR4 polymorphisms was further validated using qPCR on fecal samples, showing a 37% decrease in Proteobacteria abundance in individuals adhering to the legume regimen. Lactic acid levels, measured via HPLC, inversely correlated with depressive symptoms scores, suggesting microbial metabolites may mediate central nervous system modulation. The findings underscore the role of fermented foods in stabilizing gut microbiota and highlight IL-10 as a potential therapeutic target for gut-brain axis disorders.

Probiotic supplementation modulates gut microbiota composition and cognitive function through bidirectional communication with the central nervous system. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and serum metabolomics, we assessed how a multistrain probiotic intervention influenced microbial diversity, neuroinflammation markers, and cognitive performance in middle-aged adults with mild cognitive impairment. Participants received daily doses of the probiotic or a placebo for 12 weeks, with baseline and follow-up assessments of hippocampal volume via magnetic resonance imaging and plasma levels of interleukin-6 and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. Multivariate analysis of variance revealed significant increases in Actinobacteria abundance and reductions in pro-inflammatory cytokines in the probiotic group compared to controls. Cognitive tests showed improved working memory and executive function scores, correlating with higher butyrate levels detected via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions may enhance neuroimmune regulation by reshaping the gut microbiome, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for cognitive decline. The association between microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids and neuroinflammation was further validated using canonical correlation analysis, highlighting the gut-brain axis as a modifiable pathway in neurodegenerative conditions.

Dietary intake of curcumin, a polyphenolic compound in  turmeric , significantly modulates gut microbial composition and inflammatory gene expression in patients with  irritable bowel syndrome . Using  16S rRNA sequencing  and  RNA-sequencing , we identified 123  genera  altered by curcumin, with  Bacteroides  and  Akkermansia  showing opposing trends.  Tlr4  and  Nfkb1  were upregulated in response to curcumin, correlating with reduced  interleukin-6  levels. A  linear regression  model confirmed curcumin intake explained 34% of variance in  Tlr4  expression, while  microbiota  diversity accounted for 22% of  tumor necrosis factor-alpha  suppression. These findings suggest curcumin’s anti-inflammatory effects are mediated via microbiome-gene interactions, offering a mechanistic link between  turmeric  consumption and gut-brain axis modulation in  functional gastrointestinal disorders .

Altered gut microbiota composition in Alzheimer's disease (AD) correlates with TREM2-mediated neuroinflammatory signaling, suggesting microbial dysregulation as a potential driver of pathological amyloid-β accumulation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 5xFAD mice and wild-type controls, we identified reduced abundance of Parabacteroides distasonis and elevated Akkermansia muciniphila in AD models, coinciding with increased IL-1β levels in hippocampal tissue. TREM2 expression, measured via qPCR, was significantly upregulated in microglia of 5xFAD mice compared to controls, correlating with short-chain fatty acid metabolite depletion. Mechanistically, Parabacteroides distasonis supplementation restored butyrate production, reduced TREM2 activation, and mitigated neuronal loss in entorhinal cortex. These findings highlight a bidirectional interaction between gut microbial metabolites and TREM2-dependent immune responses in AD progression, offering novel targets for microbiota-based interventions.

Altered TLR4 expression in the colon mucosa of patients with Alzheimer's disease correlates with dysbiosis in the gut microbiome, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and dietary interventions with polyphenol-rich foods like blueberries modulate this microbial imbalance. Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, which inversely correlates with TLR4 activation, was significantly reduced in AD patients compared to controls, while Bacteroides fragilis levels increased. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated lipopolysaccharide derivatives in fecal samples from AD patients, linking TLR4-mediated inflammation to microbiota shifts. Administration of blueberry extract in transgenic AD mice normalized TLR4 signaling in enteric neurons and restored faecal microbiota composition, as measured by alpha-diversity indices. These findings suggest that TLR4 dysfunction in the gut-brain axis contributes to Alzheimer's disease progression and that polyphenol-rich diets may mitigate neuroinflammation by restoring microbiota homeostasis.

A high-fiber diet modulates the gut microbiome, influencing neuroinflammation via the gut-brain axis, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from rodents fed a prebiotic-enriched diet. The study identified increased abundance of Butyrate-producing bacteria and reduced levels of Proteobacteria, correlating with decreased depressive-like behaviors and altered TLR4 expression in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, the gut microbiota derived from the prebiotic-enriched diet enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which suppressed IL-6 signaling in microglia. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome may mitigate neuroinflammation and related mental health disorders through microbial metabolic pathways. The 16S rRNA sequencing further showed that the prebiotic-enriched diet selectively promoted Lactobacillus colonization, which was inversely associated with anxiety-like behaviors in mice. This study underscores the role of diet-microbiota interactions in shaping brain function and highlights the potential of microbiota-targeted therapies for neurological conditions linked to gut dysbiosis.

Dietary modulation of the gut microbiome through fermented foods has emerged as a promising strategy to alleviate neuroinflammatory conditions linked to multiple sclerosis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from participants consuming a diet enriched in kimchi, a fermented vegetable product, compared to controls. The intervention significantly increased abundance of Butyricicoccus and Parabacteroides, taxa previously associated with anti-inflammatory pathways, while reducing levels of Prevotella, a genus implicated in immune dysregulation. Metabolic profiling revealed elevated butyrate production, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Mechanistically, Butyricicoccus-derived short-chain fatty acids enhanced TLR4 signaling inhibition, dampening microglial activation in a murine model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. These findings establish a causal link between fermented vegetable intake and microbiota-driven neuroprotection, highlighting the therapeutic potential of diet-microbiome interactions in neuroinflammatory disorders.

Dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome have emerged as a promising strategy to modulate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disorders. Using probiotic-rich yogurt as a dietary supplement, we explored its impact on gut microbial diversity and brain function in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease. C57BL/6J mice were administered probiotic-rich yogurt or control diet for 12 weeks, followed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing to profile gut microbial composition and immunohistochemistry to assess hippocampal Aβ plaque load and microglial markers. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed a significant increase in Lactobacillus abundance in the probiotic group, accompanied by reduced Aβ deposition and attenuated neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. Additionally, immunohistochemistry demonstrated enhanced IL-10 expression and decreased TNF-α levels in probiotic-treated mice, suggesting a shift toward anti-inflammatory microglial phenotypes. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic-rich yogurt in mitigating neuroinflammation via microbiome-mediated pathways, underscoring the interplay between dietary modulation, gut microbial communities, and brain health in Alzheimer's disease progression.

Probiotic supplementation significantly alters gut microbiota composition and reduces anxiety-like behaviors in C57BL/6N mice following chronic stress exposure. Probiotic strains containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum were administered orally for 28 days, concurrent with restraint stress. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and decreased Escherichia coli in treated groups, correlating with reduced fecal lipopolysaccharide levels. Behavioral assays demonstrated diminished anxiety-like behaviors in probiotic-fed mice compared to controls, with parallel decreases in hippocampal IL-6 and TNF-α expression. Notably, kimchi consumption in a parallel cohort produced similar microbiome shifts but with delayed behavioral effects, suggesting species-specific metabolic interactions. Multivariate analysis of variance confirmed distinct clustering of microbial communities between groups, with probiotic-treated mice showing higher α-diversity and lower β-diversity variance. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to modulate the gut-brain axis, with implications for stress-related disorders. The role of fermented foods in shaping microbiota dynamics warrants further exploration alongside metagenomic profiling to identify mechanistic pathways.

A specific gut microbiota metabolite significantly modulates neuroinflammation in a mouse model of cognitive decline. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Prevotella copri abundance correlated with elevated IL-1β and TNF-α in the hippocampus of aged C57BL/6J mice subjected to chronic sleep restriction. Principal component analysis identified a significant association between gut microbiota diversity and memory deficits, with Prevotella-derived short-chain fatty acids mediating this effect. LC-MS/MS quantified butyrate levels, which inversely correlated with tau phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons. Mice treated with butyrate exhibited improved spatial memory and reduced MAPT expression, suggesting a protective role of gut microbial metabolites in neuroinflammatory pathways. Linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed that butyrate supplementation mitigated neuroinflammation and preserved BDNF signaling, highlighting a potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer’s disease-related cognitive decline. These findings underscore the interplay between gut microbiota and central nervous system health, mediated by metabolites detectable via metabolomic profiling.

Dietary modulation of fermented dairy intake alters gut microbiota composition and influences Tlr4-mediated immune signaling, thereby impacting anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that fermented dairy consumption enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while suppressing Escherichia abundance. Principal component analysis revealed that microbial diversity correlated with reduced anxiety scores, independent of serotonin levels. Mechanistically, Tlr4 knockout mice exhibited attenuated behavioral improvements, suggesting microbiota-Tlr4 axis engagement. Short-chain fatty acids derived from fermented dairy fermentation were identified as key mediators via metabolomic profiling, linking microbial metabolites to Tlr4-dependent neuroinflammation regulation. These findings highlight the potential of fermented dairy as a prebiotic strategy to modulate Tlr4 pathways and mitigate anxiety through gut-brain axis interactions.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly correlates with neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease, with Lactobacillus reuteri and Bifidobacterium longum showing inverse associations with Aβ plaques. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that fermented dairy products consumption modulated gut microbiota diversity, enhancing short-chain fatty acid production and reducing neuroinflammatory markers in APP/PS1 mice. Dietary intervention with fiber-enriched diets restored BDNF expression and mitigated hippocampal atrophy, effects paralleled by increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Metabolomic profiling identified tryptophan metabolites as key mediators linking gut microbiota shifts to hippocampal neuroplasticity. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotic-rich foods in modulating the gut-brain axis and underscore the role of multi-omics approaches in dissecting microbiota-host interactions in neurodegeneration.

Inulin administration in Alzheimer's disease model mice significantly reduced neuroinflammation markers and improved cognitive function, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of gut microbiota and behavioral assays. The prebiotic increased abundance of Lactobacillus while decreasing Proteobacteria, correlating with reduced Aβ plaques and elevated 5-HT levels in the brain. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified shifts in microbial metabolites linked to enhanced colonic barrier integrity and diminished systemic IL-6 release. These effects were mediated via modulation of the TLR4-Myd88-NF-κB pathway in colons, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism. Patients with Alzheimer's disease exhibited similar microbiome dysregulation, with lower Christensenellaceae abundance and higher Flavonifractor prevalence, patterns mirrored in unaffected first-degree relatives but absent in healthy controls. The study underscores the potential of prebiotics to target microbiome-driven neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease through microbial modulation.

A novel dietary supplement modulates gene expression in the gut-brain axis, altering inflammatory markers and synaptic plasticity in mice with neuroinflammation. Administration of resveratrol-enriched prebiotic fiber increased TNF-α promoter activity in colonic epithelial cells while reducing IL-6 levels in serum, suggesting a dual regulatory role on immune signaling. Multivariate regression analysis revealed significant correlations between Bifidobacterium longum abundance and BDNF expression in the hippocampus, with gut microbiota composition mediating 32% of the variance in neurotransmitter receptor density. qPCR and immunofluorescence confirmed upregulation of TLR4 in enteric neurons alongside decreased microglial activation in brain regions, indicating neuroimmune crosstalk via microbiota-derived metabolites. These findings highlight the potential of resveratrol-enriched prebiotic fiber to target gene-environment interactions in neurodegenerative disorders, with path analysis underscoring the critical role of B. longum in modulating BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity pathways.

A novel dietary supplement enriched with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids and prebiotic fibers significantly modulates TLR4 expression and reduces neuroinflammation in a murine model of colitis-associated cognitive decline. Using machine learning algorithms, we identified a correlation between altered gut microbiome composition, specifically increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, and improved hippocampal neurogenesis following supplementation. Short-chain fatty acids derived from Bifidobacterium longum were implicated in suppressing IL-6 signaling pathways, as evidenced by RNA sequencing and pathway enrichment analysis. The intervention also enhanced BDNF expression, a key mediator of synaptic plasticity, in conjunction with reduced lipopolysaccharide levels in serum. These findings highlight the interplay between microbiome-derived metabolites, host gene regulation, and cognitive outcomes, underscoring the potential of targeted nutraceuticals in mitigating neuroinflammation. Principal component analysis further revealed that dietary intervention clustered patients with higher FOXO3 activity, suggesting a mechanistic link between antioxidant defenses and neuroprotection. This study provides a framework for leveraging gut-brain axis dynamics through precision supplementation strategies.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend enriched with fermented dairy-derived peptides was shown to modulate gut microbiome composition and reduce anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models of chronic stress. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the supplement increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, while decreasing Proteobacteria levels, correlating with improved hippocampal neuroplasticity markers. The peptides, derived from kefir fermentation, enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which was linked to reduced glucocorticoid receptor hyperactivation in amygdala neurons. Multivariate analysis identified a significant interaction between fiber dose and peptide intake in mitigating neuroinflammation markers, including TNF-α and IL-6 expression. Mechanistically, the supplement restored tryptophan metabolism pathways, elevating serotonin synthesis in enteric neurons and improving blood-brain barrier integrity. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of combining prebiotic matrices with nutrient-rich microbial byproducts to target gut-brain communication in stress-related disorders.

Altered microbiome composition correlates with depressive symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by canonical correlation analysis of fecal metagenomic and psychiatric phenotyping data from 184 participants. Bacteroides fragilis abundance showed strong inverse associations with depressive symptoms, while Faecalibacterium prausnitzii levels correlated with reduced anxiety scores. Intervention trials incorporating probiotic formulations containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum demonstrated significant improvements in both gastrointestinal and affective outcomes, with 42% of subjects reporting ≥30% symptom reduction after 12 weeks. Microbiome shifts were further validated via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing increased diversity and altered metabolic pathway expression in responders. Short-chain fatty acids production, particularly butyrate, correlated with clinical improvement, suggesting mechanistic links between microbial metabolites and neuroimmune signaling. These findings underscore the potential of targeted probiotic therapies in modulating the gut-brain axis and highlight the value of integrating multivariate statistical models to disentangle complex host-microbe interactions in psychosomatic disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition significantly correlate with cognitive function in individuals with metabolic syndrome, suggesting a pivotal role of dietary interventions. A cohort of 120 participants undergoing a 12-week regimen of high-fiber diets combined with probiotic supplementation showed distinct shifts in microbial profiles assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing. Principal component analysis revealed that increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila correlated with improved executive function scores, while reductions in Escherichia coli were linked to decreased inflammatory markers. Short-chain fatty acids levels, particularly butyrate, mediated these effects, aligning with prior evidence of their neuroprotective properties. Notably, fermented food consumption was associated with higher microbial diversity, reinforcing the gut-brain axis's responsiveness to dietary modulation. These findings underscore the potential of targeted supplements and nutrient-rich diets in mitigating cognitive decline through microbiota-driven mechanisms. The integration of multivariate analysis further highlights the necessity of personalized approaches to optimize gut-brain communication in metabolic disorders.

A diet rich in polyphenol-containing berries significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and enhances cognitive performance in older adults, as demonstrated by principal component analysis of microbiome data. Concurrent inulin supplementation further amplified these effects, increasing the abundance of beneficial Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while reducing pathogenic species like E. coli. In a 12-week randomized trial, 120 participants received either a berry-based polyphenol extract or a placebo, alongside daily inulin or a control supplement. Cognitive assessments revealed improved memory and executive function in the intervention group, with ANOVA showing significant differences in MoCA scores compared to controls. The gut microbiome alterations correlated with increased plasma levels of short-chain fatty acids, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolism and neurocognitive outcomes. These findings highlight the synergistic potential of polyphenol-rich diets and prebiotic supplementation in promoting cognitive health through microbiome modulation, supported by multivariate regression analyses linking microbial diversity to cognitive metrics.

A high-fiber diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles, with implications for neurodegenerative disorders linked to FTO-mediated metabolic dysregulation. Using metagenomic sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 200 participants undergoing 8 weeks of legume-rich dietary intervention, revealing increased abundance of Prevotella and Butyricicoccus, alongside elevated levels of short-chain fatty acids. FTO expression correlated inversely with butyrate concentrations, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome-derived metabolites and host metabolic pathways. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a key responder to dietary fiber, with its abundance inversely associated with FTO polymorphisms. These findings highlight the interplay between dietary fiber, gut microbiota dynamics, and genetic factors in modulating neuroinflammation and cognitive decline.

Alterations in the gut microbiome associated with a Western-type diet correlate with dysregulation of the TPH1 gene in the hippocampus of rodents, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary patterns and neuroinflammatory processes.
