Using principal component analysis, we identified that Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron abundance inversely correlated with TPH1 expression levels, while Lactobacillus reuteri showed a positive association with serotonin synthesis markers. Trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) concentrations, derived from high-fat dairy consumption, were significantly elevated in animals fed the Western-type diet and directly associated with hippocampal TPH1 downregulation. Integrative metabolomic profiling revealed that tryptophan metabolism intermediates were disrupted, aligning with altered TPH1-mediated pathways. These findings highlight the role of diet-induced dysbiosis in modulating neurotransmitter-related genes and underscore the potential of prebiotic fibers to restore microbial diversity. The study provides a novel framework connecting Western-type diet components, TPH1 expression dynamics, and neurodegenerative risk via multivariate statistical modeling, emphasizing the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative disorders through the gastrointestinal tract-brain axis. Metagenomic sequencing has revealed that dysbiosis characterized by reduced microbial diversity and overrepresentation of Bacteroides species correlates with Alzheimer's disease progression. Mechanistically, dysbiotic microbial communities enhance lipopolysaccharide production, which disrupts the blood-brain barrier and exacerbates neuroinflammation. Interventions targeting these pathways, such as probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus strains, have shown promise in restoring microbial homeostasis and reducing amyloid-beta accumulation in preclinical models. These findings underscore the potential of microbiome-directed therapies in mitigating Alzheimer's disease pathology and highlight the need for further exploration of single-cell RNA sequencing to elucidate microbial-host interactions at the cellular level.

A recent study highlights the role of probiotics and fermented foods in modulating gut-brain axis activity through alterations in gut microbiota composition and metabolic signaling. Subjects consuming a regimen combining probiotics with fermented foods exhibited significant reductions in depressive symptoms and anxiety scores compared to controls, as measured by standardized clinical assessments. Mechanistically, these interventions enhanced the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which correlated with increased production of short-chain fatty acids and neuroactive metabolites like gamma-aminobutyric acid. Notably, fermented foods rich in grains and fibers amplified the efficacy of probiotics by promoting microbial diversity and mucosal immunity. Multivariate analysis revealed that the synergistic effect of probiotics and fermented foods was most pronounced in individuals with baseline dysbiosis, suggesting a tailored approach for mental health interventions. These findings underscore the potential of combining probiotic supplementation with fermented foods to target gut-brain communication pathways, offering a non-pharmacological strategy for managing depressive disorders and related conditions.

Dietary intake of prebiotic fiber significantly alters gut microbiota composition and influences neuroinflammatory markers in individuals with metabolic syndrome. Analysis of fecal samples from 85 participants revealed that high-fiber inulin consumption correlated with increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and reduced TNF-alpha expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Using multivariate analysis of variance, we identified a significant interaction between gut microbiota diversity and serum interleukin-6 levels, which were further modulated by TLR4 polymorphisms. 16S rRNA sequencing highlighted that participants consuming ≥15g/day of inulin exhibited a 2.3-fold enrichment in Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum, a butyrate producer linked to reduced neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of gut microbiota through inulin intake may mitigate systemic inflammation via TLR4-mediated pathways, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic syndrome-associated neurodegeneration. The permutation-based regression models confirmed that TNF-alpha downregulation was independently associated with higher microbial butyrate production, reinforcing the role of diet-microbiome interactions in inflammatory homeostasis.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication through microbial metabolites, with inulin-induced shifts in gut microbiota composition correlating with altered serotonin signaling in murine models. Kimchi consumption, rich in Lactobacillus species, enhanced FUT2-mediated mucin secretion, fostering bacterial adherence and modulating neuroinflammatory markers. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified Bacteroides uniformis as a key responder to inulin, with its abundance inversely linked to tryptophan metabolism in the colon. TLR4 knockout mice exhibited diminished lipopolysaccharide-driven cytokine release, suggesting a mechanistic link between TLR4 activation and microbiota-derived SCFAs in regulating hippocampal neurogenesis. Probiotic-rich dairy further amplified Lactobacillus-mediated gamma-aminobutyric acid production, aligning with reduced anxiety-like behaviors. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetic factors, fiber interventions, and fermented food in shaping neuroimmune outcomes via the gut-brain axis.

A novel dietary intervention using probiotic-enriched kefir significantly modulated TLR4 gene expression in the intestinal epithelium, enhancing barrier function and reducing neuroinflammation in a mouse model of stress-induced cognitive decline. RNA sequencing revealed that kefir-mediated Lactobacillus reuteri colonization upregulated TLR4 signaling pathways, which correlated with decreased IL-6 secretion and improved hippocampal neurogenesis. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated butyrate levels in the colon, linking microbial fermentation of kefir-derived polysaccharides to the observed TLR4-dependent anti-inflammatory effects. mice fed kefir exhibited reduced anxiety-like behaviors and improved spatial memory, with TLR4 expression in enteric neurons showing a 2.3-fold increase compared to controls. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of TLR4 through kefir-induced microbiome alterations may offer therapeutic potential for neuroimmune disorders.

Long-term consumption of fermented soybeans and supplementation with a probiotic blend significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced neuroinflammatory markers in APP/PS1 transgenic mice, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. The intervention enhanced gut microbiota diversity, with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Proteobacteria, correlating with improved spatial memory and reduced hippocampal amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques. Mechanistically, the probiotic blend upregulated Nrf2 expression, mitigating oxidative stress and activating autophagy pathways, while fermented soybeans enriched short-chain fatty acid production, modulating neuroinflammation via NF-κB suppression. Random forest classification identified microbial taxa linked to cognitive outcomes, with Lactobacillus and Enterococcus showing strongest predictive value. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbial metabolites and neurodegenerative pathways, underscoring the potential of targeted probiotic and fermented food interventions in mitigating Alzheimer’s disease progression. The integration of machine learning models further supports personalized microbiome-based therapies for neuroinflammation.

A novel dietary intervention involving blueberry extract significantly modulated the expression of the BDNF gene in patients with metabolic syndrome, alongside alterations in gut microbiota composition. qPCR analysis revealed a 2.3-fold increase in BDNF transcript levels in participants consuming 150 mg/day of blueberry extract over 12 weeks compared to controls. Concurrently, 16S rRNA sequencing identified a 40% reduction in Escherichia coli abundance and a 15% rise in Akkermansia muciniphila in the intervention group. These changes correlated with improved insulin sensitivity and reduced systemic inflammation markers. Anthocyanin content in blueberry extract appeared to drive the observed effects, as evidenced by HPLC quantification and pathway enrichment analysis linking BDNF upregulation to enhanced neurotrophic signaling. The study also highlighted a previously uncharacterized interaction between BDNF and Akkermansia muciniphila, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome-derived metabolites and neuroendocrine regulation. These findings underscore the potential of blueberry extract-mediated BDNF activation as a therapeutic strategy for metabolic and neurodegenerative conditions, warranting further investigation into the molecular crosstalk between diet-derived bioactives and host genetic pathways.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's composition are associated with mental health disorders via immune-related gene modulation. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and machine learning algorithms, we identified TLR4-dependent shifts in gut microbiota composition linked to depression in rodent models. Bacteroides fragilis abundance correlated inversely with TLR4 expression levels in the hippocampus, while short-chain fatty acids derived from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii mitigated inflammation through TLR4-mediated signaling pathways. Random forest classification revealed that TLR4 polymorphisms explained 34% of variance in microbiome-derived butyrate concentrations, which were inversely correlated with neuroinflammation markers. Cytokine profiling confirmed reduced IL-6 secretion in mice with TLR4 knockout following prebiotic supplementation. These findings suggest that targeting TLR4-mediated immune pathways could restore gut-brain axis communication and alleviate depressive symptoms, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for patients with major depressive disorder.

The gut microbiome significantly influences neurobehavioral outcomes in a mouse model of metabolic syndrome, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis. Mice subjected to high-fat diets exhibited altered intestinal microbiota composition, characterized by reduced abundance of Lactobacillus and increased Desulfovibrio, correlating with heightened anxiety-like behaviors and impaired spatial memory in the hippocampus. Metagenomic analysis revealed dysregulated pathways in short-chain fatty acid metabolism, while multivariate regression identified leptin as a key mediator linking microbiota shifts to neuroinflammation. Antibiotic-treated mice showed exacerbated neurocognitive deficits, underscoring the microbiome’s role in modulating brain function. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota and metabolic syndrome-induced behavioral pathology, suggesting microbiota-targeted interventions could mitigate neurodegenerative risks.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with cognitive decline in aging, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for probiotic supplementation via the gut-brain axis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from older adults with and without Alzheimer’s disease (AD) to identify microbial signatures linked to neurodegeneration. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were significantly depleted in AD patients, while Escherichia abundance correlated with increased beta-amyloid accumulation in hippocampal tissue. Intervention with probiotic strains containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored microbial balance, reduced systemic inflammatory cytokines in serum, and improved spatial memory in transgenic AD mice. Mechanistically, metabolomic profiling revealed elevated short-chain fatty acids production, which modulated microglial activation pathways and enhanced BDNF expression in prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota dysbiosis and neuroinflammation in AD, with probiotic interventions offering a viable strategy to mitigate cognitive decline through microbial modulation.

Consumption of fermented kimchi was associated with altered gut microbiota composition and reduced inflammatory markers in rodent models of metabolic syndrome. Using principal component analysis, we identified a distinct clustering of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in kimchi-treated groups compared to controls. These shifts correlated with downregulation of the TLR4 gene, which encodes a toll-like receptor critical for innate immune signaling. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) derived from kimchi fermentation, particularly butyrate, were linked to enhanced colonic barrier integrity and reduced lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Parabacteroides abundance inversely correlated with TLR4 expression, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between microbial metabolic products and host immune modulation. Participants in a parallel clinical trial who consumed kimchi daily exhibited lower systemic inflammatory cytokines and improved insulin sensitivity, reinforcing the translational relevance of these findings. The interplay between fermented food-derived metabolites, TLR4 signaling, and gut microbiota dynamics highlights novel therapeutic avenues for metabolic disorders.

A high-fat diets modulate gut microbiota composition and alter TMAO expression, influencing neuroinflammation and behavioral outcomes in rodent models. Administration of inulin mitigated these effects by enhancing Bifidobacterium abundance and reducing trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) levels in serum. Short-chain fatty acids derived from fiber-rich diets correlated with decreased IL-6 activation in hippocampal regions, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived metabolites and neuroimmune regulation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that inulin restored alpha diversity disrupted by high-fat feeding, while canonical correspondence analysis identified TMAO as a key mediator of anxiety-like behaviors. These findings highlight the role of prebiotic interventions in counteracting Western-style diets-induced dysbiosis and its downstream effects on mental health through modulation of immune-related pathways.

Alterations in the gut microbiome have been linked to neurodegenerative disorders, yet the interplay between microbial TLR4 signaling and host inflammatory responses remains understudied. Using a multivariate regression model, we analyzed fecal samples from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy controls, revealing that Curcumin supplementation significantly modulated Akkermansia muciniphila abundance while reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells correlated inversely with Bacteroides fragilis counts, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and neuroinflammation. Curcumin also enhanced the production of butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid known to suppress NF-κB activation. These findings highlight the role of microbial TLR4 signaling in AD progression and suggest that targeted Curcumin interventions may mitigate neuroinflammation by reshaping the gut microbiome and altering host inflammatory pathways. The multivariate regression model further identified Prevotella copri as a key predictor of cognitive decline, underscoring the value of integrating microbiome data with clinical outcomes.

A high-fiber diet (oats) significantly altered gut microbiota composition in rodent models with depression, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Concurrent administration of probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus) further attenuated anhedonia and gastrointestinal dysmotility, correlating with increased short-chain fatty acid production and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels in the colon. Metabolomic profiling identified tryptophan-derived serotonin precursors as key mediators of the gut-brain axis modulation, with multivariate regression linking specific Bacteroides taxa to improved mood regulation. These findings suggest that synergistic interventions targeting fiber intake and probiotic supplementation could represent a viable strategy to restore microbial homeostasis and mitigate neuropsychiatric comorbidities in patients with depressive disorders.

The interplay between gut microbiota and neuroinflammatory markers in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) was elucidated using 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial communities in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and postmortem brain tissue from AD patients. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios in AD cohorts compared to controls, correlating with elevated interleukin-6 levels in the hippocampus. Mechanistic insights were derived from fecal microbiota transplants, which modulated microglial activation and Aβ plaques in recipient animals. Lactobacillus reuteri supplementation attenuated neuroinflammation by upregulating TGF-β signaling pathways, as confirmed by qPCR and immunohistochemistry. These findings underscore the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target, with multivariate regression models highlighting microbial diversity as a predictive biomarker for AD progression. The integration of metabolomic profiling further linked short-chain fatty acids to reduced tau hyperphosphorylation in the cortex, reinforcing the role of microbiome-derived metabolites in mitigating neurodegeneration.

Dietary modulation of the gut microbiome through probiotic-rich foods significantly alters neuroinflammatory markers linked to neurodegenerative disorders, with TLR4 expression emerging as a critical mediator in this relationship. Using multivariate regression analysis, we found that fermented dairy products enriched with Lactobacillus rhamnosus reduced systemic inflammation by 32% in participants with Alzheimer's Disease, correlating with decreased IL-6 levels and improved hippocampal neurogenesis. Mechanistically, TLR4 activation in enteric neurons was dampened by probiotic supplementation, as evidenced by qPCR and immunofluorescence assessments of colonic mucosal immune cells. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic-rich diets in modulating the gut-brain axis, particularly through TLR4-dependent pathways that influence cognitive decline. The study further underscores the role of machine learning in identifying microbial signatures associated with TLR4 expression, offering a novel framework for personalized microbiome-based interventions targeting neuroinflammation.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are linked to cognitive and emotional dysregulation, with emerging evidence suggesting that dietary interventions may modulate this relationship. A cohort of 120 participants consuming a high-fiber diet enriched with fermented foods, such as sauerkraut, alongside a probiotic formulation containing *Lactobacillus* strains, showed distinct microbial profiles compared to a control group. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) revealed significant shifts in microbial community structures, correlating with improved mood scores and reduced anxiety symptoms. Notably, gut microbiota diversity, assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing, was positively associated with habitual intake of fiber-rich legumes and the probiotic supplement, which enhanced the abundance of *Bifidobacterium* species. These findings highlight the potential of targeted dietary strategies to influence gut-brain signaling pathways, suggesting that microbiota-derived metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, may mediate the observed behavioral effects. The study underscores the role of intestinal microbiota in modulating neuroimmune responses and identifies PERMANOVA-supported biomarkers that could inform personalized interventions for psychiatric conditions.

Chronic administration of the probiotic mixture derived from fermented dairy significantly modulated gut microbial diversity and enhanced neurobehavioral outcomes in APP/PS1 transgenic mice, a model of Alzheimer's disease. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, coinciding with elevated levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in the gut. Multivariate correlation analysis identified a strong association between butyrate production and reduced Aβ plaque deposition in the hippocampus, alongside improved spatial memory in mice. SCFAs were further shown to suppress microglial activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release in brain tissue. The probiotic intervention also restored gut barrier integrity, as evidenced by decreased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation and lower systemic inflammatory markers. Notably, the dairy-based probiotic formulation demonstrated superior efficacy compared to synthetic prebiotics in promoting gut microbiota-derived metabolites that cross-talk with central nervous system pathways. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of fermented food-derived probiotics in targeting the gut-brain axis to mitigate neurodegenerative pathology.

The gut microbiome modulates neurodegenerative disorders via metabolic signaling pathways, with fermented dairy consumption emerging as a modifiable factor. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 80 participants with and without Alzheimer’s disease, revealing that fermented dairy intake correlated with higher abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced levels of Enterobacteriaceae. Principal component analysis linked microbial shifts to plasma butyrate concentrations, which inversely correlated with TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. qPCR confirmed that TLR4 downregulation was associated with improved hippocampal neurogenesis markers in participants consuming fermented dairy for six months. These findings suggest that fermented dairy-induced microbial metabolites may mitigate neuroinflammation by altering TLR4-mediated immune responses. The permutation test further validated the significance of TLR4 as a biomarker for microbiome-brain interactions in Alzheimer’s disease progression. This study highlights the potential of dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota to modulate immune-related genes and ameliorate cognitive decline through short-chain fatty acid signaling.

The gut-brain axis modulates neurobehavioral outcomes through microbial metabolites, with fiber-rich diets enhancing short-chain fatty acid production in gut microbiota that correlates with reduced depressive symptoms. A cohort study employing multivariate analysis of variance revealed that prebiotic supplementation significantly increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which inversely associated with anxiety scores (p<0.05). Participants adhering to fermented food intake showed higher microbial diversity indices compared to controls, though serotonin transporter gene polymorphisms mediated 30% of the effect on 5-HTTLPR-linked emotional regulation. Adults with irritable bowel syndrome exhibited altered gut-brain communication patterns, detectable via electroencephalography, which normalized after 12 weeks of synbiotic therapy. These findings suggest that microbial-targeted interventions could optimize enteric nervous system function and mental health outcomes through dietary modulation of microbial communities.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's microbial tryptophan metabolism pathway are linked to bipolar disorder with major depressive episodes, revealing distinct gene expression patterns and microbiota dysbiosis. Using shotgun metagenomics sequencing, we identified significant reductions in K00658 and K01696 orthology levels in patients, alongside increased abundance of Actinobacteria and decreased Bacteroidetes. A Random Forests-based classification model achieved 0.997 area under the curve in distinguishing bipolar disorder patients from healthy controls by analyzing 38 microbial taxa and 12 KEGG orthologs. These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota in modulating tryptophan biosynthesis and suggest that microbial biomarkers could improve diagnostic precision for bipolar disorder. The study also underscores the potential of targeting gastrointestinal microbiome dysregulation via dietary interventions or probiotics to mitigate neuroinflammatory pathways associated with mood disorders. Despite limitations in sample size and cross-sectional design, the integration of 16S rRNA sequencing with machine learning provides a framework for exploring microbiome-gut-brain interactions in psychiatric conditions.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD), as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomics profiling. Interleukin-6 levels, measured via ELISA, exhibited a statistically significant inverse relationship with Bacteroides fragilis abundance, while tryptophan metabolites correlated with prefrontal cortex thickness. Principal component analysis highlighted three distinct microbial clusters associated with symptom severity, with Lactobacillus reuteri showing the strongest predictive power for anxiety scores. Positron emission tomography further demonstrated that kynurenine pathway dysregulation, linked to Escherichia coli, was significantly elevated in MDD patients compared to healthy controls. Random forest classification achieved 82% accuracy in distinguishing MDD cases from controls based on combined microbial and metabolic profiles. These findings suggest that gut microbiota-derived metabolites modulate neuroinflammation and brain structure, offering potential targets for precision therapies targeting the gut-brain axis.

Altered gut microbiota composition has been linked to neurobehavioral impairments in neurodevelopmental disorders, with emerging evidence suggesting dietary interventions may modulate these pathways. This study demonstrates that supplementation with the probiotic strain Lactobacillus rhamnosus, combined with a high-fiber diet enriched in inulin, significantly reduces repetitive behaviors in a mouse model of autism. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, we identified 12 microbial taxa exhibiting altered abundance, including increased Bacteroides uniformis and decreased Clostridium difficile, alongside shifts in short-chain fatty acid production. Correlative multivariate analysis revealed strong associations between butyrate levels and reduced stereotypy, while serotonin metabolism was linked to hindbrain expression of the Slc6a4 transporter. The gut microbiota alterations were accompanied by reduced glutamate concentrations in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial-derived metabolites and neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic and prebiotic interventions to modulate the gut-brain axis in neurodevelopmental conditions, warranting further investigation into microbial metabolic pathways as therapeutic targets.

The application of principal component analysis revealed significant shifts in gut microbiota composition following antibiotic treatment, correlating with altered serotonin levels measured via ELISA in rodents. Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis was associated with heightened anxiety-like behaviors and reduced tryptophan metabolism in the cecum, as detected by 16S rRNA sequencing. Short-chain fatty acid production by Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus declined in treated animals, while pro-inflammatory cytokine concentrations in serum rose, as quantified by cytokine array. Multivariate regression confirmed a strong inverse relationship between butyrate levels and anxiety scores, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and behavioral outcomes. Immunohistochemistry further showed increased glucocorticoid receptor expression in the amygdala of antibiotic-treated subjects, aligning with altered stress responses. These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota in modulating neurobehavioral pathways through metabolic and inflammatory signaling, underscoring the utility of integrating multivariate analysis and molecular profiling to dissect gut-brain interactions.

The administration of omega-3 fatty acids was associated with altered gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in a cohort of adults with major depressive disorder (MDD). Participants receiving the supplement showed increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli, alongside reduced inflammation markers such as IL-6 and TNF-α. These shifts correlated with improved depressive symptoms measured via Hamilton Depression Rating Scale after 12 weeks. Colonic mucosal permeability, assessed using transepithelial electrical resistance, decreased in the supplement group, suggesting enhanced intestinal barrier integrity. Notably, multivariate analysis identified Prevotella as a key mediator linking omega-3 intake to symptom reduction. The findings highlight the potential of targeted nutritional interventions to modulate the gut-brain axis through microbiota-dependent mechanisms, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for MDD management. Concurrent metabolomics profiling revealed elevated short-chain fatty acids in supplemented subjects, implicating microbial metabolic byproducts in the observed neurobehavioral improvements.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with cognitive decline in aging populations, as demonstrated by whole-genome metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from 48 older adults with Alzheimer's disease and 52 age-matched controls. Gut microbiota from Alzheimer's disease patients exhibited reduced alpha diversity and enriched taxa including Akkermansia and Parabacteroides, alongside depleted Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, compared to controls. Random forest classification identified 12 microbial taxa and 8 metabolic pathways as significant predictors of cognitive impairment, achieving 82% accuracy in distinguishing Alzheimer's disease cases from controls. Short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, correlated inversely with neuroinflammation markers TNF-α and IL-6 in plasma, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolism and neurodegeneration. Hippocampal BDNF expression levels were inversely associated with gut-derived lipopolysaccharide concentrations, highlighting potential cross-talk between the gut microbiome and central nervous system. These findings underscore the role of the gut-brain axis in neurodegenerative disease progression and advocate for microbial profiling as a diagnostic tool. Future studies should explore targeted probiotic interventions to modulate gut microbiota and mitigate cognitive decline.

Dietary fiber supplementation modulates gut microbial composition and inflammatory gene expression in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples. Inulin-rich diets significantly increased relative abundances of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while reducing Escherichia coli levels compared to control groups. Concurrently, transcriptomic profiling revealed downregulation of the Tlr4 gene, a key mediator of intestinal inflammation, in colonic epithelial cells of treated individuals. These findings correlate with reduced plasma levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α and improved symptom scores in IBS patients following 8 weeks of intervention. The observed microbiome-gene interactions suggest a mechanism wherein gut microbiota metabolites derived from dietary fiber modulate host Tlr4 signaling pathways, thereby attenuating inflammation. This study highlights the potential of targeted prebiotic interventions to alleviate IBS through microbiome-mediated regulation of immune-related genes and underscores the utility of 16S rRNA sequencing in elucidating gut-brain axis dynamics.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease patients, as demonstrated by shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealing reduced abundance of Prevotella and increased Escherichia-Shigella in 45 participants compared to 30 healthy controls. Multivariate regression analysis identified Prevotella depletion as a significant predictor of lower scores on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), while Escherichia-Shigella enrichment correlated with executive dysfunction. These findings align with prior observations linking microbiota dysbiosis to neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease models, suggesting microbial shifts may contribute to cognitive decline via altered neurotransmitter metabolism. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed alpha diversity reductions in fecal samples, with Blautia and Ruminococcus showing inverse relationships to MoCA performance. The study also detected elevated lipopolysaccharide levels in patients with Parkinson's disease, which correlation analysis linked to gut microbiota composition changes. These data support a mechanistic role for microbiota-derived molecular signals in modulating cognitive outcomes in Parkinson's disease, warranting further investigation into microbial-targeted interventions.

A diet rich in fermented foods significantly altered gut microbiota composition, increasing beneficial bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, while decreasing pro-inflammatory species like Escherichia coli. These changes correlated with enhanced expression of the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) in intestinal epithelial cells, suggesting a link between microbiota modulation and immune regulation. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and ANOSIM, we observed distinct microbial communities in subjects consuming fermented foods compared to controls. Plasma levels of short-chain fatty acids were elevated, potentially mediating anti-inflammatory effects. The gut microbiota alterations were associated with reduced inflammatory bowel disease symptoms, highlighting the therapeutic potential of dietary strategies. Notably, the fermented dairy products group exhibited higher microbial diversity and increased forkhead box O1 (FOXO1) expression, which may protect against oxidative stress. This study underscores the role of diet in shaping the gut microbiome and modulating host gene expression to influence immune and metabolic health.

Major depressive disorder is linked to altered gut microbiome composition and host genetic variants, yet the mechanistic interplay remains elusive. A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) analysis of 1,200 Chinese participants revealed that Romboutsia abundance correlated with METTL8 expression levels in peripheral blood, while Ruminococcus gnavus co-occurred with OTULIN in a gene-microbiome network. Microbial beta diversity differences between MDD and control groups were associated with rs6108 (p = 8.65 × 10-9), a single nucleotide polymorphism near ITGB2, and SERPINA5 expression in the prefrontal cortex showed inverse correlation with gut microbial alpha diversity metrics. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations, particularly butyrate, mediated interactions between PROSER3 and Actinobacteria taxa, suggesting a pathway for microbial metabolites to influence neuroinflammation. These findings highlight METTL8 and OTULIN as potential biomarkers linking depression to gut microbiome dysregulation in Asian populations, with LEfSe enabling precise identification of microbial-genetic associations. The integration of host genome-wide data with 16S rRNA sequencing underscores the need for multi-omics approaches to dissect the gut-brain axis in psychiatric disorders.

Altered gut microbiome composition in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients correlates with dietary intake of fermented soy products and dysregulation of antioxidant genes. Analysis of 150 PD cases and 150 controls revealed a significant reduction in Bacteroides fragilis abundance in individuals consuming fermented soy regularly, while Nrf2 expression was elevated in gut-derived immune cells from these subjects compared to non-consumers. 16S rRNA sequencing identified a 23% decrease in Akkermansia muciniphila in PD patients, which inversely correlated with serum lipopolysaccharide levels using principal component analysis. Co-administration of fermented soy extract with levodopa in murine models attenuated α-synuclein aggregation by 38% and normalized Nrf2-mediated glutathione production in enteric neurons. Microbial metabolic profiles showed heightened production of butyrate in fermented soy-treated cohorts, which directly upregulated Nrf2 transcription via histone deacetylase inhibition. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome may synergistically enhance Nrf2-dependent neuroprotection in PD, offering a potential therapeutic strategy to mitigate oxidative stress pathways implicated in disease progression.

A recent study highlights the role of the Tlr4 gene in modulating neuroinflammation via gut microbiota, with probiotic supplementation of Lactobacillus rhamnosus mitigating these effects in murine models of colitis-associated cognitive decline. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, researchers identified that Tlr4-mediated signaling amplifies pro-inflammatory cytokine release from enteric glial cells, exacerbating neuroinflammation through the gut-brain axis. Administration of probiotic strains enriched in Lactobacillus reduced IL-6 and TNF-α levels in serum while restoring gut microbiome diversity, as evidenced by increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant improvements in spatial memory and executive function in treated animals compared to controls. Mechanistically, Tlr4 knockout mice exhibited blunted inflammatory responses, suggesting that targeting this gene pathway could enhance the efficacy of probiotic interventions in neuroinflammatory disorders. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetics, microbial metabolites, and cognitive outcomes, offering potential therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative diseases linked to gut dysbiosis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome mediated by dietary fiber intake correlate with changes in the expression of the Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5) gene, influencing neuroinflammatory responses in the brain. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate ANOVA, we analyzed fecal samples from participants consuming a high-fiber diet (n=25) versus a low-fiber control group (n=25). The gut microbiome of the high-fiber group exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Prevotella, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acid production, which correlated with reduced TLR5 expression. This downregulation of TLR5 was associated with lower plasma levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6), suggesting a dampened neuroinflammatory profile. In contrast, the low-fiber group showed higher TLR5 activity and increased IL-6 levels, linked to dysbiosis in colonic mucosa. These findings highlight the role of dietary fiber in modulating microbial metabolites that interact with immune signaling pathways, potentially mitigating brain inflammation. The high-fiber diet may thus serve as a therapeutic strategy to target neurodegenerative disorders via microbiome-gene interactions.

Consumption of fermented dairy products significantly alters gut microbiota composition and reduces symptoms of anxiety in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, as demonstrated by a 12-week randomized controlled trial involving 120 participants. The intervention group received daily servings of kefir, a probiotic-rich fermented milk beverage, while the control group consumed non-fermented dairy. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a marked increase in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance in the kefir group, alongside reduced gut microbiota dysbiosis scores. Psychological outcomes were assessed using the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, with the kefir group exhibiting a 34% reduction in anxiety scores compared to controls. Multivariate analysis of variance confirmed significant differences in microbiota diversity and anxiety metrics between groups. Additionally, serum levels of tryptophan and serotonin were elevated in the kefir cohort, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut microbiota modulation and central nervous system function. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of fermented dairy in ameliorating gut-brain axis dysfunction through microbiota-targeted interventions.

A high-fat diet (high-fat) significantly alters gut microbiota composition, exacerbating neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits in rodents via the gut-brain axis. Administration of a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum partially restored microbial diversity, yet cognitive recovery remained incomplete. Application of 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the supplement reduced Proteobacteria abundance while enhancing Firmicutes ratios, correlating with decreased systemic inflammation but limited hippocampal neurogenesis. However, when combined with electroacupuncture at the ST36 acupoint, the probiotic intervention fully reversed spatial memory impairments, as evidenced by improved performance in the Morris water maze task. Mechanistically, the synergistic approach normalized TLR4 expression in the hippocampus and restored short-chain fatty acid signaling, highlighting a multi-modal strategy to target microbiome-brain interactions. These findings underscore the necessity of integrating microbial modulation with non-pharmacological interventions to address diet-induced neurocognitive decline.

A 12-week randomized controlled trial demonstrated that prebiotic supplementation significantly altered gut microbiota composition, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, correlating with improved anxiety and depression scores in 120 participants with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). The intervention group receiving inulin-type fructans showed a 23% reduction in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores compared to a placebo group, with microbial shifts including increased Bifidobacterium and decreased Enterobacteriaceae. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that baseline gut microbiota diversity predicted treatment response, highlighting interactions between gastrointestinal dysbiosis and central nervous system function. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations, measured via gas chromatography, correlated with mood disturbance metrics, suggesting metabolic pathways as potential mediators. The study underscores the role of prebiotic-induced microbiota modulation in alleviating psychological comorbidities in IBS, with implications for gut-brain axis-targeted therapies.

A longitudinal study reveals that supplementation with curcumin significantly modulates gut microbiota composition in patients with Alzheimer's disease, correlating with reduced neuroinflammatory markers and improved cognitive function. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) identified distinct microbial signatures in curcumin-treated cohorts, marked by elevated Akkermansia muciniphila and reduced Escherichia coli abundance compared to placebo groups. These shifts aligned with decreased systemic inflammatory cytokine levels, including IL-6 and TNF-α, suggesting a microbiome-mediated anti-inflammatory pathway. Mouse models administered curcumin exhibited analogous microbiota alterations and enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis, as measured by immunohistochemistry for BDNF. Notably, principal component analysis highlighted a strong correlation between Akkermansia enrichment and reduced amyloid-beta plaque burden, implicating gut-brain axis modulation in disease progression. The findings underscore curcumin's potential as a microbiota-targeted therapeutic, with machine learning models predicting 78% accuracy in distinguishing responders based on baseline microbiome profiles. This interplay between gut microbiota dynamics, curcumin bioavailability, and neuroinflammatory outcomes highlights novel avenues for neurodegenerative disease management.

Altered gut microbiome composition has been implicated in the progression of multiple sclerosis (MS). This study evaluated the impact of a prebiotic fiber supplement on microbial profiles and inflammatory markers in MS patients. Fecal samples from 45 participants were analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing increased abundance of butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium and reduced pro-inflammatory Escherichia following supplementation. Concurrently, serum levels of interleukin-6 were significantly lowered, suggesting a potential mechanism linking microbiota modulation to immune regulation in MS. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions targeting the gut-brain axis in autoimmune neurological conditions. Additionally, the gut microbiome changes correlated with improved central nervous system function, as measured by neurological scoring, reinforcing the role of microbiota-derived metabolites in neuroinflammation. The prebiotic fiber also enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which may mitigate patient fatigue and cognitive decline through TNF-α-mediated pathways. These data underscore the value of integrating microbiome profiling with metabolomic analysis to elucidate gut-brain-immune interactions in chronic neuroinflammatory diseases.

Probiotic supplementation significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, thereby influencing neurobehavioral outcomes in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 120 children with ASD and 120 typically developing controls, we identified 14 taxa associated with probiotic intake, including increased Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli. Logistic regression revealed that higher short-chain fatty acid production correlated with reduced severity of GI symptoms (OR = 0.32, 95% CI 0.18–0.57). Gut dysbiosis was further linked to elevated serotonin metabolite levels in colonic tissue, suggesting microbial modulation of the gut-brain axis. Notably, Lactobacillus reuteri, a key component of the probiotic formulation, exhibited strong negative correlations with autism severity scores (FDR-corrected P < 0.01). These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to ameliorate GI symptoms and neurobehavioral deficits via microbial modulation of neurotransmitter pathways. The logistic regression framework underscores the utility of integrating microbiome data with behavioral assessments to refine therapeutic strategies for ASD.

Altered lipid metabolism in the brain is strongly associated with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), highlighting the potential of lipidomic profiling as a biomarker for early detection. Using mass spectrometry, we analyzed lipid profiles in postmortem brain tissues from AD patients and age-matched controls, identifying significant reductions in phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin levels. Principal component analysis further revealed distinct lipidomic signatures correlating with disease severity, suggesting that specific lipid classes may serve as therapeutic targets. Additionally, gut microbiota dysbiosis, characterized by decreased short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria, was linked to impaired lipid metabolism in patients with AD, emphasizing the interplay between gut-brain axis communication and neurodegeneration. These findings underscore the value of integrating multi-omics approaches with machine learning to decode complex interactions between lipid metabolism, microbial activity, and cognitive outcomes in neurodegenerative disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with systemic inflammation in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), suggesting a potential role for microbiome-targeted therapies. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 120 participants with IBS and 80 controls, we identified reduced diversity in gut microbial communities and enrichment of Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis in IBS cases. Plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-6, were significantly elevated in patients with IBS, correlating with principal component analysis of microbiota data. Quantitative PCR confirmed increased tnf and il6 expression in intestinal biopsies from IBS subjects. A multivariate logistic regression model integrating microbiota profiles and inflammatory markers achieved 82% accuracy in distinguishing IBS from controls, highlighting the interplay between microbial dysbiosis and immune activation. These findings support the hypothesis that gut microbiota modulation could mitigate inflammation in IBS, warranting further exploration of prebiotic or probiotic interventions to restore microbial homeostasis.

Dietary modulation of the gut microbiome significantly influences neuroinflammatory markers in aging populations, as demonstrated by a pilot study employing whole-genome metagenomic sequencing to analyze stool samples from older adults consuming probiotic-rich yogurt daily for six months. Participants exhibited reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and altered gut microbiome composition, with increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Escherichia coli compared to a control group. Functional profiling revealed upregulation of pathways involved in short-chain fatty acid synthesis, which may mediate neuroprotective effects via the gut-brain axis. Notably, brain imaging data correlated with microbiome-derived butyrate levels, suggesting a direct link between dietary interventions and neural plasticity markers. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic-rich yogurt in mitigating age-related cognitive decline and underscore the utility of whole-genome metagenomic sequencing for dissecting microbial contributions to neurodegenerative processes. The study also identifies specific taxa that could serve as biomarkers for monitoring gut-brain axis integrity in clinical settings.

Altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is linked to specific dietary patterns and genetic factors. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified TSC2 mutations correlating with reduced abundance of Lactobacillus and increased Enterobacteriaceae, which were further modulated by fermented dairy product consumption in children aged 4–12. Microbiome profiles revealed that fermented dairy product intake was associated with elevated short-chain fatty acids levels, while TSC2 variants were linked to dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, affecting serotonin synthesis pathways. Participants following a high-fiber diet showed improved gastrointestinal symptoms and reduced behavioral manifestations of ASD, suggesting microbiota-mediated interactions between TSC2-related pathways and dietary components. These findings highlight the potential of microbiome-targeted interventions, including probiotic supplementation, to modulate gut-brain axis signaling in ASD patients. Further investigation into TSC2’s role in microbiota-host communication may uncover novel therapeutic strategies involving prebiotic-rich foods and metagenomic analysis.

Altered gut microbiota composition was linked to cognitive decline in older adults, with dietary interventions showing promise in mitigating neuroinflammation. A 12-week trial involving 200 participants consuming a fermented dairy product enriched in probiotic strains revealed significant shifts in gut microbial communities assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing. Participants with higher baseline short-chain fatty acid levels exhibited improved memory retention, correlating with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. Individuals receiving the fermented dairy showed reduced inflammatory cytokine secretion compared to controls, alongside enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis. Metabolic profiling indicated that the probiotic modulated tryptophan metabolism, elevating serotonin precursors associated with mood regulation. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiota-supportive diets to alleviate cognitive impairment through <microbiome>-mediated pathways, emphasizing the role of microbial community analysis in precision nutrition strategies.

A reduction in the expression of the fabp2 gene was associated with altered gut microbiome composition in individuals consuming a high-fiber food diet, revealing a mechanistic link between dietary fiber intake and microbial metabolism. Supplementation with the omega-3 fatty acid modulated the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a key mucosal-associated bacterium, while concurrent intake of fermented dairy enhanced the production of butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid implicated in neuroinflammation regulation. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified that fabp2 downregulation correlated with decreased butyrate synthesis, which was partially restored by probiotic administration. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, dietary interventions, and microbial-derived metabolites in shaping gut-brain communication. Microbial diversity metrics showed a significant inverse relationship with lipopolysaccharide levels in the colonic lumen, suggesting that fabp2-mediated pathways influence systemic inflammation via microbiome-modulated immune signaling. Furthermore, fiber-rich plant-based diets were linked to increased abundance of Prevotella species, which co-occurred with elevated tryptophan metabolism, a precursor to serotonin synthesis. These results underscore the potential of combining targeted nutraceuticals with dietary modifications to ameliorate gut-brain axis dysfunctions.

Alterations in gut microbial composition and function are linked to cognitive decline in aging populations, with emerging evidence highlighting the role of 16S rRNA-encoded bacterial taxa in modulating neuroinflammatory pathways. A principal component analysis of fecal samples from 120 participants revealed that Bacteroidetes abundance inversely correlated with amyloid-beta accumulation in hippocampal regions, while Firmicutes ratios were associated with tau hyperphosphorylation in entorhinal cortex. Notably, lactulose supplementation for six months significantly increased the relative abundance of Prevotella and Parabacteroides, which co-occurred with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. Arginine biosynthesis-related pathways in Eggerthella lenta showed strongest associations with executive function deficits, as measured by neuropsychological testing. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of microbial metabolic pathways via dietary interventions may offer therapeutic potential for Alzheimer's disease by restoring neuroimmune balance.

A high-fiber diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition and modulates host metabolic pathways, as demonstrated by multivariate analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 participants. Legumes, rich in resistant starch and polyphenols, were associated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced inflammation markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α. Notably, the Fto gene, previously linked to obesity susceptibility, showed enhanced expression in intestinal epithelial cells exposed to microbial metabolites derived from fiber fermentation. These findings suggest that dietary fiber may influence host physiology through microbiota-mediated signaling, with potential implications for obesity and metabolic disease management.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are strongly associated with neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s disease, as evidenced by elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the hippocampus and systemic markers of oxidative stress. Using immunohistochemistry and 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified significant shifts in microbial taxa, including reduced abundance of Bifidobacteriaceae and increased Prevotellaceae, correlating with cognitive decline in APP/PS1 transgenic mice. A multivariate linear regression analysis further revealed that microbial diversity metrics, such as Shannon index, independently predicted hippocampal amyloid-β accumulation (β = −0.42, p = 0.012). Treatment with a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus plantarum normalized cytokine profiles and restored β-diversity, as shown by flow cytometry and metabolomic profiling. These interventions also mitigated oxidative stress markers via activation of the Nrf2 pathway, as confirmed by Western blotting. The statistical model highlighted that microbial-derived butyrate levels mediated 32% of the treatment effect on cognitive scores (p = 0.008). These findings underscore the gut microbiota’s role in modulating neuroinflammation and suggest targeted microbiome interventions as a therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer’s disease.

A novel prebiotic compound significantly modulates gut microbial composition and alleviates neuroinflammation in a murine model of multiple sclerosis (MS). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in C57BL/6 mice treated with the compound, correlating with reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 detected via ELISA. Kruskal-Wallis test confirmed significant differences in colonic microbial diversity between treated and untreated groups (≤0.01). The compound also suppressed astrocytic activation and microglial infiltration in the central nervous system, as visualized by immunohistochemistry. Short-chain fatty acids produced by gut-derived bacteria were identified as key mediators, with butyrate levels correlating negatively with neuroinflammatory markers using mass spectrometry. Principal component analysis highlighted the compound’s impact on microbial metabolic pathways linked to immune regulation. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota through prebiotic supplementation could represent a therapeutic strategy for MS, bridging gut and brain pathophysiology via multi-omics integration.

Alterations in the gut microbiota associated with the TLR4 gene modulate neuroinflammation and behavioral outcomes in rodent models of chronic stress, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples and linear mixed-effects models analyzing longitudinal behavioral data. Lactobacillus reuteri abundance correlated inversely with corticosterone levels, while Parabacteroides distasonis showed heightened association with anxiety-like behaviors in mice subjected to social defeat stress. Metagenomic analysis identified TNF-α expression in intestinal epithelial cells as a downstream mediator of microbiota-induced immune signaling. Permutation testing confirmed significant interactions between gut microbial diversity and TLR4 polymorphisms in predicting hippocampal neurogenesis rates. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetic factors and microbial composition in shaping the gut-brain axis, with potential implications for microbiome-targeted therapies in psychiatric disorders.

A novel prebiotic formulation derived from fermented soybean extract significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and alleviated neuroinflammation in a rodent model of Alzheimer's disease. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, including Butyricicoccus, alongside reduced Proteobacteria levels in treated cohorts. Multivariate regression analysis revealed a strong correlation between microbiota-derived butyrate concentrations and decreased tau protein phosphorylation in hippocampal tissue. The prebiotic also enhanced glutathione synthesis and suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines via activation of the Nrf2 pathway. Longitudinal metabolomic profiling confirmed sustained improvements in intestinal barrier integrity markers, with principal component analysis highlighting scfa metabolism as a key mediator of neuroprotection. These findings establish a mechanistic link between microbiota modulation via prebiotics and therapeutic outcomes in neurodegenerative disorders, underscoring the potential of gut-brain axis interventions in clinical settings.

Altered gut microbiota composition has been linked to dysregulated inflammatory bowel disease progression, prompting investigations into dietary interventions. A pilot study evaluated the effects of a high-fiber diet enriched with prebiotic oligofructose on microbial diversity using 16S rRNA sequencing in 30 patients with ulcerative colitis. Baseline gut microbiota profiles revealed reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated Escherichia coli in active cases compared to healthy controls. Post-intervention, fecal samples showed a 28% increase in Bifidobacterium and a 19% decrease in Escherichia coli, correlating with improved endoscopic scores. Alpha diversity metrics improved significantly (P < 0.01), suggesting restored microbial balance. Notably, fermented dairy products consumed as part of the high-fiber diet were associated with higher Lactobacillus counts, while oligofructose supplementation correlated with reduced lipopolysaccharide levels in stool. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted dietary strategies in modulating gut microbiota dynamics and inflammatory pathways in inflammatory bowel disease, warranting larger trials to validate efficacy.

Dietary supplementation with fermented dairy products modulates neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in APP/PS1 transgenic mice by altering gut microbiota composition and mitigating ApoE4-mediated amyloid accumulation. Models exhibited impaired spatial memory and elevated Aβ42 levels in hippocampus, alongside dysregulated Tlr4 signaling and reduced BDNF expression. Feeding fermented dairy products enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum and colon. ApoE4 carriers showed heightened vulnerability to Alzheimer’s disease pathology, but fermented dairy products ameliorated Aβ plaque burden and restored BDNF expression through microbiota-dependent mechanisms. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus abundance inversely correlated with Aβ42 levels in brain tissue. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Bifidobacterium were linked to reduced Tlr4 activation in microglia, suggesting a microbiota-gut-brain axis pathway for fermented dairy products-mediated neuroprotection. These findings highlight the interplay between ApoE genotype, microbiota-modulating diets, and cognitive decline in neurodegenerative models.

Altered expression of the TLR5 gene in gut epithelial cells correlates with dysbiosis in patients with neurocognitive impairment, revealing a molecular link between immune signaling and gut-brain communication. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified distinct gut microbiota profiles in individuals consuming a diet high in processed carbohydrates, characterized by reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated levels of proinflammatory Escherichia coli. These findings align with prior observations that short-chain fatty acids produced by butyrate-producing microbes modulate hippocampal neurogenesis via HDAC-dependent mechanisms. A dietary intervention incorporating fermented dairy enriched in Lactobacillus significantly restored TLR5 expression and improved memory retention in a murine model of age-related cognitive decline. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing confirmed that microbial diversity increased alongside reduced systemic IL-6 levels, suggesting a therapeutic pathway through which microbiota modulation could counteract neuroinflammation. These data highlight the interplay between host genetic regulators, microbial composition, and dietary factors in shaping cognitive outcomes.

A high-fiber Mediterranean diet modulates neuroinflammatory pathways through microbiome-driven NLRP3 expression changes in Parkinson's disease models, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR. Bacteroidetes abundance correlated with reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced microglial activation in substantia nigra of α-synuclein overexpressing mice, while olive oil-rich interventions enhanced gut microbiota diversity and suppressed IL-1β upregulation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that intestinal flora metabolites, particularly butyrate, modulated TLR4 signaling in microglia, attenuating neuroinflammation and α-synuclein aggregation. Fermented dairy consumption further altered microbial argR expression, linking dietary patterns to motor dysfunction mitigation. These findings highlight the interplay between plant-based diets, gut microbiome dynamics, and immune-related pathways in neurodegenerative disease progression, suggesting targeted prebiotic strategies could ameliorate chronic inflammation and neurodegeneration.

Modulation of the Tlr5 gene by a prebiotic fiber significantly alters gut microbiota composition and reduces neuroinflammation in a Alzheimer's disease murine model. C57BL/6J mice fed a inulin-enriched diet exhibited increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Prevotella, correlated with reduced IL-6 and TNF-α expression in hippocampal tissues. 16S rDNA sequencing revealed enhanced α-diversity alongside elevated short-chain fatty acid production, which co-occurred with improved spatial memory in APP/PS1 transgenic mice. Tlr5 knockout mice showed exacerbated microbiota dysbiosis and heightened systemic inflammation compared to wild-type controls, underscoring its role in mediating gut microbiota-brain communication. The prebiotic intervention normalized BDNF levels in the cortex and restored retinol homeostasis, linking Tlr5-mediated immune regulation to Alzheimer's pathology. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting Tlr5 signaling via prebiotic modulation to counteract neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.

A TLR2-mediated signaling pathway in enteric neurons was identified as a critical mediator of neuroinflammation linked to gut dysbiosis in C57BL/6J models. Analysis of multivariate PCA on fecal metagenomic data revealed distinct clustering of Prevotella and Bacteroides taxa in subjects consuming a high-fiber diet compared to those on a low-fiber regimen. TLR2 knockout mice exhibited reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion following Escherichia coli challenge, correlating with altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. qPCR confirmed upregulation of IL-6 and TNF-α in wild-type animals, while ANOVA highlighted significant differences in butyrate levels between dietary groups. These findings suggest that TLR2 activation by gut-derived metabolites may amplify neuroimmune responses, with dietary modulation of fiber intake offering a potential therapeutic avenue. The interplay between microbial composition, TLR2 signaling, and metabolite dynamics underscores the need for targeted interventions in neurodegenerative disorders associated with gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Interventions targeting the gut-brain axis have revealed novel links between microbial dysbiosis and neurodegenerative disorders, with fermented dairy products showing potential to modulate TREM2-mediated immune responses in Alzheimer’s disease models. A 12-week intervention in aged C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet supplemented with kefir (a probiotic-rich fermented milk) demonstrated altered gut microbiota composition, characterized by increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium alongside reduced Escherichia coli. 16S rRNA sequencing correlated these shifts with decreased systemic inflammation, as evidenced by lower plasma IL-6 levels. qPCR analysis further revealed upregulation of TREM2 expression in hippocampal tissue, coinciding with improved performance in novel object recognition tests. Mechanistically, kefir-induced microbiota changes were associated with elevated production of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, which may act as a signaling molecule to enhance TREM2-dependent phagocytosis of Aβ plaques. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome through fermented foods could synergize with genetic pathways like TREM2 to mitigate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, offering a dual-targeted therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer’s disease.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition are strongly correlated with anxiety severity, as revealed by LEfSe analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from 180 participants. Lactobacillus abundance inversely correlated with serotonin levels, while Bacteroides showed positive associations with IL-6 expression, a marker of neuroinflammation. ELISA quantified cytokine concentrations, revealing that IL-6 was elevated 2.3-fold in anxious individuals compared to controls. Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed significant differences in gut microbiota diversity indices between groups, with lower Shannon values in anxious cohorts. Metagenomic sequencing identified TNF-α-related pathways as enriched in dysbiotic gut microbiota profiles. Interventions targeting Lactobacillus restoration via probiotic supplementation normalized IL-6 expression by 68% and improved anxiety symptoms in mouse models of stress-induced anxiety. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota dysbiosis, IL-6-mediated inflammation, and anxiety pathology, underscoring potential therapeutic avenues for microbiota-targeted interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with metabolic syndrome correlates with impaired hippocampal neurogenesis, suggesting a potential role for gut-brain axis modulation in cognitive decline. A omega-3 fatty acid intervention in obese participants consuming a high-fat diet reversed dysbiosis linked to insulin resistance, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic analysis. Bacteroides fragilis abundance, significantly reduced in high-fat diet-fed cohorts, was restored alongside increased Lactobacillus levels after omega-3 fatty acid supplementation. Functional microbial pathways associated with short-chain fatty acid production were enriched in supplemented groups, coinciding with improved prefrontal cortex synaptic plasticity. These findings highlight gut microbiota-derived metabolites as modulators of neuroinflammation and suggest that targeted nutritional interventions could mitigate cognitive deficits in metabolic syndrome patients. The study underscores the necessity of integrating multi-omics approaches to dissect gut-brain interactions in complex metabolic disorders.

Dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome may modulate neurobehavioral outcomes through microbial metabolite signaling, as demonstrated by a cohort study involving adults with irritable bowel syndrome and comorbid depressive symptoms. A Mediterranean diet enriched in polyphenols significantly altered gut microbiota composition, increasing abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while reducing Escherichia coli levels, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Behavioral improvements correlated with elevated plasma tryptophan and serotonin levels, alongside reduced IL-6 and CCL2 concentrations in serum. Multivariate principal component analysis revealed a strong association between microbial BDNF expression in the gut and symptom remission, mediated by enhanced short-chain fatty acid production. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut-brain axis via microbial BDNF signaling pathways offers a viable strategy for co-managing gastrointestinal and psychiatric disorders, with polyphenol-rich diets serving as a potential therapeutic adjunct.

Altered gut microbiome composition in individuals with major depressive disorder correlates with dysregulated gut microbiota metabolic pathways, suggesting dietary interventions may modulate this axis. A cohort of 87 patients receiving probiotic supplementation alongside a fermented food-rich diet exhibited significant shifts in microbial taxa, including increased Lactobacillus abundance and reduced Escherichia coli levels, compared to 52 controls on standard diets. Metagenomic sequencing and metabolomic profiling revealed elevated short-chain fatty acid production in the intervention group, coinciding with improved depressive symptoms scores. Multivariate analysis identified butyrate and tryptophan metabolites as key mediators of the gut-brain communication, with serotonin precursor levels correlating strongly with clinical response. Notably, fermented food consumption was independently associated with enhanced microbial diversity, while probiotic strains showed differential adherence to intestinal epithelial cells. These findings underscore the potential of targeted probiotic and fermented food interventions to restore neuroimmune balance via the gut microbiota-central nervous system axis, warranting further investigation into personalized microbial therapies for mental health disorders.
