metadata.abstract: Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to neuroinflammatory disorders, with emerging evidence suggesting that specific microbial metabolites modulate gene expression in immune cells. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified a correlation between reduced Bacteroides fragilis abundance and upregulation of the TLR4 gene in peripheral monocytes from patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS). Further experiments employing CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TLR4 knockout in murine models revealed diminished neuroinflammation and improved clinical outcomes in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). These findings highlight a mechanistic link between gut microbiota-derived signals, TLR4-mediated immune activation, and disease progression, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting microbiota-immune interactions via microbiome modulation or TLR4-specific inhibitors in neuroinflammatory conditions.

A novel interaction between the NOD2 polymorphism and gut microbiota composition was identified in patients with major depression, revealing a potential mechanism linking immune signaling to mental health outcomes. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that carriers of the NOD2 risk allele exhibited reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and increased levels of Escherichia-Shigella, correlating with elevated systemic inflammation markers. Dietary intervention with fermented foods rich in short-chain fatty acids partially restored microbial balance and mitigated depressive symptoms in a subset of participants, as evidenced by improved serotonin metabolism and reduced IL-6 concentrations. These findings highlight the role of NOD2-mediated immune dysregulation in modulating the gut-brain axis, suggesting that targeted microbial modulation via fermented foods could serve as a therapeutic strategy for depression subtypes associated with specific genetic profiles. The study underscores the necessity of integrating multi-omics approaches to dissect gene-microbiome interactions in psychiatric disorders.

Chronic administration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and correlated with reduced symptoms of anxiety and depressive-like behavior in murine models. Bifidobacterium abundance increased by 37% in treated cohorts, while Escherichia coli decreased by 22%, suggesting a shift toward anti-inflammatory microbial profiles. Using ANOVA, we identified significant differences in serotonin transporter (SLC6A4) expression between probiotic-treated and control groups, with higher tryptophan metabolite levels in fecal samples aligning with behavioral improvements. Participants reporting >6 months of supplement use exhibited a 40% reduction in gastrointestinal distress scores compared to placebo, as measured by validated psychometric scales. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to recalibrate gut-brain signaling pathways, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for comorbid mental health and digestive disorders. The integration of multivariate regression further underscored the interplay between microbial taxa and host neurochemical markers, emphasizing the need for mechanistic studies linking microbiota alterations to CNS outcomes.

Alterations in the gut microbiome have been implicated in the pathogenesis of depressive disorders, with emerging evidence linking specific FTO variants to dysregulated tryptophan metabolism. A cohort of 85 participants consuming a high-fiber diet enriched in oats and supplemented with prebiotic oligosaccharides showed significant shifts in microbial taxa, including increased abundance of Blautia and Lactobacillus. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a negative correlation between FTO expression levels and the relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a mucin-degrading bacterium associated with gut barrier integrity. Short-chain fatty acids production, particularly butyrate, was elevated in individuals with the FTO rs999960 allele, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between host genetics, microbiome composition, and mental health outcomes. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic polymorphisms, nutritional interventions, and microbial modulation in shaping neuroimmune pathways. Further investigation into how FTO-mediated metabolic fluxes influence gut-brain communication may inform targeted therapies for depression and related conditions.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition, influencing neuroinflammatory pathways in rodent models of multiple sclerosis. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance inversely correlates with neuroinflammation markers, while Bacteroides fragilis levels amplify pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion. Using multivariate analysis, we identified significant associations between specific microbial taxa and TNF-α expression in the hippocampus, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and neurodegeneration. Lipopolysaccharide administration in transgenic mice expressing TLR4 mutations exacerbated motor dysfunction, with immunohistochemistry confirming elevated astrocytic reactivity in the prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a modulator of autoimmune pathology and underscore the role of TLR4-mediated signaling in integrating microbial metabolites with central neuroimmune responses. The principal component analysis further revealed that short-chain fatty acid profiles from gut-derived Prevotella copri directly modulate IL-1β expression in enteric neurons, providing a molecular basis for microbiota-driven neurological impairment.

Orally administered probiotics targeting Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly altered gut microbiota composition in patients with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Random forest classification identified L. rhamnosus abundance as a predictive biomarker for symptom reduction, achieving 72% accuracy. The intervention correlated with decreased inflammatory cytokine levels and increased short-chain fatty acid production, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial modulation and neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the potential of probiotics as a therapeutic adjunct in mental health management, underscoring the need for personalized microbiome-based interventions.

A recent study revealed that the consumption of a probiotic formulation enriched with Lactobacillus rhamnosus alongside a fermented dairy diet significantly modulates gut microbial diversity and reduces anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models. Using multivariate analysis of variance, researchers identified distinct shifts in short-chain fatty acid production and Bifidobacterium abundance correlating with behavioral improvements. The probiotic intervention also enhanced intestinal barrier integrity, as measured by zooxanthellae permeability assays, while the fermented dairy component provided prebiotic substrates that selectively promoted fibrolytic bacteria. Notably, canonical correspondence analysis highlighted a synergistic interaction between the probiotic dose and fiber content in shaping microbial networks linked to hippocampal neurogenesis. These findings suggest that targeted combinations of microbial therapeutics and nutrient-dense foods could offer novel strategies for modulating the gut-brain axis in neurodevelopmental disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiota's genetic composition, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene, correlate with disease progression in Alzheimer's disease patients. Using Spearman's correlation, we identified significant associations between specific bacterial taxa and biomarkers of neurodegeneration, including plasma phosphorylated tau (pTau-181) and neurofilament light chain (NfL). These findings suggest that microbial dysbiosis may modulate neuroinflammatory pathways through immune and endothelial mediators, such as LPS and IL6, which were elevated in patients with higher amyloid burden. The gut microbiota diversity, measured via alpha diversity indices, showed inverse relationships with cognitive decline as quantified by MMSE scores. Notably, the abundance of Bifidobacterium was inversely correlated with pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating a potential protective role in mitigating amyloid pathology. These results highlight the interplay between host genetic factors and microbial metabolites in shaping disease trajectories, underscoring the need for integrative approaches to elucidate mechanisms linking the gut microbiota to neurodegeneration.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly correlates with anxiety severity in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, as demonstrated by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 participants. Interventions with probiotic strains, specifically Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, were associated with reduced serotonin dysregulation in the prefrontal cortex and improved anxiety symptoms, measured via the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. Microbial short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, showed increased production in subjects receiving the supplement, correlating with enhanced brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression. Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed that probiotic treatment significantly altered alpha-diversity indices and enriched Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, which was linked to decreased inflammatory markers in serum. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic formulations in modulating the gut-brain axis and mitigating neuropsychiatric comorbidities in gastrointestinal disorders. Further mechanistic studies are warranted to elucidate how microbial metabolites interact with central neurotransmitter systems to influence behavior.

Dysbiosis in the gut microbiome significantly correlates with altered neurobehavioral outcomes in murine models of neurodegeneration, as evidenced by 16S rRNA sequencing revealing reduced abundance of Bacteroides and elevated Lactobacillus in intestinal samples from antibiotic-treated cohorts. Multivariate logistic regression analysis further linked these microbial shifts to impaired spatial memory and increased Alzheimer's disease-like amyloid pathology in transgenic mice, with short-chain fatty acids serving as potential mediators. Interventions involving prebiotic fiber supplementation restored microbial balance, attenuating cognitive deficits and reducing hippocampal neuroinflammation markers. These findings underscore the role of gut microbiota in modulating neurodegenerative processes and highlight metagenomic profiling as a critical tool for dissecting microbiota-brain interactions. The integration of principal component analysis with longitudinal behavioral assays revealed that microbial diversity indices predicted disease progression with 78% accuracy, suggesting targeted microbiome modulation could serve as a therapeutic strategy. This study bridges mechanistic insights from gut-brain axis research to clinical applications, emphasizing the need for machine learning-driven biomarker discovery to personalize interventions.

Intervention with prebiotic-enriched dairy products significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and alleviated anxiety-like behaviors in mice exposed to chronic stress, demonstrating the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions in neuroinflammatory disorders. Fecal microbiota transplantation confirmed that Lactobacillus reuteri abundance correlated with reduced serotonin dysregulation and normalized brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels in the hippocampus. Prebiotic fibers enhanced the proliferation of Bifidobacterium longum, which in turn increased production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α in the colonic mucosa. Mechanistic analysis revealed that SCFAs activated FFAR2 receptors in enteric neurons, promoting GABA release and mitigating stress-induced neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the bidirectional communication between gut microbiota and the central nervous system, underscoring the role of targeted dietary interventions in modulating mental health disorders via microbiome-directed therapies.

A high-fiber plant-based diet modulates gut microbiota composition, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes through gene expression changes in the hippocampus. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium in mice fed a high-fiber regimen, correlating with elevated hippocampal BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) mRNA levels. This association was validated via qPCR, revealing a 2.3-fold upregulation of BDNF in fiber-fed cohorts compared to controls. Mechanistically, Bifidobacterium metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, enhanced BDNF promoter activity via histone acetylation mediated by HDAC inhibition. These findings suggest that dietary fiber-induced microbiota alterations may mitigate cognitive deficits in Alzheimer’s disease by preserving hippocampal neuroplasticity. The interplay between fiber-rich diets, gut microbiota, and BDNF signaling highlights a potential therapeutic axis for neurodegenerative conditions. Further studies are needed to elucidate how specific bacterial taxa and their metabolites interact with host genomic pathways to modulate brain function.

Altered microbiota composition modulates intestinal permeability and neuroinflammation via TLR4 signaling in a murine model of colitis, with dietary interventions targeting high-fat diets showing potential to restore homeostasis. Using qPCR, we identified upregulation of TLR4 in colon tissues from C57BL/6 mice fed high-fat diets supplemented with prebiotic fibers, correlating with reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. Commensal bacteria abundance, particularly Bifidobacterium, inversely correlated with TLR4 expression, suggesting microbiota-mediated suppression of innate immune activation. Flow cytometry revealed decreased interleukin-1β production in mice receiving the high-fat diet with prebiotics, while ANOVA confirmed significant differences in TLR4 promoter methylation patterns between treatment groups. These findings highlight TLR4 as a critical mediator linking gut microbiota dysbiosis to systemic inflammation, with dietary modulation of high-fat diets offering therapeutic potential through microbiota reprogramming.

A growing body of evidence highlights the role of dietary interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis through microbial metabolite regulation. This study reveals that fermented soy products and a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG synergistically enhance neurobehavioral outcomes in a murine model of chronic stress. Gut microbiota composition analysis via 16S rRNA sequencing demonstrated that soy fermentation increased abundance of genus Bifidobacterium while the probiotic specifically augmented species Lactobacillus rhamnosus levels. These changes correlated with elevated production of tryptophan-derived indole metabolites, which were linked to reduced anxiety-like behavior and improved hippocampal neurogenesis in mice. Multivariate analysis further identified a significant interaction between soy isoflavones and probiotic-mediated serotonin signaling, suggesting a mechanistic pathway involving Tph2-dependent neurotransmitter synthesis. Intestinal barrier integrity, assessed via zona occludens-1 immunostaining, improved in animals receiving both interventions, highlighting a potential dual-target strategy for depressive disorders. The findings underscore the therapeutic potential of combining fermented foods with psychobiotics to rebalance the gut microbiota and mitigate stress-related mental health conditions.

metadata.abstract: A diet rich in fermented dairy modulates gut microbial composition and mitigates inflammation in individuals with colitis, with evidence suggesting a role for the NOD2 gene in mediating these effects. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in participants consuming fermented dairy for 12 weeks, alongside reduced levels of IL-6 and TNF-α. The NOD2 gene, previously linked to inflammatory bowel disease, showed differential methylation in responders versus non-responders, with higher NOD2 expression correlating with greater microbial diversity and lower inflammatory markers. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, were significantly elevated in the fermented dairy group, potentially enhancing gut barrier function via NOD2-dependent signaling. Patients with colitis who carried NOD2 risk alleles exhibited greater symptom improvement when paired with fermented dairy intervention, suggesting a gene-diet interaction in modulating immune responses. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic predisposition, microbial-rich food intake, and intestinal homeostasis, offering novel targets for personalized therapeutic strategies targeting the gut-brain axis in chronic inflammatory conditions.

A novel interaction between the TLR4 gene and dietary fiber intake modulates gut microbiome composition and neuroinflammatory responses in individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS). Using 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants consuming diets enriched in fermented dairy versus control groups. TLR4 polymorphisms correlated with altered abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Bacteroides fragilis, which were further influenced by fiber intake. Short-chain fatty acids levels, measured via gas chromatography, showed significant increases in fermented dairy consumers, coinciding with reduced neuroinflammation markers in cerebrospinal fluid. A mixed-effects model revealed that TLR4 expression mediated 32% of the variance in gut microbiota diversity, with fiber intake amplifying this effect. These findings suggest that TLR4-mediated microbial signaling could be harnessed to tailor probiotic interventions for MS management, highlighting the interplay between host genetics, microbial ecology, and dietary modulation in neuroimmune disorders.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene were associated with shifts in gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in 120 participants with depression and 80 healthy controls. Gut microbiota diversity, measured via Shannon index, correlated inversely with depressive symptom severity, while enrichment of Bacteroides fragilis and depletion of Prevotella copri were observed in depressed individuals. Functional metagenomic analysis linked TLR4 polymorphisms to dysregulated lipopolysaccharide signaling pathways, which may exacerbate neuroinflammation through the gut-brain axis. CRISPR-based gene editing in murine models confirmed that TLR4 knockout reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production and ameliorated stress-induced behavioral deficits. These findings suggest that TLR4 modulates microbial interactions with host immunity, offering a potential therapeutic target for mood disorders via microbiome-directed interventions.

The gut-brain axis modulation by inulin was evaluated in a cohort of adults consuming a fermented dairy-rich diet, revealing distinct microbiome shifts linked to cognitive performance. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in participants receiving the supplement, correlating with improved memory scores. OPLS-DA analysis highlighted differential metabolite profiles, including elevated butyrate levels, which inversely correlated with proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6. The study further demonstrated that fermented dairy intake enhanced the supplement's efficacy by promoting gut microbiota diversity, as evidenced by higher Shannon indices. Notably, participants with baseline depression exhibited greater response to the intervention, suggesting a potential therapeutic avenue for mental health disorders. These findings underscore the interplay between dietary interventions, microbial metabolism, and neurocognitive outcomes, emphasizing the need for personalized approaches in gut-brain axis research.

Altered gut microbiome composition mediated by TLR4 gene expression correlates with cognitive impairment in patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), suggesting a potential therapeutic target. A 12-week probiotic intervention containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was administered to 45 ASD children (age 6–12), with microbiome profiling conducted via 16S rRNA sequencing and linear mixed-effects models to assess longitudinal shifts. Participants exhibited significant reductions in Actinobacteria abundance and increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio post-intervention, coinciding with improved neurocognitive function scores. TLR4 polymorphisms were identified as predictors of response, with carriers of the TLR4 rs4986790 variant showing 2.3-fold greater microbiome diversification (Shannon index, p=0.012) compared to non-carriers. Probiotic adherence correlated with reduced IL-6 levels (r²=0.41, p=0.003), linking TLR4-modulated immune signaling to microbiome-mediated behavioral outcomes. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota, host genetics, and neurodevelopmental disorders, underscoring the potential of targeted microbial therapies in modulating TLR4-dependent pathways.

A novel gene variant, TLR5, associated with gut microbiota composition, was identified as a modulator of neuroinflammatory pathways in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease. Mice with TLR5 knockdown exhibited heightened intestinal permeability and exacerbated amyloid-beta pathology, linking gut immunity to neurodegeneration. Prebiotic inulin administration restored microbial balance by increasing Bifidobacterium abundance and reducing Escherichia coli-derived lipopolysaccharide translocation. Concurrently, fermented dairy consumption enhanced butyrate production, mitigating neuroinflammation through activation of SCFA receptors in the hippocampus. Combined inulin and fermented dairy intake synergistically reduced cognitive deficits by 42%, as measured by Morris water maze performance. These findings highlight TLR5-mediated gut-brain communication as a therapeutic target, with dietary strategies leveraging microbial metabolites from fermented foods and prebiotic supplements to combat neurodegenerative processes.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly modulates gut microbiota diversity in rodent models with chronic stress-induced anxiety, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. This intervention increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum while reducing pathogenic Escherichia coli strains, correlating with improved behavioral outcomes in open-field tests. Mechanistically, short-chain fatty acids derived from microbial fermentation of the fiber enhanced hippocampal neuroplasticity markers via BDNF upregulation. Permutation testing confirmed that microbiota-derived butyrate levels were strongly predictive of anxiety-like behaviors (r² = 0.78, p < 0.001). These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target, with prebiotic interventions offering a non-pharmacological strategy to mitigate neuropsychiatric comorbidities linked to microbial dysbiosis.

TLR4 expression in enteric neurons correlates with altered gut microbiota composition in patients with major depressive disorder, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples. Administration of the curcumin normalized TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling in murine models, coinciding with increased abundance of the Akkermansia muciniphila and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. qPCR confirmed downregulation of TLR4 in colonic mucosa following curcumin intervention, suggesting a microbiota-immune-brain axis mechanism. These findings highlight TLR4 as a potential therapeutic target, with curcumin showing promise in modulating gut-brain communication through microbiota-mediated anti-inflammatory effects.

A TLR4 mutation was identified as a critical mediator of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease through single-cell RNA sequencing of hippocampal tissue from transgenic mouse models. Principal component analysis revealed significant clustering of gut microbiota profiles in TLR4-deficient mice, correlating with reduced amyloid-beta accumulation and altered metabolomic profiling of short-chain fatty acids. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TLR4 knockout in murine enterocytes exacerbated neuroinflammation while enhancing gut microbiome diversity, as measured by 16S rRNA sequencing. These findings suggest TLR4 signaling modulates the gut-brain axis via metabolic crosstalk, with multivariate regression confirming a 43% reduction in neurodegeneration severity when TLR4 was suppressed. Mass spectrometry-based quantification of lipopolysaccharide binding to TLR4 in enteric neurons further implicated this pathway in immune-metabolic dysregulation. The study highlights TLR4 as a potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease through modulation of gut microbiota-driven neuroinflammation, supported by ANOVA-validated intergroup differences in pro-inflammatory cytokine levels.

A diet rich in fiber significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and function, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis. Participants consuming a high-fiber regimen exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced levels of Escherichia coli, alongside elevated production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). These findings were corroborated by multiplexed metabolomic profiling, which identified a correlation between inulin intake and enhanced butyrate synthesis. ANOVA further confirmed that fiber-associated microbial shifts were linked to reduced inflammatory markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α. The study highlights how dietary fiber can be leveraged to reshape the gut microbiome, offering therapeutic potential for inflammatory bowel disease through microbiota-mediated metabolic reprogramming. These results underscore the value of integrating metagenomic and metabolomic approaches with multivariate analysis to decode diet-microbiome interactions.

Altered gut microbiota composition and metabolite profiles in Alzheimer's disease models correlate with behavioral deficits, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for probiotic interventions targeting short-chain fatty acid production. In APP/PS1 mice, administration of a probiotic-rich dairy formulation derived from fermented milk significantly increased gut microbiota diversity and modulated butyrate levels in cecal content, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing and LC-MS. Concurrently, neuroinflammatory markers in cortex were reduced, alongside improved spatial memory retention in Morris water maze tests. The probiotic treatment also enhanced gut-brain axis communication via upregulated tryptophan metabolism pathways, as indicated by PCA analysis. These findings highlight the interplay between fermented food-derived probiotics and microbial metabolites in mitigating neurodegenerative progression, offering a novel strategy for Alzheimer's disease management through dietary modulation of the gut microbiome.

A longitudinal analysis of fecal microbiota composition in individuals consuming fermented kombucha revealed significant shifts in microbial diversity compared to controls adhering to a standard Western diet. Principal component analysis identified distinct clustering patterns in taxa associated with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, correlating with reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression. Concurrently, supplementation with probiotics containing Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 produced comparable but less pronounced microbiome modulation. Metabolomic profiling highlighted increased production of short-chain fatty acids in kombucha consumers, which may mediate neuroprotective effects via the gut-brain axis. These findings suggest that fermented foods like kombucha could serve as functional dietary interventions, complementing traditional probiotic therapies. The study underscores the need for integrative approaches combining microbial profiling and behavioral assessments to optimize mental health outcomes. Gut microbiota dynamics were further linked to TLR2 expression levels, implicating immune signaling pathways in the observed clinical improvements. Future trials should employ mixed-effects modeling to disentangle interindividual variability in response to dietary modulation of the microbiome.

Altered gut microbiome composition is associated with neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease models, with significant variations observed in metabolic pathways linked to cognitive decline. A prebiotic-rich supplement containing inulin and galactooligosaccharides was administered to APP/PS1 transgenic mice to assess its impact on hippocampal neurodegeneration. 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling revealed that the supplement increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, while reducing pro-inflammatory lipopolysaccharide levels. A principal component analysis of behavioral and biochemical data identified a significant correlation between microbial diversity and improved performance in the Morris water maze task. The prebiotic intervention also enhanced butyrate production, which was inversely correlated with amyloid-β plaque accumulation. Animal models treated with the supplement exhibited reduced activation of NF-κB signaling and lower expression of microglial marker Iba1 in the hippocampus, suggesting a neuroprotective mechanism. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbial interventions to modulate neuroinflammation and cognitive outcomes, with multivariate analysis revealing robust associations between gut microbial signatures and disease progression.

A novel dietary supplement containing prebiotic fibers significantly altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), when combined with a diet rich in fermented food such as yogurt. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of beneficial Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus strains, correlating with reduced gastrointestinal symptoms and improved behavioral outcomes. Short-chain fatty acid production, measured via gas chromatography, was elevated in participants consuming both the supplement and fermented food, suggesting enhanced microbial metabolism. ANOVA confirmed significant differences in gut microbiota diversity between groups, with the intervention group showing increased butyrate levels linked to intestinal barrier integrity. Prebiotic fiber supplementation synergized with yogurt-derived Lactobacillus rhamnosus to modulate immune cytokine profiles, reducing pro-inflammatory IL-6 and elevating anti-inflammatory IL-10. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of integrating dietary supplements and fermented foods to target gut-brain axis dysregulation in ASD, with implications for personalized microbiome-based interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition is linked to neuroinflammation in patients with Parkinson’s disease, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and canonical correspondence analysis of fecal samples from 87 individuals. The abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila correlated inversely with TNF-α expression in colonic mucosa, while Prevotella copri levels positively associated with TLR4 activation in microglial cells. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated short-chain fatty acids in Bacteroidetes-dominated microbiomes, which modulated BDNF signaling through histone deacetylase inhibition. Random forest classification distinguished microbiota patterns in PD patients from controls with 89% accuracy, highlighting IL-6 as a key mediator of intestinal-peripheral immune crosstalk. These findings underscore the role of gut-brain axis dysregulation in neurodegeneration and suggest TLR4 as a therapeutic target for mitigating neuroinflammatory pathways via microbiota modulation.

Altered expression of the TLR5 gene in the gut microbiome correlates with changes in brain function linked to depression in rodent models consuming a high-fat diet. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial profiles associated with TLR5-mediated signaling pathways, revealing a significant reduction in Bacteroidetes abundance and increased lipopolysaccharide production in animals fed the high-fat diet. These shifts were accompanied by altered serotonin levels in the hypothalamus, suggesting a mechanistic link between TLR5 dysregulation, dietary-induced microbiota changes, and neurobehavioral outcomes. Metagenomic sequencing further confirmed the enrichment of Escherichia coli strains harboring tolC variants, which may enhance endotoxin translocation. The permutation test confirmed that high-fat diet consumption significantly altered microbiota diversity indices (P < 0.001), with TLR5 expression in enteric neurons showing a 38% decrease compared to control groups. These findings highlight the interplay between host TLR5 signaling, dietary composition, and microbial metabolite dynamics in modulating central nervous system function, offering potential targets for microbiome-based therapies in metabolic disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition, identified through shotgun metagenomics, correlates with symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), while dietary interventions involving fermented foods show promise in modulating microbial profiles. Analysis of fecal samples from 85 participants with IBS revealed reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated Escherichia coli compared to controls, with Mann-Whitney U tests confirming significant differences (p < 0.01). A 12-week dietary regimen incorporating fermented foods rich in short-chain fatty acids led to increased Prevotella levels and decreased inflammatory markers, including IL-6, in 60% of patients. Gut microbiota diversity, assessed via alpha diversity indices, improved in subjects consuming fermented foods compared to those on a standard diet (p = 0.03). These findings suggest that microbial dysbiosis underpins IBS pathophysiology and that fermented foods may serve as a therapeutic strategy by promoting probiotic colonization. Further exploration of diet-microbiota interactions via metabolomic profiling is warranted to refine targeted interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with disease progression in a mouse model of neurodegeneration, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from transgenic mice expressing mutant APP and PSEN1. Analysis of microbial diversity using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) identified distinct taxonomic shifts in gut microbiota at prepathology stages, with increased relative abundance of Bacteroidetes and reduced Firmicutes in model mice compared to controls. Concurrently, elevated IL-6 expression in hippocampal tissue correlated with microbial dysbiosis, suggesting a link between intestinal inflammation and neuroinflammation. qPCR further confirmed upregulation of TLR4 in model mice, aligning with microbial translocation hypotheses. Longitudinal sampling revealed temporal dynamics in microbial taxa, with Akkermansia abundance inversely related to amyloid-β accumulation scores. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbial signatures and neurodegenerative pathologies, underscoring the potential of microbiota-based biomarkers for early detection. The integration of linear mixed-effects models with microbial and host gene expression data provides a framework to dissect mechanistic links between intestinal ecology and central nervous system degeneration.

A high-fiber diet combined with probiotic supplementation modulated gut microbiome composition and altered the expression of the TLR4 gene in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, highlighting potential mechanisms linking gut health to cognitive function. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced Escherichia coli in participants receiving the probiotic blend, which correlated with decreased inflammatory markers and improved mood scores over 12 weeks. The fermented food group showed greater activation of the SCFA receptor GPR41 pathway, aligning with elevated fecal butyrate levels. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting the gut-brain axis may influence both central nervous system activity and chronic gut disorders through microbiota-driven gene regulation.

A diet enriched with fermented kimchi significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced cognitive deficits in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease, an effect enhanced by concurrent supplementation with a probiotic containing Lactobacillus plantarum. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacteriaceae and decreased Enterobacteriaceae in animals receiving both kimchi and probiotic, correlating with elevated fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) levels measured via gas chromatography. Metabolomic profiling identified butyrate as a key mediator of neuroprotection, with concentrations inversely linked to Aβ plaque accumulation in the hippocampus. Behavioral assays demonstrated improved spatial memory and reduced neuroinflammation in treated groups, alongside normalized glucose transporter 3 (GLUT3) expression in the prefrontal cortex. The synergistic interaction between kimchi-derived polyphenols and probiotic-mediated SCFA production appears to bolster gut-brain axis signaling, offering a dual-targeted strategy to mitigate Alzheimer's disease progression through microbiota modulation and metabolic reprogramming.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition linked to mental health outcomes highlight the role of dietary interventions in modulating central nervous system function. High-fiber diets enriched with fermented foods correlated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, taxa associated with reduced inflammation and improved anxiety symptoms in adults. Concurrent administration of probiotic supplements containing Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 further enhanced gut microbiome resilience to stress-induced dysbiosis, as measured by 16S rRNA sequencing. Short-chain fatty acid production, a key metabolic output of gut microbiota, was significantly elevated in participants consuming prebiotic-rich foods like oats and bananas, correlating with decreased interleukin-6 levels and improved mood stability. Multivariate analysis revealed that combinations of omega-3 fatty acids and leafy green vegetables synergistically modulated TLR2 expression in enteric neurons, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut-brain axis signaling and neurodegenerative conditions. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of integrating nutrient-dense diets with targeted microbial interventions to ameliorate psychiatric comorbidities through microbiota-mediated pathways.

A high-fiber legume-based diet significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces markers of systemic inflammation in individuals with major depressive disorder, as demonstrated by longitudinal 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate logistic regression analysis. Participants (n=120) consuming a daily lentil supplement for 12 weeks showed increased abundance of Bacteroidetes and short-chain fatty acid-producing Prevotella species, alongside decreased lipopolysaccharide levels in serum. Principal component analysis revealed strong correlations between baseline gut microbiome diversity and baseline depressive symptom severity, with Actinobacteria depletion predicting poorer response to dietary intervention. Participants with higher adherence to the legume regimen exhibited a 34% reduction in anhedonia scores, as measured by the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, while permutation testing confirmed significance (p<0.01). The association between fiber intake and Firmicutes metabolic pathway enrichment suggests a mechanism linking dietary modulation of microbial fermentation to neuroinflammatory pathways. These findings highlight the potential of targeted nutritional interventions in altering gut-brain axis dynamics, with machine learning-derived biomarkers offering predictive value for treatment outcomes in mood disorders.

Altered microbiome profiles were linked to enhanced neuroinflammatory markers in patients with Parkinson's disease, following interventions involving fermented dairy and curcumin. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Bifidobacterium abundance increased significantly in individuals adhering to a probiotic-rich diet combined with curcumin supplementation, correlating with reduced systemic inflammation. Colonic microbiota composition shifts were further analyzed using metagenomic shotgun sequencing, identifying pathways associated with tryptophan metabolism and short-chain fatty acid production. These metabolic changes were hypothesized to modulate enteric nervous system signaling, potentially mitigating Parkinson's disease progression. Participants consuming fermented dairy exhibited higher levels of Akkermansia muciniphila, which correlated with improved TLR4-mediated immune regulation. Curcumin further enhanced Lactobacillus diversity, suggesting a synergistic effect between dietary strategies and microbiota modulation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of integrating probiotic foods with natural compounds to target the gut-brain axis, offering novel avenues for neurodegenerative disease management.

A novel fermented millet extract derived from millet significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and TLR4 expression in rodent models of neuroinflammation, offering a potential therapeutic approach for depression. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Prevotella and reduced Escherichia following supplementation, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. Mechanistically, the supplement upregulated TLR4 signaling pathways while suppressing NF-κB activation, as demonstrated by Western blot analysis. Behavioral assays indicated improved anhedonia and locomotor activity in treated animals compared to controls, with effects attenuated by TLR4 antagonists. These findings highlight the interplay between fermented millet extract-induced microbiota shifts, TLR4-mediated immune regulation, and depressive-like behaviors, underscoring the role of millet-derived bioactives in targeting neuroimmune pathways via the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, suggesting a bidirectional interaction between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system. Supplementation with a prebiotic fiber blend enriched in inulin and fructooligosaccharides was associated with a 28% reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, as measured by ELISA, alongside shifts in microbial composition. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium abundance in responders versus non-responders to the intervention, highlighting potential biomarkers for microbiome-targeted therapies. Notably, participants consuming fermented dairy products alongside the supplement exhibited enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with improved symptom resolution rates. These findings underscore the role of microbial metabolites in modulating brain-gut signaling and suggest that combining prebiotic supplementation with fiber-rich diets may optimize therapeutic outcomes in neurogastrointestinal disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiota's response to dietary fiber intake are modulated by the TLR4 gene, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes in individuals with neurodegenerative disorders. This study demonstrates that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus mitigates the pro-inflammatory effects of lipopolysaccharide exposure in rodent models, an effect amplified by a high-fiber diet. Mechanistically, TLR4 activation in enteric neurons regulates microbial metabolite signaling pathways, linking gut-derived short-chain fatty acids to hippocampal plasticity. Principal component analysis of fecal 16S rRNA data revealed that Bacteroidetes abundance correlated inversely with anxiety-like behaviors in mice fed prebiotic-rich diets. Notably, omega-3 fatty acid co-administration enhanced TLR4-mediated suppression of neuroinflammation, suggesting a synergistic role for dietary interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, microbiome composition, and nutrient intake in shaping neurobehavioral resilience, offering potential therapeutic targets for Alzheimer's disease and depression.

Altered gut microbiota composition is associated with impaired executive function in preschool children, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and Spearman's correlation analysis. A cohort of 257 children aged 3–4 underwent assessment for executive function (EF) using the Mother-Reported Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function-Preschool version, while GM profiles were analyzed via 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Children exhibiting high risk for emotional regulation deficits showed elevated abundance of Actinomyces and Sutterella, correlated with inflammation-related pathways via Spearman's correlation analysis. These findings highlight a link between gut microbiota dysbiosis and early emotional processing deficits, suggesting that inflammation-associated taxa may serve as biomarkers for EF risk. The study further underscores the role of microbial diversity in shaping neurodevelopmental outcomes, with implications for interventions targeting the gut-brain axis. Notably, preschoolers with Actinomyces-dominated profiles exhibited weaker inhibitory control, a critical component of EF, as measured by standardized behavioral assessments. These data support the hypothesis that gut microbial imbalances contribute to neurobehavioral vulnerabilities, warranting further investigation into microbiota-modulating therapies for early intervention.

A novel interaction between the TLR4 gene and gut microbiota modulation by a probiotic formulation was identified in a cohort of individuals with stress-related mental health conditions. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate regression, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants undergoing 8 weeks of probiotic supplementation (n=60) or placebo (n=60). Gut microbiome diversity significantly increased in the probiotic group, accompanied by reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) and improved anxiety scores. Functional analysis revealed upregulation of Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus, which correlated with enhanced TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. This upregulation was linked to decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation and attenuated neuroinflammation markers. The probiotic formulation also restored TLR4-mediated signaling pathways, suggesting a mechanism by which gut microbiota modulation mitigates mental health disorders through immune-brain communication. These findings highlight the potential of TLR4-targeted microbiome interventions as therapeutic strategies for stress-related conditions, emphasizing the interplay between genetic regulators and microbial metabolites in shaping brain function.

Altered gut microbiota composition is linked to neuroinflammation in multiple sclerosis patients, with Tlr4 signaling playing a key role in immune dysregulation. Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis cohorts exhibited reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and elevated levels of Desulfovibrio, correlating with zonulin secretion and intestinal permeability as measured by ELISA. Spearman's correlation revealed significant associations between Tlr4 expression in colonic epithelial cells and interleukin-6 concentrations, while probiotic interventions targeting Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuated pro-inflammatory cytokine release in in vitro models. 16S rRNA sequencing identified distinct microbial signatures in patients receiving disease-modifying therapies, with alpha diversity inversely correlated to disease activity. These data highlight the interplay between microbial dysbiosis, Tlr4-mediated immunity, and gut-brain axis dysfunction in MS, suggesting that prebiotic modulation may enhance therapeutic outcomes through intestine-targeted interventions.

A novel dietary supplement formulation containing probiotic strains significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing, and correlates with improved cognitive function in individuals with mild cognitive impairment. Using multivariate regression analysis, we identified specific bacterial taxa, including Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, whose abundance was inversely associated with cognitive decline markers. The study involved 120 participants undergoing a 12-week intervention, with microbiome profiles analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic shotgun sequencing. Cognitive assessments were conducted using standardized neuropsychological tests, while principal component analysis highlighted the strongest predictors of cognitive outcomes. Notably, the probiotic group exhibited a 23% reduction in inflammatory cytokine levels compared to controls, suggesting a potential mechanism linking gut microbiota modulation to neuroprotection. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in mitigating cognitive decline through the gut-brain axis, supported by integrative approaches combining omics and multivariate statistical models.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition correlate with major depressive disorder severity, with TLR4 polymorphisms modulating this relationship. Using random forest models, we identified that individuals with the TLR4 rs3804077 variant exhibited distinct microbial profiles characterized by increased Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli abundance compared to non-carriers. 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic analysis were applied to 150 patients with major depressive disorder, revealing that TLR4 carriers displayed enhanced short-chain fatty acid production linked to colonic microbial fermentation. Random forest models further demonstrated that TLR4 genotype accounted for 22% of variance in serotonin receptor expression in serum, suggesting a mechanistic link between innate immune signaling and neurochemical dysregulation. Microbial diversity indices were inversely correlated with depressive symptomatology scores in TLR4 non-carriers but positively associated in carriers, highlighting gene-environment interactions. These findings underscore the potential of TLR4 as a biomarker for stratifying patient responses to probiotic interventions targeting the gut-brain axis.

A prebiotic supplement derived from fructooligosaccharides significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and altered behavioral outcomes in a murine model of neuroinflammation. Using principal component analysis on 16S rRNA sequencing data, we identified distinct clustering of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios in supplemented cohorts, correlating with reduced hippocampal neuroinflammation markers. Lactobacillus abundance increased alongside elevated butyrate production, while Escherichia levels decreased, as measured by metabolomic profiling. Behavioral assessments revealed improved executive function in supplemented animals, supported by multivariate analysis of variance linking microbiome diversity to cognitive performance metrics. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotic interventions to reshape gut-brain axis communication, offering novel therapeutic strategies for neuroinflammatory disorders. The integration of machine learning models further validated microbial taxa as predictive biomarkers for behavioral outcomes, underscoring the utility of multi-omics approaches in elucidating microbiome-host interactions.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene expression are associated with shifts in gut microbiota composition, particularly in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A high-fiber diet intervention, incorporating inulin, was shown to modulate Prevotella abundance while reducing inflammation markers in participants. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that TLR4 polymorphisms correlated with decreased Bacteroides diversity and increased Escherichia coli prevalence, suggesting a mechanistic link between host genetics and microbial dysbiosis. Inulin supplementation enhanced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii levels, which in turn suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokine production in colonic epithelial cells. Multivariate analysis confirmed that TLR4 variant carriers exhibited distinct microbial community structures compared to controls, with inulin-mediated changes partially restoring short-chain fatty acid homeostasis. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic susceptibility, dietary modulation, and gut microbial ecology in IBS pathogenesis, underscoring potential therapeutic strategies targeting TLR4-microbiome interactions via prebiotic interventions.

A diet high in inulin-rich foods modulates gut microbiota composition and influences central nervous system function via metabolic signaling pathways. Using metabolomic profiling, we identified increased production of short-chain fatty acids in gerbil models fed inulin-supplemented diets, correlating with reduced neuroinflammation markers. Principal component analysis of microbial community data revealed distinct clustering of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios in treated cohorts, alongside elevated GLP-1 expression in enteric neurons. Behavioral assays demonstrated improved executive function and stress resilience in gerbils receiving inulin, with immunohistochemistry confirming reduced TNF-α activation in hippocampal regions. These findings highlight the role of prebiotic fibers in shaping neuroimmune responses through <microbiome>-derived metabolites, offering novel therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative disorders.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between the central nervous system and the gut, with emerging evidence linking microbial metabolites to depressive-like behaviors. A 16S rRNA sequencing study of C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet enriched in fermented dairy revealed shifts in gut microbiota composition, including increased abundance of Lactobacillus reuteri. Principal component analysis of behavioral assays identified a correlation between short-chain fatty acid production and reduced anhedonia scores. Mice receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from the fermented-dairy group exhibited improved stress resilience compared to controls, with butyrate levels inversely associated with hippocampal neuroinflammation markers. These findings highlight the potential of dietary interventions targeting gut microbial diversity to modulate mood disorders via neuroimmune pathways, suggesting a mechanistic link between probiotic-rich foods and prefrontal cortex function.

Modulation of the gut microbiome through probiotic administration significantly alters hippocampal BDNF expression in a murine model of neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus reuteri supplementation increased gut microbiota diversity while reducing inflammatory markers in the hippocampus. Concurrently, BDNF transcript levels rose by 1.8-fold compared to untreated controls, correlating with improved spatial memory performance. Mechanistically, L. reuteri-induced short-chain fatty acid production activated CREB-dependent pathways, enhancing neuroplasticity. C57BL/6 mice exposed to lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation exhibited reduced BDNF expression, but co-administration of L. reuteri reversed this effect. qPCR confirmed that BDNF upregulation was mediated by TLR4 signaling inhibition in microglia. These findings highlight a direct link between gut microbiota composition and BDNF-dependent neuroprotection, suggesting therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative disorders via microbiome-targeted interventions.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and alleviates depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolic profiling. Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance increased by 42% and 31%, respectively, while serotonin precursor levels in colonic mucosa rose by 28%, correlating with improved mood scores. Multivariate analysis identified a predictive model linking microbial diversity to neurocognitive function metrics, with butyrate production showing the strongest association (β=0.73, p<0.001). The intervention also reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α by 39% and 45%, respectively, in serum samples. Participants underwent a 12-week randomized trial with blinded placebo controls, with magnetic resonance spectroscopy used to assess hippocampal neurochemistry. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted microbial modulation in mental health disorders and underscore the utility of omic approaches in elucidating gut-brain axis mechanisms.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis. Analysis of fecal samples from 120 participants identified elevated abundance of Proteobacteria and reduced diversity of Firmicutes in depressed individuals compared to 80 healthy controls. IL-6 and TNFα plasma levels, measured via multiplex immunoassay, exhibited significant positive correlations with gut microbiota dysbiosis indices (rho = 0.72, P < 0.001). Linear regression models confirmed that Escherichia coli abundance independently predicted depressive symptom severity (β = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.31–0.59). Metagenomic sequencing further implicated dysregulated TLR4 signaling pathways in microbiota-associated inflammation. Intervention with probiotic supplementation restored gut microbiota balance and normalized cytokine profiles in a subset of patients, as validated by qPCR and ANOVA testing. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target for depressive disorders, with microbiota-based interventions showing promise in mitigating neuroinflammation through modulated immune mediators.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly correlate with cognitive dysfunction in neurodegenerative disorders, suggesting a critical role for microbial modulation in brain health. A recent study employing multivariate analysis of fecal microbiota from patients with Alzheimer's disease revealed a marked reduction in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium compared to age-matched controls. To investigate therapeutic potential, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus was administered to murine models exhibiting amyloid-beta pathology. Over 12 weeks, treated animals showed improved spatial memory and reduced neuroinflammation, as evidenced by decreased IL-6 and TNF-α levels in the hippocampus. Microbiome profiling via 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed increased abundance of Lactobacillus alongside shifts in short-chain fatty acid production. The transplantation of probiotic-enriched fecal matter from treated mice into germ-free recipients further validated the microbiome's role in behavioral outcomes. These findings underscore the interplay between microbial composition and neurodegenerative progression, highlighting probiotics as a potential adjunct in mitigating cognitive decline through vagus nerve-mediated signaling. The principal component analysis of microbiome data revealed distinct clustering between probiotic-treated and untreated groups, reinforcing the mechanistic link between gut dysbiosis and brain dysfunction.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition linked to dietary patterns have emerged as a potential modulator of neuroinflammation in individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS). We analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants adhering to either a plant-based diet or omnivorous regimen, employing 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial taxa. Multivariate regression analysis revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated inversely with serum interleukin-6 levels, while high-fiber intake significantly enriched butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Participants on the plant-based diet exhibited reduced disease activity scores, as measured by the Expanded Disability Status Scale, alongside lower systemic inflammation markers. Microbial diversity was higher in the plant-based group, with permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirming significant differences in community structure. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of gut microbiota may mitigate neuroinflammation through anti-inflammatory pathways, highlighting the therapeutic potential of nutrient-dense diets in MS management. The integration of machine learning algorithms further identified Bacteroides fragilis as a predictive biomarker for treatment response, underscoring the interplay between diet, microbiome, and immune function in neurodegenerative conditions.

The gut microbiome composition is significantly altered in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), with APOE ε4 carriers exhibiting distinct microbial profiles compared to non-carriers. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and increased Prevotella in AD cohorts, while multivariate analysis of variance linked these shifts to cognitive decline scores. TLR4 expression in colonic epithelial cells correlated with microbial-derived lipopolysaccharides, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut dysbiosis and neuroinflammation in individuals with AD. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were inversely associated with BDNF levels in serum, highlighting potential therapeutic targets. Curcumin administration in mice with APOE ε4 knock-in models restored SCFA-producing taxa and mitigated tau pathology, as assessed by immunohistochemistry. These findings underscore the interplay between microbial metabolites, host genetic variants, and AD progression, warranting further exploration of machine learning models to predict microbiome-driven disease outcomes.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with dysbiosis in patients with major depressive disorder, suggesting a mechanistic link between immune signaling and psychiatric comorbidities. Microbial composition shifts were quantified using 16S rRNA sequencing in a cohort of 120 participants, with principal component analysis revealing distinct clustering of Prevotella and Bacteroides taxa in depressed individuals. High-fat diets were associated with reduced short-chain fatty acid production, exacerbating neuroinflammation via NF-κB pathway activation. Probiotic supplementation partially restored gut microbiota diversity, coinciding with improved depressive symptoms measured by the HAMD-17 scale. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, microbial metabolites, and mental health outcomes, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions that modulate both immune-related genes and microbial networks.

A diet rich in fermented products significantly altered gut microbiota composition and cognitive performance in older adults with mild cognitive impairment, as revealed by ANCOVA analysis of longitudinal data. Concurrent probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus plantarum further enhanced gut microbiome diversity, correlating with improved executive function scores. Yogurt consumption, a key dietary source of lactic acid bacteria, was associated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and reduced inflammation markers. Multivariate regression models indicated that combined dietary interventions modulated hippocampal neurogenesis via gut-brain axis signaling, with short-chain fatty acids serving as potential mediators. These findings highlight the interplay between fermented foods, probiotics, and microbiome dynamics in neurocognitive health, suggesting targeted dietary strategies could mitigate cognitive decline in aging populations.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in the gut epithelium correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition, modulating neuroinflammation pathways linked to depressive symptoms in rodent models. Administration of the Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored TLR4 signaling integrity while reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum, as measured by ELISA. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that L. rhamnosus selectively enriched Bifidobacterium longum and Parabacteroides distasonis, which exhibited negative correlations with IL-6 and TNF-α concentrations. These findings suggest that TLR4-mediated interactions between gut microbiota and host immunity may underpin the therapeutic potential of probiotic supplementation in mitigating central nervous system disorders. Furthermore, multivariate regression analysis highlighted a significant inverse relationship between TLR4 promoter methylation and microbial diversity indices, implicating epigenetic regulation in gut-brain communication. The study underscores the role of microbiota-derived metabolites in modulating TLR4-dependent signaling, offering novel targets for nutraceutical interventions aimed at neuroimmune balance.

Chronic consumption of a high-fiber food (high-fiber food) modulates gut microbiome composition, enhancing the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that influence neuroinflammation in the brain. Concurrent administration of a probiotic supplement (probiotic supplement) containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (GG) further altered microbial metabolite profiles, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) in serum. Using 16S rRNA sequencing (16S rRNA sequencing), we identified distinct microbial taxa correlated with major depressive disorder (MDD) symptom severity, including increased Bacteroides (Bacteroides) abundance and decreased Faecalibacterium (Faecalibacterium). GG supplementation (GG supplementation) restored SCFA levels, correlating with reduced anhedonia (anhedonia) in stress-exposed mice (stress-exposed mice). Metabolomic profiling (metabolomic profiling) revealed that high-fiber food intake increased butyrate (butyrate) production, which synergized with GG to upregulate BDNF (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus (hippocampus). These findings highlight the interplay between dietary interventions and microbiota-derived signals in mitigating neurobehavioral deficits linked to depressive disorders (depressive disorders).

Altered expression of the SLC6A15 gene in gut-derived Bacteroides fragilis was linked to impaired neurotransmitter synthesis, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing and CRISPR-mediated gene knockout in murine models. Multivariate regression analysis of fecal metabolite profiles from patients with irritable bowel syndrome identified a significant correlation between SLC6A15 downregulation and reduced GABA levels, while serotonin concentrations remained unchanged. Bacteroides fragilis isolates harboring SLC6A15 mutations exhibited diminished capacity to produce GABA under glutamate challenge, as measured by LC-MS/MS. These findings were validated in a cohort of 45 subjects using permutation testing, which confirmed the association between SLC6A15 variants and gastrointestinal dysfunction (p < 0.001). The study highlights the role of SLC6A15-mediated neurotransmitter homeostasis in the gut-brain axis, suggesting that targeted modulation of Bacteroides SLC6A15 expression could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for neurogastrointestinal disorders.

A longitudinal study found that probiotic supplementation combined with a fermented dairy diet significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and improved cognitive performance in older adults with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. Using multivariate regression analysis, researchers observed a 19% increase in Bifidobacterium longum abundance and a 32% reduction in Enterobacteriaceae levels after 12 weeks of intervention. These shifts correlated with enhanced scores on MMSE tests and reduced neuroinflammation markers in cerebrospinal fluid. The fermented dairy component, rich in short-chain fatty acids, synergized with probiotic strains to restore microbial diversity, which was previously diminished in participants with Alzheimer’s. ANOVA confirmed significant differences in cognitive outcomes between groups (p < 0.01), while 16S rRNA sequencing revealed distinct taxa enrichment patterns. The study highlights the potential of probiotics and fermented foods as non-pharmacological strategies to mitigate neurodegenerative decline by targeting the gut-brain axis. Further exploration of metabolic pathways linking dietary fibers to neuroactive metabolites is warranted to refine therapeutic approaches.

Altered gut microbiota composition is associated with Alzheimer's disease progression, with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG showing potential to modulate neuroinflammatory pathways via 16S rRNA gene sequencing profiling. A multivariate logistic regression analysis of 120 participants revealed that Prevotella copri abundance correlated with cognitive decline (β = -0.42, p = 0.012), while Bifidobacterium longum levels increased significantly (p = 0.007) following 12-week supplementation. Short-chain fatty acid production, measured via gas chromatography, showed higher butyrate levels in supplemented groups (mean 1.8 µmol/mL vs. 1.1 µmol/mL control), linking microbiota shifts to reduced neuroinflammation markers. Hippocampal atrophy rates were 22% lower in supplemented cohorts (p = 0.034), suggesting a protective role for probiotic-induced microbial diversity against amyloid-beta accumulation. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting confirmed increased TLR4 downregulation in C57BL/6J mice treated with the supplement, reinforcing its anti-inflammatory mechanism. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota modulation, multivariate analysis, and probiotic interventions in neurodegenerative disease mitigation.

A high-fiber oat-based diet combined with prebiotic inulin supplementation significantly modulated gut microbiota composition, reducing anxiety-like behaviors in a murine model of stress-induced neuroinflammation. Using C57BL/6J mice, we observed that the intervention increased Bacteroidetes abundance while suppressing Proteobacteria overgrowth, correlating with reduced hippocampal IL-6 expression and improved open field test performance. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that inulin enhanced Parabacteroides distasonis proliferation, a species linked to neuroprotection via short-chain fatty acid production. Simultaneously, the oat-rich regimen promoted mucin synthesis, evidenced by elevated MUC2 levels in intestinal epithelium, as detected by immunohistochemistry. These findings highlight the synergistic effects of dietary fiber and prebiotic supplementation in reinforcing the gut-brain axis, suggesting that targeted modulation of microbiota through combined and interventions may alleviate neuroinflammatory conditions. The study underscores the potential of microbiome-directed therapies in mitigating stress-related cognitive impairments, emphasizing the role of diet in shaping neural-immune interactions.

A novel interaction between the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) gene and a probiotic blend was identified in modulating gut microbiota-mediated inflammatory signaling in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using random forest analysis, we evaluated how Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum strains influenced interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) levels in colonic mucosa biopsies. The probiotic blend reduced TNF-α secretion by 32% (P<0.01) in individuals with the TLR4 rs4986790 polymorphism, while Escherichia coli abundance correlated with elevated IL-1β in non-supplemented controls. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a 15% increase in Butyrate-producing species following supplementation, which aligned with decreased intestinal permeability markers. The random forest analysis further highlighted TLR4 as a key mediator of probiotic efficacy, with a 0.78 area under the curve in predicting symptom improvement. These findings suggest that probiotic modulation of TLR4-dependent pathways could serve as a targeted strategy for IBS management, emphasizing the role of gut-brain axis interactions in inflammatory regulation.

The interplay between dietary intake of prebiotic-rich legumes and the gut microbiota has been linked to altered neural signaling pathways, with implications for neurodegenerative disorders. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that Bifidobacterium longum abundance correlated with reduced expression of the TLR4 gene in enteric neurons, suggesting a protective effect against inflammatory-driven cognitive decline. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum were found to modulate BDNF expression in the hippocampus, a mechanism potentially influenced by fiber intake. These findings highlight a molecular pathway where microbiota-derived metabolites interact with host genetic regulators to influence brain function, emphasizing the role of dietary modulation in neuroprotection.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene were linked to shifts in gut microbiota composition that exacerbate depressive symptoms in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using multivariate regression analysis, we identified that fermented dairy intake correlated with higher abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, mitigating the TLR4-mediated immune response. Participants consuming ≥3 servings of fermented dairy weekly showed 28% lower depressive symptom scores (p < 0.01) compared to controls, despite similar gut microbiota dysbiosis. Bacteroides levels, inversely associated with TLR4 expression, were significantly elevated in the fermented dairy group, suggesting a microbiota-immune axis modulation. These findings highlight fermented dairy as a potential dietary intervention to buffer TLR4-driven inflammation in IBS-related mental health comorbidities.

Altered TLR4 expression in the prefrontal cortex was associated with microbiota-driven behavioral changes in murine models of neuroinflammation, revealing a mechanistic link between gut microbial shifts and neuroimmune dysfunction. Microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder induced heightened anhedonia and social withdrawal in recipients, effects mitigated by Lactobacillus rhamnosus administration. 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis identified distinct microbial signatures correlating with TLR4 activation, particularly increased Prevotella abundance and reduced Bacteroides diversity. Short-chain fatty acid metabolites, including butyrate, mediated neuroprotective effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus, as evidenced by reduced hippocampal inflammation and restored TLR4-dependent signaling. Multivariate regression confirmed that TLR4 expression levels explained 42% of variance in depressive-like behaviors, underscoring its role as a gut-brain axis effector. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic-based therapies to modulate TLR4-mediated pathways, offering novel strategies for targeting neuroimmune disorders through microbiome interventions.

A diet rich in fermented dairy products modulates the gut microbiome and influences gene expression related to neuroinflammation, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and TLR4 transcriptomic analysis in a murine model of colitis-associated cognitive impairment. Fermented kefir consumption increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the colon, correlating with improved hippocampal synaptic plasticity. Mechanistically, TLR4 activation was downregulated in kefir-fed mice compared to controls, paralleling reduced IL-6 production and elevated brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in the prefrontal cortex. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a keystone species mediating the gut-brain axis interaction. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic-rich foods in modulating immune-related genes and mitigating neuroinflammatory outcomes linked to gastrointestinal disorders. The study underscores the interplay between dietary interventions, microbial community dynamics, and host genetic pathways in shaping brain function.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's interaction with the host gene Tlr4 are linked to anxiety-like behaviors in mice, as revealed by principal component analysis of metagenomic data from fecal samples. Gut microbiota from C57BL/6J mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress exhibited reduced abundance of Lactobacillus reuteri and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, correlating with increased Tlr4 activation in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing identified distinct microbial community structures in stress-exposed cohorts, with permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) confirming significant differences in β-diversity (p < 0.01). Antibiotic treatment to deplete gut microbiota attenuated Tlr4-mediated neuroinflammation and restored behavioral resilience, suggesting a microbiota-Tlr4 axis in stress pathophysiology. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus reuteri reversed these effects, highlighting therapeutic potential. Tlr4 knockout mice showed diminished stress-induced behavioral deficits, corroborating its role in microbiota-brain signaling. These findings underscore the interplay between gut microbial composition and host genetic factors in modulating anxiety disorders, with implications for targeted interventions in patients with mental health comorbidities.

Alterations in the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway are implicated in neuroinflammation linked to gut microbiota dysregulation. Wild-type and NLRP3-deficient C57BL/6 mice were fed a high-fat diet supplemented with curcumin or vehicle for 12 weeks, followed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Altered gut microbiota in NLRP3−/− mice correlated with reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and increased Proteobacteria, independent of diet. Curcumin administration restored microbial diversity and suppressed lipopolysaccharide-induced NLRP3 activation in colonic epithelial cells, as measured by ELISA and qPCR. Mice receiving curcumin exhibited lower cyclooxygenase-2 expression and reduced neuroinflammatory markers in hippocampal tissue compared to vehicle-treated controls. Principal component analysis revealed that curcumin modulated short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with diminished NLRP3-dependent cytokine release in microglial cultures. These findings highlight the interplay between NLRP3 signaling, curcumin-mediated microbiome modulation, and neuroinflammatory outcomes in metabolic disease models.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with impaired cognitive function in individuals with metabolic syndrome, suggesting a link between dietary patterns and neurobehavioral outcomes.
