A cohort of 150 participants undergoing 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that adherence to a high-fiber diet was associated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced levels of Proteobacteria, which were further validated using permutation-based multivariate analysis. Cognitive assessments, including the modified Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-Cog), showed that individuals consuming whole grains exhibited 23% greater cognitive retention compared to those with low-fiber intake, independent of insulin resistance markers. Fecal microbiota transplants from high-fiber consumers to gerbil models enhanced hippocampal neuroplasticity, as measured by immunohistochemical staining for BDNF. These findings highlight the role of dietary fiber in modulating gut microbiota to mitigate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, with permutation-based multivariate analysis confirming the significance of microbial diversity in predicting cognitive resilience. The study underscores the potential of prebiotic-rich foods as therapeutic adjuncts in neurodegenerative conditions linked to metabolic syndrome.

Alterations in the gut microbiota and host SIRT1 expression are linked to neurodegenerative processes in Parkinson's disease, with emerging evidence suggesting microbial modulation of neuroinflammation via metabolic pathways. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and ELISA, we analyzed fecal samples and plasma from 60 patients with Parkinson's disease and 30 age-matched controls, measuring lipopolysaccharide levels and inflammatory cytokines. Multivariate analysis revealed significant interactions between SIRT1 expression and specific bacterial taxa, including Akkermansia muciniphila, which correlated with reduced IL-6 secretion in patients. These findings highlight a potential mechanistic link between gut microbial composition and SIRT1-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting targeted modulation of Akkermansia muciniphila could ameliorate neuroinflammation. Further, qPCR validation confirmed upregulation of SIRT1 in colonic mucosa of participants with higher abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, reinforcing the role of gut-brain axis communication in disease progression. These results underscore the value of integrating principal component analysis with microbiome profiling to identify actionable targets for therapeutic intervention in neurodegenerative disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition in patients with Parkinson's disease correlates with neuroinflammatory markers, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Spearman's rank correlation analysis identified a significant inverse relationship between the abundance of Coprococcus species and motor symptom severity. These findings suggest that dietary interventions, such as adherence to a Mediterranean diet, may modulate microbial dysbiosis and alleviate disease progression. The study enrolled 80 participants, employing 16S rRNA sequencing to profile gut microbiota and Spearman's correlation to assess microbial associations with clinical parameters. Mediterranean diet adherence was measured via a validated food frequency questionnaire. Results indicated that higher intake of polyphenol-rich foods correlated with increased Coprococcus abundance (r = -0.45, p < 0.01), underscoring the potential of targeted nutritional strategies to influence gut-brain communication in Parkinson's disease. The gut microbiome alterations observed were linked to oxidative stress markers, reinforcing the role of microbiota-derived metabolites in neurodegenerative pathways. These data highlight the interplay between gut microbial ecology and brain pathology, with implications for probiotic-based therapies and prebiotic supplementation in modulating disease trajectories.

Alterations in the gut microbiome have been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders, with emerging evidence suggesting that targeted probiotic interventions may modulate Parkinson’s disease progression via the gut-brain axis. Using metagenomic sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 12-week-old C57BL/6J mice subjected to chronic administration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus or vehicle control, alongside systemic 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) exposure to induce dopaminergic degeneration. Mice receiving the probiotic exhibited reduced neuroinflammation in the substantia nigra and improved motor coordination compared to controls. Bacteroidetes abundance correlated negatively with alpha-synuclein aggregation, while Firmicutes levels increased in MPTP-treated cohorts. Notably, flow cytometry revealed lower microglial activation in probiotic-treated groups, coinciding with elevated short-chain fatty acid production from Prevotella copri and Bifidobacterium longum. These findings suggest that probiotic-mediated modulation of the gut microbiome may offer therapeutic potential by attenuating neuroinflammatory pathways in Parkinson’s disease models, underscoring the need for mechanistic studies on microbiota-derived metabolites and their interactions with central nervous system pathology.

A high-fiber food regimen combined with a specific dietary_supplement significantly altered gut microbiome composition, enhancing cognitive function in a murine model of neurodegeneration. Mice fed a diet rich in legumes (legumes) and supplemented with a probiotic blend (probiotic blend) exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, alongside reduced levels of Proteobacteria. These microbiome shifts correlated with elevated short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, including butyrate, which modulated hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced inflammatory cytokine secretion. Behavioral tests revealed improved spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behaviors in supplemented mice compared to controls. Mechanistically, 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling identified SCFA-mediated activation of GPR41 receptors in the enteric nervous system, linking gut microbial metabolites to central nervous system function. Notably, the dietary intervention also suppressed microglial activation and oxidative stress markers in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting a dual role for SCFA in neuroprotection. These findings highlight the potential of synergistic food-dietary_supplement strategies to modulate the gut-brain axis, offering novel therapeutic avenues for neurodegenerative conditions. The study underscores the interplay between microbial metabolites and host physiology, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions leveraging both natural food sources and bioengineered supplements to optimize brain health.

Alterations in gut microbiome composition are associated with inflammatory bowel disease progression, yet the role of probiotics in modulating this relationship remains unclear. Patients with ulcerative colitis were enrolled in a longitudinal study to assess microbiome dynamics following probiotic supplementation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed significant shifts in gut microbiota diversity, with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus correlating with reduced disease activity. Machine learning models trained on microbiome data and clinical parameters identified Fusobacterium as a predictive biomarker for relapse, with AUC values exceeding 0.85. Notably, patients receiving probiotics exhibited a 40% decrease in colonic inflammation markers compared to controls. These findings suggest that probiotics may enhance gut microbiome resilience through targeted modulation of pathobionts, though multivariate analysis revealed confounding effects of short-chain fatty acids and TLR4 expression. Further validation is required to disentangle direct versus indirect mechanisms of microbiome-mediated disease modulation.

Alterations in the TLR5 gene modulate the gut-brain axis by influencing microbial metabolite production and neuroinflammation in subjects with neurodegenerative disorders. A dietary intervention using inulin-enriched diets was tested in murine models to assess its impact on gut microbiome composition and cognitive function. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated with improved spatial memory in TLR5-knockout mice, while short-chain fatty acids levels rose significantly following inulin supplementation. TLR5 deficiency was linked to heightened neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus, which were mitigated by inulin-induced shifts in gut microbiota diversity. Butyrate production, a metabolite associated with metabolomic profiling, showed a direct inverse relationship with Alzheimer's disease progression in cohort studies. These findings suggest that TLR5-mediated microbial signaling pathways are critical in translating dietary interventions into neuroprotective effects, highlighting the potential of prebiotic fibers as therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative conditions.

Modulation of the gut microbiome via probiotic supplementation with <bacteria>Lactobacillus plantarum</bacteria> has shown promise in mitigating depressive-like behaviors in rodent models of chronic stress. This study employed a chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) protocol in rats to assess the impact of fermented wheat germ (FWG) on behavioral, neurochemical, and microbial outcomes. FWG treatment significantly reduced immobility in the forced swim test and elevated serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex. Microbial 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that FWG altered the gut microbiota composition, with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Fecalibacterium species. A permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) confirmed significant differences in microbial community structure between FWG-treated and control groups (F = 4.23, P < 0.01). Correlations between short-chain fatty acid production and reduced anxiety scores were further validated using Spearman’s rank correlation. These findings suggest that FWG-mediated modulation of the gut-brain axis may represent a viable adjunct therapy for stress-related mental health disorders, highlighting the role of microbial metabolites in neurobehavioral regulation.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative progression in Parkinson's disease, with emerging evidence highlighting the role of specific microbial metabolites in modulating dopaminergic pathways. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified significant shifts in the abundance of Lactobacillus and Bacteroides in patient cohorts compared to controls. These changes correlated with altered expression of the SNCA gene, a key player in alpha-synuclein aggregation. Concurrently, administration of the probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum was associated with reduced systemic inflammation and improved motor function in a murine model of Parkinson's disease. The observed microbiota-gene interactions suggest a potential therapeutic strategy targeting both microbial dysbiosis and pathological protein aggregation. These findings underscore the interplay between gut microbiome dynamics and genetic factors in Parkinson's disease pathogenesis, offering novel insights into microbiome-based interventions for neurodegenerative disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition and 16S rRNA gene expression patterns in response to a prebiotic fiber intervention were identified using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, revealing significant shifts in microbial diversity and functional pathways. C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet supplemented with inulin exhibited increased abundance of Butyricicoccus and Blautia, coupled with reduced levels of pro-inflammatory Escherichia species, compared to controls. Metagenomic functional profiling further highlighted upregulation of genes encoding short-chain fatty acid synthesis enzymes, correlating with improved insulin sensitivity markers. These findings suggest that targeted prebiotic supplementation may modulate gut microbiota metabolic pathways through taxonomic and functional metagenomic analysis, offering therapeutic potential for metabolic disorders linked to microbiome dysregulation. The study underscores the utility of integrating multimodal microbiome analysis to dissect the interplay between nutritional interventions and host genomic responses in complex disease models.

Altered expression of the SLC6A4 gene in gut epithelial cells correlates with increased intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as demonstrated by confocal microscopy and qPCR analysis of mucosal biopsies. Altered gut microbiota composition, characterized by reduced abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, was linked to SLC6A4 dysregulation via canonical correlation analysis of longitudinal data from 120 participants. Functional validation using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated SLC6A4 knockout in murine models confirmed heightened gut barrier dysfunction and elevated serum IL-6 levels, consistent with clinical observations. Microbial metabolites such as butyrate partially reversed these effects, suggesting a mechanistic interplay between SLC6A4-mediated transport and microbial signaling. Random forest modeling identified SLC6A4 expression as a top predictor of disease severity, outperforming traditional IBS subtyping metrics. These findings highlight a novel axis connecting genetic susceptibility, intestinal microbiota dynamics, and inflammatory pathways in IBS, with implications for precision diagnostics and microbiota-targeted therapies.

A high-fiber flaxseed diet supplemented with inulin significantly alters gut microbial composition and mitigates neuroinflammation in aged C57BL/6 mice, offering novel insights into gut-brain axis modulation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and neuroinflammatory biomarker profiling, we observed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus alongside reduced interleukin-6 levels in the hippocampus. The flaxseed-rich regimen enhanced production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which correlated with improved performance in Morris water maze tests. Inulin further amplified SCFA synthesis by promoting fiber-degrading taxa, suggesting synergistic effects between dietary fiber and prebiotic supplementation. These findings highlight the potential of combining plant-based foods with prebiotic interventions to target gut microbiota-derived metabolites involved in neuroprotection, particularly in aging populations with early-stage neurodegeneration. The study underscores the role of gut microbiota in modulating brain health through metabolic signaling pathways, supporting the development of microbiota-targeted nutritional strategies for cognitive preservation.

Chronic consumption of kimchi has been associated with altered gut microbiota composition, prompting investigations into the role of probiotic supplementation in modulating these effects. Using principal component analysis, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants to assess microbial diversity and functional pathways linked to gut health. Probiotic supplementation significantly increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, while reducing Escherichia coli levels compared to kimchi-only diets. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of microbial communities in the probiotic group, characterized by enhanced production of short-chain fatty acids and reduced inflammation-related lipopolysaccharides. These findings suggest that probiotics may synergize with fermented foods to reinforce gut barrier integrity and suppress pathogenic overgrowth. Additionally, multivariate regression confirmed a strong correlation between kimchi-derived Lactobacillus and improved intestinal permeability markers. The study highlights the potential of combining traditional fermented foods with targeted probiotics to optimize microbiome health, underscoring the need for mechanistic studies on their combined impact on metabolic disorders and autoimmune conditions.

The co-administration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus with standard pharmacological therapy significantly altered gut microbiota composition and improved clinical outcomes in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). A 6-week double-blind, randomized controlled trial involving 85 MS patients demonstrated that those receiving the probiotic exhibited a 23% reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine levels compared to the placebo group, alongside a 17% increase in short-chain fatty acid production. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus rhamnosus enriched Allobaculum and Parabacteroides while suppressing Prevotella abundance, correlating with decreased TNF-α and IL-17 secretion. Notably, Allobaculum showed a strong negative correlation (r = -0.64, P < 0.01) with fatigue scores assessed via the Fatigue Severity Scale. Metabolomic profiling further identified elevated butyrate levels in the probiotic group, which inversely correlated with brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) decline observed in untreated controls. These findings suggest that Lactobacillus rhamnosus-mediated microbiota modulation may alleviate neuroinflammation and support neuroplasticity in MS through mechanisms involving SCFA-driven immune regulation and BDNF preservation.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative disorders, with emerging evidence suggesting that targeted dietary interventions can modulate systemic inflammation and disease progression. In a cohort of transgenic mice modeling Alzheimer’s disease, we evaluated the combined effects of a postbiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium longum lysate and a fermented soy product rich in isoflavones on cognitive decline and amyloid pathology. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the microbiota in treated mice exhibited increased abundance of Prevotella and Butyricimonas, alongside reduced Proteobacteria levels, compared to controls fed a standard diet. Western blot analysis detected decreased Aβ-40 aggregation in the hippocampus of supplemented groups, correlating with elevated LONP1 activity in mitochondrial fractions. Notably, serum IgA titers against gut commensals were significantly higher in mice receiving both postbiotic and fermented soy, suggesting enhanced immune tolerance. These results highlight synergistic mechanisms where postbiotic modulation of microbial metabolism and phytochemical anti-inflammatory properties jointly mitigate neurodegeneration, offering a dual-targeted strategy for Alzheimer’s disease management.

Administration of the prebiotic fiber inulin significantly altered the gut microbiota composition in male C57BL/6 mice, leading to changes in the expression of the BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor) gene in the hippocampus, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Mice receiving inulin exhibited increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, while short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels correlated with upregulated BDNF transcripts. Behavioral testing demonstrated reduced anxiety-like behavior in inulin-treated groups, paralleling elevated serotonin concentrations in the prefrontal cortex. ANOVA confirmed significant interactions between microbiome diversity and BDNF expression, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial modulation and neuroplasticity. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotic interventions to target BDNF-mediated pathways, offering novel strategies for managing depression and anxiety disorders via the gut-brain axis. The integration of multivariate analysis with microbiome profiling underscores the complexity of host-microbe interactions in modulating brain function.

Chronic consumption of sauerkraut enriched with Lactobacillus plantarum was found to modulate gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. In C57BL/6 mice subjected to chronic unpredictable stress, this intervention mitigated anhedonia and reduced serotonin dysregulation in the prefrontal cortex. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan derivatives in the serum, correlating with normalized Htr1a expression in the medial prefrontal cortex. L. plantarum also restored butyrate levels, a short-chain fatty acid critical for gut-brain axis signaling. Behavioral testing confirmed improved spatial working memory and reduced neuroinflammation markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α, in the hippocampus. These findings highlight the role of fermented foods in reshaping gut microbial communities to alleviate stress-induced cognitive deficits through tryptophan metabolism and butyrate-mediated neuroimmune modulation. The integration of multi-omics approaches underscores the complexity of gut-brain axis interactions in neurobehavioral disorders.

Consumption of fermented soybeans, a traditional food rich in isoflavones, significantly modulates the expression of the Nrf2 gene in intestinal epithelial cells, thereby enhancing antioxidant defenses. Using a combination of qPCR and multivariate analysis, we observed that the bioactive compounds in fermented soybeans upregulate Nrf2, leading to increased production of glutathione and decreased oxidative stress markers in the colon. This effect was associated with a shift in the gut microbiome composition, including increased abundance of Bacteroides species linked to anti-inflammatory responses. The study also revealed that Nrf2 activation through dietary intervention mitigates colitis progression in C57BL/6 mice, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for fermented soybeans in inflammatory bowel disease. These findings highlight the interplay between dietary components and genetic pathways in modulating gut health and systemic inflammation, underscoring the value of fermented soybeans as a functional food to target Nrf2-mediated antioxidant pathways.

Consumption of fermented dairy products, rich in Lactobacillus strains, correlates with altered TLR4 expression in the hippocampus, modulating neuroinflammation and synaptic plasticity via microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Using RNA sequencing and qPCR, we observed that TLR4 upregulation in hippocampal neurons was associated with increased Lactobacillus abundance in the gut, which in turn elevated butyrate levels, a known SCFA that enhances neurogenesis. Gut microbiota modulation through probiotic-rich diets significantly reduced neuroinflammation markers in mice with chronic stress-induced cognitive deficits, as evidenced by improved performance in Morris water maze tests. TLR4 knockout models exhibited diminished responses to fermented dairy-induced neuroprotection, implicating this gene in the mechanistic link between gut microbiota and brain function. Metabolomic profiling revealed that butyrate levels correlated inversely with TLR4 activation, suggesting a feedback loop between microbial SCFAs and innate immunity in the central nervous system. These findings highlight the role of diet-induced microbiota shifts in shaping TLR4-mediated immune signaling, offering novel targets for neurodegenerative disorders linked to gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Recent evidence suggests that modulating gut microbiota through probiotic administration alters inflammatory pathways linked to cognitive decline in aging populations. Using multivariate regression analysis, we evaluated longitudinal data from 628 participants with early-stage Alzheimer's disease who received daily probiotic formulations containing *Lactobacillus* and *Bifidobacterium* strains over 12 months. Baseline gut microbiota profiles were assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing that participants with higher baseline abundance of genus Bacteroides showed greater cognitive preservation after intervention. Probiotic use correlated with reduced plasma levels of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, markers of systemic inflammation, while multivariate regression analysis identified a significant interaction between family Ruminococcaceae enrichment and improved performance on mini-mental state examination scores. Notably, probiotic efficacy varied by intestinal permeability status, with individuals exhibiting higher gastrointestinal leakiness showing greater neurocognitive benefits. These findings underscore the potential of probiotic-mediated gut-brain axis modulation as a therapeutic strategy, though further validation through randomized controlled trials is needed to confirm causal relationships and optimize microbial formulations for neurodegenerative conditions.

High-fiber diet consumption significantly alters gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in participants with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 60 individuals randomized to either a high-fiber or standard diet for 12 weeks. PERMANOVA revealed distinct microbial community structures between groups, with the high-fiber cohort showing increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, alongside decreased Enterobacteriaceae. ANOSIM further confirmed separation of gut microbiome profiles, while qPCR quantified SCFA-producing enzyme transcripts linked to butyrate synthesis. Anxiety scores, assessed via Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, declined by 32% in the high-fiber group, correlating with microbial shifts. Linear regression identified Bifidobacterium abundance as a significant predictor of symptom improvement. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of gut microbiota via fiber intake may represent a viable strategy for managing IBS-associated psychological comorbidities, warranting further investigation into microbial metabolite-mind interactions.

Altered gut microbiome composition in patients with Parkinson's disease correlates with dysregulated gut-brain axis signaling, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between Enterobacteriaceae overgrowth and neuroinflammation. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified distinct microbial signatures in 120 patients undergoing probiotic supplementation trials, with significant shifts in Bifidobacterium abundance observed alongside symptom modulation. A logistic regression analysis confirmed that higher baseline Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios predicted poorer response to probiotic supplementation (

 < 0.01). Furthermore, 16S rRNA profiling revealed that short-chain fatty acid production by Prevotella strains was inversely correlated with Parkinson's disease progression rates ( = -0.34,

 = 0.002). These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota in modulating neurodegenerative pathways and underscore the need for personalized probiotic interventions targeting specific taxa to optimize therapeutic outcomes. The integration of machine learning models with longitudinal gut microbiome data may further refine predictive biomarkers for disease stratification.

The TLR4 gene variant rs3804077 was significantly associated with altered gut microbiota composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by logistic regression analysis of 120 fecal metagenomic datasets. Concurrently, administration of the curcumin supplement (500 mg/day for 8 weeks) modulated microbial taxa, reducing abundance of proinflammatory Escherichia coli and elevating anti-inflammatory Bifidobacterium longum in IBS subjects. This intervention correlated with decreased systemic IL-6 levels and improved gastrointestinal motility scores, as measured by manometry. TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells was further validated as a mediator of curcumin’s anti-inflammatory effects via qPCR and Western blot in vitro models. The logistic regression results highlighted a 2.3-fold increased likelihood of microbiota normalization in curcumin-treated individuals compared to placebo, with TLR4-mediated signaling pathways identified as key regulators of microbial-immune crosstalk. These findings suggest that targeting TLR4 through curcumin may represent a viable strategy to restore gut-brain communication in IBS by reprogramming the gut microbiome and dampening inflammatory cascades.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's interaction with the host immune system, mediated by the TLR4 gene, are linked to neuroinflammation in irritable bowel syndrome patients. Gut microbial dysbiosis correlated with elevated proinflammatory cytokine levels, as measured by ELISA, and was analyzed using multivariate ANOVA to assess associations between microbial taxa and immune markers. Patients with IBS exhibited reduced abundance of Bacteroides and increased Enterococcus, which were significantly associated with TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Butyricimonas showed inverse correlations with IBS severity scores, suggesting a protective role. Principal component analysis revealed that microbial community structure explained 32% of variance in TLR4 activation pathways, highlighting a mechanistic link between microbiome composition and immune dysregulation. These findings underscore the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target, with TLR4 signaling emerging as a key mediator of microbial-immune crosstalk in gastrointestinal disorders.

16S rRNA sequencing revealed that fiber-rich diets modulate gut microbiota composition in older adults with early-stage Alzheimer's disease, correlating with reduced amyloid-beta accumulation in hippocampal regions. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids in participants consuming fermented dairy products, which co-occurred with improved executive function scores. Lactobacillus abundance, linked to probiotic supplementation, showed inverse associations with neuroinflammation markers in prefrontal cortex biopsies. Functional MRI confirmed heightened insula connectivity in subjects following six months of omega-3 fatty acid intake, alongside shifts in gut microbiome taxa such as Akkermansia. These findings suggest that targeted dietary interventions and multi-omics approaches may synergistically enhance neuroprotective pathways by bridging intestinal dysbiosis and neurodegeneration in vulnerable populations.

Alterations in the gut microbiota of patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) correlate with shifts in fermented food consumption and probiotic intake, revealing potential modulators of neurodevelopmental outcomes. Analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from fecal samples of ASD children and neurotypical controls identified Bacteroides fragilis and Parabacteroides distasonis as significantly depleted in ASD cohorts, while Lactobacillus abundance rose in individuals consuming kimchi regularly. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored tryptophan metabolism pathways in mice models of ASD, aligning with reduced social interaction deficits and improved serotonin synthesis. These findings suggest that fermented food-derived microbial metabolites and probiotics may normalize gut-brain axis signaling by targeting TNF-alpha-mediated inflammation in prefrontal cortex neurons. The integration of multivariate analysis further highlighted short-chain fatty acids as key mediators linking fermented food intake to ASD symptom mitigation, underscoring dietary interventions as promising strategies for microbiome-based therapies.

A novel interplay between dietary intake and genetic regulation in the gut-brain axis has been uncovered through analysis of fermented dairy consumption and its impact on TNF-α-mediated inflammation in gut microbiota of subjects with irritable bowel syndrome. Administration of probiotic strains enriched in Lactobacillus alongside fiber-rich diets significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, correlating with improved anxiety symptoms. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that TNF-α expression was downregulated in response to probiotic intervention, while short-chain fatty acids production increased, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived metabolites and neural signaling. Pathway analysis highlighted the role of TLR4 in mediating lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation, which was attenuated by fermented dairy consumption. These findings underscore the potential of combining prebiotic and probiotic strategies to modulate immune-related genes and alleviate gut-brain axis dysfunction, offering a targeted approach for neuroimmune disorders linked to gut dysbiosis.

Modulation of gut microbiota through multi-strain probiotic administration significantly attenuates cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD) models, as evidenced by improved performance in Morris water maze tasks and reduced neuroinflammatory markers. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in treated SAMP8 mice, correlating with elevated serum short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) levels. These findings suggest a mechanistic link between probiotic-induced microbial shifts and mitigation of Aβ pathology via modulation of the AKT/GSK-3β signaling pathway. Notably, transcriptomic profiling identified upregulation of neuroprotective genes in the hippocampus of supplemented animals, highlighting potential therapeutic strategies for cognitive impairment associated with neurodegenerative disorders. The study underscores the role of gut microbiome engineering as a viable adjunct to conventional AD therapies, with probiotics showing promise in targeting both metabolic and neuronal pathways implicated in disease progression.

A novel prebiotic formulation significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and TNF-α expression in rodent models subjected to chronic social defeat stress, revealing a mechanistic link between microbial-derived metabolites and neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR, we identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced lipopolysaccharide levels in colonic contents following prebiotic administration. Concurrently, TNF-α mRNA levels in hippocampus were suppressed by 40% in treated animals, correlating with attenuated depressive-like behaviors and enhanced vagal nerve connectivity. Metabolic profiling revealed elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in the cecum, which directly inhibited TNF-α promoter activity via histone deacetylase modulation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotics in targeting neuroimmune pathways governed by TNF-α, offering a dual strategy to restore microbial balance and mitigate stress-induced neuroinflammation. The interplay between gut microbiota-derived SCFAs and host gene regulation underscores the complexity of the gut-brain axis in psychiatric disorders.

The gut-brain axis modulates neurobehavioral outcomes via serotonergic signaling, with the SERT gene playing a critical role in serotonin transporter regulation. Inulin supplementation in adults with irritable bowel syndrome was linked to altered gut microbiota dynamics, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and canonical correspondence analysis. Analysis of fecal serotonin metabolites showed a 28% increase in 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels correlating with SERT expression in enteric neurons. Inulin-induced shifts in Bacteroidetes abundance were associated with reduced anxiety-like behavior in rodent models using open field testing. Multivariate regression models confirmed that SERT polymorphisms interacted with microbial short-chain fatty acids to predict depressive symptom severity in cohort studies. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic variants, prebiotic interventions, and microbial metabolites in shaping gut-brain communication pathways. The path analysis further revealed that 63% of the variance in neurocognitive function scores could be attributed to combined effects of SERT activity, inulin dosage, and microbial diversity indices. This integrative approach underscores the potential of targeted fiber-based therapies to modulate serotonin-related neurobiology through microbiota-mediated mechanisms.

A dietary supplement intervention significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and cognitive performance in aging participants, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and random forest classification. The study enrolled 120 older adults with mild cognitive impairment, randomly assigned to receive either a probiotic-rich synbiotic formulation or a placebo over 12 weeks. Microbial alpha-diversity increased in the synbiotic group, with notable enrichment of Bifidobacterium longum and Prevotella copri, while Escherichia coli abundance decreased. Cognitive assessments using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment showed a 15% improvement in the synbiotic cohort compared to controls. Permutation-based multivariate analysis linked shifts in gut microbiota β-diversity to changes in memory and executive function scores. The synbiotic formulation also correlated with reduced inflammation markers, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome modulation and neurocognitive benefits. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiota-directed interventions to mitigate cognitive decline, supported by high-resolution microbial profiling and machine learning-driven biomarker identification. The integration of gut-brain axis dynamics with clinical outcomes underscores the value of combining omic technologies and predictive modeling in precision health strategies.

The TLR4 gene exhibits altered expression in the hippocampus of individuals with major depressive disorder, correlating with dysbiosis in the gut microbiome and impaired neuroplasticity markers. A qPCR-based study revealed that patients receiving Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG for 12 weeks demonstrated a 32% reduction in TLR4 mRNA levels compared to controls (ANOVA, p=0.012), alongside increased abundance of Bacteroides uniformis and Lactobacillus in fecal samples. These changes coincided with improved depressive symptoms measured via HAMD-24 scores and enhanced serotonergic signaling in prefrontal cortex tissue. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified Prevotella copri as a predictive biomarker for TLR4 dysregulation (AUC=0.81). The Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG intervention also modulated BDNF expression and 5-HT levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome-targeted therapies and neuroimmune pathways. These findings highlight the potential of microbiome-derived probiotics in ameliorating depression by restoring TLR4-mediated immune homeostasis and promoting neuroplasticity via the gut-brain axis.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in the gut epithelium correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition that influence neurobehavioral outcomes in rodents. Dietary interventions targeting inulin, a prebiotic fiber, partially reversed these effects by enriching Bifidobacterium populations and reducing inflammation. qPCR confirmed TLR4 upregulation in colonic tissues of mice fed a high-fat diet, while 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a decrease in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Behavioral assays showed that mice with obesity exhibited heightened anxiety-like behaviors, which were mitigated by inulin supplementation. The gut microbiome mediated this effect, as fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors normalized TLR4 signaling and improved cognitive flexibility in recipient mice. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4 expression, microbial metabolism, and dietary modulation in shaping brain function. The study underscores potential therapeutic strategies leveraging prebiotics to target immune-related genes and restore gut-brain communication in metabolic disorders.

A novel dietary intervention combining probiotic supplementation with fermented vegetable intake significantly modulated gut microbiota profiles in adults exhibiting chronic gastrointestinal dysfunction and neurocognitive decline. 16S rDNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Prevotella and Bifidobacterium alongside reduced Escherichia coli in participants following a 12-week regimen, correlating with improved short-chain fatty acid production. Serum tryptophan metabolite levels, measured via LC-MS/MS, showed elevated kynurenine ratios, suggesting enhanced tryptophan metabolism pathways. Concurrently, butyrate concentrations rose, aligning with reduced inflammatory markers IL-6 and TNF-α detected by ELISA. Cognitive assessments demonstrated improved executive function scores and reduced anxiety symptoms, potentially mediated by microbiome-derived SCFAs influencing hippocampal neuroplasticity. The study underscores the therapeutic potential of fermented food-mediated microbiome reprogramming, augmented by probiotic interventions, in targeting gut-brain axis dysregulation linked to neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders. Mechanistic insights from metabolomic profiling further highlight the role of microbial metabolites in bridging gastrointestinal and central nervous system homeostasis.

A diet rich in fermented dairy products combined with probiotic supplementation significantly modulated gut microbiome composition and reduced neuroinflammatory markers in patients with depression. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we analyzed fecal samples from 85 participants randomized to receive either a fermented dairy-based intervention or a placebo, alongside probiotic administration for 12 weeks. The intervention group exhibited a 23% increase in beneficial bacterial taxa such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside decreased plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α and IL-6. Metabolomic data revealed elevated short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which correlated with improved depressive symptoms measured via the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Notably, the probiotic alone did not alter microbiome diversity, but synergized with the fermented dairy to enhance mucosal barrier integrity, as evidenced by reduced zonulin levels. These findings suggest that integrative approaches combining prebiotic-rich diets with probiotic therapies may offer a viable strategy to target gut-brain axis dysregulation in psychiatric disorders, highlighting the role of microbiome-derived metabolites in modulating central nervous system function.

A high-fiber plant-based diet supplemented with prebiotic oligosaccharides significantly alters gut microbiota composition and modulates inflammatory signaling pathways in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Analysis revealed that the NOD2 gene, critical for intestinal epithelial cell immunity, exhibits differential expression correlated with shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios. Metagenomic sequencing identified 15 species whose abundance inversely predicted colonic inflammation severity, while multivariate regression models linked higher fiber intake to reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced cytokine production. The prebiotic intervention increased Akkermansia muciniphila levels, which co-occurred with upregulation of TLR4 and enhanced mucosal barrier integrity. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of microbial communities through diet and supplements can influence host genetic responses, offering novel therapeutic strategies for chronic gut disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), with genetic variants in the IL6 gene modulating this relationship. A random forest algorithm identified IL6 as a key predictor of systemic inflammation levels, validated through cross-validation (k=10) and adjusted for confounding variables such as age, diet, and medication use. Patients with the IL6-174G/C polymorphism exhibited a 38% higher risk of elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) levels compared to non-carriers (p=0.003). These findings suggest that IL6 gene variants may influence the gut-brain axis through immune signaling pathways, highlighting potential targets for microbiome-directed therapies in IBS management. The integration of microbiome profiling with genomic data revealed distinct microbial taxa, including Akkermansia muciniphila, that interacted with IL6-dependent inflammatory responses. Multivariate analysis confirmed that principal component analysis reduced dimensionality of gut microbial features, aligning with inflammatory biomarkers. This interplay between host genetics and microbial composition underscores the role of gut microbiota in shaping neuroimmune outcomes, offering novel insights for precision medicine in functional gastrointestinal disorders.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene modulate gut microbiota composition and inflammatory signaling, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models of depression. Dietary interventions targeting probiotics and fermented dairy products were tested for their capacity to restore microbial homeostasis and mitigate neuroinflammation. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that Bifidobacterium abundance correlated inversely with IL-6 levels in colonic tissues of TLR4-deficient mice, while probiotics supplementation increased Lactobacillus populations and reduced quorum sensing markers. Fermented dairy products enriched the microbiome with Streptococcus thermophilus, which co-occurred with elevated tryptophan metabolites linked to serotonin synthesis in the serotonin-producing neurons of the raphe nuclei. Multivariate analysis confirmed that TLR4 expression levels predicted response to probiotics in patients with major depressive disorder, suggesting a genetic determinant of microbiota-based therapeutic efficacy. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4, microbial metabolites from fermented dairy, and probiotic interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition associated with depression were linked to dietary intake of fermented foods, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples from 60 participants. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance correlated inversely with symptom severity, while Enterobacteriaceae levels increased in individuals reporting low fiber consumption. Patients adhering to fermented dairy intake exhibited higher short-chain fatty acid production, potentially modulating hippocampal neuroplasticity via tryptophan metabolism pathways. Multivariate analysis identified omega-3 fatty acids from fish as a protective factor against gut microbiota dysbiosis, with TLR2 expression levels in colonic epithelial cells showing significant interaction with dietary patterns. These findings underscore the bidirectional communication between gut microbiota and central nervous system, highlighting the therapeutic potential of targeted prebiotic interventions in mental health disorders.

A MAOA polymorphism is associated with altered gut microbiota composition in patients with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate analysis. Analysis of fecal samples from 120 participants identified reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and increased prevalence of Escherichia coli in carriers of the MAOA variant, correlating with higher serotonin metabolite levels in plasma. ANOVA confirmed significant differences in microbial diversity indices between genotype groups, while metagenomic shotgun sequencing uncovered pathway enrichment in tryptophan metabolism. These findings suggest a mechanistic link between MAOA-mediated neurochemical signaling and dysbiosis, potentially modulating the gut-brain axis via tryptophan-derived serotonin production. The principal component analysis further highlighted distinct clustering of microbial taxa in patients with major depressive disorder, emphasizing the role of microbial community structure in psychiatric phenotypes. These data underscore the importance of integrating genetic and microbial biomarkers in understanding depressive disorders and may inform targeted probiotic interventions.

A polymorphism in the FMO3 gene was associated with altered gut microbiome composition, as revealed by multivariate regression analysis in a cohort of 500 participants. This genetic variant correlated with shifts in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and increased production of trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a metabolite linked to neuroinflammation. Subjects carrying the FMO3 allele exhibited higher scores on depression and anxiety scales, independent of dietary choline intake. Gut microbial TMAO synthesis was validated via metabolomic profiling, revealing a 2.3-fold elevation in TMAO levels among FMO3 carriers. The multivariate regression analysis further identified Escherichia coli as a mediator of TMAO-induced neuroinflammation, with FMO3 polymorphism explaining 18% of variance in inflammatory markers. These findings suggest a mechanistic link between genetic variation in host metabolic enzymes, gut microbial metabolism, and mood disorders, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for depression through microbiome modulation.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition are strongly associated with the severity of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 150 participants. Using differential abundance analysis, we identified significant enrichment of Bacteroides and depletion of Faecalibacterium in IBS patients compared to healthy controls. These microbial shifts correlated with increased inflammation markers and altered neurotransmitter production in the gut. Furthermore, a random forest classifier trained on microbial taxa achieved 82% accuracy in distinguishing IBS subtypes based on symptom profiles. The findings highlight the potential of microbiome-targeted therapies and underscore the role of machine learning in personalized diagnostics. Statistical validation through permutation tests confirmed the robustness of these associations, suggesting that gut microbial profiling could serve as a non-invasive biomarker for IBS management. These results align with growing evidence that gastrointestinal dysbiosis modulates central nervous system function via immune and neural pathways, offering novel avenues for therapeutic intervention.

Altered gut microbiome composition correlates with depressive symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 120 participants. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) identified significant differences in microbial beta diversity between IBS patients with depression and those without, with Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium showing inverse associations with depressive severity. TLR4 expression in intestinal biopsies, measured via quantitative PCR, correlated with gut microbial dysbiosis and inflammation markers like IL-6. Random forest modeling further validated that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance predicted remission of depressive symptoms after 12 weeks of prebiotic intervention. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbial dysregulation, immune signaling, and mood disorders in IBS, suggesting targeted modulation of Akkermansia could improve psychiatric comorbidities through the gut-brain axis.

A diet rich in fermented foods modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces neuroinflammation in murine models of Alzheimer's disease, with mechanisms linked to the FMO3-mediated metabolism of trimethylamine. Intervention with fermented foods altered gut microbial taxa associated with TMAO production, decreasing systemic TMAO levels and mitigating neurodegeneration in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid producers, while metabolomic profiling identified reduced lipid peroxidation markers. FMO3 knockout mice exhibited exacerbated neuroinflammation and elevated neurotoxic metabolites, highlighting its role in mitigating TMAO-driven pathogenesis. These findings underscore the interplay between fermented foods-induced microbial shifts and FMO3-dependent metabolic pathways in modulating Alzheimer's disease progression.

A novel probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum significantly modulates gut microbiome composition in obese adults consuming a high-fat diet, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Participants receiving the supplement exhibited increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, including Butyricimonas, alongside reduced levels of Escherichia coli and Enterobacter, compared to control groups on a high-fat diet. Metabolic profiling indicated elevated butyrate and propionate concentrations in the colonic lumen of supplemented individuals, correlating with improved insulin sensitivity and reduced inflammatory biomarkers in serum. Machine learning analysis further identified distinct microbial signatures associated with probiotic adherence, emphasizing the role of microbial interactions in mediating metabolic benefits. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions could mitigate metabolic syndrome risk by reshaping gut microbial ecology through nutritional modulation and omic profiling.

A high-fiber diet supplemented with probiotics significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, enhancing colonic short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa and reducing inflammation in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 80 participants consuming either a fermented vegetable-rich regimen or a standard diet, alongside probiotic supplementation. LEfSe identified increased abundance of Faecalibacterium and Butyricicoccus in the supplemented group, correlating with lower IL-6 levels. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated butyrate concentrations, linked to improved depressive symptoms via serotonin signaling pathways. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of integrating fermented foods and probiotic interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis for mental health disorders.

The gut microbiota's modulation of the gut-brain axis influences neurobehavioral outcomes, as demonstrated by the impact of probiotic supplementation on specific SIRT1 expression in a rodent model of stress-induced depression. Using a rat model subjected to Chronic Unpredictable Mild Stress (CUMS), we found that administration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly reduced depressive-like behaviors in open field and forced swim tests while restoring gut microbiota diversity via 16S rDNA sequencing. Mechanistically, qPCR analysis revealed enhanced SIRT1 expression in the hippocampus, correlating with decreased inflammatory markers such as TNF-α and IL-6. This SIRT1-mediated effect was linked to shifts in Bifidobacterium abundance, suggesting a bidirectional interaction between microbiota-derived metabolites and host neuroimmune pathways. Furthermore, Western blot confirmed phosphorylation of AKT downstream of SIRT1 activation, implicating the PI3K-AKT signaling cascade in the antidepressant response. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted interventions, particularly probiotic formulations, in modulating SIRT1-dependent neuroplasticity and mitigating stress-related pathologies through the gut-brain axis.

A high-fat diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition and exacerbates metabolic dysfunction, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing using Illumina MiSeq. Analysis of 120 male C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) or standard chow showed that HFD-induced obesity correlated with reduced alpha diversity and shifts in bacterial taxa. Statistical techniques, including ANOVA and PERMANOVA, identified significant differences in microbiome structure between groups. The gene encoding the 16S rRNA was critical in profiling these changes, revealing a dominance of Firmicutes over Bacteroidetes in HFD-fed animals. Additionally, dietary intervention with a probiotic supplement partially restored microbial balance, suggesting a potential therapeutic role. These findings highlight the interplay between diet, microbiota, and metabolic health, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. The statistical significance of these results underscores the importance of gene-based microbiome analysis in understanding diet-related diseases.

A high-fiber legume-based diet supplemented with the curcumin extract significantly altered gut microbiota composition and modulated inflammatory TNF-α expression in adults with metabolic syndrome. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR, we observed a 40% increase in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance alongside reduced Escherichia coli levels in participants receiving the curcumin intervention compared to controls. These shifts correlated with a 25% decrease in circulating IL-6 and a 15% reduction in TNF-α mRNA expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The legume-based diet enriched for inulin and polyphenols likely enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which may have indirectly suppressed TNF-α signaling through butyrate-mediated histone acetylation. Notably, curcumin supplementation alone increased Lactobacillus plantarum abundance by 30%, suggesting a synergistic effect with dietary fiber in reshaping the gut microbiome. These findings highlight the interplay between nutrient intake, phytochemicals, and host immune-related genes in modulating systemic inflammation and metabolic health.

The role of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in modulating neurobehavioral outcomes remains understudied despite their established link to gut microbiota dynamics. A SCFA-acylated starch was administered to mice to target intestinal SCFA release, followed by assessments of neurobehavioral and microbiomic changes using high-resolution 16 S rRNA marker gene sequencing. Elastic net regression identified microbial features correlating with reduced depressive symptoms and altered glutamate metabolism in chronically stressed cohorts. Increased abundance of <bacteria>Bifidobacterium</bacteria> and decreased histamine synthesis were associated with improved anxiety-like behaviors, while Intestinibacter depletion linked to heightened cognitive impairment risk. Quantitative PCR confirmed upregulated ZO-1 and Claudin gene expression in treated groups, mitigating colonic permeability. Butyrate enrichment from the starch correlated with normalized IL-6 levels and enhanced tryptophan synthesis pathways. These findings suggest that microbiome-targeted SCFA delivery may offer a novel strategy for mental health interventions, with machine learning models providing predictive value for microbial biomarkers of psychiatric resilience.

metadata.abstract: The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between intestinal microbiota and central nervous system function, with emerging evidence linking dysbiosis to neuroinflammation in depression. A Tlr4-deficient murine model revealed heightened susceptibility to anxiety after exposure to a high-fat diets enriched in trans fats, suggesting immune signaling pathways modulate this interaction. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified altered gut microbiota composition in rodents fed processed foods containing emulsifiers, correlating with elevated lipopolysaccharide levels and reduced Tlr4 expression in hippocampus neurons. These findings align with clinical data showing that patients with major depressive disorder exhibit decreased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a gut microbiome member implicated in intestinal barrier integrity regulation. Dietary interventions targeting fiber intake restored Tlr4-dependent neuroimmune homeostasis in preclinical models, highlighting the therapeutic potential of prebiotics to normalize gut microbiota dysbiosis and mitigate neuroinflammatory pathways. This work underscores the role of Tlr4 in mediating diet-induced microbial shifts that influence brain function, offering novel biomarkers for stratifying mental health disorders based on microbial metabolite profiles.

A dietary supplement containing probiotic strains significantly altered gut microbiome composition and modulated immune gene expression in patients with metabolic syndrome. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and reduced levels of Escherichia coli in supplemented individuals, correlating with decreased systemic inflammation. The TLR4 gene, a key mediator of innate immune signaling, showed elevated expression in response to microbial metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids produced by the enriched Bifidobacterium species. This upregulation was associated with reduced plasma concentrations of interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein, markers of metabolic dysregulation. Furthermore, administration of prebiotic fiber synergistically enhanced the probiotic effects, promoting alpha diversity and stabilizing gut barrier integrity. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the microbiome via dietary interventions may ameliorate inflammation-driven pathologies by influencing host gene networks. The interplay between microbial-derived signals and host TLR4 activation highlights potential therapeutic strategies for chronic metabolic disorders, emphasizing the need to integrate microbiome profiling with genetic analyses in precision medicine approaches.

Interventions targeting the gut microbiome may modulate neuroinflammation in patients with major depressive disorder by altering microbial metabolites linked to brain function. A 12-week randomized trial evaluated the impact of prebiotic supplementation on gut microbiota composition and inflammatory markers in 150 individuals with major depressive disorder. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in the prebiotic group, correlating with reduced plasma levels of interleukin-6. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed a significant interaction between treatment and baseline microbial diversity in predicting symptom improvement. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotic interventions as adjuncts in managing major depressive disorder, with <statistical_technique>statistical_technique> analysis revealing that individuals with lower initial microbial diversity experienced greater benefits. The study underscores the role of the gut-brain axis in neuroinflammation and supports personalized approaches to microbiome-based therapies.

Modulation of the gut-brain axis by a curcumin-rich diet ameliorates neuroinflammation in murine models of Alzheimer’s disease through suppression of the TNF-α pathway. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that curcumin enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in colonic samples, coinciding with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. TNF-α expression in hippocampal tissue was significantly attenuated (p < 0.01), alongside improved BDNF signaling and synaptic plasticity markers. LEfSe analysis identified Prevotella as a keystone taxon inversely correlated with TNF-α activation, suggesting microbial metabolites may mediate this effect. Metabolomic profiling detected elevated butyrate levels in feces, aligning with butyrate-producing bacteria abundance shifts. These findings highlight the interplay between curcumin-induced microbiome remodeling and TNF-α-driven neuroinflammation, offering a mechanistic link between dietary modulation and cognitive outcomes in neurodegenerative conditions.

Altered expression of the TLR5 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in a cohort consuming a high-fiber diet. This study identified that individuals with irritable bowel syndrome exhibited reduced TLR5 activity alongside decreased abundance of Bifidobacterium and increased Escherichia coli, a pattern reversed by dietary intervention with fermented dairy. Metagenomic analysis further linked TLR5-mediated signaling to dysregulated production of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, which were restored to baseline levels after six weeks of resistant starch supplementation. The gut microbiota of participants receiving prebiotic-rich foods showed enhanced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii colonization, associated with improved gastrointestinal motility and reduced inflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between host immune-related genes, microbiome dynamics, and dietary modulation in managing gastrointestinal disorders, underscoring the potential of targeted nutritional strategies to restore microbial homeostasis through multi-omics profiling.

A variant in the Tlr4 gene was found to modulate gut microbiota composition, correlating with altered neuroinflammation in individuals with major depressive disorder. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified distinct microbial profiles in subjects with the Tlr4 variant, characterized by reduced Bifidobacterium abundance and elevated Proteobacteria levels. These microbial shifts were associated with increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in intestinal epithelial cells, suggesting a mechanistic link between host genetics, microbiome dysbiosis, and psychiatric comorbidities. Notably, inulin supplementation in a murine model of Tlr4-mediated gut dysbiosis reversed microbial imbalance, restored barrier integrity, and attenuated depressive-like behaviors. This effect was accompanied by enhanced Bifidobacterium colonization and reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced cytokine release. Our findings highlight the interplay between host gene variants, microbiome composition, and mental health outcomes, with dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota offering a promising strategy to mitigate inflammation-driven psychiatric disorders. The integration of metagenomic sequencing with functional assays underscores the potential of precision nutrition in modulating the gut-brain axis.

The gut microbiota modulates central nervous system function through metabolic and immune pathways, with TNF-α expression emerging as a critical mediator in this interaction. A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus plantarum was administered to aged C57BL/6J mice to assess its impact on microbial composition and neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Prevotellaceae and reduced Desulfovibrionaceae in supplemented groups, correlating with decreased IL-6 levels in hippocampus tissue. Principal component analysis of metagenomic data highlighted significant shifts in pathways related to short-chain fatty acid production and TLR4 signaling. Notably, TNF-α expression in microglia was downregulated by 42% in supplemented animals compared to controls, accompanied by improved performance in novel object recognition tasks. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of gut microbial communities via probiotics may alleviate neuroinflammation by suppressing TNF-α-driven pathways, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for age-related cognitive decline. The multivariate analysis further identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a key predictor of treatment response, underscoring the complex interplay between microbial taxa and host genetic regulators in the gut-brain axis.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly modulates gut microbiota composition in adults with irritable bowel syndrome, correlating with reduced anxiety symptoms and altered TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Using multivariate regression analysis, we identified a strong inverse relationship between Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and gastrointestinal pain scores, while butyrate production correlated with increased BDNF mRNA levels in the prefrontal cortex of rodent models. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiota modulation via prebiotics to influence neuroimmune signaling pathways, as evidenced by significant ANOVA-detected differences in TLR4 activation between intervention and control cohorts. The association between microbial diversity and mental health outcomes was further validated using principal component analysis, revealing that Prevotella copri abundance explained 23% of variance in depressive symptomatology scores. This study underscores the interplay between gut microbial metabolites, host immune-related genes, and psychiatric comorbidities, suggesting that microbiota-targeted therapies may offer novel avenues for treating gut-brain axis disorders.

A high-fiber supplement regimen significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and metabolic outcomes in individuals with type 2 diabetes, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Analysis of fecal samples demonstrated a 37% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance and a 22% reduction in Escherichia coli relative to baseline, with PERMANOVA confirming significant shifts in microbial community structure. Concurrently, serum levels of short-chain fatty acids correlated with improved insulin sensitivity, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial-derived metabolites and host metabolic regulation. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing further identified upregulation of carbohydrate metabolism pathways in responders, while canonical correspondence analysis highlighted associations between specific bacterial taxa and glycemic control. These findings underscore the potential of targeted fiber interventions to reshape the gut microbiome and mitigate diabetes-related complications through modulation of intestinal microbial functions and metabolic signaling.

A 12-week intervention with a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum significantly altered gut microbiota composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Short-chain fatty acid production correlated with reductions in gastrointestinal distress scores, while random forest analysis identified Blautia and Parabacteroides as key predictors of symptom improvement. Microbial diversity increased in responders, contrasting with non-responders who showed persistent proinflammatory cytokine elevation. Fecal butyrate levels rose in parallel with serotonin receptor 5-HT4 expression, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and visceral hypersensitivity. The metagenomic sequencing further uncovered ARG1 upregulation in Peptostreptococcus, associated with metabolic endotoxemia reduction. Kruskal-Wallis testing confirmed significant intergroup differences in microbial taxa abundance, while SCFA ratios correlated inversely with IBS severity indices. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic therapies to modulate gut-brain axis signaling, with multi-omics approaches enabling precise predictive modeling of treatment outcomes in functional gastrointestinal disorders.

A high-fiber diet modulates gut microbiota composition in patients with Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from fecal samples. Prebiotic fiber supplementation increased the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Butyricicoccus while reducing Escherichia coli in 30 participants over 12 weeks, correlating with reduced neuroinflammation markers. Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids were quantified via gas chromatography, revealing elevated butyrate levels linked to improved cognitive scores on the Mini-Mental State Examination. ANOVA confirmed significant differences in alpha-diversity indices between the intervention and control groups (p < 0.01). Mechanistically, butyrate enhanced TLR4 expression in enteric neurons, mitigating blood-brain barrier permeability. These findings suggest that prebiotic fiber may exert neuroprotective effects through the microbiota-gut-brain axis, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease management.

Alterations in the Tlr4 gene were associated with changes in gut microbiome composition linked to anxiety-like behaviors in mice fed a high-fiber diet enriched in inulin. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that Bacteroidetes abundance correlated inversely with Tlr4 expression, while Firmicutes levels rose in animals with anxiety-related phenotypes. Short-chain fatty acids derived from fiber fermentation modulated Tlr4-mediated inflammatory signaling, as evidenced by ANOVA analysis of cytokine profiles. Lactobacillus spp. showed increased abundance in high-fiber-treated groups, coinciding with reduced anxiety scores in behavioral assays. Mechanistically, Tlr4 knockdown in colonic epithelial cells attenuated the pro-inflammatory effects of lipopolysaccharides from Escherichia coli, suggesting a direct link between Tlr4 function and microbial metabolites. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic regulators, nutritional inputs, and microbial dynamics in shaping neurobehavioral outcomes, underscoring potential therapeutic strategies targeting gut-brain axis interactions.

Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus modulates gut microbiota composition and enhances short-chain fatty acid production in individuals consuming a fiber-rich diet high in whole grains, correlating with reduced anxiety symptoms. Mechanistically, this intervention upregulates TLR4 expression in the hypothalamus, linking microbial metabolites to central nervous system signaling. qPCR confirmed increased BDNF levels in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting a neuroprotective effect mediated by butyrate derived from resistant starch fermentation. Multivariate analysis of faecal metagenomic data revealed a significant inverse correlation between Bacteroides fragilis abundance and serotonin levels in the serum, highlighting the role of probiotics in stabilizing 5-HT transporter activity. These findings underscore the interplay between nutritional intake, microbial diversity, and neuroimmune pathways in regulating mood disorders, with probiotic-based therapies offering a targeted approach to modulate the gut-brain axis through TLR4-mediated signaling.

Chronic consumption of fermented kimchi modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models of stress-related disorders. Lactobacillus plantarum abundance increased alongside elevated short-chain fatty acid production in colonic samples from kimchi-fed rats, while serotonin levels in the hippocampus decreased compared to controls. Principal component analysis revealed significant correlations between microbial taxa and behavioral metrics, with Parabacteroides distasonis showing inverse associations with hyperactivity. Kimchi-induced alterations in gut-brain signaling were linked to downregulated Il6 expression in the prelimbic cortex, suggesting anti-inflammatory effects. Butyrate levels, a SCFA produced by Lactobacillus, correlated with reduced neuroinflammatory markers in microglia from treated animals. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of fermented foods in modulating the gut microbiota to alleviate neuropsychiatric symptoms via metabolite-mediated neuroimmune interactions.

A high-fiber whole grain diet supplemented with the probiotic strain Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces systemic inflammation in patients with irritable bowel syndrome. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we identified a 32% increase in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance and a concurrent decline in Escherichia coli in supplemented groups compared to controls. This shift correlated with a 28% reduction in plasma interleukin-6 levels and improved gastrointestinal symptoms as measured by the IBS-SSS score. Notably, whole grain consumption alone increased short-chain fatty acid production, while the probiotic intervention enhanced mucosal barrier integrity via upregulation of claudin-4 expression. These findings highlight synergistic effects of dietary fiber and targeted probiotic administration in reshaping the gut microbiome to alleviate inflammatory gut disorders. The metabolomic profiling further revealed altered bile acid conjugation patterns, suggesting microbiota-mediated modulation of host metabolic pathways. This study underscores the potential of combining fiber-rich diets with probiotics to therapeutically target the gut-brain axis in chronic digestive conditions.

A novel dietary intervention targeting the gut-brain axis has demonstrated efficacy in modulating neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in a murine model of Alzheimer’s disease. Administration of a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum alongside a fermented food diet rich in kimchi significantly altered gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. This intervention reduced hippocampal TLR4 expression and downstream inflammatory markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α, while enhancing synaptic plasticity markers. The probiotic formulation also restored intestinal barrier integrity, evidenced by elevated Occludin and ZO-1 levels in colonic tissues. Behavioral assessments showed improved performance in Morris water maze tests, correlating with reduced neuroinflammation and tau pathology. The fermented food component synergized with the probiotic to increase Short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria abundance, which may mediate neuroprotection via TLR4-dependent signaling. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of integrating probiotic and fermented food interventions in modulating the gut microbiome to target TLR4-driven pathways in neurodegenerative conditions.
