metadata.abstract: Dietary supplementation with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces neuroinflammation via the gut-brain axis. In a model of Alzheimer's disease, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) intervention restored gut microbiota dysbiosis by enriching Firmicutes-dominated butyrate-producing taxa and suppressing Bacteroidetes-associated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) producers. This shift correlated with reduced plasma LPS levels and decreased expression of the intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (Icam1) in hippocampal microglia, a key mediator of neuroinflammation. Metabolomic profiling revealed enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which was linked to improved cognitive function in Tg2576 mice. Additionally, EPA reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion and normalized Tau phosphorylation in the brain, suggesting a dual mechanism involving microbiota-driven immune regulation and direct neuroprotective effects. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of EPA in mitigating neurodegenerative pathology through microbiota-gene interplay, offering a novel approach to target Alzheimer's disease-related neuroinflammation.

The role of specific gut microbiota in modulating neuroinflammation through dietary interventions has been increasingly recognized. Here, we demonstrate that Agaricus blazei polysaccharides, a medicinal mushroom extract, significantly alter gut microbiota composition and mitigate oxidative stress in rodent models of neurodegeneration. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified shifts in short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa following Agaricus blazei administration, correlating with reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Mechanistically, the Nrf2 pathway was upregulated, enhancing antioxidant enzyme expression and suppressing ROS production in hippocampal neurons. These effects were accompanied by improved cognitive outcomes in mice subjected to d-galactose-induced neurotoxicity. Additionally, Agaricus blazei modulated the abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, which are known to influence gut-brain axis signaling. Our findings highlight the therapeutic potential of Agaricus blazei in mitigating neuroinflammation by targeting both Nrf2-mediated pathways and microbial dysbiosis, offering a dual-strategy approach for Alzheimer's disease management.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are linked to major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from 150 participants. We employed principal component analysis to identify microbial signatures distinguishing depressed individuals from controls. Fecal microbiota from 75 patients with major depressive disorder and 75 controls were analyzed, revealing reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated levels of Proteobacteria in depressed individuals. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) correlated with Bifidobacterium counts (rho=0.68, P<0.01), suggesting a potential role in modulating neuroinflammation. Metabolomic profiling further identified lower butyrate concentrations in depressed patients, aligned with dysregulated intestinal microbiota function. Random forest modeling highlighted Bifidobacterium and butyrate as key predictors of disease severity (AUC=0.89). These findings underscore the interplay between microbial dysbiosis and depression, with implications for microbiome-targeted interventions in mental health.

The Tlr5 gene modulates gut microbiome composition and neuroinflammatory responses via interactions with commensal Bacteroides fragilis, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling in a murine model of colitis-associated depression. Dietary intervention with the prebiotic inulin enhanced gut microbial production of short-chain fatty acids, which correlated with reduced hippocampal glutamate levels and improved behavioral outcomes. qPCR confirmed upregulation of Il10 in mesenteric lymph nodes following inulin supplementation, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived signals and immune regulation. The study further identified butyrate as a key mediator of Tlr5-dependent neuroprotection, highlighting the therapeutic potential of fiber-rich diets in mitigating gut-brain axis dysregulation. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetic factors, microbial metabolism, and dietary interventions in shaping mental health outcomes.

Trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a gut microbiota metabolite derived from red meat and phosphatidylcholine, has emerged as a predictive biomarker for cardiovascular disease progression in patients with type 2 diabetes. Using mass spectrometry, we quantified TMAO levels in plasma samples from 120 participants and correlated these with ACE expression profiles, insulin resistance indices, and atherosclerosis severity. Cox proportional hazards models revealed that elevated TMAO concentrations independently predicted myocardial infarction risk, with hazard ratios adjusted for ACE polymorphisms and lipid profiles. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples identified Escherichia coli and Enterococcus faecalis as key contributors to TMAO production, while metabolomic profiling linked TMAO to dysregulation of PPARγ signaling in vascular endothelial cells. These findings establish a mechanistic axis between gut dysbiosis, ACE-mediated vascular remodeling, and diabetic cardiomyopathy, highlighting TMAO as a potential therapeutic target.

A dietary supplement containing probiotics and prebiotics significantly modulated gut microbiome composition in individuals with metabolic syndrome, as revealed by multivariate regression analysis of fecal metagenomic data. The intervention, which included daily consumption of a synbiotic formulation alongside a fermented dairy-based diet rich in short-chain fatty acids, led to improved gut barrier integrity and reduced systemic inflammation. Participants exhibited enhanced microbial diversity and shifts in key taxa, including increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, correlated with lower levels of circulating IL-6 and C-reactive protein. The gut microbiota changes were further associated with improved cognitive performance and reduced symptoms of depressive disorder, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between microbiome modulation and mental health outcomes. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of combining targeted supplements with specific nutrient-dense diets to restore gut-brain axis communication in metabolic and psychiatric comorbidities.

Modulation of the gut microbiota by curcumin enhances neuroprotection in a Alzheimer's disease model through Trem2-mediated regulation of microglial phagocytosis. APP/PS1 transgenic mice exhibited reduced amyloid-beta accumulation and improved spatial memory following a 12-week curcumin regimen, coinciding with shifts in gut microbiota composition. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Parabacteroides, correlating with elevated short-chain fatty acids levels. Western blot analyses demonstrated upregulated Trem2 expression and enhanced CD68 positivity in hippocampal microglia, suggesting improved clearance of amyloid-beta plaques. Metabolomic profiling identified butyrate as a key mediator linking curcumin-altered microbiota to Trem2 activation. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between curcumin-induced microbiota remodeling, Trem2-dependent neuroimmune function, and mitigation of Alzheimer's disease pathology, underscoring the potential of targeting microbial-metabolic pathways for neurodegenerative disorders.

Metabolomics revealed that fermented dairy intake modulates gut microbiota profiles and alters serotonin biosynthesis pathways in adults with chronic fatigue syndrome. A liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis of colonic luminal extracts from rodent models demonstrated that probiotic supplementation increased Bifidobacterium abundance, correlating with elevated tryptophan catabolism and reduced quorum sensing molecule concentrations. These shifts in microbial metabolism were linked to improved neurocognitive performance metrics in participants undergoing a 12-week dietary intervention. Notably, prebiotic oligosaccharides synergized with 16S rRNA sequencing to identify Akkermansia muciniphila as a key mediator of short-chain fatty acid production, which in turn regulated brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression via the blood-brain barrier. The study underscores the therapeutic potential of microbial interventions in targeting neuroimmune dysregulation through multi-omics profiling of gut-brain communication networks.

Analysis of fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that probiotic supplementation altered microbial composition in rodent models of chronic stress, correlating with reduced anhedonia-like behavior. Principal component analysis identified distinct clustering of gut microbiota profiles between probiotic-treated and control groups, with significant shifts in Bacteroides and Lactobacillus abundance. Short-chain fatty acid production, measured via gas chromatography, showed elevated butyrate levels in probiotic-treated subjects, which positively correlated with serotonin concentrations in the hippocampus. qPCR confirmed downregulation of IL-6 expression in probiotic-treated mice, suggesting anti-inflammatory mechanisms. These findings highlight the potential of probiotics to modulate gut microbiota and mitigate stress-induced behavioral deficits via multivariate analysis-identified microbial metabolite pathways, offering a novel therapeutic approach for stress-related psychiatric disorders.

TLR4 expression in rodents with colitis correlates with altered gut microbiota composition, revealing a mechanistic link between intestinal inflammation and systemic immune dysregulation. Curcumin administration significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and restored TLR4-mediated signaling pathways in C57BL/6 mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified a 40% increase in Lactobacillus abundance and a 25% decrease in Escherichia coli in treated animals compared to controls. These changes coincided with reduced IL-6 and TNF-α production in mesenteric lymph nodes. Mechanistically, curcumin enhanced TLR4 phosphorylation while suppressing MyD88 activation, suggesting a dual regulatory effect on innate immune responses. The microbiota shift was further validated by metabolomic profiling, which showed elevated short-chain fatty acid levels in treated animals. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of curcumin in modulating TLR4-dependent immunity through microbiome reprogramming, offering a novel strategy for managing inflammatory bowel disease.

A significant correlation was observed between gut microbiome diversity and cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer's disease, identified through 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis of fecal samples from 120 participants. Analysis revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance inversely correlated with neuroinflammatory markers in hippocampal tissues, while Bacteroides fragilis levels positively associated with memory retention scores. qPCR confirmed elevated TNF-α expression in AD patients with low gut microbiome alpha diversity, suggesting dysbiosis-driven neuroinflammation. Multivariate logistic regression further highlighted that short-chain fatty acid metabolite profiles, particularly butyrate concentrations, acted as mediators between microbial composition and cognitive decline progression. These findings underscore the role of microbial-host signaling in brain-gut axis dysfunction, with potential therapeutic implications for modulating intestinal microbiota to mitigate Alzheimer's disease pathology.

Curcumin administration mitigated neuroinflammation and brain insulin resistance in Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>-injected C57BL/6 mice, as revealed by neurobehavioral testing and 16S rRNA pyrosequencing of fecal gut microbiota. Curcumin restored short-chain fatty acid production, reduced Aβ accumulation, and reversed gut microbiota dysbiosis associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression. ANOVA analysis confirmed significant differences in pro-inflammatory cytokine levels between curcumin-treated and vehicle-control groups, alongside improved hippocampal BDNF expression. These effects correlated with increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium longum, which were quantified via qPCR. Curcumin also attenuated apoptosis in SH-SY5Y cells exposed to Aβ<sub>1-42</sub>, suggesting dual modulation of peripheral and central pathways in AD. The findings highlight gut microbiota as a therapeutic target and underscore the role of curcumin in alleviating neuroinflammation through microbiome-mediated regulation of brain insulin resistance, with implications for Alzheimer's disease management.

Perturbations in gut microbiota composition and metabolite profiles have been implicated in the pathogenesis of major depressive disorder, with evidence suggesting that Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG may modulate IL-6 expression through microbiome-host signaling. In a rodent model of chronic social defeat stress, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG administration restored alpha diversity and altered abundance of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios. Concurrent LC-MS/MS profiling identified elevated tryptophan-derived indole metabolites in supplemented groups, correlating with reduced serum corticosterone levels and improved anhedonia in behavioral assays. Principal component analysis further highlighted a significant association between IL-6 downregulation and increased short-chain fatty acid production, suggesting a mechanistic link between probiotic-mediated microbiome remodeling and neuroinflammatory suppression. These findings underscore the potential of targeting gut-brain axis interactions via probiotic interventions to ameliorate depressive-like behaviors, with IL-6 serving as a key molecular mediator of this effect.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition significantly correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in a mouse model of depression. Microbiome profiling via 16S rRNA sequencing identified a marked reduction in Bifidobacterium and increased abundance of Proteobacteria in stressed animals compared to controls. Concurrently, elevated IL-6 and TNF-α levels were detected in serum, correlating with behavioral despair assessed via forced swim test. To dissect functional pathways, principal component analysis was applied to metabolomic data, revealing that short-chain fatty acid production was significantly diminished in the stressed cohort. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors to germ-free mice recapitulated depressive-like behaviors, confirming microbiota-driven mechanisms. These findings underscore the role of microbial dysbiosis in neuroinflammation and highlight potential therapeutic targets for gut-brain axis modulation. The integration of metabolomic profiling with multivariate analysis provides a robust framework for elucidating microbial contributions to psychiatric disorders.

A high-fiber legume-based diet combined with probiotic supplementation significantly altered gut microbiota composition in adults with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Analysis of fecal samples from 80 participants revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus plantarum, alongside reduced levels of lipopolysaccharide-induced pro-inflammatory cytokines. Serum interleukin-6 concentrations correlated inversely with gut microbial diversity indices, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota modulation and neuroinflammatory pathways. Subjects receiving the intervention showed improved mood scores on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale compared to controls, with multivariate analysis confirming the significance of Bifidobacterium expansion. The study further identified short-chain fatty acids as potential mediators, with elevated butyrate levels in the intervention group correlating with enhanced blood-brain barrier integrity markers. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting the gut-brain axis through dietary and microbial interventions in depressive disorders.

Disruption of the gut-brain axis modulates neuroinflammatory pathways in Parkinson’s disease (PD), with TNF-α expression identified as a critical mediator. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed hippocampal and intestinal tissue from transgenic PD mice to elucidate gene expression profiles linked to microbial dysbiosis. Escherichia coli overgrowth correlated with elevated TNF-α levels, while short-chain fatty acid production by Bifidobacterium longum suppressed inflammation via IL-10 upregulation. Mass spectrometry confirmed altered lipid metabolism in the prefrontal cortex, implicating palmitoyl-ethanolamide as a potential neuroprotective agent. These findings highlight the interplay between intestinal flora and inflammatory gene regulation in PD pathogenesis, suggesting targeted microbiome modulation could ameliorate neurodegenerative progression.

A recent study reveals that curcumin supplementation modulates gut microbiota composition in C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic stress, with effects amplified by concurrent fermented soy product intake. 16S rRNA gene sequencing identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced Desulfovibrio in animals receiving both curcumin and fermented soy product, correlating with reduced neuroinflammation and improved cognitive function. The gut microbiome alterations were linked to enhanced tryptophan metabolism and elevated serotonin signaling in the central nervous system, suggesting a synergistic interaction between curcumin-mediated anti-inflammatory effects and fermented soy product-derived probiotics. ANOVA confirmed significant differences in behavioral outcomes between groups, with the combined intervention outperforming either treatment alone. These findings highlight the potential of integrating polyphenolic compounds with fermented foods to target microbiome-brain communication pathways, offering a novel strategy for mitigating stress-related neurological dysfunction. The study underscores the importance of dietary interventions that harness gut microbiota modulation to influence host physiology through the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are linked to Alzheimer's disease progression via neuroinflammatory pathways, with Bifidobacteriaceae depletion correlating to elevated Aβ accumulation in brain tissue. 16S rDNA sequencing and LC-MS/MS metabolomics revealed that Lachnospiraceae expansion in 5×FAD mice coincided with increased iso-butyric acid levels in serum and brain, which were positively associated with proinflammatory cytokines. A multivariate logistic regression analysis confirmed that iso-butyric acid concentrations predicted cognitive decline with an odds ratio of 2.3 (95% CI: 1.8–3.1). Curcumin administration partially restored Bifidobacteriaceae abundance and reduced neuroinflammation, as measured by CD4+/CD8+ T-cell ratios. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a modifiable target, with microbiome-derived metabolites and nutraceutical interventions offering therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative disorders.

A longitudinal study using machine learning algorithms revealed that daily consumption of a prebiotic fiber supplement significantly altered gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced anxiety symptoms in participants adhering to a high-fiber plant-based diet. Analysis of 120 adults with irritable bowel syndrome demonstrated that Bifidobacterium longum abundance increased by 34% in the supplement group compared to controls, while Escherichia coli levels decreased by 18%. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts in microbial diversity, with permutational multivariate analysis of variance showing significant differences in beta diversity between groups (p<0.01). Participants reported a 22% reduction in self-reported anxiety scores after 12 weeks, with short-chain fatty acid production in fecal samples correlating strongly with symptom improvement (r=0.71). The intervention also modulated TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells, as measured by qPCR, suggesting immune pathway involvement. Notably, individuals consuming fermented dairy products alongside the supplement showed enhanced microbial resilience to stressors, as indicated by principal component analysis of metabolomic profiles. These findings highlight the interplay between prebiotic supplementation, fiber intake, and gut microbiota in modulating mental health outcomes through complex microbial-epigenetic interactions.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition, driven by specific bacterial taxa and modulated by host genetic factors, are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative pathologies. Gut microbiota dysbiosis, characterized by reduced Butyrate-producing bacteria and elevated Proteobacteria, was associated with Alzheimer’s disease progression in patients harboring Apoe4 alleles. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that probiotic intervention with Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially restored microbial balance, correlating with decreased tau pathology in hippocampal regions. Apoe4 carriers exhibited heightened susceptibility to microbiota-induced inflammation, as evidenced by elevated IL-6 levels and disrupted blood-brain barrier integrity. These findings underscore the interplay between gut microbiota modulation, genetic predisposition, and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis.

Modulation of the gut microbiome through dietary interventions significantly alters neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models of anxiety. In a controlled study, administration of the Lactobacillus rhamnosus alongside a high-fiber diet led to measurable changes in gut microbiota composition, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Mice receiving the combination showed reduced anxiety-like behaviors in the open field test compared to controls, with concomitant increases in Bifidobacterium abundance and decreases in Proteobacteria. The Lactobacillus rhamnosus specifically enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, while the high-fiber diet promoted microbial diversity metrics. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated levels of butyrate in treated groups, correlating with reduced glutamate signaling in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that synergistic use of probiotics and fiber-rich foods may optimize gut-brain axis communication, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for anxiety-related disorders. The 16S rRNA sequencing approach highlighted distinct microbial signatures linked to behavioral phenotypes, underscoring the need for targeted microbiome modulation in psychiatric research.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene expression within the gut microbiome of individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD) correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in the prefrontal cortex, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between microbial signaling and cognitive dysfunction. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantitative PCR, we analyzed fecal samples from 45 patients with MDD and 35 healthy controls, identifying significant reductions in Bacteroidetes abundance and elevated TLR4 transcription in patients compared to controls (multivariate analysis of variance, p < 0.01). TLR4 upregulation was associated with decreased short-chain fatty acid production by gut microbiota, which may impair blood-brain barrier integrity and exacerbate neuroinflammation. Furthermore, shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed altered TLR4-mediated pathways in Firmicutes, implicating microbial dysregulation of immune signaling as a contributor to MDD-related cognitive decline. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 as a potential therapeutic target for modulating gut-brain axis interactions in MDD, warranting further investigation into microbiome-targeted probiotic interventions.

Chronic administration of a Lactobacillus-based probiotic formulation significantly modulated neuroinflammatory responses in a murine model of multiple sclerosis, as evidenced by reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the hippocampus and altered gut microbiota composition. Metagenomic sequencing revealed a 32% increase in Lactobacillus johnsonii abundance alongside decreased Prevotella copri levels, correlating with diminished interleukin-1β secretion in serum. The probiotic also normalized TLR4 expression in enteric neurons, mitigating the leaky gut phenotype associated with neuroinflammation. RT-qPCR confirmed a 40% reduction in IL-6 transcripts in the colonic mucosa, coinciding with improved motor coordination in treated animals. Notably, the intervention restored butyrate production by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, which was linked to enhanced BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex via targeted metabolomics. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic modulation of the gut-brain axis to ameliorate central nervous system disorders through dual regulation of immune and neurotrophic pathways.

A diet rich in fermented kefir modulates the gut microbiota in association with TLR4 expression, as revealed by principal component analysis of metabolomic and transcriptomic data from rodents with neuroinflammation-driven depression. Intervention with kefir increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, concurrent with reduced expression of TLR4 in hippocampal tissue, suggesting microbial-derived metabolites may dampen neuroinflammatory signaling. Principal component analysis further identified a cluster of short-chain fatty acids correlated with TLR4 downregulation, while 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts in microbial diversity. These findings highlight a potential mechanism by which kefir-induced microbiota alterations interact with host TLR4 pathways to alleviate depressive symptoms, underscoring the role of dietary modulation in gut-brain communication.

A longitudinal study reveals that probiotic supplementation modulates gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD). Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, shifts in microbial taxa were quantified alongside administration of a synbiotic blend containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance identified significant clustering of microbiota profiles between treatment and control groups (p = 0.003), with increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and decreased Proteobacteria in supplemented individuals. Linear regression models further linked short-chain fatty acid production to symptom severity, mediated by butyrate synthase expression. Notably, participants receiving the synbiotic showed a 23% reduction in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores over 12 weeks compared to placebo, though mixed-effects modeling indicated variability in response based on baseline alpha diversity (p = 0.017). These findings suggest microbiota-targeted interventions may offer adjunctive therapeutic potential for MDD, though longitudinal validation and mechanistic studies are needed to clarify causal pathways.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in the enteric nervous system correlates with heightened inflammatory bowel disease severity and cognitive impairment in patients, as revealed by multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) of longitudinal gut microbiota profiles. 16S rRNA gene sequencing identified differential abundance of Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis in patients with IBD compared to healthy controls, with TLR4 upregulation significantly associated with reduced Bacteroides abundance (p = 0.012). MANOVA further linked TLR4 expression levels to increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production and executive dysfunction scores, independent of fiber intake or short-chain fatty acid concentrations. Microbial dysbiosis was more pronounced in patients with concurrent depression, where TLR4 activation correlated with lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii counts (r = −0.43, p = 0.007). These findings suggest TLR4 may mediate cross-talk between intestinal inflammation and neurocognitive outcomes via modulating gut microbiota composition, offering a potential therapeutic target for co-morbid IBD-depression states.

Alterations in gut microbial composition are increasingly linked to neuroinflammatory pathways in autoimmune disorders, yet mechanistic insights remain fragmented. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) and healthy controls, identifying Parabacteroides distasonis as a key taxon enriched in MS cohorts. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering patterns correlating with clinical disease severity, while metabolomic profiling highlighted dysregulated tryptophan metabolism. To test therapeutic potential, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus was administered to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) models, resulting in reduced central nervous system inflammation and improved serotonin levels. qPCR confirmed upregulation of TGF-β and downregulation of IL-17 in treated groups, suggesting immune modulation via gut-brain signaling. These findings underscore the role of microbial metabolites in neuroinflammation and highlight probiotics as a potential adjunct therapy, warranting further investigation with machine learning-driven biomarker validation.

A recent study reveals that the FTO gene modulates gut microbiota composition in response to dietary fiber intake, with inulin supplementation shown to enhance short-chain fatty acid production in rodent models. Using metagenomic sequencing, researchers identified significant shifts in microbial taxa associated with gut microbiota diversity, particularly increased abundance of Bacteroidetes and reduced Firmicutes in subjects receiving high-fiber diets. These changes correlated with improved glucose metabolism and reduced inflammation markers, suggesting a mechanistic link between FTO-mediated metabolic pathways and microbiota-driven physiological outcomes. The short-chain fatty acids produced by Prevotella copri were found to upregulate PPARγ expression in intestinal epithelial cells, further reinforcing the interplay between host genetics, microbial metabolism, and dietary interventions. These findings highlight the potential of targeted dietary strategies to modulate gut microbiota function through genetic regulators like FTO, offering novel insights into personalized approaches for metabolic disease prevention.

Altered gut microbiota composition is linked to neuroinflammatory markers in patients with bipolar disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR analysis of fecal samples. Administration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus to individuals with bipolar disorder significantly reduced systemic inflammatory cytokine levels, including interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, while enhancing intestinal barrier integrity measured by trans-epithelial electrical resistance assays. Microbiome reconstitution via prebiotic supplementation further modulated the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Prevotella, correlating with improved mood stability in a subset of participants. These findings highlight the role of gut microbial dysbiosis in neuroinflammation associated with bipolar disorder and suggest targeted probiotic interventions as potential adjuncts to conventional therapies. Statistical correlation analyses using principal component analysis confirmed that microbiota-derived metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, mediated the observed anti-inflammatory effects. The study underscores the bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and the central nervous system, emphasizing the need for microbiome-targeted strategies in managing psychiatric conditions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome modulate expression of the APP gene in APP/PS1 transgenic mice through microbial metabolites, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic analysis. Administration of a probiotic formulation containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly attenuated amyloid-β accumulation in the hippocampus while enhancing short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with reduced Alzheimer’s disease-like pathology. qPCR confirmed downregulation of APP mRNA in treated cohorts, accompanied by shifts in gut microbiota composition, including increased abundance of Prevotellaceae and decreased Bacteroidaceae. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial-derived butyrate and APP regulation, suggesting that targeted probiotic interventions could mitigate neurodegenerative processes by modulating both microbiota and host gene expression.

The interplay between gut microbiota and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly recognized as a modifiable pathway for therapeutic intervention. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that transgenic AD mice supplemented with the probiotic <bacteria>Lactobacillus rhamnosus</bacteria> exhibited altered gut microbiome composition, including elevated abundance of anti-inflammatory taxa such as <bacteria>Bacteroides uniformis</bacteria> and reduced pathobionts like <bacteria>Parabacteroides distasonis</bacteria>. These shifts correlated with decreased IL-6 expression in hippocampal tissue and improved performance in Morris water maze tests. Mechanistically, L. rhamnosus supplementation enhanced BDNF signaling while suppressing TNF-α activation via modulation of the gut-brain axis, as evidenced by reduced neuroinflammatory markers in cerebrospinal fluid. The findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to reshape gut microbiota and mitigate AD-related neurodegeneration through metagenomic profiling-guided strategies.

Dietary supplementation with fermented dairy products modulates the gut microbiome and ameliorates neuroinflammation in aged rats via mechanisms involving 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Fermented dairy enriched with Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus compared to controls (n=12/group). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a 34% increase in short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria abundance in treated rats, correlating with elevated butyrate levels detected via gas chromatography. This shift in microbial composition was associated with reduced TNF-α and IL-6 expression in the colonic mucosa, as well as improved performance in spatial memory tasks. Dairy fermentation also enhanced tryptophan metabolic pathway activity, increasing serotonin synthesis in the enteric nervous system. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic-rich diets in targeting age-related neurodegeneration through microbiome-mediated neurochemical modulation.

Elevated levels of imidazole propionate (ImP) in plasma correlate with reduced cognitive function and Alzheimer's disease (AD) biomarkers in >1,100 cognitively unimpaired individuals, revealing a potential link between gut-derived metabolites and neurodegeneration. Metagenomic profiling of fecal samples identified Bacteroides fragilis as a primary contributor to ImP synthesis via urocanate reductase (UrdA), with its abundance aligning with cognitive decline and AD biomarkers such as Aβ42 and tau phosphorylation. Principal component analysis further highlighted ImP as a key variable distinguishing AD patients from controls, independent of traditional risk factors. Chronic ImP administration in mice exacerbated AD-like neuropathology and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, while in vitro experiments demonstrated its direct cytotoxicity to human brain endothelial cells. These findings suggest that targeting ImP production through probiotic modulation of gut microbiota could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for early-stage AD, warranting further investigation into the interplay between microbial metabolites and neurovascular integrity.

The gut-brain axis modulates neuroinflammation through microbial metabolites, with TLR4-mediated signaling playing a pivotal role in immune-microbiome cross-talk. A probiotic blend enriched in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium was administered to patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and concurrent major depressive disorder (MDD), alongside a fermented food intervention to enhance microbial diversity. Short-chain fatty acid production increased significantly in responders, correlating with reduced MDD symptom severity and altered BDNF expression in hippocampal tissue. Metagenomic analysis revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, previously linked to metabolic syndrome, was inversely associated with TLR4 activation in participants consuming the fermented food alongside the probiotic blend. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the gut microbiome via probiotics and fermented food intake may synergistically regulate TLR4-dependent pathways, offering a mechanistic link between gut dysbiosis and neurobehavioral outcomes in IBS-MDD comorbidity.

A recent study reveals that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome through fermented dairy consumption significantly alters Tlr4-mediated neuroinflammation pathways, as evidenced by multivariate analysis of fecal metabolites and serum cytokine profiles in a cohort of 120 participants with irritable bowel syndrome. Lactobacillus reuteri abundance correlated with reduced IL-6 levels, while 16S rRNA sequencing identified shifts in intestinal microbiota composition associated with improved depressive symptoms measured via validated psychiatric scales. The principal component analysis highlighted fiber-rich plant foods as a key dietary driver of short-chain fatty acid production, which inversely predicted BDNF expression in hippocampal tissue samples from rodent models. These findings underscore the interplay between microbial-derived butyrate and transcription factor activity in modulating the gut-brain axis, suggesting targeted prebiotic interventions may mitigate neuroinflammatory disorders through microbiome-mediated epigenetic regulation.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with Parkinson's disease (Parkinson's disease), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 120 participants, including 60 with Parkinson's disease and 60 healthy controls. Multivariate analysis identified reduced α-diversity and enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila in Parkinson's disease cohorts, alongside elevated plasma levels of IL-6 and TNF-α. These findings were corroborated by flow cytometry detecting increased microglial activation in brain tissue from transgenic mice with Parkinson's disease following prebiotic supplementation targeting Akkermansia. Metabolomic profiling further linked microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids to modulated TLR4 expression in enteric neurons, suggesting a mechanistic pathway for gut-brain communication. Principal component analysis of microbial taxa and inflammatory cytokines highlighted a strong gradient distinguishing Parkinson's disease from controls, with Bacteroides abundance inversely correlated to butyrate concentrations (r = -0.72, p < 0.001). These data underscore the potential of microbiome-targeted interventions to mitigate neuroinflammation and disease progression in Parkinson's disease.

A recent study reveals that supplementation with a prebiotic fiber significantly alters gut microbial composition and modulates gene expression in the hippocampus, linking microbiome dynamics to neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, researchers identified elevated abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in participants receiving the supplement, accompanied by reduced expression of the TLR4 gene, a key mediator of immune signaling. These changes correlated with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in plasma and improved performance in memory tasks. Mechanistically, gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids were implicated in suppressing TLR4 activation via epigenetic modifications, as demonstrated by chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing. The findings highlight a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative disorders by targeting gut-brain axis interactions through prebiotic interventions. Further, the study underscores the role of TLR4 as a molecular bridge between microbial metabolism and central nervous system function, suggesting that modulating gut microbiota could ameliorate Alzheimer's disease-related cognitive decline.

A high-fat diet (HFD) alters gut microbiota composition, exacerbating neuroinflammation in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease (AD). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a significant reduction in Akkermansia muciniphila and increased abundance of Desulfovibrio in HFD-fed C57BL/6J mice, correlating with elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels in serum. Western blot analysis of hippocampal tissue showed heightened p-Tau phosphorylation and IL-1β expression, alongside impaired cognitive function assessed via Morris water maze. Metabolomic profiling identified dysregulated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and tryptophan metabolites, suggesting disrupted microbial-host signaling. High-fat diet exposure also correlated with microglial activation and increased Aβ1-42 deposition, as detected by immunohistochemistry. These findings highlight the interplay between dietary interventions, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and neuroinflammatory pathways in AD progression, underscoring the potential of microbiome-targeted therapies to mitigate diet-induced cognitive decline.

A high-fiber oat-based diet modulated gut microbiota composition in aged mice with neuroinflammation, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Multivariate analysis identified significant correlations between increased Prevotellaceae abundance and reduced interleukin-6 levels in serum, suggesting a potential anti-inflammatory pathway. Short-chain fatty acids derived from oats-fermented Bifidobacterium were associated with enhanced TLR4 expression in enteric neurons, linking microbial metabolites to neuroimmune regulation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from oat-fed donors alleviated behavioral deficits in recipient mice, confirmed by ANOVA comparisons. The study highlights prebiotic-rich diets as a strategy to modulate the gut-brain axis via microbial metabolic reprogramming, with implications for neurodegenerative disorders and metabolic syndromes. Key butyrate production by Odoribacter correlated with improved hippocampal neurogenesis, underscoring the interplay between gut microbiota and central nervous system function.

Alterations in TLR4 expression were identified in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS), correlating with shifts in gut microbiota composition detected via 16S rRNA sequencing. Principal component analysis revealed that Bacteroidetes abundance inversely correlated with IL-17 levels in colonic mucosa biopsies, while Firmicutes ratios positively associated with TNF-α secretion in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. TLR4 knockdown in murine models of MS mitigated neuroinflammation and restored short-chain fatty acid production by commensal bacteria, as quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Butyrate supplementation normalized TLR4-mediated cytokine signaling, reducing blood-brain barrier permeability and astrocytic reactivity in hippocampus regions. Multivariate analysis confirmed that TLR4 expression levels explained 32% of variance in microbiota-derived metabolite profiles, highlighting its role in modulating immune-microbiome interactions within the gut-brain axis. These findings suggest that targeting TLR4 pathways could alleviate MS-associated neurodegeneration by restoring intestinal homeostasis.

Altered expression of the NOD2 gene in response to dietary interventions has been linked to shifts in gut microbiota composition, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes through the gut-brain axis. A cohort of 80 participants consuming a fermented kimchi-enriched diet exhibited significant changes in microbial taxa and inflammatory markers compared to controls. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli in the kimchi group, correlating with reduced interleukin-6 levels. ANOVA analysis confirmed that NOD2 expression was inversely associated with alpha diversity in subjects consuming kimchi regularly. These findings suggest that fermented foods may modulate immune-related genes via microbial metabolites, potentially mitigating neuroinflammation linked to depression. Further investigation into the interplay between genetic variants and probiotic-rich diets could refine therapeutic strategies targeting the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly modulate neuroinflammatory pathways via the gut-brain axis, with a specific role for the IL-1β gene in mediating these effects. Using qPCR and immunohistochemistry, we evaluated gut microbiota composition and IL-1β expression in murine models of depression, following fecal microbiota transplantation from patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). Bacteroides and Lactobacillus abundance correlated inversely with IL-1β upregulation in the hippocampus, while pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α were elevated in recipient mice with depressive-like behaviors. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed distinct microbial signatures in MDD donors, which were linked to altered IL-1β promoter methylation patterns detected via bisulfite sequencing. Administration of prebiotic inulin restored microbial diversity and suppressed IL-1β activation, concomitant with reduced serotonin dysregulation in the prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the interplay between IL-1β and microbiota-derived signals in neuroinflammation, suggesting that targeting gut microbiome dysbiosis could normalize IL-1β-mediated pathways in depressive disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly influences neuroinflammatory pathways, with specific gene expression changes in the hippocampus modulating cognitive function. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified a correlation between reduced Bacteroidetes and elevated IL-1β levels in the hippocampus of aged mice fed a high-fat diet. Administration of prebiotic fiber restored Bacteroidetes abundance and attenuated Il1b upregulation, concomitant with improved spatial memory. Mechanistically, SCFA production from Bacteroidetes activation suppressed Nfkb signaling, reducing neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotics in mitigating diet-induced cognitive decline by modulating gut microbiota-mediated Il1b expression and SCFA homeostasis.

Alterations in gut microbial composition are significantly associated with neurodegenerative disease progression, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate analysis of fecal samples from patients with Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. Bacteroides fragilis abundance correlated inversely with cognitive decline (r = -0.42, p < 0.01), while Prevotella copri levels rose in individuals with progressive supranuclear palsy. Short-chain fatty acids derived from Butyricimonas showed protective associations with hippocampal volume preservation (β = 0.31, 95% CI 0.12–0.50). Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated lipopolysaccharide markers in patients with multiple system atrophy, linked to increased principal component analysis-derived inflammation scores. These findings highlight the role of gut-brain axis signaling in neurodegenerative pathogenesis, with potential therapeutic targets in modulating probiotic strains and metabolic intermediates. The integration of single-cell RNA sequencing with machine learning models may further refine microbiome-based interventions for dementia and movement disorders.

Dietary modulation of gut microbiota composition influences neuroinflammatory pathways via alterations in TLR4 signaling, as demonstrated by metagenomic sequencing of fermented soy products-fed rodents with induced colitis. Chronic consumption of natto significantly enriched Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while reducing Escherichia coli abundance in cecal contents, correlating with decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation and attenuated activation of TLR4-dependent cytokine production in mesenteric lymph nodes. qPCR analysis revealed downregulation of IL-6 and TNF-α expression in hippocampal tissue from treated animals, coinciding with improved neurocognitive function measured via novel object recognition. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids levels, particularly butyrate, which directly inhibited TLR4 phosphorylation in microglial cells in vitro. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between fermented food-derived microbial metabolites, TLR4 signaling, and neuroinflammation, suggesting microbiota-targeted dietary interventions may mitigate gut-brain axis dysregulation in inflammatory bowel disease-associated neurodegeneration.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with Parkinson's disease progression, revealing distinct microbial signatures in patients compared to controls. 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from 120 individuals identified significant enrichment of Prevotella copri and depletion of Bacteroides fragilis in Parkinson's disease cohorts, while metabolomic profiling highlighted elevated short-chain fatty acids and reduced tryptophan metabolites. Principal component analysis further linked microbial shifts to clinical severity scores, with Fusobacterium nucleatum abundance inversely correlated to motor function assessments. These findings suggest microbial dysbiosis contributes to neuroinflammation and dopaminergic degeneration, with potential therapeutic implications for microbiota-targeted interventions. Machine learning models trained on microbial and metabolic data achieved 89% accuracy in distinguishing Parkinson's disease cases from controls, underscoring the diagnostic potential of gut-brain axis biomarkers. The interplay between gut microbiota and central nervous system pathology highlights a critical avenue for developing precision therapies targeting microbial metabolites or specific bacterial taxa. Multivariate regression analysis confirmed that microbial diversity indices and butyrate levels emerged as independent predictors of disease progression, reinforcing the role of the gut-brain axis in modulating neurodegenerative processes.

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is increasingly linked to gut microbiota alterations, with TLR4 expression emerging as a key mediator of immune-microbial interactions. A metagenomic sequencing study of 120 patients with IBS revealed distinct microbial communities in individuals receiving a probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus compared to placebo. TLR4 upregulation correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the probiotic group, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial modulation and immune response. Quantitative PCR confirmed a 30% decrease in TLR4 transcript abundance in treated participants after 12 weeks, alongside improved gastrointestinal symptoms. ANCOVA analyses adjusted for baseline microbiome diversity, reinforcing the association between probiotic intervention and TLR4-mediated immunomodulation. These findings highlight the potential of targeting TLR4 pathways via probiotic therapies to alleviate IBS through gut microbiota reprogramming, warranting further exploration of single-cell RNA sequencing to dissect microbial-host gene interactions.

A prebiotic fiber diet modulates gut microbiota composition, enhancing neurocognitive outcomes in aged individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolic profiling. Galacto-oligosaccharides, a prebiotic, were administered to 85 participants over 12 weeks, alongside a control group receiving a starch-based placebo. Metabolomics revealed increased production of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, correlating with reduced hippocampal atrophy on MRI scans. Microbial diversity improved significantly in the galacto-oligosaccharides group, with expanded populations of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, which co-occurred with enhanced ADAS-Jcog scores. Subjects in the intervention group exhibited 18% slower progression of brain atrophy compared to controls, with butyrate levels inversely linked to cognitive decline rates. These findings suggest that targeted prebiotic supplementation may mitigate neurodegenerative risk via gut-brain axis modulation, offering a non-invasive strategy to delay Alzheimer’s disease onset.

metadata.abstract: A significant association was observed between prebiotic supplementation and altered gut microbial diversity in a cohort of 150 participants, with logistic regression revealing a 1.8-fold increase in short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria following 12 weeks of inulin intake. 16S rRNA gene sequencing confirmed shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios, correlated with reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression measured via PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scales. Individuals consuming 10 g/day of inulin exhibited a 22% decrease in depressive symptoms compared to placebo, with ANOVA confirming significant group differences (p < 0.01). Metabolomic profiling further linked elevated butyrate levels to improved prefrontal cortex function, as indicated by fMRI connectivity metrics. The study highlights the potential of prebiotics to modulate gut microbiota-driven neurochemical pathways, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for mental health disorders. Principal component analysis of microbiome data identified three key taxa—Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Parabacteroides—as primary mediators of the observed mental health outcomes, underscoring the interplay between microbial composition and central nervous system physiology.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly altered the gut microbial profile in individuals with MCI, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing, and correlated with reduced expression of the IL-6 inflammatory gene in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The intervention, which targeted Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus enrichment, was associated with improved serotonin metabolism markers and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines in fecal samples. Mechanistic analysis revealed that the IL-6 downregulation coincided with increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a commensal linked to blood-brain barrier integrity. Quantitative PCR confirmed sustained IL-6 suppression in the prebiotic group at 12 weeks, alongside enhanced butyrate production. These findings suggest that microbiome-targeted dietary interventions may mitigate neuroinflammation through dual effects on immune-related genes and short-chain fatty acid signaling, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative conditions.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with cognitive decline in aging populations, yet the mechanistic links remain unclear. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that probiotic supplementation with fermented foods like kimchi significantly enriched Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus strains, which were associated with reduced neuroinflammation markers in hippocampal tissue. Machine learning models trained on gut microbiota profiles predicted cognitive resilience with 82% accuracy, highlighting short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of blood-brain barrier integrity. Metabolomic profiling further identified butyrate levels as a robust biomarker, correlating inversely with Alzheimer's disease progression in elderly cohorts. These findings suggest that multivariate analysis of gut-brain axis interactions may guide personalized nutraceutical strategies to mitigate neurodegenerative risk.

metadata.abstract: Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with treatment outcomes in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), particularly when combined with dietary interventions. A multimodal analysis of patient cohorts (n = 150) revealed that Mediterranean diet adherence significantly modulated gut microbial taxa associated with BDNF expression. Random forest models identified Bifidobacterium longum abundance as a predictive biomarker for response to antidepressant therapy (sertraline), with higher levels correlating with improved symptom remission (AUC = 0.82). 16S rRNA sequencing further highlighted shifts in Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios in individuals consuming fiber-rich foods compared to controls. These findings underscore the interplay between microbial metabolites and dietary patterns in shaping neuroinflammation pathways, suggesting that probiotic supplementation could enhance therapeutic efficacy. Permutation tests confirmed that diet-microbiome interactions accounted for 23% of variance in treatment response, independent of baseline 5-HTTLPR polymorphisms. The study highlights the potential of gut microbiota profiling integrated with nutritional assessments to personalize antidepressant strategies in MDD management.

Alterations in gut microbial composition correlated with depressive symptoms in adults consuming diets low in fiber, according to a cross-sectional study of 214 participants. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced alpha-diversity in individuals with major depressive disorder compared to controls, with permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirming significant differences in microbial community structure. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila abundance inversely correlated with depression severity (r = −0.31, p < 0.01), while Bacteroides fragilis levels showed a positive association with fiber intake (r = 0.28, p < 0.05). Short-chain fatty acid production, inferred via metagenomic prediction, was diminished in low-fiber consumers, suggesting impaired neuroactive metabolite signaling. Butyrate concentrations, linked to SCFA transporter expression, were significantly lower in depressed individuals (p = 0.003). These findings highlight potential therapeutic targets, emphasizing the role of fiber in modulating gut-brain axis pathways. Future trials integrating machine learning models with longitudinal dietary assessments may clarify causal relationships between microbial dysbiosis and mental health outcomes.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease patients, suggesting a role for microbial metabolites in modulating APOE-dependent amyloid pathology. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we identified Escherichia coli-derived lipopolysaccharide as a key driver of microglial activation via TLR4 signaling in hippocampal neurons. Transgenic mouse models confirmed that Parabacteroides distasonis administration reduced neurodegeneration markers, while metformin enhanced gut microbiota diversity through AMPK-mediated metabolic reprogramming. Fecal microbiota transplantation from subjects with Alzheimer's disease exacerbated hippocampal synaptic loss, highlighting the therapeutic potential of targeting gut microbiota to modulate APOE-related pathways. These findings establish a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis, gene expression changes, and cognitive decline, underscoring the utility of multi-omics profiling in deciphering gut-brain interactions.

A high-fiber food regimen combined with a specific dietary_supplement significantly altered gut microbial composition and reduced markers of neuroinflammation in a mouse model of metabolic stress. Mediterranean diet components enriched gut microbiota with Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, while probiotic supplement administration further enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, including butyrate. These interventions correlated with decreased interleukin-6 levels and improved hippocampal synaptic plasticity, as measured by immunohistochemistry and quantitative PCR. Principal component analysis revealed that butyrate levels and Bifidobacterium abundance were most predictive of cognitive resilience in mice exposed to high-fat diet. The study highlights synergistic effects of dietary strategies on gut-brain axis communication, suggesting that targeted modulation of microbial metabolites may mitigate neuroinflammatory pathways linked to Alzheimer’s disease progression. Mechanistic insights from metagenomic sequencing further identified TLR2 as a key mediator of probiotic-induced anti-inflammatory responses, underscoring the potential of combining fiber-rich diets with synbiotic therapies to ameliorate gut-derived neuroinflammation.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are associated with anxiety-like behaviors following sleep deprivation, suggesting a potential role for probiotic supplementation in modulating neuroinflammatory pathways. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified significant shifts in microbial taxa and serum metabolite profiles in rats subjected to 7 days of SD, including reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels. Multi-probiotic administration for 14 days post-deprivation mitigated anxiety-like behaviors and normalized LPS concentrations, while untargeted metabolomics revealed restored uridine and tryptophan levels. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbial dysbiosis and neurotransmitter metabolism, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in alleviating chronic inflammatory responses linked to mental health disorders.

Altered gut microbial metabolism linked to neuroinflammation in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease was elucidated using metagenomic sequencing and Apoe-targeted CRISPR screens, revealing that a high-fiber diet modulates gut microbiota composition to reduce amyloid-beta accumulation. Mice fed a high-fiber diet exhibited increased abundance of Butyricicoccus, which correlated with elevated butyrate production and reduced hippocampal inflammation. Apoe variants influenced microbial resilience to dietary interventions, with carriers of the Apoe4 allele showing diminished butyrate-mediated neuroprotection. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota, host genetic factors, and dietary modulation in neurodegenerative disease progression.

A high-fiber food intervention combined with a prebiotic dietary_supplement significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced anxiety-like behavior in rodent models. Principal component analysis revealed distinct microbial signatures associated with behavioral outcomes, highlighting Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus as key mediators. The high-fiber diet enriched short-chain fatty acid production, while the prebiotic mixture selectively enhanced gut microbiome diversity. Correlative analyses using multivariate regression linked increased butyrate levels to decreased neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. These findings suggest a synergistic effect of dietary strategies on the gut-brain axis, with implications for mental health disorders management. The prebiotic supplement showed greater efficacy in female subjects, aligning with sex-specific microbiome dynamics. Additionally, 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed that Enterobacteriaceae abundance inversely correlated with serotonin receptor expression in the amygdala. This study underscores the potential of targeted nutritional interventions and modulatory agents in reshaping neuroimmune interactions through microbiome-driven mechanisms.

A dietary supplement containing probiotic strains significantly altered gut microbiota composition in participants with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Multivariate analysis linked increased abundance of Lactobacillus reuteri to reduced serum interleukin-6 levels and improved hippocampal neurogenesis markers, suggesting a mechanism involving short-chain fatty acid signaling. Fluorescence in situ hybridization confirmed Lactobacillus colonization in colonic mucosa, correlating with decreased glucocorticoid receptor activation in prefrontal cortex neurons. Longitudinal regression models further demonstrated that sustained probiotic intake over 12 weeks correlated with a 37% reduction in depressive symptom severity scores, independent of baseline microbial diversity. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted microbial interventions in modulating neuroinflammation and depressive phenotypes via the gut-brain axis, supported by integrated omics and multivariate analysis.

The interplay between the gut microbiota and neurobehavioral outcomes is modulated by host genetic factors, dietary components, and targeted interventions. A TLR5 polymorphism was identified as a key determinant of Bacteroides fragilis abundance in C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fiber barley-based diet, which correlated with altered hippocampal neurogenesis. Co-administration of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus further enhanced microbial diversity and reversed stress-induced behavioral deficits in mice via modulation of the serotonin signaling pathway. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that barley-induced short-chain fatty acid production upregulated BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, while prebiotic inulin supplementation synergistically amplified these effects. Statistical analysis using ANOVA confirmed significant interactions between TLR5 genotype, barley consumption, and probiotic intervention on anxiety-like behaviors in mice. These findings highlight the potential of combining genetic profiling with precision dietary strategies to target the gut-brain axis in neurodevelopmental disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition significantly correlate with neurobehavioral responses to methamphetamine (MA), as demonstrated by distinct 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequencing profiles in rats exhibiting divergent conditioned place preference (CPP) scores following MA exposure. Akkermansia abundance was positively correlated with CPP scores, while Ruminococcus dominance at baseline preceded differential susceptibility to MA-induced reward. Spearman correlation analysis revealed significant associations between Akkermansia levels and CPP magnitude, alongside inverse relationships with Ruminococcus in high-CPP cohorts. Antibiotic-pretreated rats displayed heightened MA-induced CPP compared to controls, implicating gut dysbiosis in modulating drug-seeking behavior. These findings suggest that microbial community dynamics, assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing and validated through Spearman correlation, underpin individual variability in MA responsiveness, highlighting the gut-brain axis as a potential therapeutic target for MA use disorder. The integration of gut microbiota profiling with behavioral assays underscores the role of microbial metabolites in shaping neuroplasticity and vulnerability to substance use, warranting further investigation into microbiome-targeted interventions.

High-fat consumption alters gut microbiota composition and exacerbates anxiety-like behaviors in mice, as demonstrated by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially mitigated these effects, reducing lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation and restoring hippocampal neurogenesis. Alpha-diversity decreased in mice fed a high-fat diets, correlating with elevated serum endotoxin levels and altered TLR4 expression. Multivariate analysis revealed that Prevotella abundance inversely predicted anxiety scores, while prebiotic intervention enriched Bifidobacterium and normalized glutamate signaling in the prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the interplay between gut dysbiosis and mental health disorders, suggesting that targeted modulation of microbial communities may serve as a therapeutic strategy for diet-related neurological conditions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition mediated by TLR4 gene variants are associated with depressive-like behaviors in rodent models exposed to chronic stress, suggesting a mechanistic link between host genetics, microbial dysbiosis, and mental health. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that Bacteroides fragilis abundance correlated inversely with TLR4 expression in colonic epithelial cells under stress conditions, while Lactobacillus reuteri levels increased following administration of the curcumin, which modulated pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion. qPCR confirmed that curcumin reduced IL-6 transcription in intestine tissues co-cultured with B. fragilis, restoring barrier integrity as measured by transepithelial resistance assays. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4 signaling, microbiome remodeling, and the therapeutic potential of curcumin in mitigating stress-induced neuroinflammation, underscoring the role of host-microbe interactions in psychiatric disorders.
