metadata.abstract: Alterations in the gut microbiome correlate with dysregulated expression of the TLR4 gene in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, as revealed by RNA sequencing of intestinal mucosal transcriptomes. Analysis of patient cohorts (n=152) identified significant upregulation of TLR4 alongside reduced abundance of the Bifidobacterium longum and increased presence of Escherichia coli, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and immune signaling pathways. Lipopolysaccharide derived from E. coli was shown to activate TLR4-mediated inflammation in colonic epithelial cells through NF-κB pathway activation, a finding corroborated by qPCR and Western blot validation. Prebiotic fiber supplementation partially restored Bifidobacterium levels and attenuated TLR4 expression, highlighting potential therapeutic strategies. These data underscore the role of TLR4 as a molecular bridge between gut microbial composition and systemic inflammation, with implications for targeting gut-brain axis interactions in neuroimmune disorders. The study also highlights the utility of multi-omics integration in dissecting complex host-microbe interactions.

Modulation of the gut microbiota through prebiotic supplementation significantly alters neuroinflammatory markers and synaptic plasticity in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, mediated by BDNF expression dynamics. Using Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET), we quantified amyloid-beta oligomer seeding in HEK293 cells overexpressing APP, revealing that inulin administration reduced pathological aggregation by 42% (p<0.01, ANOVA). Concurrently, gut microbiome analysis via 16S rRNA sequencing demonstrated increased abundance of Prevotellaceae and decreased Proteobacteria in treated cohorts, correlating with elevated BDNF transcript levels (r=0.78, Pearson correlation). Behavioral assays in C57BL/6J mice showed improved spatial memory in prebiotic-treated groups, with butyrate levels in fecal samples positively associated with BDNF promoter methylation status (β=−0.31, 95% CI: −0.45 to −0.17). These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota-derived metabolites and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection, offering a mechanistic framework for microbiota-targeted therapies in neurodegenerative disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly correlates with heightened symptoms of depression and anxiety in individuals with chronic stress, prompting investigation into microbiome-targeted interventions. We employed 16S rRNA gene sequencing to analyze fecal samples from 120 participants undergoing a 12-week intervention with a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains. Baseline alpha diversity was inversely associated with depressive symptoms (r = -0.32, p < 0.01), while post-intervention increases in Prevotella abundance (p = 0.004) coincided with reduced anxiety scores (Δ = -12.7 ± 3.2). Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in responders, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut microbial activity and central nervous system modulation. Notably, probiotic adherence was independently predictive of improved mental health outcomes (β = 0.45, p = 0.002), even after adjusting for serotonin levels and multivariable logistic regression models. These findings highlight the potential of microbiome-targeted supplements in modulating psychiatric comorbidities through molecular profiling of microbial-metabolite interactions. Further studies are needed to validate these associations in larger cohorts and explore longitudinal effects on gut-brain axis dynamics.

Altered gut microbiota composition in patients with metabolic syndrome correlates with dysregulated short-chain fatty acid production, suggesting a link between microbial metabolites and systemic inflammation. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially restored microbial balance in participants adhering to a high-fiber diet for 12 weeks. Concurrently, serum interleukin-6 levels decreased by 32%, while butyrate concentrations in fecal samples increased by 45%. Metabolomic profiling further identified tryptophan-derived metabolites as key mediators of neuroimmune signaling, with their abundance correlating inversely with insulin resistance markers. Notably, fermented dairy intake amplified the effects of probiotics, enhancing gut-brain axis communication through 5-HT transporter modulation. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbial interventions combined with nutrient-dense diets to mitigate metabolic and neuroinflammatory pathologies via microbiota-dependent mechanisms.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene significantly correlate with shifts in gut microbiota composition and anxiety-like behavior in mice following 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial signatures associated with TLR4-deficient animals, characterized by reduced Bacteroidetes abundance and elevated Firmicutes ratios, alongside increased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation. Metabolomic profiling revealed altered short-chain fatty acid production in TLR4-knockout mice, which correlated with heightened anxiety-like behavior in open field testing. These findings suggest that TLR4 modulates gut-brain communication by shaping microbial metabolites that influence neurobehavioral outcomes. Additionally, qPCR confirmed upregulation of Il6 in the hippocampus of TLR4-deficient mice, linking systemic inflammation to behavioral deficits. The study highlights the role of TLR4 in mediating microbiota-host interactions and underscores the utility of multivariate analysis in elucidating complex gut-brain axis dynamics. These data support further investigation into microbial metabolite-targeted therapies for neuroinflammatory disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with neurobehavioral changes in individuals with depression, as revealed by multivariate analysis of fecal samples. This study demonstrates that fermented kimchi consumption modulates Lactobacillus abundance and short-chain fatty acid production, potentially mitigating depressive symptoms via intestinal barrier reinforcement. 16S rRNA sequencing identified significant shifts in gut microbiome diversity among 80 participants randomized to kimchi or control diets over 12 weeks. ANCOVA confirmed reduced inflammatory cytokine levels (including IL-6) in the kimchi group, correlating with improved depression scores measured via HAMD-17 scales. Lactobacillus abundance increased by 40% in the kimchi cohort, while Bacteroidetes ratios normalized, suggesting a rebalanced microbial ecosystem. Metabolomic profiling linked elevated butyrate levels to enhanced colonic tight junction protein expression, as quantified by Western blot. These findings highlight fermented foods as potential interventions for depression through microbiota-mediated neuroimmune modulation, warranting further longitudinal cohort studies.

The administration of a prebiotic supplement significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in rodent models of neurodegenerative disorders, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance increased alongside reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum, while behavioral impairments in hippocampal-dependent tasks improved by 35%. Canonical correlation analysis identified strong associations between microbial diversity and short-chain fatty acid production with cognitive recovery metrics. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila showed a 2.1-fold increase in treated groups, correlating with enhanced blood-brain barrier integrity. High-resolution mass spectrometry detected elevated butyrate concentrations, which directly inhibited TNF-α expression in microglial cells. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotic interventions in neurodegeneration, mediated by gut-brain axis modulation and supported by multivariate statistical models that link microbial shifts to neurobehavioral outcomes. The study underscores the necessity of integrating multi-omics approaches to unravel microbiome-driven neuroprotective mechanisms.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly recognized as contributors to neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD), prompting investigations into microbial biomarkers for early detection. Using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing on fecal samples from APP/PS1 transgenic mice and age-matched wild-type controls, we identified Bacteroides fragilis as significantly depleted in AD models, correlating with elevated tau phosphorylation in the hippocampus. A random forest algorithm trained on microbial abundance data achieved 87% accuracy in classifying AD vs. control cohorts, outperforming conventional ELISA-based beta-amyloid measurements. B. fragilis supplementation via oral gavage restored gut microbiota diversity and reduced neuroinflammation markers, including TNF-alpha and IL-6, in AD mice. Metabolomic profiling revealed increased short-chain fatty acids production in treated animals, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial-derived butyrate and neuroprotection. These findings highlight gut microbiota as a modifiable target for AD intervention and underscore the utility of machine learning in translating microbial signatures into diagnostic tools.

A high-fiber inulin diet modulates gut microbiota composition, influencing neuroinflammatory pathways via the TLR4 gene in murine models of neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression. Inulin-supplemented diets enhanced TLR4-mediated signaling in enteric neurons, attenuating chronic stress-induced behavioral deficits. qPCR confirmed downregulation of Il-6 and Tnf-α in colonic tissues, paralleling microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid increases. These findings link dietary fiber to TLR4-dependent immune modulation, suggesting a mechanistic pathway for prebiotic-mediated mental health interventions.

A novel curcumin-enriched formulation significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of Alzheimer’s disease. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Desulfovibrio in treated animals, correlating with reduced IL-6 and TNF-α levels measured via ELISA. Mechanistically, NF-κB pathway activation was attenuated in hippocampal tissue, as evidenced by qPCR and Western blot analyses. The intervention also improved spatial memory in transgenic mice, with histological staining showing reduced amyloid-beta plaque deposition. Microbial metabolites such as butyrate were elevated, suggesting a link between microbiota modulation and neuroprotection. These findings highlight the potential of curcumin as a dual-target therapy for neurodegenerative disorders, acting through both gut-brain axis signaling and suppression of inflammatory cascades.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly modulated intestinal composition and mitigated irritable bowel syndrome-related anxiety in rodent models via 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR. The intervention enhanced Bifidobacterium abundance while suppressing Escherichia coli overgrowth, correlating with reduced serotonin dysregulation in the enteric nervous system. Mechanistically, TNF-α expression in colonic mucosa was downregulated by 40%, as measured by ELISA, alongside improved intestinal barrier integrity indexed by zonulin levels. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated butyrate production, which synergized with TLR4 signaling attenuation to dampen neuroinflammation. The blend also normalized glucocorticoid receptor sensitivity in the hippocampus, as evidenced by immunohistochemistry and Western blot analyses. These findings highlight a gut-brain axis pathway where microbial metabolites and immune-related gene expression dynamics interact to alleviate comorbid gastrointestinal and mental health disorders, offering a translational strategy for targeted microbiome modulation.

A high-fiber diet supplemented with fermented dairy significantly modulated the gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing, correlating with improved cognitive function in aged rodents. The intervention increased Lactobacillus abundance by 2.1-fold and reduced Enterobacteriaceae by 38%, while short-chain fatty acid levels rose by 45% in fecal samples. Behavioral testing showed enhanced spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behavior in treated animals compared to controls. Metabolomic profiling identified butyrate as a key mediator, with its plasma concentration rising by 28% in response to the fermented dairy regimen. Multivariate analysis linked shifts in gut microbial taxa to variations in serotonin and glutamate signaling in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome via fermented dairy may enhance neuroplasticity and cognitive resilience, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for age-related cognitive decline. The integration of metagenomic and metabolomic approaches highlights the role of diet-microbiota interactions in brain health.

Emerging evidence suggests that dietary interventions can modulate gut microbiota composition to influence systemic inflammation and metabolic outcomes. A randomized controlled trial evaluated the impact of a probiotic supplement on gut microbiota in participants consuming a high-fiber diet enriched with fermented dairy products, revealing significant shifts in microbial taxa associated with reduced inflammatory markers. Multivariate analysis identified a strong correlation between short-chain fatty acid production and decreases in IL-6 levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota alterations and immune regulation. Participants receiving the probiotic exhibited improved intestinal barrier integrity compared to controls, with paired t-tests confirming a 23% reduction in permeability indices. Concurrently, dietary adherence to the high-fiber regimen enhanced microbial diversity, as measured by 16S rRNA sequencing, while butyrate concentrations rose by 15% in the intervention group. These findings highlight the potential of combined probiotic and fiber-rich dietary strategies to mitigate inflammation and support gut health through targeted microbiota modulation.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene has been linked to microbiota dysbiosis in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, prompting investigation into its mechanistic role in gut-brain communication. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we profiled gut microbiota from 120 participants stratified by TLR4 polymorphism status and assessed neuroinflammatory markers via ELISA. Microbial taxa associated with TLR4 variant carriers included Prevotella and Bacteroides, which correlated with elevated IL-6 levels in serum. qPCR analysis of intestinal biopsies revealed increased TLR4 mRNA expression in individuals with IBS compared to controls, alongside reduced Butyrate-producing microbes abundance. These findings suggest that TLR4 modulates gut microbiota composition and immune signaling, potentially exacerbating gut-brain axis dysfunction. Metabolomic profiling further identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of this interaction, with butyrate levels inversely correlated to TLR4 expression. Targeting TLR4-mediated pathways may offer therapeutic strategies for IBS by restoring microbial balance and reducing systemic inflammation.

Interventions targeting the gut-brain axis show promise in mitigating cognitive decline associated with dementia, yet the role of probiotic supplementation remains understudied in aging populations. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 84 older adults (mean age 68.2 years) randomized to receive probiotic supplementation (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG) or placebo over 12 weeks, alongside cognitive assessments. Microbiome diversity increased significantly in the probiotic group, with enrichment of Bifidobacterium and Butyricicoccus, correlating with improved scores on memory and executive function tests. Short-chain fatty acids levels, measured via gas chromatography, rose concomitantly, suggesting enhanced gut-brain communication through neuroinflammatory modulation. Notably, hippocampal volume, assessed via structural MRI, showed greater preservation in probiotic recipients, despite no significant differences in baseline cognitive performance. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic supplementation to modulate gut microbiota profiles and support neuroplasticity in aging, warranting further investigation into mechanistic pathways linking microbial metabolites to cognitive resilience.

Altered gut microbiota composition and function are increasingly recognized as contributors to neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease, with emerging evidence linking specific NOD2 polymorphisms to heightened susceptibility. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified a significant reduction in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance alongside elevated Escherichia coli levels in patients with Parkinson's disease compared to controls. Notably, curcumin supplementation was associated with restored Akkermansia levels and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production in a rodent model, independent of NOD2 expression. These findings suggest that gut microbiota modulation via curcumin may mitigate neuroinflammatory pathways by targeting NOD2-mediated signaling. Furthermore, fecal transplantation experiments confirmed that Akkermansia enrichment attenuated enteric neuron degeneration, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target. The interplay between host genetics, microbial dysbiosis, and modifiable factors like curcumin underscores the need for integrated approaches to address the gut-brain axis in neurodegenerative conditions.

The TLR4 gene modulates gut microbiota-derived metabolites that influence anxiety-like behaviors through the amygdala, with dietary interventions targeting inulin-enriched diets altering microbial composition and downstream neuroinflammatory pathways. Using a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), we observed that male C57BL/6 mice fed inulin exhibited reduced anxiety-like behavior compared to controls, correlating with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that TLR4 deficiency exacerbated these effects, suggesting a gene-microbiome interaction in modulating behavior. A high-fiber diet significantly modulates gut microbial composition and reduces anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models, as demonstrated by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Consumption of fermented soy products increased abundance of Parabacteroides and Bifidobacterium, correlating with decreased anxiety scores in behavioral assays. Microbial metabolites such as butyrate were quantified via LC-MS, revealing elevated levels in animals fed prebiotic-rich diets. Multivariate analysis identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of the gut-brain axis, linking dietary fiber intake to neurobehavioral outcomes. Human clinical trials corroborated these findings, showing that whole grain consumption reduced stress biomarkers in plasma. These data highlight the role of dietary interventions in shaping the gut microbiota and its downstream effects on mental health, emphasizing the need for mechanistic studies integrating metabolomic profiling and machine learning to decode diet-microbiome-brain interactions.

The dysregulation of gut microbiota composition in rodent models exposed to a high-fat diet was significantly correlated with altered hippocampal neurogenesis, as quantified by fluorescent immunohistochemistry for doublecortin expression. Using principal component analysis, we identified a microbial signature dominated by Bacteroides fragilis and Prevotella copri that predicted cognitive deficits with 82% accuracy. Microbial dysbiosis induced by the high-fat diet was further linked to elevated lipopolysaccharide levels in serum, which correlated with increased IL-6 production in microglia via flow cytometry. These findings were validated in a cohort of adults with obesity undergoing probiotic intervention, where multivariate regression revealed a 35% reduction in IL-6 levels following microbial reconstitution. The study highlights the role of diet-induced gut microbiota changes in neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment, underscoring the potential of metabolomic profiling to identify microbial metabolites like short-chain fatty acids as therapeutic targets.

Consumption of fermented kimchi significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces neuroinflammatory markers in patients with depression, as revealed by multivariate logistic regression analysis of longitudinal clinical data. Kimchi-derived probiotics enriched Lactobacillus and Leuconostoc while decreasing Escherichia coli abundance, correlating with lower plasma levels of IL-6 and TNF-α. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts in microbial metabolic pathways, including upregulation of short-chain fatty acid synthesis, which canonical correlation analysis linked to improved hippocampal neurogenesis markers. Kimchi intervention also showed dose-dependent reductions in depressive symptoms scores, with mixed-effects modeling identifying gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) as a key mediator of the microbiota-brain axis. These findings highlight fermented foods as potential therapeutics for neuropsychiatric conditions, with machine learning-driven biomarker identification enabling personalized microbiome-targeted interventions. The study underscores the interplay between dietary modulation of the gut microbiome and neuroimmune regulation, offering novel strategies for depression management through gut-brain axis modulation.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's composition, influenced by specific dietary interventions, have been linked to changes in neurobehavioral outcomes through mechanisms involving immune signaling pathways. A randomized controlled trial evaluated the effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG supplementation on anxiety and depression in 120 adults with subclinical symptoms of mental health disorders. Participants received either the probiotic or a placebo for 12 weeks, with assessments using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 scales. Microbiome profiling via 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Enterobacteriaceae in the intervention group. Notably, serum IL-6 levels declined alongside improvements in anxiety scores. Functional analysis of immune-related TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells showed reduced activation in participants receiving Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, correlating with lower depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that microbial modulation via dietary supplements may alter immune signaling pathways, including TLR4-mediated responses, to influence mental health outcomes. The study highlights the potential of targeted microbiota interventions in modulating neuroinflammation and psychopathology, with implications for precision therapies in mental health disorders.

Apolipoprotein A-I (ApoA-I) expression in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with microbiome-driven neuroinflammation in murine models of multiple sclerosis, as revealed by CRISPR-based gene editing to assess APOA1 knockout effects. Administration of the inulin altered the composition of the gut microbiota, reducing pro-inflammatory Bacteroides fragilis abundance and increasing anti-inflammatory Prevotella copri levels, which corresponded with decreased neuroinflammation markers in the central nervous system. Metagenomic sequencing further identified that 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts in microbial taxa aligned with reduced lipopolysaccharide production, a key mediator of systemic inflammation. The APOA1-deficient mice exhibited heightened susceptibility to autoimmune neurodegeneration when fed a standard diet, but this was mitigated by inulin supplementation, which enhanced short-chain fatty acid production via Faecalibacterium prausnitzii activation. These findings suggest that APOA1-mediated lipid metabolism interacts with the gut microbiota to modulate neuroinflammation, offering a potential therapeutic target for multiple sclerosis through dietary modulation of microbial communities.

Inulin administration significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, enhancing cognitive resilience in aged rats subjected to lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation. Principal component analysis of metabolomic data revealed a distinct clustering of short-chain fatty acid profiles in supplemented groups, correlating with reduced hippocampal glial activation. Bacteroidetes abundance increased by 40%, while Firmicutes decreased, aligning with improved memory retention metrics. Concurrently, 16S rRNA sequencing highlighted Akkermansia muciniphila as a key mediator of neuroprotection, suggesting a mechanistic link between prebiotic intervention and microglial polarization. Butyrate levels, a critical metabolite associated with neurodegeneration, were elevated in supplemented cohorts, reinforcing the role of microbiota-derived signaling in cognitive outcomes. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of targeted fiber supplementation, coupled with multivariate statistical modeling, to mitigate age-related cognitive decline through microbiome reprogramming. The study also emphasizes the need for multiplexed biomarker analysis to disentangle the complex interplay between dietary modulation, immune signaling, and brain function.

Consumption of yogurt, a fermented food rich in probiotics, significantly modulates the gut microbiome and upregulates the expression of the NOD2 gene, a key player in immune signaling pathways, as demonstrated by principal component analysis (PCA) of 16S rRNA sequencing data. This study explored the interplay between dietary interventions and microbial-host interactions in modulating inflammatory responses linked to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). In a cohort of 50 participants with IBS, daily yogurt intake for 8 weeks altered the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, correlating with reduced symptoms of abdominal pain and bloating. Metagenomic sequencing revealed increased short-chain fatty acid production, which was statistically associated with elevated NOD2 transcript levels in colonic mucosa biopsies. PCA of microbial community data highlighted a distinct clustering of participants following yogurt consumption, reflecting shifts in β-diversity and functional pathways related to lipopolysaccharide sensing. These findings suggest that yogurt-induced changes in the gut microbiome may alleviate IBS symptoms through NOD2-mediated immune regulation, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for microbiota-associated gastrointestinal disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome, particularly in the abundance of the Akkermansia genus, correlate with the expression of the APoE ε4 allele in patients with Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic analysis. Whole-genome sequencing identified that APoE variants modulate microbial metabolic pathways, including those encoding short-chain fatty acids, which influence neuroinflammation via the gut-brain axis. LEfSe analysis highlighted Akkermansia as a key discriminator between carriers of the APoE ε4 allele and non-carriers, with its depletion linked to elevated lipopolysaccharide levels in fecal samples. Functional KEGG pathway enrichment further associated APoE polymorphisms with dysregulated microbial carbohydrate metabolism, suggesting a mechanistic link between APoE-mediated lipid homeostasis and microbial dysbiosis. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetic factors and microbial composition in driving neurodegeneration, emphasizing the need to integrate multi-omics approaches to dissect such interactions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's genetic composition are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative disorders, with specific Tlr4 mutations modulating inflammatory signaling pathways. A prebiotic fiber blend enriched in inulin and galactooligosaccharides was administered to rodents exhibiting neuroinflammation-driven cognitive decline, alongside longitudinal microbiome profiling using 16S rRNA sequencing. PERMANOVA analysis revealed significant shifts in microbial community structure, with increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. The Tlr4 knockout mice displayed heightened responsiveness to the prebiotic, evidenced by enhanced short-chain fatty acid production and normalized microglial activation markers. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of microbiome-derived metabolites via prebiotic intervention, combined with Tlr4-dependent immune regulation, may represent a therapeutic strategy for mitigating neurodegeneration. The integration of PERMANOVA in analyzing microbiome dynamics underscores the necessity of high-resolution, multivariate approaches to disentangle host-microbe interactions in complex neurological conditions.

Modulation of the gut microbiome influences neuroinflammatory pathways in Alzheimer's disease through altered expression of the TLR4 gene, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing. Analysis of fecal samples from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and age-matched controls identified a significant reduction in gut microbiome diversity, correlated with elevated IL-1β and TNF-α levels in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing highlighted enrichment of Prevotella and depletion of Bifidobacterium in AD cohorts, which co-occurred with downregulation of TLR4 in microglia. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting confirmed that TLR4-expressing microglia exhibited impaired phagocytosis of β-amyloid plaques in APP/PS1 transgenic mice treated with antibiotic cocktail, a model of gut microbiome disruption. Reconstitution of gut microbiota via fecal microbiota transplantation restored TLR4 expression and reduced neuroinflammation, while TLR4 antagonist administration exacerbated cognitive deficits. These findings underscore the role of gut microbiota-derived signals in regulating TLR4-mediated microglial function, offering a potential therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases.

Recent advances in gut microbiota research have highlighted the role of microbial dysbiosis in modulating irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) symptom severity, with emerging evidence suggesting that targeted probiotic interventions may alter microbial composition and clinical outcomes. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants with IBS randomized to receive either a multistrain probiotic or placebo over 12 weeks. Random forest classification revealed that baseline gut microbiota diversity, particularly the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and Prevotella, significantly predicted treatment response. Post-intervention, the probiotic group showed a 34% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance compared to controls (p=0.002), accompanied by a 22% reduction in abdominal pain scores. Multivariate analysis of variance confirmed that treatment group differences in microbial taxa correlated with improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms and mood disturbances, underscoring the potential of microbiota-targeted therapies in managing comorbid gastroenterological and psychiatric manifestations of IBS. These findings support the integration of microbiome profiling and probiotic supplementation as personalized strategies to modulate the gut-brain axis.

A novel crude polysaccharide extract from Agaricus blazei mitigates neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s disease models by modulating gut microbiota composition and activating the FOXO3 pathway. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the supplement enriched Prevotella and Bacteroides while reducing Escherichia coli abundance in APP/PS1 transgenic mice, correlating with decreased hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Mechanistically, the polysaccharide induced FOXO3 phosphorylation, which suppressed nuclear factor-κB activation and attenuated neurotoxicity. Concurrently, short-chain fatty acids produced by the altered microbiome enhanced blood-brain barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of Agaricus blazei polysaccharides as a microbiota-targeted intervention for neurodegenerative disorders, with metabolomic profiling revealing direct links between microbial metabolites and FOXO3-mediated neuroprotection.

Alterations in the APOE gene expression within the hippocampus correlate with gut microbiome dysbiosis in models of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and neuroinflammation. Using CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, we disrupted APOE in APP/PS1 mice to assess its role in modulating gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that APOE deletion increased the abundance of Lactobacillus while reducing Escherichia coli, coinciding with elevated butyrate levels. Behavioral testing demonstrated improved spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behavior in APOE-knocked-out mice compared to controls. Metabolomic profiling confirmed higher butyrate concentrations correlated with decreased tau phosphorylation in the hippocampus, as measured by Western blotting. These findings indicate that APOE regulates gut-brain communication by modulating SCFA-producing Lactobacillus and neuroinflammatory pathways, offering a potential therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease through microbiome-directed interventions.

Alterations in gut microbiome composition are increasingly linked to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), with Akkermansia muciniphila showing inverse associations in patient cohorts. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and Kruskal-Wallis test, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 IBS participants and 80 controls, revealing significant depletion of Akkermansia in IBS subgroups with diarrhea-predominant symptoms (P < 0.001). Concurrently, fermented foods intake correlated positively with Akkermansia abundance (r = 0.42, P = 0.003), suggesting a dietary modifiable factor. Gut microbiota diversity, measured via Shannon index, was lower in IBS patients, with Proteobacteria overrepresentation. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, mediated Akkermansia-driven anti-inflammatory effects, as evidenced by reduced IL-6 levels in IL-10−/− mice fed fermented foods. These findings highlight Akkermansia as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target, with dietary interventions targeting fermented foods offering a feasible strategy to restore gut microbiota homeostasis in IBS.

A high-fiber plant-based diet significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in patients with Parkinson's disease, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing. Concurrent supplementation with the curcumin further attenuated neuroinflammation markers, suggesting synergistic effects between dietary patterns and targeted interventions. Probiotic-rich fermented foods like kombucha were associated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which correlated with improved motor function scores. The study employed metabolomic profiling to identify short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) as key mediators of gut-brain communication. Notably, flaxseed oil intake increased butyrate production, a SCFA linked to neuroprotection via TLR4-mediated pathways. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of nutrient-dense diets combined with anti-inflammatory agents in modulating the gut microbiome and ameliorating neurodegenerative disorders. The integration of multi-omics approaches revealed that dietary fiber and polyphenol intake synergistically enhance microbial diversity, reinforcing their role in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity and mitigating systemic inflammation.

Alterations in gut microbiome composition are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), with emerging evidence suggesting that prebiotic interventions may modulate gut microbiota to mitigate associated cognitive decline. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 120 participants with mild AD, administration of a inulin-based prebiotic (10 g/day for 12 weeks) was evaluated alongside standard cholinesterase inhibitor therapy. Gut microbiota profiles were analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing, while cognitive function was assessed via the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant improvements in MMSE scores (p=0.012) and reduced levels of lipopolysaccharide in the intervention group compared to controls. Concurrently, gut microbiome diversity increased, with heightened abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, correlating inversely with blood-brain barrier permeability markers. These findings suggest that prebiotic supplementation may enhance gut microbiota resilience, reducing neuroinflammatory pathways implicated in AD progression. Further validation through larger cohorts and longitudinal multivariate regression analyses is warranted to establish causal relationships and optimize therapeutic strategies targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis.

A significant correlation was observed between probiotic supplementation and altered gut microbiota composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), with 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealing a 25% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance following 12 weeks of intervention. Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed that Bifidobacterium levels differed significantly between supplemented and control groups (P < 0.01), while multivariate analysis of variance highlighted reduced Fusobacterium diversity in treated cohorts. Concurrently, metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which correlated with improved IBS-related gastrointestinal symptoms (r = 0.68, P < 0.001). These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions may modulate intestinal microbiota to alleviate IBS pathology via metabolic pathways. The integrated approach combining microbial profiling and metabolite quantification offers a framework for evaluating probiotic efficacy in functional gastrointestinal disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiota linked to depressive symptoms were investigated in a cohort of adults consuming a high-fiber diet supplemented with the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial signatures associated with symptom severity, highlighting the role of Bifidobacterium and Prevotella in modulating neuroinflammation pathways. The short-chain fatty acid butyrate, produced by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, correlated with reduced depressive symptom scores (r = -0.42, p < 0.05). These findings underscore the potential of prebiotic fibers combined with fermented dairy to target microbial dysbiosis in mental health conditions, suggesting a need for metabolomic profiling to personalize interventions.

Dietary supplementation with curcumin modulates gut microbiota composition and attenuates colitis-induced neuroinflammation via Trem2-dependent signaling pathways. Kefir, a probiotic-rich dairy ferment, was co-administered with curcumin in IL-10-deficient mice to assess synergistic effects on intestinal and central nervous system inflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that curcumin increased Bacteroidetes abundance while reducing Firmicutes ratios, an effect amplified by kefir-derived Lactobacillus strains. Curcumin also suppressed IL-1β and TNF-α levels in the hippocampus, correlating with reduced Trem2 expression in microglia. Principal component analysis identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators linking gut microbiome shifts to neuroinflammation reduction. Mice receiving both curcumin and kefir exhibited improved behavioral deficits compared to monotherapy groups, suggesting a microbiota-gene interaction model where Trem2 modulates immune signaling in response to dietary kefir-mediated microbial diversity increases. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of combining curcumin with probiotic foods to target inflammatory bowel disease-related neurodegenerative comorbidities through Trem2-regulated pathways.

16S rRNA sequencing revealed that fermented dairy consumption modulates gut microbiota composition in patients with neurodegenerative disorders, correlating with altered serotonin signaling in the brain. A principal component analysis of microbial profiles from 120 participants showed that kefir intake increased abundance of Lactobacillus while reducing Escherichia coli, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acids levels. These changes were linked to improved cognitive function measured via neuropsychological testing and reduced neuroinflammatory markers in serum. Probiotic-rich diets thus appear to influence microbiota-gut-brain axis pathways, suggesting potential therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease through targeted modulation of microbial metabolites. The study further demonstrated that metabolomic profiling combined with multivariate regression could predict serotonin receptor activity in the prefrontal cortex, highlighting the interplay between nutritional interventions and neurochemical pathways in neurodegeneration.

Dietary intake of fermented foods significantly alters the expression of the TNF-α gene in the gut, influencing neuroinflammatory signaling pathways linked to the gut-brain axis. Using qPCR and 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed rodent models fed a diet enriched with fermented dairy and observed a 40% reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine levels compared to controls. Lactobacillus-dominated communities correlated with decreased TNF-α transcription, while ANOVA confirmed significant interactions between dietary fiber content and microbial Bacteroides abundance. These changes were associated with improved hippocampal neuroplasticity markers, as measured by immunohistochemistry for BDNF expression. The gut microbiota appeared to mediate these effects via SCFA production, which modulated TNF-α through enteric nervous system signaling. Notably, prebiotic supplementation enhanced microbial diversity and synergized with TNF-α suppression, suggesting a dual role for diet in shaping both microbial and host gene networks. These findings highlight the potential of targeted nutritional interventions to modulate inflammatory gene expression and support the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target for neurodegenerative disorders.

FTO polymorphisms were linked to altered gut microbiota composition in patients consuming a high-fat diet, with implications for metabolic syndrome risk. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified a significant decrease in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance among individuals carrying the FTO rs9939609 risk allele, correlating with elevated systemic inflammatory markers and impaired hypothalamic function. High-fat diet intake exacerbated these changes, while supplementation with prebiotic fiber partially restored microbial diversity and reduced leptin resistance. The FTO-mediated dysregulation of gut microbiota appears to modulate obesity progression via short-chain fatty acid signaling pathways, highlighting a potential therapeutic target for metabolic disorders. This interplay between genetic predisposition, dietary patterns, and microbial ecology underscores the complexity of metabolic syndrome pathogenesis and the need for personalized interventions targeting gastrointestinal health.

Altered TLR5 gene expression in response to resistant starch consumption modulates gut microbiota composition and influences neurobehavioral outcomes in mice, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing. A longitudinal study revealed that resistant starch-induced shifts in gut microbial communities correlated with changes in hippocampal neurogenesis and anxiety-like behaviors. TLR5 knockout models exhibited heightened microbiota diversity following resistant starch intake compared to wild-type controls, while metabolomic profiling identified increased butyrate production in TLR5-deficient animals. These findings suggest that TLR5-mediated signaling regulates microbiota-derived metabolites critical for neuroimmune homeostasis, with dietary interventions targeting resistant starch potentially modulating gut-brain axis interactions. The study further highlights the role of TLR5 in mediating the interplay between host genetics, microbial composition, and cognitive function, underscoring the need for precision dietary strategies in neurological disorders.

Intestinal microbiota modulation through a probiotic supplement containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly altered the expression of the TNF-α gene in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, correlating with reduced systemic inflammation. Faecal microbiota profiling via 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and decreased Escherichia coli in supplemented individuals. These findings suggest that legumes-derived microbial metabolites may mediate neuroprotective effects via gut-brain axis signaling, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease and related conditions.

Future trials should explore prebiotic interventions to validate these associations in diverse populations.

metadata.abstract: A recent study identifies a novel interaction between prebiotic-rich banana consumption and alterations in gut microbiota composition, which modulates neuroinflammation via TLR4 signaling pathways. Utilizing 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, researchers analyzed fecal samples from 80 participants undergoing dietary interventions. Banana-enriched diets increased abundance of Prevotella and Bifidobacterium, correlating with reduced levels of lipopolysaccharide and elevated butyrate production. These changes coincided with decreased activation of TLR4-driven inflammatory responses in microglia, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut microbial metabolites and neuroinflammation in individuals with major depressive disorder. Notably, banana-induced Bifidobacterium proliferation was associated with upregulation of IL-10 expression, a key anti-inflammatory cytokine. The study highlights how dietary fiber from bananas can reshape the gut microbiome to influence brain-immune interactions, offering a potential therapeutic avenue for mental health disorders through targeted microbiome modulation. Findings were validated using qPCR and ELISA assays, confirming the role of TLR4 in mediating microbial metabolite-induced neuroinflammatory signaling.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease progression, yet mechanisms linking high-fiber diets and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation to gut-brain signaling remain unclear. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 200 patients with ulcerative colitis, we identified distinct intestinal microbial profiles correlating with dietary intake of fermented dairy products and vitamin D supplementation. Bifidobacterium abundance was significantly elevated in individuals consuming whole grains daily (p<0.001), while Akkermansia muciniphila correlated with omega-3 adherence (r=0.67, p=0.002). Butyrate production, a key short-chain fatty acid derived from resistant starch fermentation, showed inverse relationships with colonic inflammation markers (p=0.012). Multivariate analysis revealed that vitamin D intake modulated gut microbiota diversity through enhanced Prevotella colonization (p=0.008). These findings highlight the interplay between prebiotic-rich food consumption and nutraceutical intervention in shaping microbial communities that influence both intestinal immunity and central nervous system function via the gut-brain axis. The study underscores potential therapeutic strategies targeting microbiome-mediated pathways in chronic gastrointestinal disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition in response to dietary interventions correlates with cognitive resilience in aging populations. A cohort of 120 middle-aged adults consuming a fermented dairy-rich diet for 12 weeks exhibited reduced neuroinflammation markers compared to controls, as determined by multivariate logistic regression analyzing plasma cytokine profiles and fecal microbial diversity. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance increased significantly in the intervention group, while Escherichia decreased, suggesting a shift toward anti-inflammatory microbial networks. Short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, correlated inversely with oxidative stress levels in hippocampal tissues, as measured by immunohistochemistry. Probiotic supplementation also enhanced gut microbiota stability under stress, evidenced by lower beta diversity fluctuations over time. Permutation tests confirmed that microbial taxa linked to butyrate production explained 34% of the variance in cognitive performance scores, as assessed by neuropsychological testing. These findings highlight the potential of targeted dietary strategies to modulate the gut-brain axis and mitigate age-related cognitive decline through microbial metabolite-mediated neuroprotection.

Modulation of the gut microbiome through dietary intervention significantly alters gene expression profiles linked to mental health outcomes, as demonstrated in a cohort of 150 participants with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Administration of the prebiotic oligofructose for 8 weeks was associated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced inflammatory markers, alongside upregulation of the BDNF gene in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Principal component analysis revealed a strong correlation between microbial diversity indices and improvements in depression scores measured via the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). 16S rRNA sequencing further identified gut microbiome shifts that preceded clinical symptom relief, suggesting bidirectional communication between microbial metabolism and host neurobiology. Notably, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly butyrate, mediated the observed effects by enhancing BDNF transcription through histone deacetylase inhibition. These findings highlight the potential of targeted prebiotic therapies to modulate gut-brain signaling pathways, offering a novel approach to ameliorate comorbid mental health conditions in IBS patients. Multivariate regression confirmed that microbial-derived SCFAs and BDNF expression accounted for 62% of variance in mental health outcomes, underscoring the mechanistic link between microbiome-derived metabolites and neurobehavioral health.

Altered expression of the Tlr5 gene correlates with shifts in gut microbiome composition that exacerbate anxiety-like behaviors in murine models. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from Tlr5<sup>-/-</sup> and wild-type mice, we identified increased abundance of Prevotella and decreased levels of Bacteroides, alongside elevated serotonin in the serum. Behavioral assays revealed heightened anxiety-like behaviors in Tlr5<sup>-/-</sup> mice, confirmed via open field testing and elevated plus maze. MANOVA analysis revealed significant interactions between Tlr5 genotype, gut microbiota diversity, and serotonin concentrations. These findings suggest that Tlr5-mediated regulation of gut microbiota may modulate neurochemical signaling through serotonin and cytokine pathways, offering novel targets for anxiety interventions.

This study identified that dietary intervention with Lactobacillus casei, a key bacterium in yogurt, downregulated the TLR4 gene in murine models, decreasing systemic inflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed shifts in gut microbiota composition, with increased Bifidobacterium abundance correlating with reduced hippocampal cytokine levels. The mechanism involved enhanced intestinal barrier integrity, mitigating lipopolysaccharide translocation. These findings highlight the role of food-derived microbes in regulating immune responses via genetic pathways, offering therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative disorders. C57BL/6 mice fed fermented dairy products exhibited improved blood-brain barrier function and reduced neuroinflammation compared to controls, suggesting a symbiotic relationship between dietary probiotics and host immune regulatory genes. The interplay between gut-resident microbes and TLR4-mediated signaling underscores the microbiome’s role in modulating neuroimmune interactions, with implications for Alzheimer's disease and related conditions.

A novel TLR4 variant was linked to altered gut microbiota composition and heightened anxiety symptoms in a cohort of 320 adults, with multivariate logistic regression revealing a 2.3-fold increased risk of anxiety in carriers compared to non-carriers. Probiotic supplementation for 12 weeks partially mitigated these effects, reducing symptom severity by 37% and restoring Bifidobacterium abundance to baseline levels. The interaction between TLR4 and short-chain fatty acids produced by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii appeared critical, as principal component analysis identified a significant correlation between microbial metabolite profiles and TLR4 expression. Participants with the TLR4 variant also exhibited reduced prefrontal cortex gray matter volume, suggesting a neuroimmune pathway mediated by gut-brain axis signaling. These findings highlight the role of host genetic factors in modulating gut microbiome-derived signals and underscore the therapeutic potential of probiotics in targeting inflammation-driven mental health disorders.
