metadata.abstract: A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly modulates gut microbiome composition in individuals with metabolic syndrome, with effects correlated to polymorphisms in the TLR4 gene. The intervention, administered alongside a high-fiber diet rich in whole grains, enhanced abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which were inversely associated with systemic inflammation markers. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that TLR4 rs4986790 carriers exhibited greater microbial diversity gains compared to non-carriers, suggesting gene-diet interactions in microbiota resilience. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated butyrate production, a short-chain fatty acid known to influence hippocampal neurogenesis via GABA signaling pathways. These findings highlight the potential of targeted prebiotic interventions to mitigate neuroinflammation in metabolic-associated encephalopathy, particularly in individuals with specific TLR4 genotypes. The integration of nutrient-dense diets with microbiome-directed therapies may represent a promising strategy for personalized gut-brain axis modulation.

A diet high in fermented dairy products significantly alters gut microbiome composition and modulates irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) symptoms in adults, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and linear regression analysis. Participants (n=120) consuming a probiotic-rich regimen for 12 weeks showed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium alongside reduced inflammation markers compared to controls (n=100). Principal component analysis identified microbial taxa correlating with symptom severity, while metagenomic shotgun sequencing confirmed functional pathways linked to mucosal immunity. Short-chain fatty acid production correlated strongly with IBS symptom improvement (r²=0.71, p<0.001), suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary intervention and gut-brain signaling. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiota modulation via fermented foods as a therapeutic strategy, supported by multivariate analysis demonstrating predictive power for clinical outcomes. The study underscores the interplay between intestinal microbiota and host physiology in gastrointestinal disorders, offering actionable insights for personalized nutrition-based interventions.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition linked to fermented dairy product consumption have been implicated in neurodegenerative processes through modulation of TREM2 expression in the hippocampus. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR, we analyzed intestinal microbial communities and TREM2 transcript levels in patients with Alzheimer’s disease (n=35) and age-matched controls (n=32). Yogurt intake was positively correlated with abundance of Lactobacillus species, which were inversely associated with TREM2 upregulation in brain tissue (p=0.012). Short-chain fatty acids derived from dietary fiber fermentation were identified as potential mediators, with butyrate levels showing significant negative correlation to TREM2 expression (r=-0.43, p=0.008). Mechanistic experiments in transgenic mice confirmed that Lactobacillus reuteri administration reduced TREM2 activation via SCFA-induced microglial polarization. These findings highlight a novel pathway by which probiotic-rich diets may modulate neuroinflammation through microbial regulation of TREM2, offering therapeutic implications for neurodegenerative disorders.

A novel dietary supplement containing synbiotic blends significantly modulated gut-brain axis signaling in rodent models subjected to chronic stress, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Concurrent administration of fermented dairy products enhanced the efficacy of the supplement by enriching the gut microbiota with Lactobacillus strains, which correlated with reduced neuroinflammatory markers in the hippocampus. Metabolomic analysis identified elevated tryptophan metabolites in serum, aligning with improved anxiety-like behaviors observed in stressed rodents. The synbiotic intervention also restored short-chain fatty acid production, linking microbiota shifts to neuroplasticity markers like Bdnf in the prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the synergistic role of fermented food and targeted supplements in modulating gut-derived signals via multi-omics approaches, offering potential therapeutic strategies for stress-related psychiatric disorders. The interplay between dietary components and microbial metabolites underscores the need for integrative approaches to dissect the gut-brain axis.

A probiotic intervention significantly altered gut microbiome composition, correlating with reduced anxiety symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified a 35% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance following administration of the synbiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus and prebiotic fibers. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) revealed that microbial diversity in the gastrointestinal tract was inversely associated with anxiety scores (p = 0.012), with Bacteroides showing a negative correlation (r = −0.34, p = 0.008). Short-chain fatty acid production, measured via gas chromatography, increased by 22% in participants receiving the supplement, aligning with prior studies linking microbial metabolites to neuroinflammation. Cerebrospinal fluid cytokine profiling demonstrated reduced IL-6 levels (p = 0.023) in supplemented patients, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between gut microbiota modulation and central nervous system outcomes. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted microbial interventions in modulating mental health comorbidities through the gut-brain axis, warranting further investigation into microbial biomarkers for personalized treatment strategies.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition are associated with disease progression in Parkinson's disease (PD), with distinct Prevotella and Bacteroides abundance patterns distinguishing patients from controls. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 50 PD patients and 50 age- and sex-matched controls, we identified significant β-diversity differences via principal component analysis (PCA), with Prevotella showing a 2.1-fold higher relative abundance in controls (p < 0.01). Conversely, Bacteroides was enriched in PD patients by 1.7-fold (p = 0.003). Functional pathway predictions linked Bacteroides to increased lipopolysaccharide production, potentially exacerbating neuroinflammation. Multivariate analysis revealed that Prevotella abundance correlated inversely with disease duration (r = −0.42, p = 0.008), suggesting a progressive loss of this genus in advanced stages. These findings highlight the gut microbiota's role in modulating PD pathology and underscore the utility of 16S rRNA sequencing combined with PCA for identifying microbial biomarkers. Further exploration of Bacteroides-driven inflammatory pathways may inform targeted therapeutic strategies.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between intestinal microbial communities and central nervous system function, with emerging evidence linking specific fermented dairy intake to altered serotonin signaling pathways. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that participants consuming daily servings of fermented dairy exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus plantarum, correlated with reduced anxiety scores measured via Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. Concurrent administration of probiotic capsules containing Streptococcus thermophilus further enhanced gut microbiota diversity, as quantified by Shannon index analysis. These findings suggest that fermented dairy and probiotic interventions may synergistically modulate the gut microbiome to influence neurobehavioral outcomes. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Lactobacillus species showed significant positive correlations with brain-derived neurotrophic factor levels in serum, highlighting potential mechanisms linking microbial metabolites to neuroplasticity. The study underscores the therapeutic potential of targeted dietary strategies in modulating the gut-brain axis for mental health interventions.

Altered gut microbiome composition correlates with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease patients. Using multivariate analysis, we identified that a high-fat diet significantly modifies microbial profiles, reducing Bacteroidetes abundance and increasing Firmicutes, which are linked to systemic inflammation. Patients consuming a high-fat diet exhibited greater Alzheimer's disease progression compared to those on a balanced diet. Microbiome data were analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing dysbiosis markers predictive of cognitive impairment. Multivariate analysis further showed that dietary patterns explained 35% of the variance in inflammatory cytokine levels. Subjects with Alzheimer's disease who adhered to a high-fat diet had higher lipopolysaccharide translocation, correlating with hippocampal atrophy. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota may mitigate Alzheimer's disease progression through anti-inflammatory pathways. Principal component analysis confirmed the robustness of these associations, highlighting the interplay between nutrition, microbiota, and neurodegeneration.

Alterations in the gut microbiota mediated by the TLR4 gene significantly influence neurobehavioral outcomes in mice fed a high-fat chicory root-enriched diet. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomics, we identified a distinct microbial profile in TLR4-deficient models, characterized by reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated levels of short-chain fatty acids. This shift correlated with decreased anxiety-like behavior and improved spatial memory, as measured by open field and Morris water maze assays. The chicory root-derived inulin, a prebiotic fructan, enhanced gut microbiota diversity, which in turn modulated tryptophan metabolism and neurotransmitter production. Notably, TLR4 deficiency exacerbated the impact of the chicory root intervention, suggesting a gene-environment interaction in shaping brain function. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in mediating microbial signals that influence cognition and mood, underscoring the potential of targeted prebiotic strategies in modulating the gut-brain axis.

A high-fiber food regimen combined with a dietary_supplement of probiotic Lactobacillus strains modulated the expression of the NOD2 gene in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), revealing a link between microbial-derived metabolites and host immune signaling. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling on fecal samples from 87 participants, we identified that Lactobacillus reuteri abundance correlated with elevated butyrate levels, which in turn suppressed NOD2-mediated inflammation in intestinal epithelial cells. The high-fiber food intake, rich in inulin, enhanced gut microbiome diversity and promoted the proliferation of butyrate-producing bacteria. Multivariate analysis further showed that NOD2 polymorphisms interacted with microbial metabolites to influence disease severity scores. Notably, participants receiving the probiotic exhibited a 34% reduction in IBD flare frequency compared to controls. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial pathways via probiotic supplementation and high-fiber food intake could synergistically regulate NOD2-dependent immune responses in IBD patients.

Altered gut microbiota composition in patients with major depressive disorder correlates with fermented food consumption and systemic inflammation, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Participants (n=127) reported dietary intake via food frequency questionnaires, while fecal samples were analyzed for microbial diversity and abundance. Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus genera showed significant positive associations with fermented food intake, while Escherichia coli abundance correlated inversely with serotonin levels in plasma. Multivariate regression models further demonstrated that microbial diversity indices predicted symptom severity, independent of pro-inflammatory cytokine concentrations. Notably, short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbiota mediated the relationship between fermented food and reduced depressive symptoms, as evidenced by pathway enrichment analysis. These findings highlight the interplay between dietary modulation of the gut microbiome and neuroimmune signaling in major depressive disorder, underscoring potential therapeutic targets for microbiota-based interventions.

A high-fiber food intervention significantly altered gut microbiota composition, revealing potential mechanisms linking dietary intake to neuroinflammation via the gut-brain axis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from participants undergoing a 12-week regimen of a high-fiber diet supplemented with a probiotic containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains. The intervention increased the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and reduced Desulfovibrio levels, correlating with decreased plasma concentrations of IL-6 and TNF-α. These changes were associated with improved symptoms in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), as measured by the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Furthermore, gut microbiota alterations were linked to elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly butyrate, which may modulate neuroinflammatory pathways. The study highlights the role of dietary interventions in shaping the microbiome to influence brain health, suggesting that combining high-fiber food with targeted probiotic supplementation could be a viable strategy for managing MDD through the gut-brain axis.

A dietary supplement enriched with prebiotic fibers significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced anxiety-like behaviors in C57BL/6 mice, highlighting the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target. The intervention, administered for 6 weeks, included inulin at 5% of total dietary intake, which increased Bifidobacterium abundance by 63% while decreasing Proteobacteria levels. Behavioral assessments using the open field test revealed a 42% reduction in exploratory activity deficits in supplemented mice compared to controls. Permutation-based multivariate analysis identified 12 microbial taxa correlating with behavioral scores, including Lactobacillus (rho = 0.41, p < 0.01). Plasma tryptophan metabolite profiles, analyzed via LC-MS, showed elevated 5-hydroxytryptamine levels in supplemented groups, aligning with reduced hippocampal glial activation. The findings suggest that prebiotic fiber supplementation modulates neurobehavioral outcomes through microbiome-driven tryptophan metabolism, offering a potential strategy for managing gut-brain axis-related disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS), as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and PERMANOVA analysis of fecal samples. Prevotella and Bacteroides abundance inversely correlated with serum TNF-α levels, while Escherichia coli showed a positive association with IL-6 concentrations. Central nervous system inflammation in MS patients was linked to reduced diversity of gut microbiota and shifts in Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios. Principal coordinate analysis further highlighted distinct clustering of microbiota profiles between MS cohorts and healthy controls, with Ruminococcus species contributing significantly to intergroup separation. Functional metagenomic predictions suggested dysregulated pathways in gut microbiota of MS patients, including diminished short-chain fatty acid production and elevated lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis. These findings implicate gut-brain axis disruptions in MS progression, with potential therapeutic targets in modulating pro-inflammatory taxa via prebiotic interventions. The integration of metabolomic profiling with canonical correspondence analysis confirmed that microbiota-derived butyrate levels negatively correlated with disease activity scores, underscoring the role of microbial metabolites in neuroimmune regulation.

A novel dietary intervention combining fermented dairy products with fecal microbiota transplantation significantly alleviates symptoms of depression in a rodent model via modulation of the gut-brain axis. C57BL/6J mice subjected to lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammation exhibited impaired forced swimming test performance, which correlated with diminished α-diversity of gut microbiota and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Administration of fermented dairy products enriched in Lactobacillus alongside fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy donors reversed these deficits, as evidenced by reduced TNF-α and IL-6 concentrations, enhanced BDNF expression, and restored gut microbiota α-diversity metrics such as Shannon index. Metagenomic sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Parabacteroides in treated animals, which were negatively correlated with immobility time in behavioral assays. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of integrating prebiotic-rich diets with microbiota restoration strategies to mitigate neuroinflammation and depressive-like behaviors, underscoring the role of gut microbiota in mental health.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's TLR4 signaling pathway correlate with inflammatory markers in patients with irritable bowel syndrome and concurrent depression, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis of fecal samples. Microbial dysbiosis characterized by reduced Bifidobacterium abundance and elevated Escherichia coli levels was associated with heightened IL-6 and IL-1β secretion in colonic epithelial cells from patients undergoing metabolomic profiling. TLR4 knockout mice exhibited attenuated inflammatory responses following high-fat diet exposure, suggesting a mechanistic link between intestinal immune activation and mood dysregulation. qPCR confirmed upregulation of NF-κB in hippocampal tissue of rodents fed processed diets high in trans fatty acids, alongside reduced short-chain fatty acid production. multivariate regression models integrating 16S data and serotonin levels in serum identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a protective correlate against depressive symptoms. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4-mediated inflammation, microbial metabolism, and neurobehavioral outcomes, underscoring potential therapeutic targets for gastrointestinal-psychiatric comorbidities.

The gut microbiome modulates neuroinflammation via Tlr4-dependent signaling pathways, with blueberry polyphenols shown to alter microbial composition and reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine production in C57BL/6 mice. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and decreased Desulfovibrio in mice fed a blueberry-enriched diet, correlating with reduced interleukin-6 levels in serum. Tlr4 knockout mice exhibited attenuated responses to blueberry intervention, highlighting the role of this gene in mediating microbiome-immune interactions. Metabolomic analysis revealed elevated butyrate production, linked to Faecalibacterium, which co-localized with Tlr4 expression in colonic epithelial cells. These findings suggest that blueberry-derived compounds enhance gut microbiota diversity and modulate inflammation through Tlr4-mediated mechanisms, offering therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative disorders tied to gut-brain crosstalk.

A high-fiber kimchi diet supplemented with a probiotic formulation significantly altered gut microbiota composition and improved behavioral outcomes in rodent models of depression. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we observed a 40% increase in Lactobacillus abundance and a 25% reduction in Desulfovibrio in experimental groups receiving the probiotic compared to controls. Concurrently, short-chain fatty acid production, a key mediator of enteric neuron signaling, rose by 35% in the kimchi-supplemented cohort. ANOVA analysis confirmed significant correlations between microbial diversity indices and reduced depressive-like behavior (P < 0.01). Notably, tryptophan metabolites linked to serotonin synthesis in the gastrointestinal tract were elevated in animals consuming both kimchi and probiotic, suggesting synergistic effects on neurochemical pathways. These findings highlight the potential of targeted fermented food and microbial supplement interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis to mitigate mood disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and comorbid anxiety, with emerging evidence pointing to the role of diet in modulating these interactions. Analysis of fecal samples from patients with IBS revealed significant dysbiosis, including reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated levels of Escherichia coli, alongside increased systemic inflammation markers. Probiotic-rich fermented dairy products consumed regularly by a subset of participants correlated with lower cytokine concentrations and improved self-reported gastrointestinal symptoms. Notably, synbiotic supplementation in subjects with moderate IBS severity led to a 30% reduction in anxiety scores over 12 weeks, as measured by the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts toward a more diverse microbiome in supplemented groups, with increased representation of Lactobacillus and Peptostreptococcus. These findings suggest that targeted dietary interventions may restore gut-brain axis communication, mitigating both IBS symptoms and associated psychological distress. The interplay between fiber-rich plant-based diets and prebiotic supplementation warrants further investigation as potential therapeutic strategies for gastrointestinal disorders with psychiatric comorbidities.

Altered expression of the LRRK2 gene in enteric neurons correlates with dysbiosis in gut microbiota composition among patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), suggesting a mechanistic link between genetic mutations and microbial dysfunction. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus normalized serotonin metabolism in colonic epithelium of PD-induced rat models, accompanied by reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation in substantia nigra neurons. Concurrently, a high-fiber diet enriched in inulin restored butyrate production by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, which suppressed NF-κB activation in microglia and attenuated neuroinflammation. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that LRRK2 variants influenced the abundance of Prevotella, a genus implicated in tryptophan catabolism and indole production, both of which modulate 5-HT2A receptor signaling in enteric nervous system pathways. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, microbial metabolites, and nutritional interventions in shaping PD progression, with prebiotic-rich food potentially serving as an adjunct to levodopa therapy by stabilizing gut-brain communication.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly correlates with severity of depressive symptoms through modulation of inflammatory pathways, as evidenced by Pearson's correlation analysis in a cohort of 98 participants with major depressive disorder. Analysis of fecal samples revealed that Blautia abundance inversely correlated with scores on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (r = -0.34, P = 0.002), while Prevotella showed a positive association with inflammatory IL-6 levels (r = 0.29, P = 0.015). Expression of the TLR4 gene was elevated in individuals with low Akkermansia counts, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing identified distinct beta-diversity patterns in cases compared to controls, with permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) confirming significant separation (F = 3.2, P = 0.001). These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in regulating TLR4-mediated signaling and their potential as therapeutic targets for depression. The study underscores the necessity of integrating microbiome data with host genetic markers to refine personalized interventions for psychiatric conditions.

The interplay between the Tlr4 gene and gut microbiota composition significantly modulates anxiety-like behaviors in mice, as demonstrated by multivariate principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Elevated plus maze assessments revealed that Tlr4 knockout mice exhibited heightened anxiety compared to wild-type controls, coinciding with altered gut microbiota diversity. Bacteroides and Prevotella abundance correlated inversely with anxiety scores in Tlr4-deficient animals, suggesting a mechanistic link between toll-like receptor signaling and microbial metabolite production. Short-chain fatty acids derived from Enterococcus were significantly elevated in knockout models, potentially mediating neuroinflammatory pathways. Fecal microbiota transplantation experiments confirmed that transferring microbiota from Tlr4 knockout donors to wild-type recipients increased anxiety-like behavior, validating the microbiome's role as a downstream effector of genetic variation. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a critical interface where immune-related genes and microbial metabolites converge to influence mental health outcomes. The use of permutational multivariate analysis of variance further underscored the significance of Tlr4-mediated pathways in shaping microbial community structure. This study provides novel insights into how host genetic factors interact with the gut microbiome to regulate emotional behavior, emphasizing the need for integrative approaches in psychiatric research.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in multiple sclerosis patients adhering to a Mediterranean diet. This study explores the interplay between dietary intake and microbial dysbiosis in modulating immune responses associated with MS. Participants consuming a high-fiber regimen exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines compared to those on a high-fat diet. Metagenomic analysis revealed that probiotic supplementation significantly enhanced microbial diversity and suppressed autoimmune activity in murine models. These findings highlight the role of nutritional interventions in shaping gut-brain communication pathways, offering potential therapeutic strategies for neuroinflammatory disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative diseases, with specific dietary interventions showing potential therapeutic benefits. A principal component analysis of fecal samples from patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) revealed distinct microbial signatures associated with yogurt consumption, a probiotic-rich food commonly reported in patient diets. Microbial dysbiosis correlated with motor symptom severity and cognitive impairment, while higher abundance of Bifidobacterium was observed in individuals consuming yogurt regularly. Short-chain fatty acid levels, measured via gas chromatography, were significantly elevated in these cohorts, suggesting a mechanistic link between yogurt-mediated microbiome modulation and neuroinflammatory attenuation. Mouse models of PD fed a yogurt-supplemented diet exhibited improved motor coordination and reduced striatal α-synuclein aggregation, findings corroborated by multivariate regression analyses. These data highlight the role of diet-microbiome interactions in modulating PD progression, with yogurt consumption emerging as a modifiable factor warranting further investigation in longitudinal studies.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition and Bdnf expression profiles in the hippocampus are linked to cognitive decline in aging populations. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and increased Enterobacteriaceae in individuals with Alzheimer's disease, correlating with decreased Bdnf transcriptional activity. Principal component analysis of metagenomic data identified three microbial clusters significantly associated with neuroinflammation markers, including elevated IL-6 levels. Single-cell RNA sequencing further localized Bdnf downregulation to glial cells in rodent models subjected to high-fat diets, which also disrupted gut microbiota homeostasis. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and Bdnf-mediated neuroplasticity impairment, suggesting targeted microbiota modulation as a therapeutic strategy. Multivariate regression confirmed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance independently predicted Bdnf expression levels (β = -0.43, p < 0.01), reinforcing the role of gut-brain axis signaling in neurodegenerative progression.

Modulation of the TLR4 gene by curcumin, a polyphenolic compound derived from Curcuma longa, significantly reduces neuroinflammation in a murine model of gut-brain axis dysfunction. In a cohort of 120 rodents with induced intestinal permeability, curcumin supplementation (200 mg/kg/day) for 8 weeks led to a 42% decrease in hippocampal TLR4 expression compared to controls. This downregulation correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and improved executive function scores, as measured by behavioral assays. Gut microbiota analysis revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Escherichia coli, suggesting a microbiome-mediated mechanism. The TLR4 pathway's modulation by curcumin highlights its potential as a therapeutic target for neurodegenerative disorders linked to gut dysbiosis. The study further demonstrated that curcumin enhanced gut microbial diversity while suppressing lipopolysaccharide translocation, a key driver of systemic inflammation and cognitive decline. These findings underscore the interplay between TLR4-mediated signaling, microbiome dynamics, and neurobehavioral outcomes, offering novel insights into diet-gene interactions in brain health.

A dietary supplement containing probiotic Lactobacillus strains significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and improved behavioral outcomes in a preclinical model of chronic stress-induced depression. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified distinct shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios following 4-week supplementation, correlating with reduced anhedonia and enhanced Shannon diversity indices. Male C57BL/6 mice exposed to repeated social defeat stress exhibited increased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and altered intestinal microbial metabolites, which were partially reversed by the supplement. Notably, the Prevotella genus showed a strong inverse relationship with depressive-like behaviors in multivariate regression models, suggesting potential microbial biomarkers. The intervention also restored hippocampal Bdnf expression, a key mediator of neuroplasticity, linking microbiome alterations to neurobiological changes. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic formulations in modulating the gut-brain axis via microbiome profiling and mechanistic pathways involving neurotrophic factor regulation.

Altered microbial metabolism of polyphenol-rich foods correlates with cognitive resilience in amyloid precursor protein (APP) transgenic models, as demonstrated by metagenomic sequencing and metabolomic profiling of fecal samples from APP/PS1 mice fed a diet enriched in blueberries. Multivariate analysis revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance inversely correlated with hippocampal Apoe expression levels, while microbial-derived tryptophan metabolites showed positive associations with spatial memory tasks. Gut microbiota diversity, quantified via alpha-diversity indices, was significantly higher in participants consuming fermented dairy compared to controls, suggesting dietary modulation of neuroinflammatory pathways. TLR4 activation in microglia, inferred from qPCR data, aligned with shifts in gut microbiota composition, particularly increased Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus rhamnosus taxa. These findings highlight the interplay between polyphenol intake, Apoe-mediated lipid metabolism, and canonical correlation analysis of microbial biomarkers in modulating neurodegenerative risk via the gut-brain axis.

The gut microbiome modulates hippocampal neurogenesis through TLR4-dependent signaling pathways, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and transcriptomic profiling in a murine model of chronic stress. Prevotella copri-dominated microbiota enhanced synaptic plasticity by upregulating BDNF expression, while Escherichia coli abundance correlated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in the amygdala. Mechanistically, TLR4 activation in enteric glial cells promoted secretion of IL-6, which crossed the blood-brain barrier to modulate BDNF transcription. This interaction was disrupted by TLR4 antagonists, restoring depression-like behavior in rodent subjects. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, further influenced HDAC2 activity, altering chromatin accessibility at BDNF promoter regions. These findings highlight TLR4 as a critical mediator linking the gut microbiome to neurodegenerative disorders, with implications for targeted metabolomic interventions in mental health disorders.

Trem2 expression in microglia was significantly upregulated in Alzheimer's disease models following curcumin supplementation, correlating with reduced amyloid-beta plaque burden. Oat beta-glucan-enriched diets synergized with curcumin to enhance gut microbiome diversity, as evidenced by 16S rRNA sequencing, while Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated with Trem2 activation. Multivariate analysis revealed that Trem2 modulation was linked to altered short-chain fatty acid profiles, particularly elevated butyrate levels from oat-fermented Bacteroides strains. Curcumin also suppressed Nlrp3-mediated inflammasome activation in hippocampal neurons, reducing neuroinflammation markers. These findings suggest that curcumin-mediated Trem2 regulation and oat-derived prebiotics act through convergent pathways to mitigate Alzheimer's disease progression by harmonizing gut-brain signaling.
