metadata.abstract: 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus plantarum significantly altered gut microbiota composition in adults consuming a high-fiber diet enriched in fermented vegetables. These changes correlated with reduced inflammation markers and enhanced expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota modulation and immune homeostasis. Metabolomic profiling identified increased production of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, which were associated with improved irritable bowel syndrome symptoms. The prevailing microbiota in participants receiving the probiotic showed elevated abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, while Faecalibacterium prausnitzii levels correlated with FOXO3 activation, a key regulator of cellular stress responses. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions combined with fiber-rich diets to modulate the gut-brain axis via immune-related pathways, offering novel strategies for managing neuroimmune disorders.

Manipulating gut microbiota via fermented kimchi and inulin supplementation significantly modulates neuroinflammatory responses in C57BL/6 mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that kimchi-enriched diets increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, while inulin promoted Prevotella expansion, both correlating with reduced IL-6 and TNF-α levels in hippocampal tissues. ELISA confirmed lower serum glucocorticoid concentrations in supplemented groups, alongside improved depressive-like behavior in forced swim tests. Inulin also enhanced BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex, whereas kimchi-derived short-chain fatty acids suppressed microglial activation via TLR4 signaling. Microbial diversity shifts aligned with altered serotonin metabolism in the enteric nervous system, suggesting a bidirectional gut-brain communication pathway. These findings highlight the potential of fermented foods and prebiotics to mitigate neuroinflammation and behavioral deficits through microbiota-mediated immune regulation, with multi-omics approaches essential for dissecting these mechanisms.

Altered gut microbiota composition in individuals consuming high-saturated-fat diets correlates with variations in the TLR4 gene and is associated with neuroinflammation markers via canonical correlation analysis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 120 participants with depression and 120 controls, we identified that red meat intake was strongly linked to reduced gut microbiota diversity and elevated lipopolysaccharide levels. TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells was positively correlated with IL-6 production, which in turn showed a significant association with principal component analysis-derived microbiota clusters. Participants with depression exhibited distinct microbial taxa profiles, including increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and decreased Bifidobacterium levels, patterns that aligned with TLR4 polymorphisms. Multivariate analysis revealed that the interaction between red meat consumption and TLR4 genotype explained 32% of the variance in neuroinflammation scores. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between dietary patterns, microbial dysbiosis, and immune signaling pathways, suggesting that targeting TLR4-mediated inflammation could mitigate depression risk in individuals with dysbiotic gut microbiomes.

Modulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome by curcumin in colonic epithelial cells correlates with altered gut microbiome composition and reduced neuroinflammation in murine models of Alzheimer's disease. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Prevotella and decreased levels of Bacteroides in Curcuma longa-treated cohorts, alongside elevated butyrate production. Curcumin suppressed NLRP3-mediated caspase-1 activation, attenuating microglial activation in hippocampal regions. These effects were accompanied by improved spatial memory in mice fed a high-fat diet and co-administered curcumin. Multivariate analysis revealed significant correlations between microbial taxa shifts and NLRP3 expression levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut dysbiosis and neurodegenerative progression. Curcumin treatment also restored intestinal barrier integrity by upregulating Occludin and ZO-1 expression, mitigating systemic inflammation. These findings highlight the potential of curcumin-mediated NLRP3 inhibition as a therapeutic strategy targeting both gut-brain axis dysfunction and Alzheimer's disease pathology.

L-Leucine supplementation modulated gut microbiota dynamics and BDNF expression in rodent models of metabolic syndrome, as demonstrated by canonical correspondence analysis of 16S rRNA profiling. L-Leucine administration for 8 weeks increased abundance of Odoribacter and Parabacteroides while decreasing Prevotella, correlating with enhanced BDNF mRNA levels in hippocampal tissue. MANOVA revealed significant associations between leucine-induced microbial shifts and improved insulin resistance metrics. BDNF upregulation paralleled reduced inflammatory cytokines in serum, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut microbiota remodeling and neuroplasticity pathways. qPCR confirmed BDNF expression changes, while metabolomics identified elevated short-chain fatty acids as potential mediators. These findings highlight L-Leucine's dual role in shaping gut microbiota and modulating BDNF-dependent neuroendocrine signaling, offering a novel strategy for targeting metabolic syndrome through the gut-brain axis.

The modulation of gut microbiota through dietary supplementation with Lactobacillus reuteri significantly alters neurobehavioral outcomes in a murine model of anxiety, as evidenced by reduced exploratory behavior and altered hippocampal neurogenesis. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a marked increase in Lactobacillus abundance alongside decreased Desulfovibrio levels in treated C57BL/6 mice, correlating with diminished anxiety-like traits in the elevated plus maze. Principal component analysis further highlighted distinct microbial clustering between supplemented and control groups, with short-chain fatty acid production rates showing significant variance. These changes were accompanied by elevated brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the hippocampus, suggesting microbiome-driven neuroplasticity. Notably, the gut-brain axis appears to mediate these effects through serotonin signaling pathways, as inferred from gene expression profiling. The findings underscore the therapeutic potential of probiotic interventions in modulating neurobehavioral disorders, with multi-omics approaches revealing intricate interactions between microbial metabolites and central nervous system function. Pathway enrichment analysis confirmed significant overlaps between microbial-derived butyrate metabolism and neuroinflammatory markers, reinforcing the role of the gut microbiome in neurodevelopmental processes.

TLR4 signaling in enteric neurons modulates neuroinflammation via interactions with gut microbiota metabolites derived from fiber-rich foods and prebiotic fiber. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes in the colon influence TLR4-mediated pathways, altering Alzheimer's disease progression in rodent models. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that TLR4 expression correlates with butyrate levels in patients consuming fermented dairy supplemented with inulin. Butyrate enhanced TLR4 activation, reducing neuroinflammatory markers in hippocampal regions while promoting gut microbiota diversity. qPCR analysis confirmed that TLR4 upregulation in subjects with Alzheimer's disease was inversely proportional to whole grain intake and resistant starch supplementation. These findings suggest that TLR4 serves as a molecular link between gut microbiota metabolism of fiber-derived substrates and cognitive decline, highlighting prebiotic interventions as potential therapeutic strategies.

A high-fiber legume-based diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition, as demonstrated by permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealing distinct microbial community structures in individuals consuming ≥3 servings daily compared to controls. This shift correlated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila, while short-chain fatty acid production rates rose by 42% (p<0.001). Analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from 120 participants showed that dietary fiber intake explained 28% of variance in gut microbiome alpha diversity, with FUT2 polymorphisms moderating this relationship. Functional pathway predictions indicated enhanced butyrate synthesis via Blautia and Ruminococcus, which inversely correlated with systemic IL-6 levels (r=-0.39, p=0.002). Notably, participants with >10% of energy from legumes exhibited 35% lower incidence of metabolic syndrome over 18 months, suggesting a mechanistic link between fiber-mediated microbiota remodeling and systemic inflammation. These findings underscore the potential of targeted prebiotic interventions to modulate gut-brain signaling pathways, with implications for managing neuroinflammatory disorders through dietary strategies.

Altered expression of the TLR5 gene in mice was found to dysregulate the gut microbiota, resulting in heightened anxiety-like behaviors and impaired hippocampal neuroplasticity. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified significant shifts in microbial taxa, including increased abundance of Escherichia coli and reduced diversity of Butyricimonas, correlating with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the blood-brain barrier. Mechanistically, TLR5 deficiency disrupted short-chain fatty acid production by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a gut-derived metabolite critical for modulating glial cell activation. Transplantation of TLR5-deficient microbiota into wild-type mice recapitulated anxiety-like behaviors and altered serotonin signaling in the prefrontal cortex, while 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed microbial translocation to the brain via lymphatic pathways. These findings highlight TLR5 as a key regulator of gut-brain communication and underscore the role of metagenomic analysis in elucidating microbial contributions to neurobehavioral disorders. The study further reveals potential therapeutic targets for modulating gut microbiota-mediated neuroinflammation in psychiatric conditions.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly influences neuroinflammatory pathways in multiple sclerosis patients, as evidenced by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealing reduced diversity of commensal bacteria linked to immune dysregulation. Intervention with curcumin modulated microbial taxa associated with immune regulation, including increased abundance of Bacteroides and Parabacteroides, while decreasing Akkermansia and Ruminococcus levels. Metabolic profiling via mass spectrometry revealed elevated butyrate levels, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-17 in peripheral blood samples. Longitudinal analysis of patient cohorts demonstrated that curcumin supplementation synergized with flow cytometry-derived immune cell phenotyping to identify shifts in gut-associated lymphoid tissue activation states. These findings suggest that targeted supplementation may restore microbiota-immune homeostasis, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for multiple sclerosis management by leveraging microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids as anti-inflammatory mediators.

Chronic dietary fiber deficiency disrupts hippocampal synaptic integrity and cognitive function via dysregulation of the gut microbiota-SCFA axis. A 15-week murine model of fiber restriction revealed significant cognitive impairment alongside hippocampal synaptic ultrastructural abnormalities, including widened synaptic clefts and thinned postsynaptic densities. Hippocampal proteomic analysis identified reduced expression of the CaMKIId gene and its associated synaptic proteins, including GAP43, coupled with neuroinflammation and microglial engulfment of synapses. Concurrent gut microbiota dysbiosis featured decreased Bacteroidetes and increased Proteobacteria populations, linked to compromised intestinal barrier function and reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production. Notably, oral SCFA supplementation partially restored synaptic protein levels and mitigated cognitive deficits in SCFA receptor knockout mice, underscoring SCFAs as critical mediators of gut-brain communication. These findings establish a mechanistic pathway connecting dietary fiber intake to hippocampal health through microbiota-derived metabolites, highlighting potential therapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota-SCFA axis for neurodegenerative conditions.

Alterations in the gut microbiota have been implicated in the pathogenesis of autoimmune encephalitis, yet the mechanisms linking microbial dysbiosis to neuroinflammation remain poorly defined. This study identified resveratrol-mediated modulation of gut microbial communities as a potential therapeutic strategy, using a murine model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Resveratrol supplementation significantly reduced clinical scores and central nervous system infiltration of Proteobacteria while enriching Prevotella and Bacteroides taxa associated with anti-inflammatory profiles. Multivariate analysis revealed strong correlations between resveratrol-induced shifts in microbial composition and decreased cytokine levels, particularly TNF-α and IL-17. Additionally, 16S rRNA sequencing highlighted a 40% reduction in EAE-related microbial diversity, with resveratrol partially restoring alpha diversity metrics. These findings suggest that resveratrol exerts neuroprotective effects by reshaping the gut microbiome to suppress pro-inflammatory pathways, underscoring the potential of resveratrol as a microbiota-targeted intervention for autoimmune neurological disorders.

Altered expression of the Tlr4 gene in the prefrontal cortex correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition following chronic stress in C57BL/6J mice. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified a significant depletion of Lactobacillus reuteri and an enrichment of Desulfovibrio piger in Tlr4 knockout mice exposed to repeated social defeat stress, which was linked to elevated quorum sensing signaling molecules in fecal samples. L. reuteri supplementation reversed stress-induced behavioral deficits, including anhedonia and social avoidance, while qPCR confirmed downregulation of Tlr4-mediated pro-inflammatory cytokine pathways in the amygdala. These findings highlight the role of Tlr4 in modulating gut-brain communication via microbial metabolites, suggesting L. reuteri as a potential therapeutic target for depressive-like states driven by neuroinflammation. The interplay between host immune signaling and microbial diversity underscores the complexity of the central nervous system-gastrointestinal tract axis in stress-related disorders.

Prebiotic supplementation modulates neuroinflammatory pathways through regulation of TLR4 expression in the gut-brain axis, as demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis of murine models with colitis-associated cognitive decline. Inulin administration altered gut microbiota composition, increasing Prevotella abundance while reducing pro-inflammatory Fusobacterium levels. Concurrently, TLR4 transcript abundance in hippocampal tissues correlated inversely with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) concentrations in systemic circulation. Mechanistically, inulin enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which suppressed TLR4-mediated activation of NF-κB signaling in enteric neurons. This effect was corroborated by ELISA quantification of IL-6 and TNF-α in serum, showing 40% and 35% reductions, respectively, in inulin-treated cohorts. Functional enrichment analysis revealed TLR4-regulated pathways, including axon guidance and microglial activation, were significantly altered. These findings highlight a potential therapeutic axis where prebiotic intervention could mitigate neuroinflammation by targeting TLR4 expression, offering new strategies for neurodegenerative disorders linked to gut dysbiosis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative conditions, with emerging evidence suggesting that probiotic supplementation may modulate this relationship. A cohort study of 120 individuals with Parkinson’s disease (PD) and 80 healthy controls utilized 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial composition. Participants received a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium for 12 weeks, while controls received a placebo. PERMANOVA revealed significant differences in beta diversity between PD patients and controls, with probiotic treatment correlating with increased abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and reduced Prevotella. These findings suggest that microbiome-targeted therapies could alleviate PD-related gastrointestinal symptoms, though larger trials are needed to confirm efficacy and explore mechanisms underlying microbial shifts in neurodegenerative disease.

A high-fiber oat-based diet significantly modulates gut microbiota composition in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by canonical correspondence analysis. Participants (n=45) consumed a standardized oat supplement for 12 weeks, with baseline and post-intervention faecal microbiome profiles analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing. Alpha diversity increased by 18% (p=0.012), while <bacteria>Bifidobacterium longum</bacteria> abundance rose by 40% (p=0.003), correlating with reduced abdominal pain scores (r=-0.52, p=0.018). <bacteria>Faecalibacterium prausnitzii</bacteria> showed a 25% decline (p=0.021), coinciding with elevated serotonin levels in plasma (Δ=12.4 ng/mL, p=0.032). Permutational multivariate analysis identified distinct microbial community clusters between IBS groups, with <bacteria>Prevotella copri</bacteria> enrichment (p=0.007) in non-responders. The oat intervention also improved sleep quality (PSQI score reduction: 2.3 points, p=0.011) and mental health (PHQ-9 decrease: 4.1 points, p=0.024), suggesting microbiota-mediated neuroimmune pathways. These findings highlight the potential of targeted prebiotic diets to alleviate gastrointestinal and psychological symptoms through microbial and neurochemical modulation.

The disruption of Tlr5 signaling in murine models was linked to altered gut microbiota composition and heightened anxiety-like behavior, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays. This gene-mediated dysregulation correlated with reduced abundance of Bacteroidetes and elevated levels of Firmicutes, suggesting a mechanistic role for Tlr5 in modulating microbial communities that influence neurobehavioral outcomes. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Prevotella were identified as potential mediators of this interaction, with their concentrations quantified via gas chromatography. Further, Tlr5 knockout models exhibited diminished IL-6 expression in the hypothalamus, linking immune signaling to gut-brain communication. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic factors and the microbiome in shaping anxiety phenotypes, underscoring the need for targeted interventions that address both microbial and host-derived pathways.

Altered expression of the BDNF gene in the prefrontal cortex is linked to cognitive deficits in offspring exposed to a high-fat diet during lactation, as evidenced by mice models and RNA sequencing analysis. Maternal consumption of the high-fat diet led to dysregulated gut microbiota composition and reduced serotonin metabolite levels in offspring, which correlated with impaired spatial memory and attention. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated lipopolysaccharide concentrations, suggesting increased gut permeability, while ANOVA confirmed significant interactions between BDNF expression and gut microbiota diversity. These findings highlight the role of BDNF-mediated neuroplasticity in modulating the gut-brain axis and underscore the impact of high-fat diet exposure on cognitive development. Mechanistically, qPCR identified downregulation of BDNF target genes in the hippocampus, alongside shifts in gut microbiota taxa associated with inflammatory signaling pathways. The study further suggests that interventions targeting BDNF expression or high-fat diet-induced microbiota alterations may mitigate cognitive impairment in early life.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression is significantly modulated by gut microbiome dysbiosis, with microbial metabolites influencing neuroinflammation and Aβ pathology. Curcumin (CUR), a spice derivative, has shown in vivo potential to alter GM composition and reduce Aβ accumulation in transgenic AD mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from CUR-treated donors to germ-free AD mice resulted in decreased Aβ plaque load and enhanced IL-10 expression in hippocampal microglia. CUR administration increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a probiotic species linked to blood-brain barrier integrity, while reducing Proteobacteria levels associated with oxidative stress. Multivariate analysis revealed CUR-induced GM shifts correlated with reduced cytokine secretion and improved spatial memory in recipient mice. These findings highlight CUR as a nutraceutical that enhances gut-brain axis communication via FMT, offering therapeutic potential for AD through microbiome-directed interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition is strongly correlated with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with major depressive disorder, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for targeted dietary interventions. Metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from 120 participants revealed reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated levels of Escherichia coli in individuals receiving probiotic supplementation compared to controls. Cytokine profiling demonstrated decreased IL-6 and TNF-α concentrations in the probiotic group, alongside improved mood scores assessed via Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Microbial metabolite analysis identified increased butyrate production in probiotic-treated subjects, correlating with enhanced prefrontal cortex activity on functional MRI. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a modifiable pathway for depression management, with probiotics potentially restoring microbial balance and reducing systemic inflammation. The study underscores the value of multi-omics integration in elucidating microbiota-driven mechanisms of psychiatric disorders. Further clinical trials are warranted to validate these associations and optimize microbiome-targeted therapies.

A novel dietary supplement containing prebiotic fibers significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, enhancing neural plasticity through the gut-brain axis. Mouse models fed a high-fat diet alongside the supplement showed altered Bacteroidetes abundance and increased production of short-chain fatty acids, which correlated with improved hippocampal function. Using random forest analysis, we identified the FABP2 gene as a key mediator of these effects, linking microbiota-derived metabolites to synaptic density in the prefrontal cortex. The prebiotic blend also reduced inflammatory markers, as evidenced by decreased IL-6 levels in serum. These findings suggest that targeting intestinal microbial diversity via dietary interventions may ameliorate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in conditions like Alzheimer's disease, where FABP2 dysregulation is implicated. Additionally, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the supplement preserved Lactobacillus populations, which were previously linked to depression in human cohorts. This study underscores the interplay between microbiota composition, host genetic factors, and brain function, offering a potential therapeutic avenue for gut-brain axis-related disorders.

A polymorphism in the FMO3 gene modulates gut microbiota-derived metabolites linked to cognitive function in middle-aged adults, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples. Participants consuming a high-choline diet exhibited altered microbiome composition, with increased abundance of Prevotella and reduced Bacteroides, correlating with elevated plasma TMAO levels. These changes were amplified in individuals harboring the FMO3 rs1799831 variant, which encodes a less active flavin monooxygenase enzyme critical for choline metabolism. Cognitive assessments using the Trail Making Test showed that carriers of this variant demonstrated slower processing speed after 12 weeks on the high-choline regimen, suggesting a gene-diet-microbiome interaction affecting neurocognitive outcomes. Notably, the gut microbiome of variant carriers displayed reduced diversity and enrichment in Enterobacteriaceae, potentially contributing to neuroinflammation. Conversely, non-carriers showed stable microbiota profiles and improved memory retention, as measured by verbal learning tasks. These findings highlight the role of FMO3 in mediating how dietary choline influences the gut-brain axis through microbial metabolic pathways, with implications for personalized nutrition strategies targeting cognitive health.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), yet mechanisms linking microbial dysbiosis to disease progression remain underexplored. Using 16S rDNA sequencing, we identified Bacteroides fragilis as a key taxon inversely associated with TNF-α expression in colonic mucosa from C57BL/6 mice subjected to 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) exposure. Dietary intervention with curcumin restored Bacteroides abundance and suppressed TNF-α activation via modulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reducing PD-like motor deficits by 35%. Metabolomic profiling revealed curcumin-enhanced production of indole-3-propionic acid, a tryptophan-derived microbial metabolite with neuroprotective properties. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting gut microbiota-derived metabolites to modulate inflammatory pathways in neurodegenerative disorders, with natural compounds like curcumin offering a viable strategy to restore gut-brain communication.

A novel interaction between the Ephx2 gene and fermented food consumption modulates gut microbiota composition, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models. Fermented dairy products enriched in Lactobacillus were administered to wild-type and Ephx2 knockout mice, followed by principal component analysis (PCA) of 16S rRNA sequencing data to evaluate microbial shifts. Mice with Ephx2 deletion exhibited heightened resilience to chronic stress when fed fermented dairy, correlating with increased abundance of Lachnospiraceae and reduced Escherichia-Shigella relative to controls. PCA revealed distinct clustering of microbiota profiles in Ephx2 knockout groups, aligning with lower interleukin-6 levels and preserved synaptic protein expression in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that fermented food intake may mitigate stress-induced behavioral deficits via Ephx2-mediated modulation of the gut microbiota, highlighting potential therapeutic strategies for depression-related disorders. The PCA-identified microbial signatures provide a framework for targeting gut-brain axis pathways in precision nutrition interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition has been linked to depression and anxiety through the microbiota-gut-brain axis, with emerging evidence highlighting the role of fermented foods in modulating intestinal microbial communities. A 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of participants consuming sauerkraut and probiotic supplements revealed increased Lactobacillus abundance and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. These changes correlated with improved hippocampal volume and reduced anxiety symptoms as measured by validated psychiatric scales. Mechanistically, short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbes were implicated in serotonin synthesis and blood-brain barrier integrity, pathways previously associated with major depressive disorder. Prebiotic intake further enhanced microbial diversity, suggesting synergistic effects between fiber-rich diets and targeted supplementation. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of modulating gut microbiota via dietary interventions in mental health disorders, warranting further longitudinal studies to confirm clinical applicability.

A novel association between fermented dairy consumption and alterations in gut microbiota composition has been identified in individuals with depressive symptoms, highlighting potential mechanistic links to mental health outcomes. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants, stratified by intake of probiotic-enriched yogurt versus non-fermented dairy. Results revealed a significant enrichment of Blautia and Parabacteroides in the probiotic group, alongside reduced abundance of Escherichia-Shigella and Ruminococcus, correlating with lower scores on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Metabolic pathway analysis further indicated upregulation of short-chain fatty acid synthesis genes in probiotic consumers, suggesting a role for microbial metabolites in modulating neuroinflammation. Notably, fermented dairy intake was inversely associated with serum cytokine levels, while probiotic supplementation showed dose-dependent improvements in anxiety and sleep disturbances. These findings underscore the interplay between diet-derived microbial shifts and psychiatric phenotypes, implicating targeted interventions as potential adjuncts in managing depressive disorders. Validation through longitudinal studies incorporating multiplex cytokine profiling and gut-brain axis biomarkers is warranted to elucidate causal pathways.

A longitudinal study reveals that dietary interventions involving fermented products significantly modulate the gut microbiota in individuals with depressive symptoms, with multivariate analysis identifying key microbial taxa correlated to symptom severity. Participants receiving a probiotic blend showed a 28% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance compared to controls, alongside reduced inflammation markers. 16S rRNA sequencing further revealed that fiber-rich diets enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which was inversely linked to anxiety scores via canonical correlation analysis. These findings suggest that targeted psychobiotic formulations, combined with prebiotic-rich diets, may optimize neuroimmune pathways in psychiatric care. The study underscores the role of gut-brain axis dynamics in mental health, emphasizing the need for personalized microbiome-based interventions validated through machine learning models to predict therapeutic outcomes.

The TNF-alpha polymorphism modulates gut microbiota composition and inflammatory signaling, linking depression to central nervous system dysfunction via Mendelian randomization analyses. Participants with major depressive disorder exhibited altered tryptophan metabolism and reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium, correlating with TNF-alpha rs1800629 genotypes. Probiotic supplementation targeting lactobacilli improved serotonin precursor levels and mitigated depressive symptoms in mice with TNF-alpha-mediated neuroinflammation. Conditional logistic regression confirmed that TNF-alpha variants interacted with gut microbiome diversity to predict depression severity (β = -0.31, p = 0.002). Short-chain fatty acids produced by Butyricicoccus were identified as key mediators, with prebiotic fibers enhancing their bioavailability in individuals with TNF-alpha risk alleles. These findings highlight the interplay between immune-related genes, gut microbial metabolites, and interventions in modulating mental health outcomes through blood-brain barrier permeability and neurotransmitter homeostasis.

The disruption of Tlr4 signaling in C57BL/6 mice alters neuroinflammatory pathways and modifies gut microbiota composition, revealing a critical link between host immunity and central nervous system function. 16S rRNA sequencing identified significant reductions in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in Tlr4-deficient animals compared to wild-type controls, alongside elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) in colonic tissue. These microbiome shifts correlated with increased anxiety-like behavior and impaired hippocampal neuroplasticity, as measured by immunohistochemistry for BDNF expression. Tlr4 knockout mice exhibited heightened susceptibility to stress-induced visceral hypersensitivity, with serotonin receptor activation in enteric neurons dysregulated by altered microbial metabolites. The findings highlight Tlr4 as a pivotal mediator of microbiome-brain communication, suggesting that targeting Tlr4-regulated pathways could ameliorate neuroimmune disorders linked to gut dysbiosis.

A novel probiotic formulation derived from fermented kefir significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of metabolic syndrome, with implications for depression-related behavioral deficits. C57BL/6J mice fed a high-fat diet were supplemented with the probiotic for eight weeks, during which 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased alpha diversity and enrichment of Lactobacillus species. Behavioral testing demonstrated improved exploratory behavior and reduced anhedonia compared to control groups. Mechanistically, the probiotic attenuated pro-inflammatory cytokine production in colonic tissue, correlating with downregulation of the Tlr4 gene, a key mediator of intestinal inflammation. Western blot analysis confirmed reduced phosphorylation of NF-κB in hippocampus tissue, suggesting mitigation of neuroinflammatory pathways. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of fermented dairy products in modulating gut-brain axis signaling via Tlr4-dependent mechanisms, offering a novel approach to address comorbid metabolic and psychiatric disorders.

Our findings demonstrate that specific alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models of chronic stress, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis. Using a lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation model, we observed a significant depletion of Bacteroidetes and enrichment of Firmicutes in fecal samples, with Lactobacillus showing a negative correlation with anxiety-like behaviors (r = -0.63, P < 0.01). Metagenomic shotgun sequencing further identified tryptophanase-encoding pathways as differentially expressed in stress-exposed cohorts. Application of random forest classification confirmed that butyrate production by Ruminococcus bromii was a predictive biomarker for resilience to stress-induced cognitive deficits (<AUC> 0.89). These data highlight the utility of integrating multi-omics profiling with machine learning to dissect microbial contributions to psychiatric comorbidities, suggesting that targeting gut microbiota metabolic pathways may offer novel therapeutic strategies for stress-related disorders.

Tlr5 deficiency in mice alters gut microbiota composition and enhances neuroinflammation via 16S rRNA sequencing analysis, revealing increased Bacteroidetes and reduced Firmicutes ratios. Administration of probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum partially restored microbial balance, decreasing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in colonic tissue and improving neurobehavioral outcomes in autism spectrum disorder models. Tlr5-deficient mice exhibited heightened interleukin-6 production in enteric nervous system ganglia, which correlated with increased microglial activation in hippocampus. Probiotic supplementation reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation by modulating Tlr5-dependent signaling pathways, as evidenced by qPCR and immunohistochemistry. These findings highlight the interplay between Tlr5 expression, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and neurodevelopmental disorders, suggesting targeted microbial interventions as potential therapeutic strategies.

A 12-week intervention with fermented dairy products, rich in probiotics, significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in individuals with anxiety, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Participants consuming daily servings of kefir exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and reduced levels of Escherichia coli, correlating with improved scores on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which may mediate the observed anxiolytic effects through gut-brain axis signaling. The study also highlighted gut microbiome dysbiosis as a potential biomarker for anxiety severity, with Mann-Whitney U tests confirming significant differences between the intervention and control groups (P < 0.01). Notably, adherence to the kefir-based diet was associated with enhanced serotonin transporter expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived metabolites and neurochemical pathways. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of dietary modulation in targeting gut-brain interactions, offering a non-pharmacologic strategy for managing anxiety-related disorders. The integration of metagenomic analysis and dietary intervention highlights the role of gut microbiota as a modifiable factor in mental health outcomes, warranting further exploration of probiotic-rich foods in clinical settings.

A probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with major depressive disorder, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing, and correlated with reduced expression of the TLR4 gene, a key mediator of neuroinflammation. Analysis of fecal samples from 45 participants demonstrated that the supplement increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum while decreasing Escherichia coli, concomitant with decreased plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines. qPCR confirmed downregulation of TLR4 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota modulation and immune signaling pathways. Functional enrichment analysis identified TLR4-regulated pathways, including NF-κB signaling, as significantly attenuated in supplemented individuals. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to alleviate depression by reshaping the gut microbiome and modulating host immune-related genes. The study underscores the role of gut microbiota in neuroimmune crosstalk and supports further exploration of TLR4 as a therapeutic target in depressive disorders.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells significantly correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition that influence neuroinflammation pathways. A cohort study employing multivariate regression analysis revealed that individuals consuming a high-fiber diet enriched in inulin exhibited reduced systemic inflammation markers compared to controls. These findings were corroborated by metagenomic sequencing showing increased abundance of Bacteroidetes and decreased Firmicutes ratios in the gut of participants adhering to the dietary intervention. Mechanistically, TLR4-mediated signaling was found to modulate microbial metabolite production, including short-chain fatty acids, which in turn affected hippocampal neurogenesis in mice models. The butyrate levels, a key short-chain fatty acid, correlated strongly with cognitive performance metrics in both human and rodent subjects. Furthermore, prebiotic supplementation synergized with TLR4 downregulation to enhance neuroprotective effects, suggesting a dual-target therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease and related neurodegenerative disorders. This study underscores the interplay between host genetic factors, dietary modulation, and microbial metabolism in shaping brain health outcomes.

Altered microbial production of tryptophan derivatives in the gut correlates with neurodegenerative disorders, highlighting a potential gut-brain axis mechanism involving tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (Tph2). Using shotgun metagenomics, we analyzed fecal samples from 50 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 50 controls, identifying dysregulated pathways in Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis linked to indole synthesis. Principal component analysis revealed that Tph2 expression in the prefrontal cortex significantly predicted microbial serotonin production levels, with an AUC of 0.89. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed reduced abundance of Prevotella and increased Enterococcus in Alzheimer's cohorts, correlating with Tph2-mediated metabolic shifts. Integrating metabolomics data with random forest modeling, we identified 5-hydroxytryptamine as a key mediator between gut microbiota and neuroinflammation markers. These findings underscore Tph2's role in linking microbial tryptophan metabolism to Alzheimer's progression via the gut-brain axis, offering novel targets for therapeutic intervention.

A high-fiber legume-based diet significantly alters gut microbial diversity and correlates with reduced systemic inflammation in aging adults, as revealed by multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) of fecal metagenomic datasets. Participants consuming 200 g/day of legumes for 12 weeks exhibited a 15.6% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance and a 22.3% decrease in Escherichia coli, alongside lower plasma IL-6 levels compared to controls. 16S rRNA sequencing identified a positive correlation between legume intake and short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which was further validated using canonical correlation analysis to link microbial taxa with inflammatory biomarkers. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting fiber-rich foods may modulate the gut-brain axis by enhancing anti-inflammatory pathways, offering a potential strategy for mitigating neurodegenerative risk factors associated with chronic low-grade inflammation.

A novel TLR4 variant was associated with altered gut microbiota composition in individuals consuming fermented dairy products as part of a longitudinal cohort study examining mental health outcomes. Using principal component analysis, researchers identified distinct microbial clusters correlated with anxiety severity and tryptophan metabolism in adults with subthreshold depression. Participants adhering to a plant-based diet showed reduced lipopolysaccharide levels and enhanced SCN9A expression in enteric neurons, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary patterns, immune signaling, and neurobehavioral phenotypes. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Faecalibacterium abundance inversely predicted emotional dysregulation scores, while multivariate logistic regression confirmed the independent contribution of TLR4 polymorphism to gut-brain axis dysfunction. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetic factors, microbial ecology, and diet in modulating mental health outcomes, emphasizing the need for personalized interventions targeting intestinal dysbiosis.

Altered expression of the FTO gene has been implicated in dysregulated gut microbiota composition, which correlates with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with depression. A 16S rRNA sequencing analysis revealed that FTO variants were associated with reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium and elevated Proteobacteria, suggesting a link between host genetics and microbiome-driven inflammation. Interventions targeting fiber-rich diets and probiotic supplementation were tested in a rodent model, where prebiotic intake restored Bifidobacterium levels and mitigated depressive-like behaviors via modulation of short-chain fatty acid production. FTO knockout mice exhibited heightened lipopolysaccharide translocation and increased IL-6 secretion, which were normalized by probiotic administration. These findings highlight the interplay between FTO-mediated host-microbiome interactions, nutritional interventions, and mental health outcomes, underscoring the potential of probiotic therapies to counteract FTO-related disruptions in the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are linked to neuroinflammation via immune signaling pathways, with TLR4 playing a pivotal role in modulating host responses. This study examines the interplay between gut microbial composition and TLR4-mediated inflammation in multiple sclerosis (MS) using 16S rRNA sequencing and logistic regression to identify predictive biomarkers. Analysis of fecal samples from 85 MS patients and 50 healthy controls revealed a significant reduction in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance in MS subjects, correlated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) and increased TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Logistic regression models confirmed that TLR4 upregulation and Akkermansia muciniphila depletion were independent predictors of disease progression (AUC = 0.82, 95% CI 0.75–0.89). These findings highlight the potential of gut microbiota and TLR4 as therapeutic targets for modulating neuroinflammation in MS, underscoring the need for microbiome-directed interventions to regulate TLR4-dependent immune activation in autoimmune disorders.

Altered TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells was associated with shifts in gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in a murine model of colitis. Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated inversely with proinflammatory cytokine levels in cecum tissue, while Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron showed heightened metabolic activity in duodenum lumen. TLR4-deficient mice exhibited reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced permeability in intestinal epithelium, accompanied by increased short-chain fatty acid production from Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan derivatives in serum, linking microbiota shifts to altered hypothalamic signaling pathways. TLR4 modulation via TLR4 antagonist administration restored microbial homeostasis and attenuated neuroinflammation in hippocampus regions, as detected by immunohistochemistry. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4-mediated immune regulation and microbiota-derived metabolites in shaping gut-brain axis dynamics during inflammatory conditions.

Dietary intake of fermented foods significantly alters the expression of the TNF-α gene in gut-associated lymphoid tissue, suggesting a direct link between microbiome modulation and inflammatory responses. Kimchi consumption in a murine model increased Lactobacillus reuteri abundance, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Using qPCR and 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed upregulation of TLR4 signaling pathways concurrent with shifts in gut microbiota composition. Kimchi-enriched diets enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which suppressed TNF-α expression via histone deacetylase inhibition. ELISA confirmed decreased TNF-α in serum, while flow cytometry revealed increased regulatory T cell frequencies. These findings highlight the role of fermented foods in shaping microbiota-gene interactions that mitigate inflammation, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for inflammatory bowel disease. The ANOVA analysis confirmed significant differences in TNF-α expression across groups (p < 0.01), reinforcing the mechanistic link between dietary intervention and immune regulation.

Modulation of gut microbiota through dietary probiotics influences brain connectivity via genetic pathways, as demonstrated in a murine model of neuroinflammation. Probiotic supplementation with *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* altered gut microbial composition, which correlated with reduced hippocampal hyperconnectivity observed via resting-state fMRI. Analysis of microbiome-derived metabolites using canonical correlation analysis revealed significant associations with hippocampal neuroinflammatory markers. These effects were further linked to polymorphisms in the TLR4 gene, which encodes a toll-like receptor critical for innate immune signaling. Mice with *TLR4* mutations exhibited diminished responses to probiotic-induced microbiota shifts, underscoring the gene’s role in mediating gut-brain communication. Gut dysbiosis in control groups correlated with elevated lipopolysaccharide levels, exacerbating neuroinflammation. The study highlights how probiotic interventions may target TLR4-dependent pathways to modulate brain connectivity, offering therapeutic potential for neurological disorders linked to gut-brain axis dysfunction. Canonical correlation analysis confirmed that microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, acted as mediators between TLR4 expression and synaptic plasticity. These findings suggest a mechanistic bridge between microbiota modulation and neural circuitry, emphasizing the need for personalized microbiome-targeted therapies.

Alterations in the gut microbiota mediated by a probiotic supplement were linked to improved cognitive function in individuals with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for microbial modulation in neurodegeneration. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed significant enrichment of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in participants receiving the intervention, alongside reduced abundance of Escherichia coli and Enterococcus. Principal component analysis identified a microbiome cluster associated with decreased levels of the inflammatory cytokine IL-1β and increased expression of the TREM2 gene, which is implicated in microglial phagocytosis and neuroinflammation. Correlations between microbial taxa and cognitive scores were further validated using multivariate linear regression, revealing that Lactobacillus abundance explained 18% of variance in memory recall tests. Participants with higher TREM2 expression also exhibited lower plasma beta-amyloid levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial-derived metabolites and neurodegenerative pathology. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic therapies to modulate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline via gut-brain signaling pathways. Further studies are needed to dissect the role of TREM2 in microbiome-host interactions and to optimize microbial interventions for clinical translation.

A dietary_supplement probiotic blend administered to pregnant women was associated with reduced anxiety symptoms and altered gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis of fecal microbial networks. Participants receiving the supplement showed a 23% decrease in anxiety scores compared to controls, alongside increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and reduced Escherichia coli levels. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with improved mental health outcomes through modulation of the gut-brain axis. Multivariate logistic regression confirmed that baseline butyrate concentrations predicted greater response to the dietary_supplement, with a 1.7-fold increase in symptom reduction for individuals with higher pre-intervention butyrate levels. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to enhance maternal mental health via microbiome-mediated neuroimmune pathways, supported by longitudinal cohort analyses and mixed-effects modeling of longitudinal outcomes. The study underscores the role of microbial-derived metabolites in shaping psychological resilience during pregnancy, suggesting that microbiome-directed therapies could complement conventional antidepressant regimens in perinatal care.

A diet rich in fermented dairy products significantly modulates the gut microbiome and alleviates depressive-like behaviors in rodents subjected to chronic unpredictable mild stress, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Intervention with fermented dairy restored tryptophan metabolism pathways and increased abundance of Lactobacillus species, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. 16S rRNA sequencing identified 12 microbial taxa significantly altered by the intervention, with multivariate analysis highlighting Bifidobacterium as a key mediator of behavioral improvement. The study further demonstrated that fermented dairy-induced microbiome shifts were associated with enhanced serotonin signaling in the hippocampus, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary modulation of the gut microbiome and depression mitigation. These findings underscore the potential of fermented foods as functional interventions targeting the gut-brain axis, with machine learning-driven microbial profiling offering a novel approach to personalize gut-directed therapies for mental disorders.

Altered gut microbiome composition correlates with cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disorders, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in patients with Alzheimer’s disease. Analysis of fecal samples using metagenomic shotgun sequencing identified reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and elevated Prevotella copri, alongside dysregulated short-chain fatty acid production. Principal component analysis of microbial taxa and clinical metrics highlighted a significant inverse correlation between Akkermansia levels and hippocampal atrophy volume. Intervention trials in transgenic mouse models demonstrated that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus reversed microbiome dysbiosis, restored butyrate levels, and mitigated spatial memory deficits. Concurrently, electrophysiological recordings showed normalized synaptic plasticity in hippocampal neurons. These findings underscore the potential of microbiome-targeted therapies, with probiotics as a viable strategy to modulate gut-brain axis signaling in neurodegenerative conditions. Integration of machine learning models trained on microbiome-clinical data further predicted response to intervention with 82% accuracy, emphasizing the value of multi-omics approaches in precision medicine.

Altered expression of the TSC2 gene in gut epithelial cells correlates with dysregulated neuroinflammatory responses in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, as demonstrated by multivariate regression analysis of fecal microbiome composition and serum cytokine profiles. A high-fiber diet enriched in prebiotic polysaccharides significantly modulated gut microbiota diversity, reducing lipopolysaccharide-induced activation of NF-κB pathways in enteric neurons. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetic determinants, microbial metabolites, and dietary interventions in shaping the gut-brain axis. Resveratrol supplementation further attenuated neuroinflammation via upregulation of SIRT1 expression in hippocampal regions, as evidenced by immunohistochemical staining in a rodent model. Principal component analysis revealed that fermented dairy products consumption clustered with lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids and neuroimmune homeostasis. This study underscores the potential of targeted genomic profiling and personalized nutrition strategies to mitigate neurodegenerative disorders through modulation of the gut-brain interface.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly modulated gut microbial composition and alleviated depressive-like behaviors in mice subjected to chronic stress, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. The intervention, which included fermented soybeans as a dietary matrix, enhanced the abundance of Bifidobacterium while reducing Enterobacteriaceae taxa linked to inflammation. Correlative analyses demonstrated that microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, mediated the anxiolytic effects observed in mice, aligning with elevated serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex. Notably, fermented soybeans alone, when consumed without the prebiotic supplement, failed to produce comparable outcomes, underscoring the synergistic role of targeted microbial modulation. These findings highlight the potential of combining prebiotic formulations with fermented foods to harness the gut-brain axis for therapeutic applications, as supported by multivariate statistical modeling linking microbial taxa to behavioral endpoints. The study further emphasizes the utility of integrated omics approaches in dissecting complex host-microbe interactions underlying mood disorders.

Recent findings highlight the role of fermented dairy products in modulating gut microbiota composition, with implications for neuroinflammation and multiple sclerosis progression. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, this study analyzed fecal samples from 87 participants to assess microbial shifts associated with lactose-containing diets. Lactobacillus abundance correlated inversely with serum interleukin-6 levels, suggesting anti-inflammatory effects linked to short-chain fatty acids production. Bifidobacterium taxa showed enhanced diversity in individuals consuming daily servings of kefir, a fermented dairy beverage rich in probiotics. Notably, butyrate concentrations, derived from Faecalibacterium activity, inversely predicted MS relapse frequency. These data underscore the potential of dietary interventions targeting gut-brain axis interactions, with metabolomic profiling revealing key microbial metabolites as biomarkers for neuroimmune regulation. The integration of dietary fiber and vitamin D supplementation further amplified microbial diversity, reinforcing the interplay between nutrition, microbial ecology, and neuroinflammatory outcomes. This study provides mechanistic insights into how probiotic-rich foods may mitigate neurodegenerative risks through microbial modulation, emphasizing the need for precision omic approaches in gut-brain research.

A high-fiber diet significantly modulates gut microbiome composition, correlating with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in mice. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified shifts in microbial taxa, with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. PERMANOVA revealed significant differences in β-diversity between high-fiber and control groups (p < 0.01). Furthermore, fecal metabolite profiling highlighted elevated short-chain fatty acids, linking dietary fiber to neuroactive compounds. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting microbiota composition may offer therapeutic potential for anxiety-related disorders, underscoring the role of fiber-rich foods in modulating the gut-brain axis. Microbial diversity was inversely correlated with anxiety scores (r = -0.45, p = 0.02), while serotonin transporter gene expression in the hippocampus showed a trend toward upregulation in the high-fiber group. The observed effects were partially mediated by altered tryptophan metabolism, emphasizing the interplay between fiber intake, microbiome dynamics, and central nervous system function. This study highlights the potential of dietary strategies to influence mental health via the gut microbiota, warranting further investigation into specific nutrient-microbe interactions.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition correlate with neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease models, as revealed by principal component analysis (PCA) of 16S rRNA sequencing data. We observed that gut microbiota dysbiosis in transgenic mice overexpressing amyloid precursor protein (APP) was associated with elevated TLR4 expression in the hippocampus, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial imbalance and neuroinflammatory signaling. Metagenomic sequencing identified a significant reduction in Bacteroidetes and an increase in Firmicutes ratios, alongside upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes, including IL-1β and TNF-α, in the colonic mucosa. Administration of curcumin partially restored microbial diversity and attenuated TLR4 activation, as measured by qPCR. Statistical analysis using ANOVA confirmed a significant interaction between microbiota composition and TLR4 expression levels across experimental groups. These findings highlight the role of gut microbial dysbiosis in modulating neuroinflammatory pathways via TLR4-dependent signaling, offering a potential therapeutic target for mitigating cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition significantly correlate with anxiety-like behaviors in rodents, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing revealing distinct microbial profiles. Administration of the probiotic blend containing <bacteria>Lactobacillus rhamnosus</bacteria> and <bacteria>Bifidobacterium longum</bacteria> ameliorated these behaviors, accompanied by increased butyrate production. Multivariate regression analysis identified a significant inverse relationship between Lactobacillus abundance and anxiety scores (β = -0.42, P = 0.012). These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions in modulating gut-brain axis interactions through short-chain fatty acids signaling, offering novel therapeutic avenues for anxiety disorders. Mechanistically, Lactobacillus-induced butyrate upregulated brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) expression in the hippocampus, while principal component analysis of microbial taxa aligned with behavioral improvements. The study underscores the role of gut microbiota in psychiatric comorbidities and validates probiotic-based therapies as a viable strategy to restore microbial homeostasis and mitigate neuroinflammation.
