A 12-week intervention involving a high-fiber diet supplemented with probiotic strains of Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly reduced fecal IL-6 levels and improved colonic barrier integrity. Metabolomic profiling revealed increased butyrate production, linked to gut microbiota shifts toward Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Christensenella minuta, while TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells decreased by 42%. qPCR confirmed reduced TLR4 activation in parallel with elevated SCFA levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and immune modulation. Butyrate supplementation alone, via synthetic butyrate capsules, replicated these effects in a subset of participants, though fiber-dependent microbial fermentation remained critical for sustained immune homeostasis. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in mediating gut-brain communication and suggest that dietary modulation of gut microbiota through prebiotics and probiotics could target inflammatory pathways in IBS.

Consumption of fermented food rich in probiotics significantly modulates gut microbial composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and correlates with reduced neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of multiple sclerosis. Kefir, a dairy-based fermented product, was administered to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE)-induced mice over 28 days, followed by analysis of fecal microbiota dynamics and systemic cytokine profiles. Relative abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium increased concomitantly with decreased interleukin-17 levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota shifts and immune regulation. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing identified upregulation of pathways encoding short-chain fatty acid synthesis, which may mediate anti-inflammatory effects via enteric nervous system signaling. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of diet-modulated gut microbiota in ameliorating neuroinflammatory disorders, with probiotic-rich food serving as a viable adjunct to conventional therapies. The study underscores the role of microbial metabolites in bridging intestinal immunity and central nervous system pathology, emphasizing the need for targeted omic approaches to decode microbiota-host interactions in autoimmune neurodegeneration.

The TLR4 polymorphism modulates gut microbiota composition and inflammatory signaling in response to omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, influencing irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) symptom severity. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants with IBS, stratified by TLR4 genotypes and omega-3 intake. Individuals carrying the TLR4 rs4986790 C allele exhibited reduced relative abundance of Bacteroides and increased Fusobacterium when supplemented with omega-3 compared to controls without the variant. This shift correlated with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels (TNF-α, IL-6) and improved IBS symptom scores, as measured by the Rome IV criteria. Multivariate analysis revealed that TLR4 genotype interacted with omega-3 dosage to predict microbial diversity (Shannon index, P < 0.01), suggesting a gene-nutrient-microbiota axis in IBS pathophysiology. These findings highlight the potential of omega-3 as a targeted intervention for individuals with TLR4-related immune dysregulation, emphasizing the need for personalized approaches in gastrointestinal disorders management.

Altered gut microbiota composition was linked to cognitive decline in aging populations, prompting investigation into modulatory interventions. A 12-week trial involving 150 participants with mild cognitive impairment evaluated the impact of inulin supplementation on microbial diversity and neurocognitive function. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed significant enrichment of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in the intervention group, correlating with improved prefrontal cortex activation during memory tasks. Cognitive performance was assessed using standardized batteries, with multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) confirming a 14.3% increase in executive function scores compared to controls. Serum short-chain fatty acids levels rose concomitantly, suggesting microbial metabolites may mediate neuroprotective effects. Microbial-derived tryptophan metabolites showed strong inverse correlations with Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers, highlighting potential therapeutic pathways. These findings underscore the gut-brain axis as a viable target for prebiotic-driven cognitive preservation strategies in aging populations.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between intestinal microbiota and central nervous system function, with emerging evidence highlighting the role of specific dietary components in modulating this relationship. A BDNF-dependent signaling pathway was identified as a critical mediator of neuroprotection following blueberry consumption, which enriches the gut with polyphenolic compounds that promote gut microbiota diversity. Concurrent administration of probiotics further enhanced BDNF expression by modulating Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations, reducing systemic inflammation via suppression of IL6 and TNF transcripts. These findings were corroborated using multivariate regression models, which linked higher blueberry intake with improved cognitive performance in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease. The quercetin-rich extract from blueberry synergized with probiotic strains to upregulate PPARγ, a transcription factor implicated in neurogenesis and metabolic homeostasis. This interaction was further validated by metagenomic analysis revealing increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a microbiome species associated with neuroimmune regulation. The study underscores the potential of blueberry-derived compounds and probiotics as adjuncts to conventional therapies targeting neurodegenerative disorders, emphasizing the need to integrate microbial and host gene expression data in mechanistic studies of dietary interventions.

Dietary supplementation with magnesium-L-threonate modulates gut microbiota composition in Alzheimer's disease model mice, as revealed by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, with principal component analysis identifying key microbial taxa associated with cognitive improvement. Magnesium-L-threonate administration reduced Allobaculum abundance while increasing Bifidobacterium and Turicibacter in APP/PS1 mice, correlating with elevated propionate production and improved intestinal barrier integrity, as measured by western blotting of zona occludens 1 and occludin expression. Serum metabolomic profiling via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry revealed enrichment of pathways linked to neuroinflammation and oxidative stress mitigation, suggesting microbiome-mediated neuroprotection. Multiple regression analysis confirmed that microbial propionate levels accounted for 32% of variance in cognitive recovery, highlighting the gut-brain axis as a potential therapeutic target. These findings underscore the role of magnesium-L-threonate in restoring microbial homeostasis and mitigating Alzheimer's disease pathology through intestinal barrier repair and metabolite regulation, with implications for microbiome-based interventions in neurodegenerative disorders.

Altered TLR4 expression in the gut epithelium correlates with shifts in microbiome composition, modulating neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD), as revealed by CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing and 16S rRNA sequencing. Using a murine model, we demonstrated that TLR4 deficiency exacerbated Aβ plaque accumulation in the hippocampus, coinciding with a reduction in Bifidobacterium and an increase in Proteobacteria. qPCR analysis confirmed upregulated IL-6 and TNF-α expression in TLR4-knockout mice, linking gut-immune signaling to brain pathology. Furthermore, fecal microbiota transplants from TLR4-deficient donors recapitulated cognitive deficits in recipient mice, highlighting the role of microbial metabolites in neurodegeneration. Metabolomic profiling identified altered short-chain fatty acid levels, suggesting dysregulated gut-brain communication. These findings underscore the interplay between TLR4-mediated immune responses and microbiome dynamics in AD progression, offering potential therapeutic targets for modulating the gut-brain axis.

A novel prebiotic fiber blend significantly altered gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles in adults with irritable bowel syndrome, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Participants (n=80) received daily doses of the fiber supplement for 12 weeks, alongside a standardized diet, while controls received a placebo. Metabolomic analysis identified elevated levels of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, correlated with reduced gastrointestinal symptom severity and improved hippocampal neuroplasticity markers measured via functional MRI. The Bacteroides fragilis and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance increased in the prebiotic group, coinciding with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine concentrations in plasma. These findings suggest that targeted microbial substrate modulation could enhance gut-brain communication, offering therapeutic potential for neurogastrointestinal disorders. The integrated multi-omics approach underscores the interplay between microbial metabolism and central nervous system function, highlighting the need for mechanistic studies on microbiota-derived metabolites in psychiatric and digestive pathologies.

A diet enriched with fermented foods significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and influences neurobehavioral outcomes through the gut-brain axis, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from C57BL/6 mice fed a fermented soy-based diet for 12 weeks. Multivariate analysis of variance revealed distinct clustering of microbial taxa, including increased abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced Escherichia coli, correlating with improved cognitive performance assessed via Morris water maze. These changes coincided with elevated short-chain fatty acid production and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome alterations and neuroprotection. qPCR confirmed upregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) in hippocampal tissue, aligning with behavioral improvements. The findings highlight the potential of dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota as a strategy to mitigate neurodegenerative risk via modulation of host-microbial signaling pathways.

Dietary intake of polyphenol-rich blueberries significantly alters gut microbiota composition, enhancing short-chain fatty acid production and mitigating depressive-like behaviors in rodent models. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Lactobacillus, correlating with elevated butyrate levels detected via gas chromatography. Principal component analysis confirmed distinct clustering of microbiome profiles in blueberry-fed groups compared to controls. Behavioral assessments using the forced swim test showed reduced immobility duration, alongside increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in hippocampus tissue. These effects were attenuated by antibiotic treatment, highlighting the role of microbiota in mediating neurobehavioral outcomes. Furthermore, blueberry-induced butyrate supplementation alone partially replicated the antidepressant effects, suggesting direct neurochemical pathways. This study underscores the interplay between polyphenol-rich diets and gut microbiota in modulating mood disorders, with implications for developing microbiota-targeted interventions. The findings also emphasize the utility of multivariate analysis in dissecting complex microbiome-host interactions.

16S rRNA sequencing revealed that curcumin administration significantly altered the gut microbiota in rodent models of inflammatory bowel disease, with TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells correlating inversely with Bacteroides fragilis abundance. Metagenomic analysis identified curcumin-induced upregulation of IL-10 and downregulation of IL-17A in lamina propria mononuclear cells, suggesting modulation of immune signaling pathways. Flow cytometry confirmed reduced colon infiltration by Fusobacterium nucleatum, a pathobiont linked to colitis severity. Curcumin also enhanced Lactobacillus colonization, which co-occurred with elevated Foxp3 expression in regulatory T cells. These findings highlight the potential of curcumin to reshape the gut microbiome and ameliorate inflammation through TLR4-dependent and -independent mechanisms, offering a novel strategy for targeting the gut-brain axis in neuroimmune disorders.

A dietary_supplement intervention with prebiotic fibers significantly modulated the expression of the Tlr4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells, altering gut microbiome composition and reducing anxiety-like behaviors in a murine model of gastrointestinal dysfunction. Using quantitative PCR, we observed upregulation of Tlr4 in response to inulin supplementation, which correlated with increased abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced levels of Escherichia coli. These microbiota shifts were linked to decreased systemic inflammation, as evidenced by lower plasma concentrations of IL-6 and TNFα. Behavioral assessments in rodents revealed diminished anxiety scores, with a statistically significant interaction between Tlr4 expression and microbial diversity indices (ANOVA, P < 0.05). Mechanistically, Tlr4 activation appeared to enhance mucosal barrier integrity, as indicated by reduced intestinal permeability markers. These findings highlight the interplay between prebiotic intake and host genetic factors in modulating neuroimmune outcomes through the gut-brain axis. The study underscores the potential of microbiota-targeted therapies in conditions where TLR signaling and fiber metabolism converge to influence mental health.

Dysbiosis in the gut microbiome significantly correlates with altered inflammatory responses in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBD), as revealed by multivariate regression analysis of longitudinal cohort data. Interventions involving fermented foods rich in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium demonstrated a 23% reduction in symptom severity over 12 weeks, with changes in microbial composition tracked via 16S rRNA sequencing. Patients consuming daily kimchi showed higher abundance of Prevotella and lower levels of Escherichia coli, alongside decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6. Microbiome diversity, measured by Shannon index, positively associated with dietary fiber intake from whole grains and legumes, suggesting a bidirectional relationship between gut microbial ecology and host immune modulation. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, derived from fiber fermentation, correlated with improved mucosal barrier integrity in colonic tissue samples. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted microbiota-modulating diets in IBD management, with machine learning models predicting clinical response based on baseline microbiome profiles and dietary patterns.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly correlates with cognitive deficits in individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD), suggesting a potential role for targeted dietary interventions. Administration of the Lactobacillus rhamnosus in a cohort of patients with MDD revealed shifts in microbial taxa associated with improved executive function, as measured by standardized cognitive tests. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced levels of Blautia in responders, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acid production in fecal samples. These changes were linked to reduced inflammation markers (IL-6, TNF-α) and enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis in preclinical models. Notably, serum metabolite profiling highlighted elevated tryptophan derivatives in supplemented groups, aligning with modulated tryptophan hydroxylase 2 expression in prefrontal cortex. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of probiotic modulation in psychiatric conditions, with metagenomic analysis serving as a critical tool to dissect microbial mechanisms underlying brain-gut interactions.

A novel glutamate decarboxylase (GAD)-encoding gene cluster was identified in Bacteroides species, revealing a conserved mechanism for GABA production in the human gut. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing of 961 Bacteroides genomes, we found 90% harbored complete GAD-system genes, including glutaminase, GAD, and glutamate/GABA antiporter components. In vitro metabolic assays confirmed GABA production (0.09–60.84 mM) across 16 isolates, regulated by glutamate and glutamine availability. Multivariate analysis of pH-dependent expression revealed the GAD-system mitigates acid-induced cellular damage, preserving microbial viability under acidic stress. This pathway not only contributes to intestinal GABA homeostasis but may also modulate host neurochemical signaling through the gut-brain axis. The findings highlight a previously underappreciated role for GAD-mediated metabolism in bacterial acid tolerance and its potential implications for neurological disorders linked to microbial dysbiosis.

A novel probiotic formulation significantly altered gut microbiome composition and mitigated depressive-like behaviors in rodent models of chronic stress, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays. Lactobacillus plantarum LP01 administration restored serotonin levels in the hippocampus and reduced plasma cytokine concentrations, indicating modulation of the microbiota-gut-brain axis. To identify predictive biomarkers, a random forest classifier was trained on microbiome data from 120 C57BL/6 mice subjected to restraint stress. The model achieved 92% accuracy in distinguishing responders from non-responders based on shifts in taxonomic abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Parabacteroides distasonis. L. plantarum LP01 also correlated with increased short-chain fatty acid production and reduced glucocorticoid receptor activation in the prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic interventions to target depressive symptoms via microbiome remodeling, with machine learning offering a robust framework for identifying mechanistic links between microbial signatures and behavioral outcomes. The study underscores the role of gut microbiota in modulating neuroinflammation and suggests that precision microbiome-based therapies may improve mental health outcomes.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition mediated by the Chrna7 gene are linked to neurobehavioral changes in mice, with probiotic supplementation modulating these effects. Using transgenic models, we found that Chrna7 knockout led to dysbiosis characterized by reduced Lactobacillus abundance and increased lipopolysaccharide levels, correlating with depression-like behaviors. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed shifts in microbial diversity, while serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex were altered. Administration of probiotic formulations containing Lactobacillus reuteri partially restored microbial balance and mitigated behavioral deficits. MANCOVA analysis confirmed that Chrna7 genotype and probiotic intervention interacted to influence tryptophan metabolite profiles, suggesting a role for microbial-derived tryptophan catabolites in neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, microbiota, and dietary modulation in shaping brain function, offering potential therapeutic targets for gut-brain axis-related disorders.

The random forest model revealed a significant correlation between resveratrol supplementation and altered gut microbiome composition in aged rats with Alzheimer's disease-like pathology, driven by shifts in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. This effect was mediated through the Trem2-dependent modulation of microglial phagocytosis and reduced tau hyperphosphorylation in the hippocampus, as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry. Concurrently, resveratrol enhanced IL-6 signaling in enteric neurons, promoting intestinal barrier integrity and reducing systemic inflammatory cytokine levels. The principal component analysis of fecal metabolites further linked specific short-chain fatty acids produced by Bacteroides fragilis to improved brain vascular perfusion, suggesting a dual role for resveratrol in modulating neuroinflammation and gut-derived signaling pathways. These findings highlight the potential of Trem2-targeted interventions combined with resveratrol to mitigate neurodegeneration via gut-brain axis remodeling.

Modulation of the gut microbiome through prebiotic administration significantly attenuates Alzheimer's disease progression in APP/PS1 mice by targeting the TLR4 signaling pathway. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS) increased the abundance of Lactobacillus while decreasing Proteobacteria, correlating with reduced Aβ plaque accumulation in the hippocampus. Western blotting confirmed that GOS suppressed TLR4-mediated NF-κB activation in the colon and brain, dampening proinflammatory cytokine production. Behavioral assays demonstrated improved cognitive function in treated mice, paralleling decreased IL-1β levels and enhanced BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Metabolomic profiling identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of TLR4 suppression, linking microbiota-derived signals to neuroinflammation regulation. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in gut-brain communication and suggest that prebiotic-induced microbiota remodeling may serve as a therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease by modulating immune signaling pathways.

Intestinal permeability alterations in multiple sclerosis (MS) patients correlate with pro-inflammatory cytokine elevation and gut microbiota dysbiosis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 142 participants (78 MS cases, 64 controls), we identified Prevotella depletion and Akkermansia enrichment in MS cohorts. A multivariate analysis of variance revealed significant differences in microbial diversity (p=0.003) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation markers. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus for 12 weeks reduced LPS serum levels by 34% (p=0.012) and improved blood-brain barrier integrity scores by 22%. Microbial shifts were associated with decreased IL-6 and TNF-α in MS patients, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut-brain axis modulation and neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotics in mitigating MS-related immune dysregulation via microbiome-targeted interventions.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlated with high-fructose corn syrup intake, mediated by the FTO variant rs9939609, as revealed by principal component analysis in a cohort of 300 adults. Bifidobacterium longum abundance decreased significantly in individuals consuming ≥150 g/day of the high-fructose corn syrup, while Escherichia coli increased, suggesting dysbiosis linked to metabolic dysregulation. Participants carrying the FTO risk allele exhibited a 2.3-fold higher incidence of insulin resistance compared to non-carriers, independent of dietary fiber intake. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified gut microbiome shifts in subjects with the FTO variant, including reduced Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, which correlated with elevated glucose levels. The permutation test confirmed these associations remained significant after adjusting for confounders like processed food consumption and gastrointestinal transit time. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic predisposition, dietary fructose exposure, and gut microbiota dynamics in metabolic disease pathogenesis, underscoring the need for personalized dietary interventions targeting FTO-related susceptibility.

Alterations in the gut microbiome mediated by dietary fiber intake significantly modulate TLR4 gene expression, influencing neuroinflammatory pathways in the brain and altering gut microbiota composition in C57BL/6 mice. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified that inulin-supplemented diets increased abundance of Bacteroidetes while reducing Firmicutes ratios, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. TLR4 knockout mice exhibited attenuated neuroinflammation markers compared to wild-type controls, suggesting microbiota-derived lipopolysaccharides as key mediators. This interplay highlights how fiber modulation of the microbiome can regulate TLR4-dependent signaling, offering therapeutic avenues for neurodegenerative disorders.

A recent study reveals that supplementation with inulin, a prebiotic derived from chicory root, significantly modulates the gut microbiome in rats subjected to chronic stress, thereby influencing anxiety-like behaviors via alterations in intestinal Parabacteroides abundance. This effect was mediated by the upregulation of the Nrf2 pathway, which regulates antioxidant responses and reduces neuroinflammation. The 16S rRNA sequencing analysis showed that inulin restored the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium and suppressed Escherichia coli overgrowth, correlating with decreased levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 in the prefrontal cortex. Concurrently, butyrate production, a short-chain fatty acid linked to neuroprotection, increased in fecal samples, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial fermentation and central nervous system plasticity. The findings highlight the role of prebiotic-induced microbiota remodeling in mitigating stress-related disorders through Nrf2-dependent pathways, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for anxiety disorders with dietary interventions targeting the gut-brain axis.

Altered gut microbial composition in individuals with major depressive disorder correlates with dietary patterns rich in processed foods, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Analysis of fecal samples from 120 participants revealed significantly lower alpha diversity and distinct beta diversity patterns in depressed cohorts compared to healthy controls (PERMANOVA, P < 0.001). Bacteroides and Firmicutes ratios were inversely correlated with whole grain intake, while Prevotella abundance increased in individuals consuming high-fat dairy (FDR-adjusted P < 0.05). Functional metagenomic analysis identified upregulation of pathways involved in tryptophan metabolism and downregulation of short-chain fatty acid production in depressed subjects. Notably, fermented food consumption was associated with higher levels of Lactobacillus and reduced inflammatory markers, suggesting a potential bidirectional interaction between microbiota-derived metabolites and neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the role of dietary modulation in shaping the gut microbiome and its implications for depressive symptoms, underscoring the need for microbiome-targeted interventions in mental health care.

Alterations in the gut microbiome were associated with colitis severity in IL-10−/− mice, where Tlr4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells correlated with microbial dysbiosis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we identified Enterococcus faecalis as a dominant pathobiont linked to inflammation, with short-chain fatty acids levels inversely proportional to disease progression. Multivariate analysis revealed that Tlr4 activation mediated E. faecalis-induced IL-1β secretion, while butyrate supplementation restored intestinal barrier integrity via upregulation of Occludin and ZO-1. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Tlr4 knockout in mice attenuated colitis, confirming its role in microbial-immune crosstalk. Butyrate treatment also reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and enhanced microbial diversity, suggesting a dual mechanism of action targeting both host signaling and microbial ecology. These findings highlight Tlr4 as a therapeutic target for inflammatory bowel disease, with butyrate and precision microbiome modulation offering potential strategies to restore homeostasis.

TPH2 polymorphisms modulate gut microbiota composition and anxiety-like behaviors in rodents via altered serotonin signaling, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays. Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated with TPH2 expression levels in colonic epithelium, while 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor activation in hippocampus neurons mediated stress-induced behavioral changes. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan derivatives in TPH2-knockout models, linking microbial short-chain fatty acid production to neuroinflammation. Participants with irritable bowel syndrome exhibited TPH2 variants associated with reduced Bifidobacterium diversity, further validated by quantitative PCR. These findings highlight TPH2's role in integrating microbial signals with central nervous system function, suggesting targeted serotonin reuptake inhibitors and prebiotic interventions may alleviate gut-brain axis dysregulation.

A high-fiber Mediterranean diet significantly alters the gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced symptoms of depression in a cohort of 120 participants. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified distinct microbial signatures in individuals adhering to the diet, marked by increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria and decreased pro-inflammatory taxa. Principal component analysis revealed that dietary fiber intake explained 42% of the variance in microbial beta-diversity, with whole grains and fermented foods emerging as key drivers. Functional metagenomic analysis further linked enhanced butyrate synthase expression to improved mental health outcomes, suggesting a mechanistic pathway involving butyrate-mediated neuroinflammation suppression. These findings underscore the role of diet in modulating the gut-brain axis and highlight the potential of targeted fiber supplementation as an adjunct therapy for mood disorders.

Intervention with fermented kimchi and probiotic capsules significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced symptoms of anxiety in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 80 adults with irritable bowel syndrome and comorbid depressive symptoms. Participants were randomized to receive daily doses of kimchi (150 g) combined with probiotic capsules containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum, or a placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum and Parabacteroides distasonis in the intervention group, correlating with reduced serotonin dysregulation and improved Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids and decreased lipopolysaccharide levels, suggesting mitigation of systemic inflammation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of combining fermented foods with targeted probiotics to synergistically restore gut-brain communication, offering a novel strategy for managing gastrointestinal-mental comorbidities. The study underscores the role of microbiota-derived metabolites in modulating neural pathways, emphasizing the need for personalized dietary interventions in neuropsychiatric disorders.

High-fiber legumes consumption significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and intestinal permeability in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and permutation-based multivariate analysis. Analysis of 120 participants revealed that increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus casei correlated with reduced IBS-specific symptom severity scores (P < 0.01), while Escherichia coli levels inversely correlated with colonic barrier integrity markers. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids production in individuals adhering to a legume-based diet, which was further validated using canonical correlation analysis to link microbial taxa with host inflammatory markers. Notably, butyrate concentrations showed a strong positive association with hippocampal neurogenesis markers in murine models, suggesting potential microbiota-brain axis mechanisms. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of dietary modulation of the gut microbiome in gastrointestinal disorders and underscore the value of integrating multi-omics approaches with machine learning for predictive modeling of gut-brain interactions.

Modulation of the gut-brain axis through genetic intervention in Tlr5-expressing neurons significantly alters microbiota composition and behavioral outcomes in C57BL/6J mice, as demonstrated by CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene disruption. Targeting Tlr5, a key mediator of intestinal immune signaling, reduced the abundance of Lactobacillus and increased Bacteroides in fecal samples analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, correlating with heightened anxiety-like behavior in open field tests. Concurrently, Tlr5 knockout mice exhibited elevated serum IL-6 levels measured by ELISA, alongside decreased qPCR-quantified Il10 expression in colon tissue, suggesting dysregulated immune homeostasis. These findings were corroborated by immunohistochemistry revealing reduced mucosal thickness and increased gut permeability markers in Tlr5-deficient animals. Statistical analyses using ANOVA confirmed significant differences in microbial diversity indices between cohorts (p < 0.01). This study underscores the pivotal role of Tlr5 in maintaining gut microbiota-brain communication and highlights CRISPR-Cas9 as a tool to dissect genetic contributions to neuroimmune disorders. The results suggest that Tlr5 signaling may serve as a therapeutic target for modulating gut-brain axis dysfunction in depression and autism spectrum disorder.

Altered gut microbiota composition has been linked to cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), with emerging evidence suggesting that dietary interventions may modulate this relationship. Here, we demonstrate that curcumin administration in APP/PS1 mice significantly reduced hippocampal inflammation and improved spatial memory, as measured by immunohistochemistry and 16S rRNA sequencing. Principal component analysis revealed that gut microbial diversity correlated with behavioral outcomes, while Akkermansia muciniphila abundance increased in curcumin-treated groups. Curcumin also suppressed IL-6 and TNF-α expression in brain tissue, alongside reduced β-amyloid plaques. These effects were associated with shifts in short-chain fatty acid production, particularly elevated butyrate levels, which were confirmed via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. The human microbiome-derived Akkermansia muciniphila was identified as a key mediator, as its depletion in AD models corresponded with worsened cognitive deficits. Collectively, these findings suggest that curcumin exerts neuroprotective effects through microbiota-dependent mechanisms, offering a novel strategy for targeting the gut-brain axis in AD progression.

Short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota exhibit significant neuroprotective effects in murine models of major depressive disorder, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA). C57BL/6J mice fed a high-fat diet exhibited altered intestinal microbial composition, marked by reduced abundance of Akkermansia_muciniphila and increased Bacteroides, correlated with elevated IL-17 levels in serum via ELISA. Pearson correlation revealed a negative association between Akkermansia_muciniphila and 5-HT concentrations in the hippocampus, while Western blot confirmed upregulated 5-HT receptor HTR2A expression in mice with depressive-like behavior. Transplantation of fecal microbiota from high-fat diet-fed mice into germ-free recipients replicated inflammatory and behavioral phenotypes, suggesting microbial dysbiosis drives neuroinflammation through SCFA modulation. These findings highlight the role of gut-brain axis signaling in mental health and underscore the utility of microbiome profiling combined with correlation analysis to identify therapeutic targets.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene significantly correlate with shifts in gut microbiota composition, influencing neuroinflammatory pathways in patients with multiple sclerosis. A probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was administered to 80 participants over 12 weeks, alongside a 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples to assess microbial diversity. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) revealed that TLR4 polymorphisms were associated with reduced abundance of Prevotellaceae and increased levels of Escherichia-Shigella, alongside elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. Intestinal permeability markers correlated with serum lipopolysaccharide levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between TLR4-mediated immune signaling and microbiome-driven inflammation. The probiotic intervention normalized cytokine profiles in 65% of subjects, while principal component analysis highlighted TLR4 expression as a key determinant of microbial resilience. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetics, microbiome dynamics, and therapeutic interventions in modulating neuroimmune responses.

A high-fat diet significantly altered gut microbiota composition in rodents, while concurrent administration of a prebiotic fiber supplement mitigated dysbiosis and restored metabolic homeostasis. Using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), we observed distinct clustering of microbial communities between groups, with Bacteroidetes abundance correlating inversely with systemic inflammation markers. High-fat diet-induced metabolic syndrome was associated with reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and elevated Firmicutes ratios, whereas the prebiotic intervention enriched Butyrate-producing taxa, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in colonic tissue. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations, measured via gas chromatography, showed significant positive correlation with prebiotic-responsive taxa abundance, suggesting microbial fermentation as a key mediator of metabolic improvement. These findings highlight the interplay between dietary modulation and microbial metabolism in regulating host physiology, emphasizing the potential of targeted interventions to counteract nutrient-dense diets-driven pathophysiology through gut microbiota reprogramming.

A probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum significantly altered gut microbiota composition and cognitive function in adults with comorbid irritable bowel syndrome and major depressive disorder, as revealed by multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA). Participants consumed the supplement alongside a high-fiber, fermented dairy-rich diet for 12 weeks, which correlated with increased butyrate production and reduced serotonin levels in serum. 16S rRNA sequencing identified significant shifts in Blautia abundance, inversely linked to executive dysfunction scores.
