metadata.abstract: Dysregulation of gut microbiota in type 2 diabetes is modulated by dietary interventions involving high-fiber legumes and prebiotic inulin, which alter microbial metabolic pathways and host glucose homeostasis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we evaluated the impact of a 12-week regimen of legume-based diets supplemented with inulin on intestinal microbial composition and systemic inflammation in ob/ob mice. The intervention significantly increased abundance of Bacteroides and Prevotella, while reducing Escherichia coli levels, correlating with decreased plasma interleukin-6 and improved insulin sensitivity. Inulin enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which was linked to reduced diabetic nephropathy markers via activation of FXR signaling. Legume intake also promoted gut microbiome diversity, which inversely correlated with hyperglycemia severity. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotic and fiber-rich dietary strategies in mitigating metabolic syndrome through microbiome-mediated anti-inflammatory effects.

Colonic inflammation and gut microbiota dysbiosis are linked to depressive-like behaviors in rodent models, yet mechanisms remain poorly defined. Blueberry consumption, rich in anthocyanins, combined with omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, was tested to modulate gut microbiota and mitigate neuroinflammation. Male C57BL/6 mice were fed a high-fat diet for 8 weeks before receiving either control, blueberry-enriched, or omega-3-supplemented diets for 4 weeks. Behavioral assessments using the forced swim test and open field assay revealed reduced immobility and increased exploratory activity in the blueberry+omega-3 group. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Prevotella and decreased Desulfovibrio in treated mice, correlating with lower plasma IL-6 levels. LC-MS/MS analysis of brain tissue showed reduced glial fibrillary acidic protein expression, suggesting neuroinflammatory suppression. These findings highlight a synergistic role of blueberry-derived polyphenols and omega-3 in restoring gut-brain axis homeostasis, offering a dual-targeted strategy for mood disorders linked to metabolic dysregulation.

A TLR4 polymorphism was associated with altered gut microbiome composition in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 120 participants. Bacteroides fragilis abundance correlated inversely with social communication deficits, while Escherichia coli levels were elevated in individuals harboring the TLR4 variant. These findings suggest immune signaling pathways mediated by TLR4 may modulate microbiota-brain interactions in ASD. Probiotic administration of Lactobacillus reuteri for 12 weeks significantly increased Bifidobacterium abundance and improved repetitive behavior scores by 23% (P=0.018). Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan metabolites in responders, linking microbial tryptophan catabolism to behavioral outcomes. The study highlights TLR4-mediated immune-microbiome interplay as a potential therapeutic target, with probiotic interventions showing promise for modulating ASD-related phenotypes through microbial metabolic pathways.

A high-fiber diet significantly alters the gut microbiome composition, which correlates with reduced anxiety-like behavior in mice, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Barley beta-glucan supplementation was associated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, alongside decreased Desulfovibrio, suggesting a potential link between microbial shifts and neurobehavioral outcomes. Principal component analysis of microbiome data identified a strong correlation between microbial diversity indices and anxiety scores measured via open-field and elevated plus maze tests. Mechanistically, Bifidobacterium metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, were implicated in modulating hippocampal neuroinflammation via TLR2 and NF-kb pathways. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions targeting the gut-brain axis for neurological disorders, emphasizing the interplay between fiber-rich diets, microbial ecology, and brain function.

A novel interaction between dietary interventions and host genetics was identified in modulating gut-brain communication, with fermented dairy products significantly altering gut microbiota composition and influencing TNF expression in rodent models. 16S rDNA sequencing revealed elevated Lactobacillus abundance in C57BL/6 mice fed fermented dairy products, coinciding with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and improved neurobehavioral outcomes. Mechanistically, TNF was found to mediate cross-talk between Lactobacillus-derived short-chain fatty acids and hippocampal CREB signaling pathways, enhancing neuroplasticity. Metabolomic profiling highlighted butyrate as a key mediator, with its levels correlating inversely with TNF transcripts in colonic tissues. These findings underscore the role of fermented dairy products in reshaping microbial communities and modulating immune-related genes to alleviate neuroinflammation, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic disorders with gut-brain axis dysregulation.

A longitudinal cohort study revealed that regular consumption of fermented milk significantly modulated the gut microbiota in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD), as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Lactobacillus abundance correlated inversely with depression severity, while Bacteroides levels rose in parallel with inflammatory markers. Multivariate logistic regression confirmed that higher Lactobacillus diversity (Shannon index ≥4.2) predicted a 34% reduction in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores after 12 weeks. Metabolomic profiling of fecal samples identified increased short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, as a potential mediator of the observed neurobehavioral effects. Notably, participants adhering to a high-fiber diet showed enhanced microbial resilience, with principal component analysis revealing distinct clustering of gut microbiota profiles compared to controls. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting intestinal dysbiosis may represent a viable adjunct to conventional therapies for depressive disorders, though longitudinal validation with larger cohorts is needed to confirm causal relationships.

A high-fiber regimen significantly alters gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced symptoms of depression in a cohort of adults. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios alongside increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, which were linked to improved neurocognitive function via multivariate regression analysis. Participants consuming ≥25 g/day of fiber exhibited a 32% reduction in depressive symptomatology compared to controls, independent of baseline demographics or serotonin levels. Metabolomic profiling further revealed elevated butyrate concentrations in the high-fiber group, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in colon biopsies. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiota through fiber intake may represent a viable strategy for mitigating mental health disorders, with machine learning algorithms confirming the predictive power of microbiota-derived metabolites in behavioral assays.

Interactions between gut microbiota and host genetic variants significantly modulate neuroinflammatory markers in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR analyses of hippocampal tissue. A Apoe polymorphism was identified as a critical mediator of this relationship, with its expression correlating inversely to Bacteroidetes abundance and positively to Fusobacterium levels in fecal samples from APP/PS1 mice. Random forest models further demonstrated that Apoe genotype accounted for 34% of variance in hippocampal IL-6 expression, while microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids explained an additional 19%. These findings underscore a bidirectional regulatory axis between gut microbiota and AD-susceptibility genes, with implications for targeted interventions. The integration of single-cell RNA sequencing and multivariate analysis of variance highlighted distinct immune cell subpopulations responsive to microbial metabolites, suggesting potential therapeutic strategies involving prebiotic modulation. This study advances understanding of how genetic and microbial factors converge to influence neuroinflammation in AD, emphasizing the need for personalized approaches to gut-brain axis modulation.

Alterations in gut microbial composition linked to major depressive disorder were significantly modulated by interventions involving fermented dairy and probiotic supplementation, as revealed by canonical correspondence analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 participants. Analysis of fecal samples collected pre- and post-intervention identified 17 operational taxonomic units exhibiting differential abundance, with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium showing marked increases correlating with reduced depressive symptom severity scores. The permutation-based multivariate analysis further highlighted interactions between short-chain fatty acid production and tryptophan metabolite levels, mediated by dietary intake of fiber-rich plant-based meals. Notably, prebiotic fiber supplementation amplified these effects, as evidenced by a 38% reduction in HAMD-17 scores compared to control groups. These findings suggest a mechanistic interplay between microbial metabolic pathways and neurobehavioral outcomes, with potential therapeutic applications in mood disorders through targeted modulation of gut microbiota via functional food and microbial interventions.

Alterations in gut microbial composition significantly correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in Parkinson’s disease patients, highlighting the microbiome’s role in neurodegeneration. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 120 subjects to identify microbial shifts associated with motor symptom severity. Prevotella copri abundance inversely correlated with alpha-synuclein levels, while Akkermansia muciniphila showed a positive association with gastrointestinal dysfunction. A parallel inulin intervention in 30 participants reduced Proteobacteria load by 40% over 12 weeks, accompanied by decreased lipopolysaccharide concentrations in serum. PERMANOVA confirmed that microbial community structure differed significantly between groups (p<0.01). These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the gut microbiome via prebiotic supplementation could mitigate neuroinflammation and improve clinical outcomes in neurodegenerative disorders. The study underscores the interplay between microbial metabolites, host immune responses, and central nervous system pathology, emphasizing the potential of microbiome-directed therapies in PD management.

Curcumin supplementation in a curcumin-enriched diet significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced inflammatory bowel disease severity in a murine model of intestinal inflammation. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside decreased pathobionts such as Escherichia coli, correlating with attenuated colonic inflammation markers. The fermented soy product natto was co-administered to assess synergistic effects, revealing enhanced butyrate production via Faecalibacterium prausnitzii activation. Curcumin also suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 in mesenteric lymph nodes, suggesting a dual mechanism targeting both microbial dysbiosis and systemic immune signaling. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of combining curcumin with natto to restore gut microbiome homeostasis in inflammatory bowel disease through metagenomic profiling-guided interventions.

Alterations in gut microbial composition significantly correlate with cognitive decline in aging populations, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from 250 participants aged 65–85. Fermented dairy consumption was inversely associated with Alzheimer’s disease progression, independent of confounding variables such as gastrointestinal health or physical activity. Random forest analysis identified Prevotella copri as a key predictor of memory impairment, while short-chain fatty acids levels mediated interactions between gut microbiota and hippocampal neuroplasticity. Antipsychotic use further disrupted microbial balance, exacerbating neurocognitive deficits. Prebiotic supplementation restored Bifidobacterium abundance, improving prefrontal cortex function in a subset of participants. These findings highlight the role of microbiota-derived metabolites in modulating brain health and suggest that targeted dietary interventions may mitigate age-related cognitive decline through metabolomic profiling and pathway enrichment analysis.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with cognitive decline in aging populations, highlighting the microbiota-gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target. A cohort of 150 participants consuming a Mediterranean diet enriched with prebiotic fiber showed improved neurocognitive outcomes compared to controls. Metagenomic sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in the prebiotic group, alongside reduced levels of Escherichia coli. Cognitive performance, assessed via MoCA and Trail Making Test, demonstrated a 12% improvement in the intervention group. Repeated-measures ANOVA confirmed significant differences in memory and executive function scores over 12 weeks. Plasma levels of tryptophan and short-chain fatty acids correlated with microbiota shifts, suggesting metabolic pathways mediate neuroprotection. Participants adhering to the Mediterranean diet also exhibited lower systemic inflammation markers, as measured by C-reactive protein assays. These findings underscore the interplay between dietary interventions, microbiota modulation, and cognitive health, emphasizing the potential of prebiotic supplementation in mitigating age-related decline. Future studies should integrate longitudinal microbiota profiling with multivariate regression models to dissect mechanistic links.

A diet enriched with fermented dairy products significantly alters gut microbiota composition, enhancing Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) signaling in enteric neurons and modulating neuroinflammatory responses via the vagus nerve. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR, we demonstrate that lactobacillus-rich fermentation increases abundance of Lactobacillus reuteri while suppressing Escherichia coli in gerbil models of metabolic syndrome. This microbial shift correlates with elevated short-chain fatty acid production, which activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) in intestinal epithelial cells, reinforcing barrier integrity. Concurrently, electrophysiological recordings reveal enhanced vagal afferent activity in proximal colon sensory neurons, linking microbiota-derived signals to hypothalamic regulation of glucose homeostasis. Mechanistically, TLR4 activation by bacterial lipopolysaccharides promotes interleukin-10 secretion from gastrointestinal lymphocytes, dampening systemic inflammation. These findings establish a causal pathway by which fermented food interventions modulate TLR4-mediated neuroimmune signaling, offering a novel strategy to mitigate obesity-associated cognitive decline through gut-brain axis reprogramming.

Altered gut microbiota composition in Parkinson's disease models is modulated by dietary interventions, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from rodents fed blueberries. Microbial diversity indices, including the Shannon index, revealed significant increases in Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance alongside reduced Proteobacteria in blueberry-treated groups compared to controls. These shifts correlated with diminished α-synuclein aggregation in midbrain dopaminergic neurons, assessed via immunohistochemistry. Anthocyanin metabolites from blueberries were identified as key mediators, interacting with TLR2 and NF-κB pathways to suppress neuroinflammation. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing further highlighted upregulated short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis genes, aligning with improved blood-brain barrier integrity in treated animals. These findings suggest that blueberry-derived compounds may mitigate α-synucleinopathy progression through microbiome-mediated neuroimmune modulation, offering a potential dietary strategy for patients with Parkinson's disease.

A high-fiber diet rich in legumes significantly modulates gut microbiota composition in patients with metabolic syndrome, as evidenced by increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria such as Bacteroides and Prevotella. Concomitant administration of a prebiotic supplement containing inulin further enhanced microbial diversity and reduced systemic inflammation markers, including C-reactive protein and interleukin-6. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we observed a 35% increase in butyrate levels in the gut microbiota of supplemented subjects compared to controls. This intervention also correlated with improved glucose homeostasis and reduced visceral fat accumulation. Notably, the legume-based diet combined with prebiotic supplementation altered the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, a mucosal-associated bacterium linked to metabolic health. These findings suggest that integrating legumes with prebiotic supplements may offer a synergistic approach to managing metabolic syndrome through microbiome modulation. The study highlights the potential of dietary strategies targeting specific microbial pathways to mitigate disease progression, emphasizing the interplay between nutrition, gut ecology, and systemic inflammation.

A novel dietary intervention significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and associated neurobehavioral outcomes in a cohort of individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders, revealing interplay between fermented dairy consumption, α-synuclein expression, and synaptic plasticity. Using a machine learning-based multivariate analysis, we identified that daily intake of a probiotic-enriched yogurt over 12 weeks correlated with reduced inflammation markers in the prefrontal cortex and altered gut microbiome profiles, particularly increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Escherichia coli. These shifts coincided with elevated BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) levels, which were statistically linked to improved social interaction scores. Short-chain fatty acids derived from microbial fermentation of fiber-rich plant matter in the diet emerged as key mediators, with principal component analysis highlighting their role in modulating α-synuclein aggregation pathways. The study underscores how targeted nutritional strategies can influence neurobiological processes through microbiota-driven mechanisms, offering potential therapeutic avenues for conditions involving neurodegeneration and autism spectrum disorder.

The gene MAOA exhibits altered expression in patients with major depressive disorder, correlating with dysbiosis in the gut microbiota and increased production of short-chain fatty acids linked to colonic inflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR, we identified a significant inverse relationship between MAOA transcript levels and abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila in cohort samples, validated by multivariate regression models accounting for confounding variables. Metabolomic profiling further revealed elevated propionate concentrations in individuals with MAOA downregulation, suggesting a mechanistic link between enzymatic activity at the serotonin transporter and microbial metabolic outputs. These findings highlight MAOA as a potential therapeutic target for modulating gut-brain communication in mood disorders, with implications for prebiotic-mediated interventions targeting Akkermansia muciniphila to normalize serotonin signaling and reduce systemic inflammation.

Altered gut microbiome composition significantly correlates with neuroinflammation markers in Parkinson's disease patients, as revealed by multivariate logistic regression analysis of longitudinal microbial and inflammatory cytokine data. Intervention studies in rodent models demonstrated that dietary modulation via Mediterranean diet-derived polyphenols and probiotic supplementation enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, reducing TNF-α levels by 32% compared to controls. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed that Bifidobacterium abundance increased by 41% in cohorts receiving prebiotic fibers, correlating with improved enteric nervous system function. principal component analysis further linked specific fermented food intake patterns to reduced neurodegeneration progression rates. These findings suggest that targeted microbiome-modulating interventions may offer a viable adjunct to conventional Parkinson's disease therapies by reinforcing gut-brain axis signaling pathways.

A novel gut-brain axis mechanism involving the Tlr4 gene was identified through single-cell RNA sequencing in a mouse model of neuroinflammation, revealing its role in modulating gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Tlr4 expression correlated with altered butyrate levels, which were linked to reduced astrocytic activation and neuroinflammatory markers in the hippocampus. Using mass spectrometry, we observed that Tlr4-mediated signaling enhanced microbial production of propionate, a SCFA that suppressed Nfkb1-driven inflammatory pathways in C57BL/6J neurons. These findings were validated in patients with multiple sclerosis, where Tlr4 polymorphisms associated with lower serum butyrate and higher interleukin-6 levels. The study highlights Tlr4 as a critical node in microbiota-brain communication, suggesting targeted modulation of SCFA metabolism via metabolomic profiling could ameliorate neuroinflammatory diseases. Further investigation into Tlr4’s interaction with Bacteroides fragilis may uncover therapeutic strategies to restore gut-brain homeostasis.

A probiotic dietary supplement modulates gut microbiota composition and alleviates stress-induced neuroinflammation via regulation of toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) signaling pathways. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that supplementation with a synbiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and prebiotic inulin significantly increased alpha diversity in rodent models exposed to chronic social defeat stress. This intervention reduced neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus, including decreased interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) expression. Mechanistically, the synbiotic blend enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which correlated with upregulation of TLR4 in intestinal epithelial cells, promoting anti-inflammatory signaling. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated butyrate levels in treated animals, directly linking microbial fermentation to TLR4-mediated suppression of microglial activation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in mitigating stress-related neuroinflammatory disorders through modulation of host-microbiota genetic interactions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome's production of specific metabolites are linked to neurodegenerative pathways through genetic determinants and microbial profiling. Escherichia coli encodes the UrdA enzyme, which catalyzes imidazole propionate (ImP) synthesis, a metabolite associated with Alzheimer's disease progression. Using metagenomic sequencing, we identified Proteobacteria-dominated gut microbiota with elevated UrdA expression in cohorts with impaired cognitive function. ImP levels correlated inversely with plasma eicosapentaenoic acid and directly with blood-brain barrier permeability in mice administered chronic ImP doses. Immunohistochemistry revealed hippocampal neuroinflammation and amyloid-β accumulation in treated animals, paralleling UrdA-driven metabolic shifts detected via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. The UrdA-encoded pathway may thus bridge microbial dysbiosis and Alzheimer's disease via neurotoxic metabolites, highlighting potential therapeutic targets in modulating gut-brain axis interactions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition are linked to neuroinflammatory markers in neurodegenerative disorders, with emerging evidence pointing to interactions between microbial metabolites and host TMAO pathways. A probiotic intervention in elderly participants with Alzheimer's disease (AD) demonstrated reduced levels of neuroinflammatory cytokines in serum, correlated with shifts in Bifidobacterium abundance. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus taxa positively associated with TMAO expression were enriched following supplementation, while Enterobacteriaceae decreased. These changes coincided with improved short-chain fatty acid production, which modulated TMAO-dependent signaling in microglia and reduced beta-amyloid accumulation in hippocampus tissue. multivariate analysis identified a significant interaction between probiotic dose and TMAO promoter methylation status, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial modulation and gene regulation in AD progression. The findings highlight potential therapeutic strategies targeting gut microbiome-host gene crosstalk to mitigate neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's disease pathology.

A novel probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in rodent models fed a high-fat diet rich in saturated fats. This intervention reduced systemic inflammation by suppressing TLR4-mediated signaling pathways in intestinal epithelial cells, as evidenced by qPCR and 16S rRNA sequencing. The probiotic blend enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which correlated with increased FXR expression in the liver and improved metabolic parameters. High-fat diet consumption alone induced dysbiosis marked by reduced Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and elevated lipopolysaccharide levels, exacerbating intestinal permeability. The probiotic blend partially reversed these effects, restoring microbial diversity and attenuating insulin resistance via multivariate analysis of metabolic profiling. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic therapies to mitigate diet-induced metabolic disorders by harmonizing gut microbiota function and regulating host immune and metabolic pathways.

A longitudinal study employing multivariate regression analysis revealed that regular consumption of fermented dairy products and supplementation with probiotic capsules were associated with reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression in adults with gut-brain axis dysregulation. Analysis of fecal 16S rRNA profiles from 200 participants showed that individuals consuming fermented dairy exhibited higher abundance of Bifidobacterium and lower levels of Proteobacteria, alongside decreased inflammatory markers such as IL-6. Those taking probiotic supplements showed similar microbiota shifts but with greater consistency in TLR4 expression modulation, suggesting a direct impact on immune signaling pathways. Mantel tests confirmed significant correlations between microbiota diversity and mental health metrics, with fermented dairy intake explaining 18% of variance in depressive symptom scores. Notably, participants adhering to both interventions demonstrated synergistic effects, with 35% greater improvement in irritable bowel syndrome-related anxiety compared to single-intervention groups. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted dietary strategies in modulating the gut microbiome to alleviate psychiatric comorbidities linked to gut-brain axis dysfunction.

A prebiotic intervention modulated neuroinflammatory markers via gut microbiota alterations in a murine model of metabolic syndrome. Inulin supplementation was associated with shifts in gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, which identified increased abundance of Christensenellaceae and reduced levels of Prevotellaceae. These changes correlated with decreased expression of the Tlr5 gene in the hippocampus, a key mediator of neuroimmune signaling. Mice receiving inulin exhibited improved spatial memory and reduced systemic inflammation, as measured by IL-6 and TNF-α plasma concentrations. Mechanistically, Tlr5 downregulation was linked to altered microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acid production, particularly elevated butyrate levels, which were confirmed via metabolomic profiling. The gut-brain axis thus emerged as a critical pathway for prebiotic-mediated neuroprotection, with Tlr5 serving as a molecular bridge between microbial metabolites and central nervous system function. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiota-modulating strategies to ameliorate neuroinflammation and cognitive deficits in metabolic disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition significantly correlate with disease progression in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. A randomized, double-blind trial evaluated the impact of probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus on neuroinflammatory markers and motor function in 84 patients undergoing standard pharmacotherapy with levodopa. Intervention groups exhibited reduced UPDRS-III scores and lower serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines compared to controls, alongside increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species. Metabolomic analysis identified elevated butyrate and tryptophan metabolites in probiotic-treated cohorts, correlating with improved gastrointestinal motility and reduced anxiety symptoms. Notably, probiotic co-administration enhanced serotonin biosynthesis pathways and modulated gut-brain axis signaling through upregulation of TMAO-related enzymes. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic therapies may synergize with conventional treatments to mitigate PD progression by restoring microbial homeostasis and modulating neuroimmune interactions.

Depression and anxiety were linked to altered gut microbiota composition in patients consuming a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. LEfSe analysis identified Akkermansia muciniphila as significantly enriched in responders compared to non-responders, while Escherichia coli abundance correlated with persistent anxiety symptoms. Short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota metabolism showed a positive association with serotonin receptor activation in the hippocampus, suggesting microbiome-driven neurochemical modulation. Participants with baseline low-grade inflammation exhibited diminished Bifidobacterium diversity, which normalized after 12 weeks of probiotic supplementation. qPCR confirmed elevated Tlr4 expression in non-responders, implicating TLR4 signaling in treatment resistance. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota dynamics, metabolite production, and mental health outcomes, underscoring the potential of microbiome-targeted interventions to modulate central nervous system function via vagal pathways.

A novel interaction between the TLR4 gene and probiotic supplementation modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces depression symptoms in individuals consuming a fermented food-rich diet. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 120 participants with major depressive disorder, we identified that TLR4 polymorphisms correlated with shifts in microbial taxa, particularly increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus among those receiving probiotic kefir daily. Multivariate analysis revealed that TLR4 variant carriers exhibited greater reductions in depressive symptoms (HAMD-17 scores: −14.2 ± 2.1 vs. −8.5 ± 3.4 in wild-type controls) when adhering to a fermented food-based diet. Mechanistically, probiotic exposure enhanced TLR4-mediated signaling, promoting anti-inflammatory cytokine production and altering short-chain fatty acid profiles. These findings highlight the role of host-genetic factors in shaping microbiome responses to probiotic interventions and fermented food consumption, offering a personalized approach to targeting depression via the gut-brain axis.

Dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome show promise in modulating neuroinflammation linked to depression. A cohort of 120 participants consuming a prebiotic-rich diet supplemented with inulin was analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance to assess microbial and host responses. Fecal samples revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus plantarum, alongside reduced levels of lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation. Serum cytokine profiling highlighted decreased IL-6 and TNF-α concentrations, correlating with lower depressive symptoms measured via the Beck Depression Inventory. Whole-genome sequencing identified TLR4 upregulation in patients with persistent inflammation, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome shifts and immune signaling. 16S rRNA gene sequencing further revealed a statistically significant inverse correlation between gut microbiome alpha-diversity and depressive symptom severity (P < 0.01). These findings underscore the role of prebiotic-mediated microbial modulation in neuroimmune regulation, with TLR4 expression emerging as a potential biomarker for therapeutic monitoring. The integration of principal component analysis enabled robust classification of microbial signatures associated with treatment outcomes, reinforcing the gut-brain axis as a viable target for dietary-based mental health interventions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are linked to neuroinflammation and behavioral dysregulation in patients with autism spectrum disorder, with Tlr4 expression in enteric neurons modulating immune signaling pathways. A 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples from rodent models revealed that Bacteroidetes abundance correlated with pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, while Lactobacillus reuteri supplementation reduced IL-6 secretion in colonic tissues. Mechanistically, Tlr4 knockout in mice attenuated gastrointestinal dysfunction and improved social interaction deficits, suggesting a role for Tlr4-mediated signaling in gut-brain communication. Co-administration of prebiotic inulin with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors enhanced serotonin bioavailability in serotonin-producing enterocytes, mitigating anxiety-like behaviors in mice with neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial metabolites, immune-related genes, and interventions in modulating neurodevelopmental disorders, with implications for personalized microbiome-targeted therapies in clinical settings.

Alterations in the gut microbiota's tryptophan metabolic pathways, influenced by host genetic factors, have been linked to neurobehavioral changes in rodent models. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling, we identified TLR4-mediated immune signaling as a critical modulator of microbial tryptophan catabolism in colonic tissue. Mice lacking functional TLR4 exhibited heightened production of kynurenine and indole-3-propionic acid in the gut lumen, correlating with elevated serotonin levels in the hippocampus and reduced anxiety-like behaviors. Gut microbiota from TLR4-deficient animals showed enriched Akkermansia muciniphila and depleted Bacteroides fragilis, suggesting a dysregulated interplay between microbial tryptophan metabolism and host immunity. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in shaping microbiota-derived neuroactive compounds and underscore the potential of targeting gut microbiota composition to modulate neurological disorders via the gut-brain axis.

Altered expression of the BDNF gene in hippocampal regions was associated with cognitive decline in a cohort of aged rats subjected to chronic stress, highlighting its role in neuroplasticity modulation via the gut-brain axis. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that gut microbiota dysbiosis correlated with reduced BDNF levels, particularly in animals with elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) concentrations. A principal component analysis of microbial profiles identified Bacteroidetes abundance as a significant predictor of BDNF downregulation, while Firmicutes ratios inversely correlated with hippocampal glutamate receptor activation. Oral administration of prebiotic inulin restored BDNF expression in stressed rats, accompanied by a shift in gut microbiota composition toward Lactobacillus dominance, as detected by qPCR. This intervention also normalized IL-6 secretion in colonic tissue and improved performance in novel object recognition assays. The findings suggest that BDNF serves as a molecular link between intestinal microbiota dysregulation and stress-induced cognitive deficits, with multivariate analysis underscoring the predictive power of microbial taxa in neurobehavioral outcomes.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with dysbiosis in the gut microbiome of individuals with major depressive disorder, as demonstrated by multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) of fecal 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 adults (60 with major depressive disorder, 60 healthy controls). Gut microbiota diversity was significantly reduced in major depressive disorder participants, characterized by decreased abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and increased Escherichia coli, alongside elevated plasma IL-6 and TNF-α levels. TLR4 expression in colonic biopsies showed a negative correlation with Faecalibacterium relative abundance (r = −0.42, p < 0.01) and a positive correlation with Escherichia (r = +0.35, p < 0.05). MANOVA revealed significant differences in microbial community structure between groups (F = 5.32, p = 0.002), with TLR4-mediated inflammation explaining 28% of variance in microbiota composition. These findings suggest a mechanistic link between immune signaling pathways and microbiome dysregulation in psychiatric conditions, highlighting TLR4 as a potential therapeutic target for modulating the gut-brain axis via microbiota-targeted interventions.

A high-fiber oatmeal intervention combined with a prebiotic powder significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and alleviated symptoms of depression in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in participants receiving the combined regimen, correlating with reduced gastrointestinal distress scores. Multivariate analysis revealed that prebiotic supplementation enhanced the efficacy of oatmeal-induced microbiota shifts, particularly in individuals with baseline low microbial diversity. Notably, antidepressant use was reduced by 30% in the intervention group, as measured by validated psychometric scales. The SCFAs-producing pathways, enriched by the oatmeal-derived polysaccharides and prebiotic fiber, were linked to improved mood stability via serotonin signaling. These findings underscore the potential of synergistic and <dietary_supplement>-based strategies to target the gut-brain axis in functional gastrointestinal disorders, offering a non-pharmacological approach to mitigate comorbid mental health conditions.

A multi-strain probiotic intervention significantly altered gut microbiota composition and modulated immune-related TLR4 expression in individuals with chronic stress. Using PERMANOVA, we found distinct β-diversity patterns in the probiotic group compared to controls, characterized by increased abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced Escherichia. Participants receiving the supplement also exhibited lower plasma levels of interleukin-6, correlating with reduced TLR4 activation. Machine learning models further identified NOD2 as a predictive biomarker for stress resilience, with higher expression in responders. These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota modulation via probiotic therapies in regulating inflammatory pathways, with implications for personalized interventions targeting TLR4-mediated neuroinflammation in mental health disorders.

Metagenomic sequencing revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance inversely correlates with depression severity in patients with major depressive disorder, with machine learning models identifying short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of this association. Targeted metabolomic profiling confirmed elevated butyrate levels in colonic luminal contents from subjects with high Akkermansia counts, while fluorescence in situ hybridization localized Akkermansia to mucosal regions. Principal component analysis of serotonin metabolite concentrations in serum and fecal samples highlighted a significant negative correlation with Akkermansia abundance, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism. CRISPR-based gene editing in C57BL/6 mice demonstrated that gut microbiota-derived tryptophan hydroxylase activity is modulated by Akkermansia, aligning with 5-hydroxytryptamine levels in hippocampal tissue. Multivariate regression further linked butyrate production to reduced neuroinflammation markers in microglial cells, implicating Akkermansia in neuroimmune regulation via short-chain fatty acid signaling. These findings underscore the potential of gut microbiota modulation as a therapeutic strategy for depressive disorders.

A diet rich in fermented dairy products significantly modulates the expression of the NOD2 gene in gut microbiota, enhancing immune response and reducing inflammation. Microbiome profiling via 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus abundance correlated with upregulated NOD2 activity in subjects consuming daily servings of kefir, a fermented milk beverage. This association was further validated through qPCR analysis, which demonstrated a 40% increase in NOD2 transcript levels compared to controls. The study also identified Bifidobacterium longum as a key mediator of this interaction, linking fermented dairy-induced changes in microbial composition to enhanced host immune signaling pathways. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were detected in higher concentrations in the colonic lumen of participants consuming the intervention, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and NOD2-driven immune modulation. These findings highlight the role of fermented dairy in shaping gut-immune crosstalk via NOD2 activation, offering potential therapeutic strategies for inflammatory bowel disease and other gut-brain axis-related conditions.

A high-fiber legume-based diet modulates gut microbial communities and TLR4 expression in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, suggesting a link between dietary interventions and neuroinflammatory pathways. Prebiotic supplementation with inulin further enhanced microbial diversity and reduced systemic inflammation markers, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing and ELISA. The gut microbiota of participants exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, alongside decreased Escherichia coli, correlating with reduced IL-6 levels. TLR4 downregulation was observed in colonic epithelial cells, coinciding with diminished neuroinflammation in hippocampus regions. qPCR confirmed altered IL-1β and TNF-α expression in subjects consuming the legume-rich regimen. Statistical PCA analysis of microbial taxa and inflammatory markers revealed distinct clustering between groups, highlighting the interplay between dietary fiber, prebiotic intake, and immune-related gene regulation. These findings underscore the potential of targeting gut-microbiota-driven TLR4 signaling to mitigate neuroinflammatory outcomes in irritable bowel syndrome and related neurodegenerative disorders.

Alterations in gut microbial composition associated with major depressive disorder were evaluated using a probiotic intervention in a cohort of 120 participants. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed significant shifts in gut microbiota diversity, with reduced abundance of Lactobacillus and increased presence of Enterobacteriaceae in untreated individuals. A PERMANOVA analysis confirmed distinct clustering of microbial communities between groups, correlating with symptom severity scores. The probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored alpha diversity indices and normalized fecal short-chain fatty acid profiles, as measured by gas chromatography. Notably, patients receiving the supplement exhibited a 32% reduction in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores after eight weeks, with microbial shifts mirrored in plasma tryptophan metabolite concentrations. Bacteroidetes abundance inversely correlated with inflammatory cytokine levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut dysbiosis and neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbial interventions to modulate the gut-brain axis, with multivariate ordination techniques critical for parsing complex interactions between microbial taxa and psychiatric phenotypes.

Tlr4 deficiency in murine models alters gut microbiota composition and enhances susceptibility to anxiety-like behaviors following high-fat diet exposure. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified Bacteroidetes depletion and Firmicutes enrichment in Tlr4-deficient mice fed high-fat diet compared to controls. Short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, particularly butyrate, correlated inversely with Tlr4 expression levels, suggesting impaired microbial metabolic function in Tlr4-knockout animals. Behavioral assessments revealed heightened open field exploration and reduced forced swim immobility in Tlr4-deficient mice on high-fat diet, consistent with paradoxical anxiolytic effects. Mechanistically, Tlr4 signaling in colonic epithelial cells modulated Lactobacillus abundance, which was linked to serotonin receptor expression in enteric neurons. These findings highlight the interplay between Tlr4-mediated immunity, dietary fat intake, and microbial metabolites in shaping gut-brain communication. The data suggest that targeting Tlr4 pathways or modulating high-fat diet-induced microbiota shifts could offer therapeutic avenues for neuroimmune disorders.

Probiotic supplementation significantly altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Lactobacillus rhamnosus administration for 12 weeks increased the relative abundance of Prevotella while decreasing Bacteroides in fecal samples compared to placebo. ANOVA analysis confirmed significant intergroup differences in microbial diversity metrics, including Shannon index values (F=4.32, p<0.05). Concurrently, serotonin levels in serum correlated with shifts in Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios (r=0.67, p=0.012), suggesting potential neurochemical mediation via the gut-brain axis. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan derivatives in the probiotic group, aligning with enhanced TPH1 expression in colonic mucosa biopsies. These findings highlight the capacity of targeted probiotic interventions to modulate intestinal microbiota dynamics and possibly influence gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric outcomes through multivariate regression models incorporating microbial and metabolic parameters.

Alterations in the Tlr4 gene were found to modulate the interaction between the gut microbiota and central nervous system function in murine models of neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we characterized shifts in microbial composition following Tlr4 deletion, revealing a significant increase in Bacteroides and Lactobacillus abundance alongside reduced Prevotella levels. These changes correlated with heightened cytokine production in serum and elevated glucocorticoid concentrations in the hypothalamus, suggesting a mechanism by which Tlr4-mediated immune signaling influences neuroendocrine responses. Real-time PCR confirmed elevated Il6 and Tnf expression in the medulla oblongata of Tlr4-deficient mice, which aligned with increased anxiety-like behaviors observed in open field tests. Furthermore, metabolomic profiling identified altered tryptophan metabolism pathways, implicating microbial-derived indole derivatives as potential mediators of neurobehavioral changes. These findings highlight the role of Tlr4 in shaping gut-brain communication and underscore the value of multimodal omics approaches for dissecting microbial-immune-neuroendocrine networks in psychiatric disorders.

Altered expression of the HLA-DRB1 gene in multiple sclerosis patients correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition driven by phytoestrogen-rich diets. A longitudinal cohort study of 120 individuals with MS revealed that HLA-DRB1 haplotype diversity modulates the abundance of Phyllobacterium and Bacteroides, which are linked to short-chain fatty acid production. Phytoestrogen intake, measured via dietary logs, showed a negative correlation with Firmicutes abundance and a positive association with butyrate levels, suggesting a microbiome-mediated anti-inflammatory pathway. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed that MS subgroups with HLA-DRB1 risk alleles exhibited distinct gut microbial profiles, particularly reduced Lachnospiraceae diversity. MANOVA analysis revealed that phytoestrogen consumption interacted with HLA-DRB1 genotypes to predict central nervous system inflammation markers. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between HLA-DRB1-mediated immune dysregulation, phytoestrogen-induced microbiome remodeling, and MS progression, offering potential therapeutic targets for microbiome-based interventions.

A diet enriched with oligosaccharides modulates gut microbiota composition and alleviates anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models via probiotic supplementation. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), we identified significant shifts in microbial diversity following interventions. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances increased in groups receiving oligosaccharides, while Enterobacteriaceae decreased, correlating with reduced anxiety scores in hippocampus-dependent tasks. Canonical correlation analysis further revealed associations between gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and behavioral outcomes. Notably, probiotic supplementation synergized with oligosaccharides to enhance microbial stability, as evidenced by higher Shannon diversity indices and reduced intergroup beta diversity. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome through prebiotic-rich foods and probiotics could represent a viable strategy for targeting neurobehavioral disorders linked to gut dysbiosis.

Short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota metabolism exhibit neuroprotective effects in models of Alzheimer's disease, with prebiotic fiber supplementation enhancing their production. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from transgenic mouse models to correlate microbial composition with cognitive outcomes following intervention. Mice receiving inulin showed increased abundance of Bacteroidetes and Prevotella, alongside elevated butyrate levels, which correlated with improved hippocampal synaptic plasticity. Metabolomic profiling revealed reduced amyloid-beta accumulation in supplemented groups, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived SCFAs and neuroinflammation modulation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted microbiota modulation in mitigating neurodegenerative disease progression, with multiplexed omics approaches providing critical insights into host-microbiome interactions.

The Tlr4 gene modulates gut microbiota composition and immune signaling pathways, influencing intestinal homeostasis and central nervous system function via the gut-brain axis. Using a 16S rRNA sequencing approach, we analyzed fecal samples from participants with and without autoimmune disorders, revealing significant Bacteroidetes-Firmicutes ratio shifts correlated with Tlr4 polymorphisms. Multivariate analysis of variance confirmed that Tlr4 rs3804077 alleles were associated with altered short-chain fatty acid profiles and increased lipopolysaccharide translocation. These findings were validated in murine models lacking Tlr4, where fluorescent in situ hybridization highlighted dysregulated mucosal Commensal microbes and heightened neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. The interplay between Tlr4-mediated immune responses and microbiota-derived metabolites appears critical in shaping neurobehavioral outcomes, suggesting targeted CRISPR-Cas9-based gene correction could restore gut-brain communication in neurological conditions. This study underscores the necessity of integrating machine learning models with microbiome-wide metabolomic profiling to decode complex gene-microbiota interactions.

Alterations in the Nrf2 gene pathway were linked to dysbiosis in Parkinson's disease patients, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. Patients exhibited reduced Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios and elevated Bacteroides abundance compared to healthy controls, correlating with increased oxidative stress markers in the substantia nigra. The Nrf2-mediated upregulation of HO-1 and NQO-1 was associated with attenuated neuroinflammation, while multiplex cytokine assays confirmed reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in mice treated with probiotic-enriched prebiotics. Metagenomic analysis further identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a keystone species whose abundance inversely correlated with alpha-synuclein aggregation in transgenic models. These findings highlight the interplay between Nrf2-regulated antioxidant defenses and gut microbiota remodeling in modulating neuroinflammation and disease progression. The integrated omics approach underscores potential therapeutic targets at the gut-brain interface, suggesting that modulating Nrf2 activity could synergize with microbiota-directed interventions to mitigate Parkinson's disease pathology.

Altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with metabolic syndrome correlates with dysregulated SIRT1 expression and impaired glucose homeostasis, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolic profiling. A high-fiber diet intervention partially restored Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, which was inversely linked to SIRT1 suppression in colonic epithelial cells, suggesting a microbiota-dependent mechanism for metabolic resilience. Short-chain fatty acids derived from prebiotic-rich foods enhanced SIRT1 activation, improving insulin sensitivity in ob/ob mice via modulation of gut-brain axis signaling. These findings highlight the interplay between SIRT1, microbial metabolites, and dietary interventions in mitigating metabolic dysfunction.

Chronic administration of a prebiotic fiber significantly altered the composition of the gut microbiota in rodents with Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. The intervention increased abundance of Bifidobacterium while reducing pro-inflammatory Escherichia coli strains, correlating with improved spatial memory and reduced neuroinflammation markers. Microbiota-derived metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, were quantified using mass spectrometry, revealing elevated butyrate levels linked to enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis. These findings suggest that modulating gut microbiota via prebiotics could mitigate cognitive decline through anti-inflammatory pathways, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative disorders.

Chronic consumption of polyphenol-rich blueberries modulates gut microbiota composition and suppresses inflammatory gene expression in the hippocampus of mice. In a 12-week intervention, C57BL/6J mice fed a diet enriched with blueberries exhibited reduced anxiety-like behaviors and altered gut microbiota profiles compared to controls. 16S rDNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and decreased Bacteroides in the cecum of blueberry-treated cohorts. Concurrently, hippocampal TNF-α and IL-6 expression levels were significantly lower, correlating with elevated short-chain fatty acid production and improved behavioral outcomes in the elevated plus maze. Mechanistically, the blueberry-induced microbiome shift enhanced butyrate synthesis, which activated FXR-mediated signaling pathways in enterocytes, dampening systemic inflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between nutraceutical interventions and host immune regulators in modulating the gut-brain axis, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for neuroinflammatory disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition induced by dietary interventions significantly modulate neuroinflammatory markers in the hippocampus. A cohort of participants consuming a probiotic-enriched dairy product for 12 weeks exhibited reduced levels of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha compared to controls. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, correlating with enhanced gut microbiota diversity. These changes were associated with improved working memory and reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models. Metabolic profiling further identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of the microbiota-brain communication. The findings highlight the potential of dietary modulation to target gut-brain axis dysregulation in neurodegenerative disorders.

Modifications in gut microbiota composition linked to depression were analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing in adults consuming a high-fiber diet supplemented with probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus. Participants (n=52) exhibited significant shifts in alpha diversity indices after 8 weeks of intervention, with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium correlating to improved mood scores. Metagenomic analysis revealed altered tryptophan metabolism pathways, suggesting microbial contributions to serotonin synthesis. Prebiotic-rich foods like oats and onions enhanced butyrate-producing bacteria, while omega-3 fatty acids co-administered with probiotics showed synergistic effects on cognitive function. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations, measured via gas chromatography, correlated with reduced inflammatory markers in serum. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial metabolites, nutrient intake, and supplement regimens in modulating mental health outcomes, underscoring the potential of targeted interventions to address depressive symptoms through gut-brain axis modulation.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are strongly linked to Parkinson's disease progression, with multivariate logistic regression highlighting Bacteroides fragilis as a key contributor to motor dysfunction severity. Interventions involving the curcumin significantly altered microbial composition, increasing Prevotella copri abundance while decreasing pro-inflammatory lipopolysaccharides production, as evidenced by qPCR and ANOVA analyses. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbial dysbiosis through curcumin may offer a therapeutic strategy for mitigating neuroinflammation in PD patients, with multivariate logistic regression further confirming the predictive value of microbial biomarkers in disease progression. The gut microbiota of patients with PD exhibited reduced butyrate-producing pathways and elevated Escherichia coli levels, which correlated with alpha-synuclein aggregation rates measured via immunohistochemistry. Notably, curcumin supplementation restored short-chain fatty acid synthesis and suppressed Escherichia coli-driven oxidative stress, as quantified by paired t-test comparisons between treatment and control cohorts. This study underscores the role of gut-brain axis interactions in PD pathogenesis and highlights curcumin as a potential modulator of microbiome-derived neuroinflammation.

A diet enriched in inulin modulates the gut microbiome and alters systemic TNF-α expression, influencing neuroinflammatory pathways linked to depression. Using Illumina MiSequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from participants undergoing a 12-week prebiotic intervention, identifying significant shifts in Blautia and Ruminococcus abundance correlated with reduced TNF-α serum levels. These changes coincided with improved mood scores on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, suggesting a microbial-mediated mechanism. Mechanistically, TNF-α downregulation was associated with increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, a species known to enhance intestinal barrier integrity. The blood-brain barrier permeability, assessed via transwell assays, showed reduced cytokine infiltration in subjects consuming inulin-supplemented diets. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotic strategies to target TNF-α-driven inflammation via microbial modulation, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for mood disorders with gut-brain axis dysregulation.

A prebiotic inulin significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and metabolic pathways in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by 16S rDNA sequencing and non-targeted metabolomics. Principal component analysis identified distinct microbial signatures associated with cognitive function, including elevated abundance of Parabacteroides and reduced Proteobacteria. The supplement restored hippocampal synaptic plasticity by mitigating neuroinflammation via bile acid signaling pathways, as evidenced by increased tauroursodeoxycholic acid levels in serum. Fecal microbiome transplantation confirmed the microbiota-dependent efficacy of inulin in reversing cognitive impairment and tau pathology in mice with Alzheimer's disease. Metabolomic profiling further linked the intervention to enhanced oleoyl-l-carnitine metabolism, which correlated with improved BDNF expression in the brain. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of inulin in targeting gut-brain axis dysregulation through metagenomic and metabolomic integration, supported by multivariate regression models that accounted for 78% of variance in cognitive outcomes.

Modulation of the gut microbiome by a probiotic formulation significantly reduced systemic inflammation and improved cognitive function in a murine model of neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified shifts in intestinal bacterial taxa correlated with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of microbial communities in treated versus control groups, with Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus showing increased abundance. These changes coincided with enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced neuroinflammatory markers in the brain and colon. Mechanistically, the probiotic formulation appeared to regulate TLR4 signaling pathways, as evidenced by qPCR and Western blot analyses. Our findings suggest that targeted microbial modulation via probiotics could offer a novel therapeutic strategy for neuroinflammatory disorders by enhancing gut-brain communication.

A recent study revealed that administration of a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus reuteri and Bifidobacterium longum significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced systemic inflammation in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, researchers identified increased abundance of anti-inflammatory bacterial taxa and decreased Proteobacteria levels following a 12-week intervention. Parallel qPCR analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells demonstrated downregulation of the TNF-α promoter region, correlating with reduced interleukin-6 secretion. The probiotic treatment also improved gastrointestinal symptoms and anxiety scores, as measured by the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. These findings highlight the role of microbial 16S rRNA-based profiling in elucidating mechanistic links between gut microbiota dysbiosis and neuroimmune dysfunction. The probiotic formulation emerged as a viable therapeutic strategy for comorbid gastrointestinal and psychiatric disorders, underscoring the necessity of integrating molecular microbiology with clinical assessments in gut-brain axis research.
