The TLR5 gene modulates gut-brain signaling via microbial metabolite recognition, as revealed by CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing in murine models. This study demonstrates that TLR5 deficiency enhances neuroinflammation and alters behavior in response to gut microbiota dysbiosis, linking immune sensing to central nervous system plasticity. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified Escherichia coli expansion in TLR5-knockout mice, correlating with elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation and hippocampal BDNF downregulation. Behavioral assays showed heightened anxiety-like responses and impaired spatial memory, mirroring autism spectrum disorder phenotypes. Mechanistically, TLR5 activation in enteric neurons suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokine release, preserving gut barrier integrity and preventing neurotoxic metabolite accumulation. These findings underscore the role of TLR5 in maintaining gut-brain homeostasis and suggest targeted modulation of microbial sensing pathways as a therapeutic strategy for neurodevelopmental disorders. The integration of single-cell RNA sequencing further mapped distinct immune cell subsets in the medulla oblongata, revealing TLR5-dependent transcriptional networks that bridge peripheral and central immune responses.

A dietary supplement containing a prebiotic fiber blend significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces systemic inflammation in individuals with metabolic syndrome, as demonstrated by longitudinal 16S rRNA sequencing and mixed-effects regression analyses. Participants (n=120) received daily doses of inulin-type fructans for 12 weeks, with baseline and follow-up assessments of fecal microbial diversity, plasma cytokine levels, and metabolic markers. Bifidobacterium and Akkermansia muciniphila abundance increased by 47% and 63%, respectively, while pro-inflammatory IL-6 and TNF-α concentrations decreased by 28% and 34%. Random forest modeling identified Bifidobacterium abundance as the strongest predictor of inflammation reduction (R²=0.61). These findings highlight the potential of targeted prebiotic interventions to restore gut microbiome homeostasis and mitigate metabolic dysregulation through immune-modulatory pathways. The mixed-effects regression approach further revealed that baseline adipose tissue inflammation severity influenced treatment response, suggesting personalized microbiome-based therapies could optimize outcomes in metabolic syndrome management.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene expression in the enteric nervous system have been implicated in the dysregulation of gut microbiota-mediated signaling pathways linked to irritable bowel syndrome and major depressive disorder. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we identified distinct Enterococcus faecalis-driven inflammatory responses in colonic epithelial cells that correlated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and altered serotonin metabolism. Microbial dysbiosis was further associated with reduced BDNF transcript abundance in the hippocampus, suggesting a bidirectional gut-brain axis disruption. Interventions targeting TLR4 via CRISPR-Cas9-mediated editing in murine models attenuated inflammatory bowel disease progression and normalized neurotransmitter profiles. These findings highlight the role of host gene-microbiome interactions in neuro-immunological disorders and underscore the therapeutic potential of precision genomic editing to restore gut-brain homeostasis.

Altered microbial gene expression in the gut microbiome correlates with neuroinflammation in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), revealing a potential link between TLR4 activation and systemic immune dysregulation. Using metagenomic sequencing and serum cytokine profiling, we analyzed fecal samples and plasma from 80 participants with IBS (n=40) and healthy controls (n=40), identifying 14 differentially expressed immune-related genes in Escherichia coli-dominated microbiota. Principal component analysis highlighted IL-1β and IL-6 as key drivers of inflammation, with lipopolysaccharide levels correlating strongly to TLR4 expression (r=0.72, p<0.001). Functional annotation of COG0495 (permease) and COG1554 (hydrolase) suggested metabolic shifts in IBS patients linked to altered short-chain fatty acid production. These findings implicate TLR4-mediated signaling in the pathogenesis of IBS and highlight the role of microbial gene networks in modulating the gut-brain axis through immune cross-talk. Further exploration of these pathways may refine therapeutic strategies targeting both microbial and host factors in IBS-related neuroinflammation.

A novel interaction between a probiotic-enriched wheat germ and the GAD1 gene was identified in a murine model of depression, highlighting the role of wheat germ fermentation in modulating neurotransmitter pathways via the gut-brain axis. Probiotic fermentation of wheat germ enhanced Lactobacillus plantarum abundance, which correlated with elevated GABA production linked to GAD1-mediated enzymatic activity in the hippocampus. Behavioral assays revealed reduced depression-like behaviors in rats treated with the supplement, alongside restored gut microbiota diversity and increased serotonin levels. Mechanistically, probiotic-enriched wheat germ upregulated GAD1 expression in enteric neurons, synergizing with Lactobacillus plantarum-derived GABA to enhance synaptic plasticity. Metabolomic profiling identified altered tryptophan metabolism, implicating TPH2-dependent serotonin synthesis in the antidepressant effects. These findings suggest that fermented wheat germ modulates GAD1 and TPH2 pathways to restore neurochemical balance, offering a potential adjunct for depression management through microbiome-targeted interventions.

Chronic administration of a multi-strain probiotic formulation significantly mitigated neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in a murine model of Alzheimer’s disease, revealing a novel interaction between gut microbiota and central nervous system pathogenesis. The intervention was coupled with 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial community shifts, revealing increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced Proteobacteria levels, correlated with decreased Aβ(1-42) accumulation and tau phosphorylation in hippocampal tissues. Transgenic 3xTg-AD mice supplemented with the probiotic exhibited enhanced BDNF expression and reduced microglial activation, suggesting modulation of neuroplasticity pathways. Concurrent metabolomic profiling identified elevated butyrate and tryptophan derivatives as potential mediators of neuroprotection. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis, with implications for neurodegenerative disorders and metabolic syndrome. The integration of multi-omics approaches highlights the necessity of mechanistic clarity in translating microbiome-based therapies to clinical practice.

Principal component analysis revealed significant associations between gut microbiota diversity and major depressive disorder severity in a cohort of adults consuming fermented dairy products regularly. Microbial taxa such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium showed inverse correlations with depressive symptoms, while Escherichia coli abundance positively correlated with anxiety comorbidities. 16S rRNA sequencing identified gut microbiome dysbiosis in patients with depression compared to controls following a probiotic-enriched diet. High-fiber intake was linked to increased Akkermansia muciniphila levels, which in turn correlated with reduced inflammatory markers via multivariate regression modeling. Gut-brain axis interactions were further supported by metabolomic profiling showing elevated tryptophan derivatives in individuals adhering to plant-based diets. These findings suggest that microbiota modulation through targeted nutritional interventions may offer novel therapeutic strategies for mental health disorders, with machine learning approaches enhancing predictive accuracy of microbiome-disease relationships.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells was linked to dysbiosis in individuals consuming a low-fiber diet, revealing a potential mechanistic pathway for gut-brain axis disruption in inflammatory bowel disease patients. Using metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from 120 participants, we identified a correlation between Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and TLR4 downregulation, which was reversed by supplementation with fermented dairy products rich in short-chain fatty acids. Butyrate levels, measured via gas chromatography, positively correlated with TLR4 expression and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, as confirmed by ANOVA analysis. Mechanistically, TLR4-mediated signaling in colonic epithelial cells was restored by probiotic-rich diets, mitigating intestinal permeability and neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between diet, microbial metabolites, and host gene regulation in modulating gut-brain communication and suggest targeted dietary interventions as a therapeutic strategy.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene variant modulate gut microbiome composition, influencing susceptibility to depressive disorders through immune-metabolic pathways. A probiotic formulation enriched with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and administered alongside fermented soybeans was evaluated in a mouse model of stress-induced anxiety. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that TLR4-deficient mice exhibited dysbiosis marked by reduced Bacteroidetes and elevated Firmicutes ratios, correlating with heightened anxiety-like behavior. Co-administration of the probiotic and fermented soybeans restored gut microbiome diversity, increased short-chain fatty acids production, and normalized TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling in the hippocampus. Multivariate analysis identified synergistic interactions between fermented soybeans-derived isoflavones and probiotic-induced SCFA-producing taxa, which dampened TLR4 activation and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4 polymorphisms, probiotic supplementation, and fermented soybeans in mitigating stress-related mental health disorders via the gut-brain axis.

Altered gut microbiota composition associated with metabolic syndrome was investigated in a preclinical model using C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet supplemented with a probiotic formulation. Analysis of 16S rRNA sequences via 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed significant shifts in microbial diversity, with gut microbiota richness decreasing by 23% in the high-fat diet group compared to controls. The probiotic formulation partially restored microbial diversity, though not to baseline levels. Metabolic parameters, including insulin resistance and lipid accumulation, correlated with specific bacterial taxa, such as the upregulated Akkermansia muciniphila and downregulated Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Functional metagenomic analysis suggested the probiotic formulation modulated pathways related to short-chain fatty acid production, potentially mitigating inflammation. However, the high-fat diet group exhibited persistent dysbiosis despite intervention, highlighting the complex interplay between dietary intake and microbiota resilience. These findings underscore the potential of targeted probiotic strategies in counteracting high-fat diet-induced metabolic disturbances, though further studies are needed to optimize microbial interventions for metabolic syndrome management.

A dietary supplement containing *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* significantly modulated the expression of the *BDNF* gene in the hippocampus of mice, as revealed by RT-qPCR, thereby reducing anxiety-like behaviors through the gut-brain axis. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples identified a shift in microbial composition, including increased abundance of *Lactobacillus* spp., which correlated with decreased plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines. The study further demonstrated that the dietary supplement's efficacy relied on its interaction with the *BDNF* gene pathway, as evidenced by gene-specific knockdown experiments. These findings suggest that microbiome-targeted interventions, when paired with genetic profiling, may offer novel strategies for treating mood disorders. Metabolomic profiling of serum samples corroborated the link between microbial metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, and altered *BDNF* signaling. This integrative approach highlights the potential of combining probiotic formulations with gene-targeted therapies to address the interplay between the microbiome and neural plasticity in psychiatric conditions.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with dysregulated lipid metabolism in obese individuals, suggesting a role for microbial modulation in metabolic disease management. Administration of a probiotic formulation containing <bacteria>Lactobacillus johnsonii</bacteria> significantly reduced systemic inflammation and normalized PPAR-γ expression in adipose tissue of obese mice fed a high-fat diet. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we observed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Fusobacterium in fecal samples, correlating with reduced plasma triglycerides and improved insulin sensitivity. PPAR-γ activation was linked to enhanced short-chain fatty acid production by Butyricicoccus, which modulated intestinal epithelial barrier integrity via zooxanthellae-mediated signaling. Notably, probiotic administration synergized with metformin to suppress adipose inflammation and restore lipoprotein lipase activity, highlighting the potential of microbiome-targeted therapies in conjunction with conventional drugs. These findings underscore the interplay between gut microbiota, host metabolic pathways, and dietary interventions in mitigating obesity-associated pathologies.

Chronic administration of the Lactobacillus rhamnosus CGMCC1.37 (Lr) significantly reduced depressive-like behaviors in mice fed a high-fat diet, accompanied by altered expression of the Htr1a gene in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). Lr treatment normalized elevated serotonin (5-HT) levels in the brain and restored Htr1a expression in stressed mice exposed to chronic unpredictable stress (CUS). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed shifts in the gut microbiota profile, with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced Proteobacteria in Lr-treated cohorts. Metabolomic profiling identified enhanced tryptophan catabolite production, correlating with Htr1a-mediated signaling modulation. AAV-shRNA targeting Htr1a in the mPFC of CUS mice reversed anhedonia, confirming the gene’s role in Lr-induced behavioral recovery. These findings highlight the interplay between high-fat diet-induced gut dysbiosis, Htr1a regulation, and the therapeutic potential of Lr in mitigating depressive-like behaviors via the gut-brain axis.

Gut microbiota dysbiosis is strongly correlated with major depressive disorder in adults, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and principal component analysis. Bacteroidetes depletion and Firmicutes overrepresentation were observed in patients with depression, alongside elevated serotonin metabolite levels in serum. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus normalized gut microbiota composition, reduced inflammatory cytokine expression, and improved depressive symptoms in a 12-week interventional trial. Short-chain fatty acids production, measured via gas chromatography, increased significantly in the probiotic group, correlating with decreased HAMD-17 scores (p < 0.01). Multivariate analysis confirmed that gut microbiota diversity predicted depressive severity independently of brain imaging markers. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic-mediated gut microbiota modulation as a therapeutic strategy for depression, emphasizing the role of gut-brain axis signaling in psychiatric disorders.

A recent study revealed that a probiotic supplement significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in geriatric rats with chronic neuroinflammation, as assessed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. The intervention targeted Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium enrichment while reducing Enterobacteriaceae abundance, correlating with improved spatial memory and reduced interleukin-6 levels in the hippocampus. Participants in the supplemented group exhibited enhanced gut-brain axis connectivity, inferred from canonical correlation analysis linking microbial taxa to neuroinflammatory markers. The probiotic also attenuated blood-brain barrier permeability, as measured by fluorescein isothiocyanate-labeled dextran leakage, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome remodeling and neuroprotection. Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, a gut microbiota marker associated with mucosal integrity, showed a statistically significant inverse correlation with TNF-α expression in the prefrontal cortex (r = -0.63, p < 0.01). These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic interventions in mitigating neuroinflammation via gut microbiota modulation, with multivariate analysis underscoring the complex interplay between microbial signatures and cerebral immune responses.

The gut microbiome's role in metabolic diseases is increasingly linked to dietary patterns, yet the interplay between specific high-fiber legumes and microbial dysbiosis remains understudied. Using multivariate regression analysis, we evaluated longitudinal data from 500 participants to assess how habitual consumption of legumes modulates gut microbial diversity and inflammatory markers. Results revealed a significant positive correlation between legume intake and abundance of Bifidobacterium, while canonical correspondence analysis highlighted that legume consumption was inversely associated with insulin resistance and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting fiber-rich foods may mitigate metabolic risk via microbiome remodeling. Notably, colonic fermentation of legume-derived polysaccharides produced elevated butyrate levels, which correlated with reduced systemic inflammation. The study also employed 16S rRNA sequencing to map microbial shifts, revealing that legume-fed cohorts exhibited a distinct taxonomic profile enriched in Akkermansia muciniphila. These data underscore the potential of plant-based diets as a modifiable factor in gut-brain-metabolism interactions, warranting further exploration of targeted prebiotic strategies. The integration of machine learning algorithms to predict individual microbiome responses to dietary changes could refine personalized therapeutic approaches.

A high-fiber diet modulates the gut microbiome, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes via the gut-brain axis, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples from mice fed probiotic-rich yogurt. The gut microbiota of animals consuming the probiotic-rich yogurt exhibited increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, alongside reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. These changes correlated with attenuated anxiety-like behavior in open-field tests and altered tryptophan metabolism pathways inferred through metagenomic functional prediction. Multivariate analysis revealed that microbial diversity, particularly Firmicutes abundance, mediated the relationship between dietary intervention and behavioral outcomes. The vagus nerve was implicated as a key conduit, with vagotomy blocking the protective effects of probiotic-rich yogurt on depression-like symptoms. These findings highlight the role of probiotic-rich yogurt in shaping the gut microbiome and its downstream impact on mental health via 16S rRNA sequencing-identified microbial pathways.

A random forest algorithm identified significant associations between high-fiber diets and alterations in the gut microbiome that correlate with depressive symptoms in a cohort of 120 participants. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that individuals consuming ≥100 g/day of whole grains exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which were inversely linked to pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed reduced hippocampal volume in participants with low-fiber intake, a finding corroborated by canonical correlation analysis linking microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids to neuroimaging metrics. The serotonin reuptake inhibitor response rate was 32% higher in high-fiber groups, suggesting microbiome-mediated modulation of serotonergic pathways. These data highlight the interplay between dietary fiber, microbial metabolites, and brain structure, with implications for major depressive disorder management. Permutation testing confirmed the robustness of these associations, underscoring the potential of fiber-rich foods as modulators of the gut-brain axis.

Chrna7 knockout in mice alters gut microbiota composition, contributing to depression-like behaviors through disrupted vagus nerve signaling. Metagenomic sequencing revealed reduced abundance of Lactobacillus species in Chrna7 KO models, correlating with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in plasma. Chrna7 encodes a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor critical for modulating immune responses via the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, yet its role in microbiota-brain interactions remains understudied. 16S rRNA amplicon analysis identified distinct microbial signatures in Chrna7 KO versus wild-type controls, with Lactobacillus reuteri showing strongest inverse association with behavioral deficits. Multivariate analysis further linked short-chain fatty acid metabolites, derived from gut microbiota, to Chrna7-mediated synaptic protein expression in the medial prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest Chrna7 regulates neurobehavioral outcomes by modulating microbiota-derived signals, highlighting the potential of targeting gut microbiome composition to ameliorate depressive disorders in individuals with Chrna7 dysfunction.

The Nrf2 gene's activation in the hippocampus was associated with reduced neuroinflammation in a mouse model of depression, suggesting a potential therapeutic target. Curcumin, a polyphenol derived from turmeric, significantly altered gut microbiota composition, as revealed by principal component analysis (PCA). The PCA highlighted distinct clustering of microbial communities in treated versus control groups, correlating with reduced depressive behaviors. These findings indicate that curcumin may exert its antidepressant effects through Nrf2-mediated pathways, modulating gut microbiota dysbiosis. Further analysis using Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed significant differences in microbial taxa abundance between groups, supporting the role of dietary interventions in neuroimmune regulation via the gut-brain axis. The study underscores the importance of Nrf2-diet interactions in mental health and highlights the utility of PCA in elucidating microbiome dynamics. Behavioral improvements were accompanied by increased antioxidant enzyme expression and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, linking curcumin to systemic and neural anti-inflammatory effects. These data suggest a novel strategy for targeting depression through microbiome remodeling and gene-specific pathways.

Curcumin-enriched  turmeric  supplementation significantly attenuated Alzheimer's disease-related Aβ pathology and neuroinflammation in a transgenic mouse model via modulation of the gut microbiota. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that  turmeric -derived curcumin enhanced abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which correlated with reduced proinflammatory cytokine levels in the brain. Mechanistically, curcumin suppressed TNF-α expression and activated the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant pathway in colonic epithelial cells, mitigating oxidative stress and preserving blood-brain barrier integrity.  Turmeric  also increased short-chain fatty acid production, which modulated TLR4 signaling in microglia to dampen neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of  turmeric  as a microbiota-targeting prebiotic to ameliorate Alzheimer's disease through gut-brain axis interactions, offering a novel strategy for disease-modifying interventions.

Altered microbial metabolites from a flavonoid-rich diet correlate with reduced neuroinflammation in aging populations, as demonstrated by principal component analysis of longitudinal cohort data. A randomized trial involving 120 participants showed that supplementation with prebiotic inulin enhanced the production of short-chain fatty acids in the gut, which were linked to improved cognitive flexibility via modulation of TLR4 expression in microglia. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that blueberry consumption increased the abundance of Bifidobacterium longum, a taxon associated with reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation and attenuated stress-induced anxiety in rodent models. Integrating multivariate analysis of variance with metabolomic profiling, we observed that individuals consuming both probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus and fermented dairy products exhibited greater alpha-diversity and lower cortisol levels compared to controls. These findings highlight the interplay between diet-modulated gut microbiota and neuroimmune signaling, suggesting that targeted interventions combined with nutrient-dense foods may optimize brain health in aging.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing, correlate with enhanced neurobehavioral outcomes in mice treated with curcumin, a polyphenolic compound derived from turmeric. This study demonstrates that chronic administration of curcumin modulates the abundance of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes while reducing pathogenic Escherichia coli levels in intestinal luminal contents of rodent models with chronic stress-induced cognitive deficits. Concurrently, metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum, suggesting microbiota-driven neuroprotection. Curcumin also increased the relative abundance of Lactobacillus, linked to tryptophan metabolism, which may mediate its effects via the gut-brain axis. These findings highlight the potential of curcumin as a modulator of gut microbiota function and its role in mitigating cognitive decline through microbiota-targeted interventions. The study underscores the interplay between nutraceuticals and microbial metabolic pathways in neurobehavioral health, offering a framework for exploring microbiome-based therapies.

A diet enriched with the probiotic *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* GG significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and alleviates behavioral symptoms of anxiety in rodent models of stress-induced dysregulation. Using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), we demonstrated that specific microbial taxa correlated with altered hippocampal neurogenesis and serotonin signaling pathways, which were further validated via 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays. The intervention reduced cytokine levels in serum, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial-derived metabolites and neuroinflammation. Hippocampal dendritic spine density, assessed via confocal microscopy, showed significant recovery in treated groups compared to controls. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic supplementation as a non-pharmacological strategy to target gut-brain axis dysregulation in mental disorders, with MANOVA revealing robust associations between microbial diversity and behavioral outcomes. The study underscores the role of microbiota-derived signaling in modulating brain function and emphasizes the need for precision in selecting microbial interventions to optimize therapeutic efficacy.

A dietary supplement containing probiotics significantly altered gut microbiota composition in individuals consuming a high-fiber food diet, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing. Analysis of fecal samples from 60 participants revealed that supplementation with *Lactobacillus rhamnosus* alongside a daily intake of oatmeal enriched the abundance of butyrate-producing bacteria, including *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, while reducing markers of intestinal inflammation. The biomedical_technique of shotgun metagenomic sequencing identified 14 differentially abundant taxa, with *Bifidobacterium longum* showing a 2.3-fold increase in the supplemented group. Concurrently, plasma levels of the food-derived metabolite inosine monophosphate correlated with improved markers of gut barrier integrity, suggesting a synergistic effect between the dietary_supplement and the food matrix. These findings highlight the potential of combining targeted probiotic supplementation with prebiotic-rich diets to modulate the gut microbiome and mitigate inflammatory conditions. The study further demonstrated that the interaction between microbial taxa and host-derived metabolites, as quantified through liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, could serve as a biomarker for therapeutic efficacy in microbiome-targeted interventions.

A high-fiber diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition, correlating with improved cognitive function in aged rats through modulation of short-chain fatty acid production. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in animals fed oat bran, which was associated with reduced inflammatory cytokine levels in the hippocampus. Principal component analysis identified a strong correlation between microbial diversity indices and spatial memory performance, measured via Morris water maze testing. Elderly participants with Alzheimer’s disease who consumed fermented dairy products showed similar microbiota shifts, though butyrate levels remained lower compared to controls. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota may mitigate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline by enhancing SCFA production, with metabolomic profiling confirming elevated acetate and propionate in model organisms fed high-fiber diets. The study underscores the role of prebiotic-rich foods in shaping neuroimmune pathways via gut-brain axis interactions, highlighting potential therapeutic strategies for age-related cognitive disorders.

A novel psychobiotic formulation significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and neuroactive metabolite production in C57BL/6 mice, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LC-MS analysis. The intervention involved administering a probiotic blend enriched with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, which enhanced γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels in colonic lumen samples while reducing glutamate concentrations. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of microbial taxa in treated groups, with increased abundance of Prevotella and decreased Escherichia coli compared to controls. The probiotic treatment also correlated with elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) production, particularly butyrate, measured via GC-MS. Behavioral assays showed reduced anxiety-like responses in mice treated with the formulation, aligning with microbiota-driven changes in GABA signaling. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to alter gut-brain axis dynamics through metabolomic profiling and multivariate statistical analysis.

Dysbiosis in the gut microbiota correlates with heightened neuroinflammation in individuals with major depressive disorder, suggesting a role for the gut-brain axis in mood regulation. A high-fiber diet modulated microbial composition and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in patients undergoing cognitive behavioral therapy, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and quantitative PCR. Analysis revealed that TLR4 expression was downregulated in the hippocampus, while Bifidobacterium abundance increased significantly in fecal samples from participants adhering to the dietary intervention. These findings suggest that microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids may mediate the anti-inflammatory effects observed, potentially via suppression of NF-κB-dependent pathways. Additionally, metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan metabolites in the serum of responders, aligning with improved serotonin signaling in enteric neurons. The study highlights the potential of dietary strategies to restore microbiome homeostasis and alleviate neuroinflammatory markers in depressive disorders, offering a novel therapeutic avenue that integrates microbial modulation with genomic and metabolic analyses.

A diet rich in fermented dairy products significantly altered gut microbiota composition in patients with anxiety disorders, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Analysis of microbial diversity showed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced levels of Escherichia coli, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine concentrations in serum. Metabolomic profiling further identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production, suggesting a mechanistic link between fermented dairy-induced microbiota shifts and improved anxiety symptoms. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiota-modulating diets in mitigating neuroinflammation-related pathologies via the gut-brain axis.

Altered expression of the TNF-α gene was observed in rodent models following chronic exposure to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a Gram-negative bacterial component that disrupts the gut microbiota. RNA-seq of intestinal epithelial cells revealed dysregulated inflammatory pathways, correlating with increased pathogenic Escherichia coli abundance and decreased short-chain fatty acid producers such as Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron. Behavioral assays demonstrated heightened anxiety-like behaviors and impaired cognitive flexibility in exposed mice, linked to elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts in microbial composition, while ELISA quantified TNF-α and IL-6 levels in serum and brain tissue. These findings highlight the role of TNF-α-mediated signaling in linking gut dysbiosis to neurobehavioral outcomes, suggesting that targeting inflammatory genes via metabolic modulation may mitigate gut-brain axis dysfunction in neurodegenerative conditions.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are strongly correlated with cognitive deficits in aged individuals, as demonstrated by multivariate regression analysis revealing significant associations between reduced Bifidobacterium abundance and impaired spatial memory. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from young donors into aged mice restored hippocampal neurogenesis and improved performance in Morris water maze tests, as assessed by immunohistochemical quantification of doublecortin-positive cells. Principal component analysis identified distinct microbial signatures linked to memory recovery, while 16S rRNA sequencing elucidated shifts in microbial taxa following intervention. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted strategies in mitigating age-related cognitive decline, underscoring the role of the gut-brain axis in neuroplasticity and behavioral outcomes. The interplay between microbial metabolites and central nervous system signaling was further validated through in situ hybridization of BDNF-expressing neurons in transplanted rodents.

A high-fiber diet modulates gut microbiota composition and enhances short-chain fatty acid production, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling in a rodent model. Oats, rich in beta-glucan, were administered to rats for four weeks, followed by analysis of microbial diversity and inflammatory markers. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, while IL-6 and TNF-α levels decreased significantly. Metabolomic data showed elevated butyrate and propionate, correlating with improved intestinal barrier integrity. These findings suggest that fiber-rich diets may mitigate inflammatory bowel disease by promoting beneficial microbial taxa and anti-inflammatory metabolites. Further studies are needed to explore clinical applications in patients with gastrointestinal disorders.

A high-fiber fermented vegetable diet significantly altered gut microbiota profiles in participants with metabolic syndrome, enhancing the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila while reducing Escherichia coli levels. Concurrent omega-3 fatty acid supplementation synergistically modulated TNF-α-mediated inflammatory signaling in enteric neurons, as evidenced by reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in ex vivo intestinal organoid cultures. These changes correlated with improved executive function scores, measured via fMRI, suggesting microbiome-brain axis reprogramming. Notably, TLR4 expression in colonic epithelial cells was upregulated by the fiber-rich diet, enhancing short-chain fatty acid sensing and downstream BDNF activation in the hippocampus. The combined intervention also restored serotonin transporter (SERT) expression in enteric nervous system neurons, aligning with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in mice models. These findings highlight the role of nutrient-microbiome interactions in neuroimmune regulation and offer potential therapeutic targets for neuropsychiatric comorbidities linked to metabolic dysregulation.

The TLR4 gene was identified as a key mediator of gut microbiota-induced neuroinflammation in multiple sclerosis (MS) through 16S rRNA sequencing and proteomic profiling. Principal component analysis revealed significant correlations between Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and TMAO levels in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) models, which were further validated by qPCR and metabolomic fingerprinting. TMAO elevation correlated with increased TLR4 activation in microglial cells, exacerbating MS pathology via IL-17 upregulation. Multivariate regression confirmed that TLR4 expression mediated 62% of the variance in MS severity scores. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TLR4 knockout in mouse models reduced TMAO-induced neuroinflammation by 43%, while flow cytometry demonstrated diminished Proteobacteria infiltration. These findings highlight TLR4 as a therapeutic target in MS, linking gut microbiota dysbiosis to neuroinflammation via metabolite-driven immune signaling pathways.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with cognitive decline in a murine model of neurodegeneration, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis. Administration of the probiotic strain <bacteria>Lactobacillus reuteri</bacteria> significantly attenuated Alzheimer's disease-like pathologies in APP/PS1 transgenic mice, evidenced by reduced Aβ plaque deposition in the hippocampus and improved spatial memory performance. Gut microbiota diversity, previously linked to neuroinflammation, showed marked restoration in treated animals, with Bacteroidetes abundance increasing by 37% relative to controls. Short-chain fatty acid levels in fecal samples, measured via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, correlated with reduced IL-6 expression in the prefrontal cortex. Notably, canonical correspondence analysis identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a key mediator of gut-brain axis signaling, with its abundance positively associated with butyrate production and synaptic plasticity markers. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of probiotic modulation in mitigating neurodegenerative cascades through microbial metabolite-driven neuroimmune regulation.

A 12-week intervention with a prebiotic-rich diet significantly altered gut microbiota composition in patients with major depressive disorder, revealing associations between specific Firmicutes taxa and symptom severity. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) identified significant shifts in microbial community structure, with Lactobacillus abundance correlating inversely with depressive symptoms (Pearson’s r = -0.42, p = 0.012). Concurrently, BDNF expression in the hippocampus was upregulated by 28% in responders, as measured by qPCR, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived metabolites and neuroplasticity. Bifidobacterium levels also showed a positive association with inverse Simpson diversity indices (β = 0.31, p = 0.007), highlighting potential biomarkers for therapeutic monitoring. These findings underscore the role of microbiota-modulating interventions in targeting BDNF-mediated pathways, with implications for personalized mental health treatment strategies.

Consumption of a fermented soybean supplement modulated gut microbiota composition and alleviated depressive-like behaviors in rodent models through microbiota-dependent mechanisms. Principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data revealed distinct microbial signatures in mice receiving the intervention, marked by increased abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced levels of Desulfovibrio. Concurrently, ELISA analysis detected lower serum IL-6 concentrations, aligning with improved open field test performance and reduced immobility in forced swim assays. Mechanistically, elevated butyrate production from short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa correlated with decreased neuroinflammatory markers, including GFAP and IL-1β, in the hippocampus. The fermented soybean-induced microbial shifts were associated with epigenetic modifications in BDNF and GLT1 promoters, as demonstrated by ChIP-seq in mice brain tissue. These findings suggest that fermented soybeans may serve as a dietary intervention targeting the gut-brain axis to mitigate depressive disorders via microbiota-mediated anti-inflammatory and neuroplasticity-enhancing effects.

A novel dietary intervention targeting the gut microbiome has revealed significant modulatory effects on neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of multiple sclerosis (MS). Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from C57BL/6 mice fed a fermented soy product (natto) enriched in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains. The intervention correlated with a 40% reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) in plasma and a 25% increase in short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) within the gut microbiota. Flow cytometry of splenocytes confirmed decreased activation of CD4+ T cells and enhanced regulatory Treg cell function. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila abundance, previously linked to neuroprotection, rose by 30% in the treated group. These findings suggest that natto-derived probiotics may ameliorate MS pathology by modulating neuroinflammation through microbiota-derived metabolites. The study underscores the therapeutic potential of diet-microbiome interactions in autoimmune neurodegenerative disorders and highlights the utility of multi-omics profiling to dissect mechanistic pathways.

The Tlr4 gene modulates neuroinflammatory responses through interactions with gut microbiota, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic analysis in a murine model of depression. C57BL/6 mice lacking Tlr4 exhibited altered gut microbiota composition, characterized by reduced abundance of Prevotellaceae and increased Bacteroidetes phyla, correlating with diminished serotonin signaling in the hippocampus. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan metabolites in Tlr4−/− animals, suggesting dysregulated tryptophan catabolism as a mediator of gut-brain communication. Multivariate analysis confirmed a significant association between Tlr4 expression and kynurenine pathway activity, highlighting its role in shaping microbiota-derived neuroactive compounds. These findings underscore the Tlr4-dependent regulation of gut microbiota-driven neuroimmune pathways, offering potential targets for microbiota-based therapies in mood disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with neuroinflammatory markers in Alzheimer's disease patients, revealing a potential mechanistic link between intestinal dysbiosis and brain pathology. 16S rRNA sequencing identified significant shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios, while principal component analysis highlighted BDNF expression as a key mediator of neurodegenerative progression. Short-chain fatty acids derived from Akkermansia muciniphila showed inverse correlations with amyloid-beta plaques in hippocampal regions, suggesting microbial metabolites modulate Alzheimer's disease through BDNF-dependent pathways. Metabolomic profiling further linked butyrate levels to reduced glial activation markers, reinforcing the role of gut microbiota in neuroinflammation. Immunohistochemistry confirmed BDNF upregulation in prefrontal cortex of transgenic mouse models treated with prebiotic fiber, aligning with multivariate regression models that accounted for 62% of variance in cognitive decline. These findings underscore the interplay between gut microbiota and BDNF in Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for modulating neurodegenerative processes via microbiome-targeted interventions.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between intestinal microbiota and central nervous system function, with emerging evidence linking specific fermented dairy products to modulated gut microbial composition and reduced anxiety symptoms in rodents. Using metagenomic sequencing, we characterized the microbiota of rats fed a high-fat diet supplemented with kimchi, a probiotic-rich fermented vegetable, and compared outcomes to controls. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance increased in the kimchi-group, correlating with decreased serotonin metabolite levels in hippocampus tissue. Behavioral assays revealed improved stress resilience and reduced compulsive grooming in treated animals, suggesting microbiota-driven neurochemical adaptations. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of fermented foods in targeting gut-brain axis dysregulation, with metagenomic analysis providing mechanistic insights into microbial-host interactions. The study underscores how dietary interventions may alter microbial ecology to influence mental health outcomes, warranting further exploration in clinical populations.

A recent study demonstrated that dietary interventions rich in fermented kimchi significantly altered gut microbiome composition in adults with depressive symptoms, correlating with reduced anxiety scores. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, researchers identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Escherichia coli in participants consuming daily servings of kimchi for 12 weeks. Principal coordinate analysis revealed distinct clustering of microbiota profiles between the intervention and control groups, with significant differences in α-diversity (P < 0.01). These changes were further associated with reduced serum levels of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome shifts and mood improvement. Notably, permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed that kimchi-induced microbiota alterations explained 18% of the variance in self-reported anxiety scores. The findings highlight the potential of fermented kimchi as a dietary strategy to modulate the gut-brain axis, though larger trials are needed to validate these preliminary results and explore strain-specific effects of Lactobacillus on mental health outcomes.

A high-fiber diet significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid production, influencing hippocampal neuroplasticity via the gut-brain axis, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from C57BL/6J mice fed a fiber-enriched diet. Bifidobacterium abundance correlated with elevated butyrate levels, which co-occurred with enhanced synaptic density in dentate gyrus neurons. Butyrate supplementation in control mice replicated these effects, suggesting a direct role for butyrate in neurodegenerative disease mitigation. Microbial shifts induced by the fiber-enriched diet also altered tryptophan metabolism, increasing serotonin precursor availability in serotonergic neurons and improving depressive-like behavior in rodents assessed via open field and forced swim tests. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotic interventions in modulating gut-brain communication through metabolite-mediated pathways, with multivariate analysis confirming the interdependence of dietary components and microbial taxa in shaping central nervous system outcomes.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in gut epithelial cells correlates with changes in gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in a murine model of metabolic dysregulation. Using obese rodents fed a high-fat diet, we identified a significant reduction in Bacteroidetes abundance and an increase in Firmicutes ratios, alongside upregulation of TLR4-mediated inflammatory signaling pathways. 16S rRNA sequencing further highlighted shifts in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production by Prevotella, which co-occurred with elevated serum lipopolysaccharide levels and neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that TLR4 activation in the gut may amplify microbiome-driven immune responses, contributing to systemic and central nervous system inflammation. Notably, 16S rRNA sequencing also detected a novel Escherichia strain with heightened lipid metabolism capacity, potentially linking gut dysbiosis to altered neurochemical signaling. The interplay between TLR4 and microbiome-derived metabolites underscores the need to integrate host genetic factors with microbial profiling when studying gut-brain axis disorders. This work provides a framework for targeting TLR4-modulating therapies to restore microbial homeostasis and mitigate neuroinflammatory outcomes in metabolic conditions.

Dietary inulin supplementation significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and enhances TPH2-mediated serotonin production in the brain of rodent models, revealing a mechanistic link between prebiotic fiber intake and neurobehavioral outcomes. Metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from conventional and germ-free mice demonstrated that inulin enriched Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus populations, which correlated with elevated serotonin levels in the hippocampus. Concurrent qPCR analysis confirmed upregulation of the TPH2 gene in enteric neurons, suggesting a direct microbial influence on peripheral serotonin synthesis. Multivariate analysis further identified Akkermansia muciniphila abundance as a predictive biomarker for depression-like behaviors in inulin-fed cohorts. These findings highlight the role of prebiotic fiber in shaping intestinal microbiota to regulate serotonin-related pathways, offering novel therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative disorders through microbiome-targeted dietary interventions.

A dietary supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was evaluated for its impact on gut microbiota composition and behavioral outcomes in patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), using 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial changes. Participants (n=45) received daily L. rhamnosus for 12 weeks, with fecal samples collected at baseline and post-intervention. The sequencing revealed a significant increase in Bifidobacterium longum abundance (relative abundance rose from 7.2% to 12.4%, P < 0.01), alongside reduced Escherichia coli levels (from 14.8% to 8.1%, P < 0.05). Concurrently, patients exhibited improved social interaction scores (mean increase of 18.3 points on the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, P < 0.001) and reduced GI symptom severity (22.6% decrease in calprotectin levels, P < 0.05). Multivariate analysis identified B. longum as a key predictor of behavioral improvements (AUC=0.83, 95% CI 0.76–0.90). These findings suggest that probiotic modulation of gut microbiota may offer a targeted therapeutic strategy for ASD by restoring microbial balance and mitigating neurobehavioral comorbidities.

Altered TLR5 expression in patients with irritable bowel syndrome correlates with dysregulated gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing. This dysbiosis was further exacerbated by a high intake of processed foods rich in emulsifiers, which disrupted intestinal barrier integrity and heightened pro-inflammatory cytokine production. A longitudinal cohort study of 120 subjects demonstrated that dietary interventions incorporating fermented foods like kimchi significantly increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, counteracting the emulsifier-induced inflammation. These findings suggest that TLR5-mediated immune signaling may serve as a therapeutic target, while modulating fermented food intake could restore microbial homeostasis. The interplay between host genetics, microbiota, and diet underscores the need for personalized strategies to mitigate gut-derived inflammation in functional gastrointestinal disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition and immune signaling pathways have been implicated in the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD). Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, we analyzed stool samples from 30 MDD patients and 30 healthy controls, identifying distinct microbial profiles linked to TLR4-mediated inflammatory responses. Bifidobacterium, a probiotic commonly associated with gut health, showed significantly reduced abundance in MDD patients, correlating with elevated systemic inflammation markers. Functional pathway analysis revealed dysregulation of tryptophan metabolism, with decreased expression of IDO1 in MDD cohorts. Notably, Prevotella abundance inversely correlated with TLR4 activation, suggesting a potential microbiome-immune crosstalk mechanism. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial dysbiosis, immune gene expression, and depressive symptomatology, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeted microbiome modulation in MDD management.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and central nervous system, with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG emerging as a promising modulator of depressive-like and anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models. In chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) rats, administration of L. rhamnosus GG significantly attenuated behavioral deficits, accompanied by altered gut microbiota composition and increased short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in the colon. Concurrently, neurotransmitter levels in the brain showed elevated γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and reduced glutamate, suggesting neurochemical reprogramming. Correlation analysis identified Lactobacillus and Bacteroides as key drivers of SCFA production, which were inversely associated with glutamate concentrations. These findings highlight the potential of L. rhamnosus GG to mitigate stress-induced mental health disruptions by modulating microbial metabolism and neurochemical pathways. The study further underscores the role of gut microbiota in shaping brain function, with correlation analysis revealing distinct microbial taxa linked to specific metabolite fluctuations. This suggests targeted probiotic interventions could offer therapeutic strategies for depression and anxiety by leveraging microbiota-driven neurochemical balance.

Mutations in the Tlr4 gene significantly alter gut microbiota composition and cognitive function, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) in C57BL/6J mice subjected to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) exposure. Gut microbiota depletion in Tlr4-deficient mice correlated with heightened pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the hippocampus and impaired performance in novel object recognition assays. Metabolomic profiling identified dysregulated short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, particularly reduced butyrate concentrations, which were linked to altered brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression via Pearson correlation. Reconstitution of gut microbiota with Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially restored SCFA levels and mitigated cognitive decline, suggesting a mechanistic interplay between Tlr4-mediated immune signaling, gut microbiota-derived metabolites, and neuroplasticity. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in modulating the gut-brain axis through microbial and metabolic pathways, with implications for therapeutic targeting of neuroinflammation and depression in patients with autoimmune disorders.

Multivariate analysis of variance revealed that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly altered gut microbiota composition in children with autism spectrum disorder, as measured by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Participants (n=45) received either the probiotic or a placebo for 12 weeks, with fecal samples analyzed for microbial taxa abundance and diversity. PERMANOVA confirmed distinct clustering of microbial communities in the probiotic group, marked by elevated Lactobacillus and reduced Bacteroides relative abundance compared to controls. Correlation analyses linked increased Lactobacillus with improved social interaction scores (r=0.32, p=0.02), while decreased Bacteroides associated with reduced repetitive behaviors (r=-0.28, p=0.04). These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions may modulate gut-brain axis signaling in ASD, though longitudinal studies are needed to assess clinical translation. The study highlights the utility of 16S rRNA profiling in elucidating microbial mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental disorders and supports further exploration of probiotics as potential adjuncts in autism management.

TMEM100 modulation in gut microbiota populations correlates with altered hippocampal neurogenesis, as demonstrated through principal component analysis of longitudinal cohort data. Curcumin administration in rodent models mitigates this effect by enhancing butyrate production via Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome-derived metabolites and neural plasticity. Subjects with major depressive disorder exhibiting TMEM100 polymorphisms showed heightened serotonin transporter expression in the prefrontal cortex, which was normalized following a 12-week regimen of curcumin combined with fermented dairy intake. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that curcumin-enriched diets increased abundance of Lactobacillus strains, which co-vary with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines levels. Multivariate analysis of metabolomic profiles further implicated short-chain fatty acids as mediators of TMEM100-dependent neuroimmune crosstalk. These findings underscore the potential of targeting TMEM100-regulated pathways via curcumin to restore gut-brain communication in depressive disorders, with implications for microbiome-based therapeutics.

TNF-α expression in patients with irritable bowel syndrome correlated with altered gut microbiota profiles following curcumin supplementation, as revealed by multivariate regression analysis. Bacteroides fragilis abundance increased in rodents administered curcumin over 12 weeks, coinciding with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in colonic mucosa. TNF-α knockdown in C57BL/6J mice attenuated IBS-related visceral hypersensitivity, suggesting a mechanistic link between TNF-α-mediated inflammation and microbiota dysbiosis. Curcumin also elevated short-chain fatty acid production by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a gut microbiota species inversely associated with chronic inflammation. Principal component analysis of fecal metabolites further identified butyrate as a key mediator of curcumin-induced anti-inflammatory effects in subjects with IBS. These findings highlight TNF-α as a therapeutic target for modulating gut microbiota-brain interactions in gastrointestinal disorders, with curcumin showing promise as a microbiota-directed intervention.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in the gut microbiome correlates with neurobehavioral deficits in murine models of neuroinflammation, suggesting a mechanistic link between immune signaling and gut-brain axis dysfunction. Using a cohort of 150 C57BL/6 mice, we applied random forest analysis to integrate 16S rRNA sequencing data with behavioral outcomes and inflammatory markers. TLR4 knockout mice exhibited reduced Lactobacillus abundance and increased Escherichia coli levels compared to wild-type controls, accompanied by heightened anxiety-like behavior in the open field test. qPCR confirmed upregulated IL-6 expression in colonic tissue of TLR4-deficient mice, while principal component analysis revealed distinct microbiome clustering between genotypes. Behavioral deficits were further associated with decreased serotonin levels in the hippocampus, as measured by HPLC. These findings highlight TLR4 as a critical mediator of microbiome-driven neuroinflammation and suggest that targeting TLR4-regulated pathways could mitigate gut-brain axis dysregulation in neurological disorders.

A multi-strain probiotic intervention significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced neuroinflammation in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and immunohistochemistry. The probiotic formulation, containing Bifidobacterium longum and Lactobacillus plantarum, increased short-chain fatty acid production in fecal samples, correlating with improved cognitive function in C57BL/6J mice subjected to amyloid-beta pathology. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated butyrate levels, which modulated blood-brain barrier permeability and suppressed neuroinflammation markers such as TNF-α and IL-6. The 16S rRNA sequencing data further highlighted shifts in alpha diversity indices, with increased abundance of Faecalibacterium and Blautia species linked to reduced tau pathology in hippocampal regions. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic modulation of the gut microbiome via metabolomic pathways may represent a viable strategy for mitigating neurodegenerative processes in Alzheimer's disease models.

Altered gut microbiota composition has been linked to neurodegenerative disorders and mental health conditions, yet mechanisms remain unclear. A 16S rRNA sequencing-based study evaluated the impact of probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG on central nervous system function in aged C57BL/6J mice with chronic stress-induced anxiety. Mice received daily doses of the probiotic for six weeks, with control groups receiving vehicle or fluoxetine. Behavioral assessments revealed that Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG significantly reduced anxiety-like behaviors in mice, comparable to fluoxetine effects, while metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids production in treated animals. Gut microbiota diversity increased in probiotic-treated groups, correlating with improved hippocampal neuroplasticity markers. Butyrate levels, specifically, were strongly associated with reduced anxiety scores. These findings suggest that probiotic-induced metabolic shifts in the gut microbiota may modulate brain function through the gut-brain axis, offering a potential non-pharmacological intervention for stress-related disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition associated with fermented milk consumption significantly modulates TLR4 expression and reduces systemic inflammation in patients with irritable bowel syndrome. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in individuals adhering to a probiotic-rich diet, correlating with decreased IL-6 levels and improved gut barrier integrity. TLR4 polymorphism analysis revealed differential activation of NF-κB pathways in subjects consuming fermented milk compared to controls, suggesting a microbiome-mediated mechanism linking dietary interventions to immune regulation. Metabolomics further showed elevated butyrate production in gut microbiota of fermented milk-treated cohorts, which inversely correlated with TLR4 phosphorylation states. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota diversity, dietary modulation via fermented milk, and TLR4-driven inflammatory signaling in IBS pathogenesis, offering potential targets for microbiome-based therapies.

A high-fiber diet modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces neuroinflammation in a murine model of depression, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays. C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fiber diet exhibited increased α-diversity of gut microbiota compared to controls on a standard diet, alongside elevated abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, taxa associated with anti-inflammatory effects. 16S rRNA sequencing further revealed reduced levels of pro-inflammatory Escherichia and Enterococcus in gut microbiota from high-fiber diet-treated animals. These microbial shifts correlated with attenuated depressive-like behaviors in the forced swimming test and reduced hippocampal expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6. Fecal microbiota transplantation from high-fiber diet-treated mice to germ-free recipients replicated the anti-inflammatory and behavioral effects, implicating gut microbiota-derived metabolites in modulating neuroinflammation. The findings highlight the role of dietary fiber in shaping gut microbiota to ameliorate depression via 16S rRNA sequencing-identified microbial signatures and downstream neuroimmune pathways.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to neuroinflammatory conditions through the gut-brain axis, with TLR4 signaling playing a critical role in immune modulation. This study explored the impact of curcumin on microbiota-associated inflammation in patients with multiple sclerosis, using 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial communities. Curcumin administration for 12 weeks significantly reduced serum IL-6 and TNF-α levels while enhancing gut microbiota diversity. Notably, taxa associated with Prevotellaceae and Bacteroidaceae expanded, correlating with decreased TLR4 activation in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. qPCR confirmed downregulation of TLR4 transcripts in inflamed intestinal tissues. These findings suggest that curcumin-mediated microbiota reprogramming may alleviate neuroinflammation by dampening TLR4-driven immune responses, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for multiple sclerosis.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with disease severity in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients, with significant shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios observed using shotgun metagenomic sequencing. A pilot study incorporating inulin supplementation in 45 PD patients revealed transient increases in Bifidobacterium abundance, coinciding with reduced motor symptom fluctuations. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified Akkermansia muciniphila abundance as a predictor of non-motor symptom severity, independent of disease duration. Concurrently, Escherichia coli overrepresentation correlated with higher levodopa-induced dyskinesia scores. Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids, quantified via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, showed inverse associations with non-ergot dopamine agonist usage. These findings suggest microbiome modulation through prebiotic interventions could influence PD progression, warranting further exploration with longitudinal mixed-effects modeling to account for confounding variables. The interplay between gut microbial metabolism and dopaminergic pathways remains a critical area for mechanistic investigation in neurodegenerative disorders.

A longitudinal analysis revealed that consumption of flavonoid-rich diets significantly correlates with enhanced cognitive performance in aging populations, mediated by alterations in the gut microbiome composition. Using multivariate regression analysis, we found that higher intake of flavonoid-containing foods was associated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, taxa linked to neuroprotective metabolite production. These microbial shifts were further correlated with reduced neuroinflammation markers and improved memory retention in rodent models supplemented with flavonoid extracts. The relationship was dose-dependent, with the strongest effects observed in individuals maintaining regular physical activity routines. Mechanistically, flavonoid metabolites generated by the gut microbiota appear to modulate BDNF expression and synaptic plasticity, as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and qPCR. Notably, the cognitive benefits were diminished in germ-free subjects, underscoring the microbiome's pivotal role. These findings highlight the potential of flavonoid-based interventions in mitigating age-related cognitive decline, with implications for Alzheimer's disease prevention strategies. The statistical significance of these associations was confirmed via ANOVA with post-hoc pairwise comparisons, reinforcing the microbiome's integration in neurocognitive health frameworks.

Altered TLR4 signaling in the gut microbiota modulates neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by multi-omics integration and principal component analysis of fecal metagenomic data from 120 patients and 80 controls. Gut microbiota profiles were correlated with plasma lipopolysaccharide levels and cognitive scores using 16S rRNA sequencing, identifying Bacteroides fragilis as a key mediator of TLR4-dependent immune activation. Principal component analysis uncovered distinct microbial networks associated with Alzheimer's disease progression, where TLR4 expression in enteric neurons was inversely linked to Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Cerebrospinal fluid cytokine profiles further validated this axis, showing elevated IL-6 in subjects with Alzheimer's disease and reduced Akkermansia counts. Metagenomic sequencing highlighted TLR4-regulated pathways, including short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis, as potential therapeutic targets. Alzheimer's disease severity correlated with microbial diversity loss, emphasizing the role of gut-brain axis dysregulation in neurodegeneration. These findings suggest that targeting TLR4-mediated gut-immune interactions via Akkermansia modulation may alleviate neuroinflammation and delay Alzheimer's disease onset, warranting clinical trials with prebiotic interventions.

Curcumin supplementation in aged C57BL/6J mice significantly altered gut microbiota composition and mitigated age-related cognitive decline, as evidenced by improved performance in novel object recognition tests. Curcumin-enriched chow increased the abundance of Prevotellaceae while reducing Bacteroides in the cecum, correlating with elevated BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Principal component analysis of metabolomic data revealed a significant inverse relationship between lipopolysaccharide levels and BDNF upregulation, suggesting microbiome-mediated neuroprotection. Curcumin also reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines in plasma, including IL-6, while TLR4 expression in the blood-brain barrier was suppressed. These findings highlight the role of curcumin in modulating the gut-brain axis via BDNF-dependent pathways, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative disorders.

Dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota composition significantly modulate neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models of anxiety-like behavior. Administration of a high-fiber diet enriched with prebiotic inulin altered microbial profiles, as assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced Desulfovibrio in aged mice exposed to chronic stress. These shifts correlated with improved performance in the elevated plus maze and reduced corticosterone levels, suggesting microbiota-mediated attenuation of stress responses. Concurrently, omega-3 fatty acids supplementation further enhanced neuroplasticity markers in the hippocampus, as evidenced by elevated BDNF expression. The synergy between fiber-derived prebiotics and omega-3s highlights potential therapeutic strategies for stress-related disorders, emphasizing the gut-brain axis as a modifiable target. Mechanistically, the observed effects align with the hypothesis that microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, influence neuroinflammation and synaptic plasticity via the vagus nerve. These findings underscore the role of integrative dietary approaches in shaping the gut microbiome and its downstream effects on mental health, warranting further investigation in human cohorts with anxiety disorders.

Curcumin supplementation modulates neuroinflammation via NOD2 expression in a gut-brain axis model of major depressive disorder, as demonstrated by quantitative PCR analysis of hippocampal tissue in rats subjected to chronic social defeat stress. Gut microbiota composition, assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealed increased Lactobacillus abundance in curcumin-treated animals, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum and prefrontal cortex homogenates. NOD2 knockdown in microglial cells attenuated the anti-inflammatory effects of curcumin, implicating this gene in mediating microbiota-derived signals. Fecal microbiota transplantation from curcumin-treated donors rescued anhedonia and social avoidance in recipient animals, while lipopolysaccharide challenge exacerbated neuroinflammatory markers in NOD2-deficient mice. These findings highlight the interplay between curcumin-induced microbiota remodeling, NOD2-dependent signaling, and depressive-like behavior, underscoring potential therapeutic strategies targeting the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in the tRNA-guanine transglycosylase (TGT) enzyme activity correlate with shifts in gut microbiota composition and dietary patterns in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Using LEfSe analysis, we identified Bacteroides as a discriminative taxon enriched in individuals consuming high fiber-rich diets, while Faecalibacterium abundance declined in those with low fiber intake. TGT expression levels in enterocytes were inversely correlated with Bacteroides abundance (r = -0.42, P < 0.05), suggesting a potential regulatory axis between host enzymatic pathways and microbial metabolism. Queuine, a dietary supplement precursor to queuosine, significantly modulated TGT-mediated tRNA modification, altering translation efficiency in colonic epithelial cells. Metabolomic profiling revealed that short-chain fatty acids produced by Bacteroides were elevated in high-fiber cohorts, correlating with reduced inflammation markers (P < 0.01). These findings highlight the interplay between TGT-dependent nucleotide modification, microbial fermentation of fiber, and intestinal homeostasis, offering novel therapeutic targets for microbiome-related disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition mediated by the Tlr4 gene significantly modulate the neurobehavioral effects of inulin consumption in rodent models. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that Tlr4-deficient mice exhibited heightened alpha diversity in fecal samples following inulin supplementation, compared to wild-type controls. This shift correlated with reduced serotonin synthesis in the enteric nervous system and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles, including elevated butyrate levels, which were linked to improved hippocampal neurogenesis. Inulin also enhanced gut microbiome resilience against lipopolysaccharide-induced inflammation, an effect amplified in Tlr4-knockout animals. These findings highlight the interplay between Tlr4-dependent immune signaling and inulin-mediated microbial metabolism in shaping brain-gut axis dynamics. The results suggest that Tlr4 polymorphisms could influence individual responses to prebiotic interventions, offering potential targets for microbiome-based therapies in neurodevelopmental disorders.

Alterations in gut microbial composition are strongly correlated with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with Parkinson's disease, revealing a critical interplay between intestinal microbiota and neurodegeneration. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium correlated with elevated NOD2 expression in the intestinal epithelium, a gene implicated in immune response modulation. Notably, high-fiber diets enriched in prebiotic oligosaccharides reversed dysbiosis, restoring short-chain fatty acid production and dampening proinflammatory cytokine release. The NOD2-mediated signaling pathway was further linked to lipopolysaccharide sensing by intestinal macrophages, which exacerbated alpha-synuclein aggregation in vitro. In a cohort of 150 patients, those adhering to fermented food regimens exhibited a 30% reduction in motor symptom progression over 12 months compared to controls. Metabolomic profiling confirmed elevated butyrate levels in the gut microbiome of individuals consuming resistant starch-rich meals, correlating with decreased TNF-α secretion. These findings highlight the NOD2-microbiota axis as a therapeutic target, with dietary modulation of fiber content offering a noninvasive strategy to mitigate neuroinflammation and delay disease progression.

A dietary supplement containing probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced neuroinflammation in a mouse model of colitis-associated depression, with effects mediated by BDNF expression in the hippocampus. Linear regression analysis revealed a significant inverse correlation between the relative abundance of Lactobacillus and plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, while BDNF upregulation was associated with improved performance in novel object recognition tasks. The gut microbiome of supplemented mice exhibited increased diversity and altered metabolic pathways, including enhanced production of short-chain fatty acids, which were linked to BDNF activation via vagal afferents. Principal component analysis further identified distinct clustering of microbiota profiles between supplemented and control groups, with Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios predictive of behavioral outcomes. These findings highlight the role of probiotic supplementation in restoring gut-brain communication, emphasizing BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity as a potential therapeutic target for depressive disorders with gut microbiota dysbiosis.

A recent study demonstrated that dietary supplementation with curcumin modulates the expression of the TNF-α gene in colonic epithelial cells, potentially altering signaling pathways linked to neuroinflammation via the gut-brain axis. Using linear mixed-effects models, researchers analyzed fecal gut microbiota composition and inflammatory markers in rodent models, revealing a significant correlation between curcumin-induced TNF-α suppression and increased abundance of Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum. These findings suggest that curcumin may mitigate neuroinflammatory disorders by modulating host-microbiome interactions, with implications for therapeutic strategies targeting enteric nervous system dysfunction. The study further highlights the role of TNF-α as a key mediator in transducing microbiome-derived signals to the central nervous system, emphasizing the need for mechanistic investigations into how curcumin-mediated gene regulation influences immune homeostasis. Analysis of variance confirmed that linear mixed-effects models effectively captured interindividual variability in microbiome responses, underscoring the complexity of host-microbe interactions in neuroimmune regulation.
