This work provides a framework for evaluating curcumin as a potential adjunct in managing central nervous system conditions with gut-brain axis dysregulation.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with multiple sclerosis, mediated by the IL-17A pathway. Psychobiotic interventions targeting Lactobacillus species modulated gut microbiota composition, reducing systemic inflammation and improving cognitive outcomes in murine models. Spearman's correlation analysis revealed a strong inverse relationship between Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratios and TNF-α levels in serum, underscoring microbiota-driven immune dysregulation. 16S rDNA sequencing confirmed shifts in microbial taxa, while qRT-PCR quantified IL-17A suppression in the central nervous system following psychobiotic administration. Concurrently, flow cytometry demonstrated reduced Th17 cell infiltration in spleen tissue, aligning with attenuated IL-17A signaling. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of psychobiotics in mitigating neuroinflammation via modulation of the gut-brain axis, supported by robust correlational evidence linking microbial diversity to immune gene expression.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in response to butylated starch administration was identified using LEfSe analysis in a murine model of chronic stress. This intervention modulated the gut microbiome by enhancing the abundance of Odoribacter and Oscillibacter, while reducing pro-inflammatory IL-6 and IL-1β levels. Butylated starch also increased tight junction protein expression (ZO-1, Claudin) and decreased intestinal permeability, correlating with reduced depression-like behaviors and corticosterone elevation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed distinct microbial pathways, including enhanced tryptophan synthesis and inositol degradation, which may mediate the observed neuroprotective effects. These findings suggest that butylated starch exerts its benefits through dual modulation of gut microbiota and host TLR4-mediated signaling, offering a novel strategy to target neuroinflammation and stress-related disorders. The integration of LEfSe with multi-omics data highlights the potential of microbiome-directed dietary interventions to ameliorate gut-brain axis dysregulation.

A diet rich in fermented food, such as kimchi, combined with probiotic supplementation, significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces depressive-like behaviors in murine models of chronic stress. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in animals receiving both kimchi and Lactobacillus plantarum, alongside reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. Behavioral assays demonstrated improved hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced anxiety scores, correlating with elevated short-chain fatty acids production. Mechanistically, Lactobacillus plantarum enhanced tryptophan hydroxylase 2 expression in the enteric nervous system, while kimchi contributed to gut microbiome diversification. These findings suggest synergistic effects of fermented food and probiotics in ameliorating stress-related mental disorders through bidirectional gut-brain axis modulation, highlighting potential therapeutic strategies for neuropsychiatric conditions linked to microbial dysbiosis.

Alterations in the TLR4 gene expression correlate with microbiome-derived metabolites from chicory root consumption and supplementation with curcumin in individuals with neuroinflammatory disorders. A cohort study involving 120 participants evaluated gut microbiome dynamics following a 12-week intervention incorporating chicory root-based prebiotic diets and curcumin administration. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Parabacteroides distasonis abundance increased significantly in subjects receiving both chicory root and curcumin, coinciding with reduced TLR4 activation in peripheral blood monocytes. PERMANOVA analysis confirmed distinct microbiome clustering between groups, with short-chain fatty acid production rates rising by 28% in the combined intervention arm compared to chicory root alone. Plasma cytokine profiling showed diminished TNF-α levels and elevated IL-10 concentrations, suggesting modulation of neuroinflammation via microbiome-TLR4 signaling. Curcumin enhanced butyrate production by Faecalibacterium spp., while chicory root selectively enriched Bifidobacterium populations. These findings highlight synergistic interactions between TLR4-mediated immunity, microbiome metabolism, and dietary interventions targeting gut-brain axis dysfunction.

A longitudinal study reveals that consumption of fermented dairy products correlates with reduced anxiety symptoms in adults, mediated by alterations in the gut microbiome. Using multivariate logistic regression, we analyzed fecal microbiota data from 220 participants, identifying a significant association between fermented dairy intake and increased abundance of Lactobacillus species. These microbial shifts were linked to decreased serotonin metabolite levels in plasma, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism. The study also found that higher fiber consumption enhanced microbial diversity, which in turn was associated with lower anxiety scores. Adjustments for confounders including 16S rRNA sequencing data and lifestyle factors confirmed the robustness of these associations. These findings highlight the potential of dietary interventions targeting specific microbiota-modulating foods to alleviate mental health disorders through the gut-brain axis, emphasizing the role of gut microbiota as a therapeutic target.

A high-fiber diet supplemented with the prebiotic inulin significantly reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodents through modulation of the gut microbiota, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Bifidobacterium abundance increased by 42% in treated groups, correlating with decreased tryptamine levels in serum, a known mediator of central nervous system function. ANOVA analysis confirmed significant differences in behavioral scores (F(2,58)=6.32, p=0.003) between the inulin-supplemented cohort and controls. Mechanistically, tryptophan hydroxylase 2 expression in the amygdala was upregulated by 28% in response to microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids, suggesting a neuroimmune pathway linking dietary fiber intake to mood regulation. These findings highlight the potential of targeted prebiotic interventions in patients with anxiety disorders, particularly when combined with fiber-rich diets to optimize microbial metabolic outputs. The study underscores the importance of integrating multivariate regression models to dissect complex interactions between dietary components, microbial taxa, and host physiology in gut-brain axis research.

Altered expression of the SLC6A4 gene in the gut microbiome of individuals consuming fermented dairy products correlates with reduced symptoms of anxiety and improved prefrontal cortical function, as revealed by qPCR and functional MRI. Lactobacillus reuteri, a predominant species in fermented dairy fermentation, was shown to modulate SLC6A4-mediated serotonin uptake in enteric neurons via short-chain fatty acid signaling, as demonstrated in murine models. Participants in a 12-week randomized controlled trial who consumed fermented dairy daily exhibited a 23% reduction in generalized anxiety disorder symptom severity compared to controls, with parallel decreases in plasma tryptophan metabolites linked to SLC6A4 activity. Multivariate analysis of microbiome profiles identified Lactobacillus reuteri abundance as a significant predictor of SLC6A4 expression levels, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary fermented dairy intake and neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of targeted fermented food interventions to modulate neurotransmitter-related genes and alleviate mood disorders through the gut-brain axis.

A diet enriched with prebiotic fiber and blueberries significantly modulates gut microbiota composition while mitigating neuroinflammation in rodent models of Alzheimer's disease. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed elevated abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, correlating with increased production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Multivariate ANOVA confirmed significant associations between SCFA levels and reduced Aβ plaques in hippocampal regions. Concurrently, blueberry-derived polyphenols enhanced BDNF expression, ameliorating synaptic dysfunction. Prebiotic fiber supplementation further diversified the gut microbiota, increasing Parabacteroides and Akkermansia taxa linked to intestinal barrier integrity. These findings suggest synergistic effects of blueberries and prebiotic fiber in modulating the gut-brain axis via microbiota-mediated neuroimmune pathways, offering a dual-targeted approach for neurodegenerative disorders.

A study reveals that combining a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus with a high-fiber diet enriched in oats significantly alters gut microbiota composition, correlating with reduced anxiety symptoms in 120 participants. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we observed increased relative abundance of Prevotella and decreased Escherichia coli in individuals adhering to the intervention compared to controls. Gut microbiome diversity, assessed via Shannon index, showed a 15% increase in the intervention group, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, linked to neuroprotective effects. Participants consuming the probiotic supplement paired with oats exhibited a 30% reduction in self-reported anxiety scores over 12 weeks, as measured by the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. Mechanistically, metabolomic profiling revealed enhanced serotonin precursor availability in the serum, suggesting a microbiota-brain axis modulation. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic supplementation combined with fiber-rich diets as a therapeutic strategy for anxiety, underscoring the interplay between gut microbiota composition and neurobehavioral outcomes.

Alterations in the gut microbiota composition mediated by the NOD2 gene are associated with changes in neuroinflammatory markers linked to depression, suggesting a molecular pathway for microbiome-brain communication. Using linear mixed models, we analyzed longitudinal data from 450 participants with major depressive disorder and 300 controls, revealing that individuals with Prevotella copri-dominated gut microbiota exhibited heightened expression of TNF-α in colonic mucosa samples. This correlation was further validated by 16S rRNA sequencing and lipopolysaccharide-induced microglial activation in murine models. Butyrate supplementation partially reversed these effects by modulating TLR4 signaling and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. The linear mixed models also identified interactions between IL10 polymorphisms and gut microbiota diversity, highlighting a gene-environment interplay in depressive symptomatology. These findings underscore the role of host genetic factors in shaping microbiota-brain interactions and suggest potential therapeutic targets for mental health disorders through microbiome modulation.

Alterations in the TPH1 gene, critical for serotonin synthesis, are linked to dysregulated intestinal motility in pediatric chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (PIPO). Using multivariate regression analysis, we identified significant associations between TPH1 expression levels and microbial dysbiosis, as measured by mucosa-associated microbiota composition. PIPO patients exhibited reduced TPH1 transcript abundance alongside shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios, suggesting a microbiome-driven modulation of serotoninergic signaling. qPCR confirmed lower SLC6A4 expression in affected individuals, correlating with diminished serotonin receptor activation. Correlation analysis further revealed inverse relationships between phenylacetylglutamine metabolite levels and TPH1 activity, implicating microbial catabolism of phenylalanine in pathway disruption. These findings highlight a bidirectional interaction between gut microbiota and intestinal serotonin pathways, with potential therapeutic targets in TPH1-modulating interventions for PIPO-related motility disorders.

A novel fiber-based prebiotic significantly modulates gut microbiome composition in murine models of neuroinflammation, correlating with reduced neuroinflammatory markers in the hippocampus. Using random forest classification, we identified distinct microbial taxa associated with cognitive improvement, including increased abundance of Lactobacillus reuteri and decreased Escherichia coli. Short-chain fatty acids derived from prebiotic fermentation were linked to enhanced brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression via BDNF promoter activation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a shift in beta diversity metrics, while principal component analysis confirmed separation of treatment groups based on microbial signatures. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted prebiotic interventions in modulating gut-brain axis communication, offering a mechanistic pathway for mitigating neuroinflammation through metabolic signaling pathways. The integration of machine learning with microbiome profiling provides a framework for personalized nutraceutical strategies in neurological disorders.

Modulation of the gut microbiota through specific dietary interventions significantly alters host Tlr4 expression and neuroinflammatory markers in C57BL/6 mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified distinct microbial community structures in fecal samples from high-fiber diet groups compared to controls, characterized by increased Bacteroidetes abundance and reduced Firmicutes ratios. Logistic regression analysis revealed that elevated butyrate levels, correlated with Butyricicoccus expansion, were independently associated with reduced EAE severity (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.22–0.66). Mechanistically, Tlr4 knockout mice exhibited attenuated IL-17 secretion and preserved blood-brain barrier integrity, suggesting microbiota-derived metabolites modulate neuroinflammation via toll-like receptor signaling. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbial composition and host immune-related genes, offering potential therapeutic targets for multiple sclerosis through microbiota-directed therapies.

metadata.abstract: Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly correlate with systemic immune dysregulation in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), as evidenced by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 150 patients and 100 healthy controls. Principal component analysis revealed distinct microbial profiles, with reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and elevated levels of Ruminococcus gnavus in SLE cohorts, coinciding with increased intestinal permeability measured via zonulin assays. Functional metagenomic analysis identified dysregulated pathways in gut microbiota linked to immune hyperactivation, while flow cytometry confirmed elevated gut-derived lipopolysaccharide translocation in SLE patients. Interventions targeting Ruminococcus gnavus with antimicrobial peptides reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in vitro, suggesting microbiome-modulated therapies could mitigate autoimmune pathogenesis. These findings underscore the role of gut microbiota as a dynamic contributor to systemic inflammation in autoimmune diseases, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for SLE management.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with dysbiosis in gut microbiota linked to inflammatory bowel disease, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing of mucosal biopsies from 45 patients. Analysis of faecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing identified Fusobacterium nucleatum as a dominant pathobiont in colonic samples from patients with active disease, whereas Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron abundance inversely correlated with TLR4 upregulation. Short-chain fatty acid profiling via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry showed reduced butyrate production in patients with IBD, coinciding with elevated lipopolysaccharide levels detected by ELISA. Functional enrichment analysis of gut microbiota data revealed impaired IL-10-mediated anti-inflammatory pathways in patients with IBD, suggesting a mechanistic link between TLR4 signaling and microbial metabolite dysregulation. These findings highlight the role of TLR4-driven immune responses in modulating gut microbiota composition and metabolic output, offering potential therapeutic targets for inflammatory bowel disease management.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to major depressive disorder, yet the role of targeted dietary interventions remains understudied. A 12-week intervention with the Lactobacillus reuteri significantly modulated the gut microbiome in 45 adults with major depressive disorder, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing. Participants receiving the supplement exhibited increased abundance of Bacteroides uniformis and Lactobacillus, alongside reduced levels of Escherichia coli, correlating with a 23% decrease in depressive symptom severity (P=0.018). Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids production, particularly butyrate, which were inversely associated with inflammatory markers IL-6 and TNF-α (r=−0.42, P=0.007). Mechanistically, TMAO pathway activation in colonic epithelial cells was suppressed, potentially mitigating neuroinflammation via serotonin receptor modulation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic supplementation in modulating the gut-brain axis, with high-throughput sequencing revealing distinct microbial signatures linked to clinical improvement. The study underscores the need for microbiome-targeted strategies in depression management, integrating multi-omics approaches to dissect complex host-microbe interactions.

Altered gut microbiota composition and TNF-α expression are linked to depressive symptoms in adults, yet the role of probiotic supplementation remains understudied. Participants (n=120) with major depressive disorder were randomized to receive Lactobacillus rhamnosus or placebo for 12 weeks. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that L. rhamnosus increased Bifidobacterium longum abundance while reducing Escherichia coli levels, correlating with reduced depressive symptoms via Spearman's correlation (r=−0.42, p<0.01). TNF-α expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells decreased by 37% in the probiotic group compared to controls (p=0.003), with qPCR validating these findings. Short-chain fatty acids levels, measured by gas chromatography, showed significant elevation in the probiotic arm (p=0.012), aligning with gut-brain axis modulation. These data suggest that probiotic intervention may alleviate depression through microbiome-mediated suppression of TNF-α signaling, highlighting a potential therapeutic strategy for mental health disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly correlates with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with Parkinson's disease, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. A cohort of 80 participants receiving a Mediterranean diet-based intervention demonstrated reduced systemic inflammation and improved motor function compared to controls. The gut microbiome of intervention recipients showed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Escherichia coli, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acids levels. Metabolomic profiling identified enhanced production of butyrate, a anti-inflammatory agent, which may mediate the observed neuroprotective effects. Notably, subjects with higher baseline alpha-synuclein levels exhibited greater responsiveness to the dietary intervention. These findings suggest that nutritional modulation of the gut microbiome could serve as a therapeutic strategy for Parkinson's disease, leveraging multi-omics approaches to link microbial changes to clinical outcomes. The study underscores the role of enteric nervous system signaling in disease progression and highlights the potential of targeted microbiota manipulation as a complementary treatment modality.

Alterations in the gut microbiota's composition significantly correlate with changes in central nervous system function, as evidenced by a study analyzing 120 participants with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and 80 healthy controls. Using principal component analysis, researchers identified a distinct microbial signature associated with heightened anxiety scores, marked by elevated levels of Escherichia coli and reduced Bifidobacterium longum. Notably, variations in the TLR4 gene were linked to differences in gut permeability and inflammatory markers, suggesting a genetic component to microbiome-brain interactions. Administration of probiotic strains led to a 30% reduction in anxiety-like behavior, accompanied by increased butyrate production. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbial diversity and hippocampal neurogenesis, with implications for targeted interventions in mental health disorders. The TLR4 gene's role in modulating immune responses to gut-derived metabolites underscores its potential as a therapeutic target. 16S rRNA sequencing further revealed that Prevotella abundance inversely correlated with serotonin transporter expression, implicating gut-brain signaling pathways in IBS pathology. This study emphasizes the necessity of integrating genetic and microbial data to unravel mechanisms underlying psychiatric comorbidities in gastrointestinal disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are strongly associated with neurodegenerative disease progression, with dietary patterns and genetic variants playing key modulatory roles. Analysis of 150 patients with Alzheimer’s disease revealed that flavonoid-rich diets correlated with elevated abundance of Bacteroidetes and reduced Firmicutes ratios, a metric linked to metabolic dysfunction. Variants in the TLR4 gene were further implicated in differential responses to gut microbiota metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids, which modulate neuroinflammation. Using multivariate logistic regression, we identified a synergistic interaction between TLR4 polymorphisms and flavonoid intake that predicted cognitive decline with 82% accuracy. This interaction was mediated by shifts in gut microbiota-derived butyrate levels, which were inversely correlated with tau pathology markers. Longitudinal data from controls showed that individuals adhering to flavonoid-rich diets exhibited a 30% lower risk of Alzheimer’s progression over 5 years, independent of TLR4 status. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic susceptibility, nutritional intake, and microbial metabolic outputs in shaping neurodegenerative outcomes, offering novel targets for disease-modifying therapies.

Modulation of the gut-brain axis through targeted dietary interventions reverses neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of metabolic dysfunction. C57BL/6 mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) exhibited increased systemic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels and neuroinflammation in hippocampal regions, correlating with altered gut microbiota composition. Administration of the probiotic Lactobacillus plantarum normalized TLR4 gene expression in microglia and reduced interleukin-6 secretion. HFD-induced obesity was accompanied by decreased abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and increased Escherichia coli, which were reversed by L. plantarum. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that L. plantarum restored microbial diversity, while ANOVA confirmed significant reductions in neuroinflammation markers. TLR4 activation was linked to microbial translocation via compromised intestinal barrier integrity, a process mitigated by L. plantarum-mediated restoration of tight junction protein occludin. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota, TLR4 signaling, and HFD-driven neuroinflammation, suggesting that dietary modulation of microbial communities could ameliorate brain dysfunction in metabolic disorders.

The TLR4 gene modulates intestinal epithelial barrier integrity and immune signaling, linking gut microbiome dysregulation to neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease. A chicory root-derived prebiotic enriched in inulin was shown to restore gut microbiome homeostasis in aged C57BL/6J mice through enhanced Bifidobacterium abundance, as assessed by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing. This intervention correlated with reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation and improved cognitive performance in aged individuals consuming a fiber-supplemented diet. qPCR confirmed decreased TLR4 expression in hippocampal neurons following prebiotic administration, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut-derived short-chain fatty acids and neuroprotection. Butyrate levels, measured via gas chromatography, were inversely associated with Alzheimer's disease-related tau hyperphosphorylation in transgenic mice. These findings highlight dietary fiber as a potential modulator of TLR4-mediated pathways in gut-brain axis dysfunction, offering novel therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative disorders.

The SLC6A4 gene demonstrates altered expression patterns in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), correlating with shifts in gut microbiota composition identified via 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing. Analysis of fecal samples from 50 participants revealed a significant negative correlation between SLC6A4 upregulation and abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, using principal component analysis to model interactions between microbial taxa and host gene expression. qPCR validation confirmed SLC6A4 mRNA levels were 38% higher in MDD cohorts compared to controls, alongside reduced microbial diversity measured by Shannon’s index. These findings suggest a bidirectional relationship between SLC6A4-mediated serotonin transport and gut microbiota dynamics, with implications for microbiome-targeted therapies in depressive disorders. Further metabolomic profiling is warranted to dissect how microbial metabolites influence SLC6A4 expression, potentially via tryptophan derivatives. The integration of multivariate regression models with longitudinal microbiome data may elucidate causal pathways in this gut-brain axis interaction.

A novel dietary supplement, Probiotic Blend X, significantly altered gut microbiota composition in a murine model, with notable changes in the expression of the TLR4 gene and increased production of short-chain fatty acids derived from the fermentation of fiber-rich vegetables. These findings were corroborated by 16S rDNA sequencing revealing elevated Bifidobacterium abundance alongside reduced inflammation markers in the colonic mucosa. The intestinal flora modifications correlated with attenuated neuroinflammation in the hippocampus, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism. Notably, fiber-rich vegetables consumption enhanced microbial butyrate synthesis, which was linked to epigenetic regulation of HDAC2 in neuronal cells. Butyrate levels inversely correlated with depressive-like behaviors observed in mice subjected to chronic stress. The TLR4 pathway was identified as a critical mediator of these effects, with IL-1β and TNF-α expression suppressed by Probiotic Blend X via modulation of microbial Escherichia coli. These data highlight the interplay between supplement-induced microbiota shifts, gene expression, and nutrient metabolism in shaping neurobehavioral outcomes, offering new therapeutic avenues for depression and inflammatory disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition linked to mood disorders in post-bariatric surgery patients was modulated by dietary interventions involving probiotics and fermented foods, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. Analysis of 200 individuals undergoing Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) or sleeve gastrectomy (SG) revealed distinct microbial profiles, with RYGB patients exhibiting elevated abundance of Veillonella and Roseburia compared to SG patients, who showed increased Christensenellaceae R-7 group and Subdoligranulum. Concurrently, 45% of participants displayed depressive symptoms, though improvements in mental health scores (BDI, HRSD) correlated with dietary changes rather than probiotic type. Enhanced intake of vegetables and whole grain cereals aligned with reduced consumption of simple sugars and saturated fatty acids, as measured by Dietary Quality Index - I (DQI-I). These findings suggest that microbiota shifts following bariatric surgery may influence mental health outcomes, with dietary strategies targeting specific microbial taxa potentially mitigating post-surgical mood disturbances. The interplay between microbial composition, dietary patterns, and neurobehavioral health underscores the need for personalized interventions in gut-brain axis research.

Altered gut microbiota composition in patients with depression is associated with dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomic profiling. A high-fiber diet intervention significantly increased Bacteroides abundance while reducing Prevotella, correlating with improved depressive symptoms over 12 weeks. The TPH2 gene, critical for serotonin synthesis, showed elevated expression in colonic mucosa samples from responders, suggesting microbiota-driven neurochemical modulation. Gut microbial-derived tryptamine levels, measured via LC-MS/MS, inversely correlated with depression severity scores. Notably, Akkermansia muciniphila abundance positively associated with SLC6A4 expression, a serotonin transporter gene, highlighting potential therapeutic targets. These findings underscore the interplay between dietary interventions, microbial metabolites, and host neurotransmitter-related genes in modulating mental health via the gut-brain axis.

A novel probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum significantly modulated SLC6A4 expression in the amygdala of rodents subjected to chronic stress, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing. This intervention was associated with reduced glucocorticoid receptor activation and altered gut microbiome composition, particularly elevated Prevotella levels, which correlated with decreased inflammatory cytokine production in colonic biopsies. The SLC6A4-mediated changes were linked to improved behavioral outcomes, including reduced anxiety-like behaviors in mice and enhanced serotonin reuptake efficiency in hippocampal neurons. Metabolomic profiling of fecal samples identified increased tryptophan metabolites, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut microbiota modulation and SLC6A4-dependent neurochemical adaptations. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbial interventions to influence neurotransmitter pathways via the gut-brain axis, offering therapeutic avenues for stress-related mental health disorders.

Alterations in the FUS gene expression correlate with dysregulated microbial metabolism in the gut, revealing a potential mechanistic link between host genetics and gut microbiota-mediated neuroinflammation. Using principal component analysis on fecal 16S rRNA data from 120 participants with depression, we identified a distinct Bacteroides-dominated cluster associated with elevated cytokine levels in plasma. Administration of the probiotic strain Lactobacillus rhamnosus for 8 weeks significantly reduced IL-6 concentrations and improved mood scores, as measured by the Beck Depression Inventory. The FUS-mediated pathway appears to modulate gut-brain axis signaling via altered short-chain fatty acid production, with multivariate analysis confirming that probiotic intervention restored microbial diversity and reduced inflammation-related TLR4 activation. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetics, microbial composition, and neuroimmune function in psychiatric disorders, highlighting probiotics as a targeted therapeutic strategy.

A diet rich in fermented miso significantly modulated gut microbial composition and altered hippocampal GAD67 expression in rodent models, correlating with improved cognitive function as assessed by novel object recognition and open field assays. Principal component analysis revealed that Lactobacillus plantarum abundance correlated strongly with increased GABA production in the cecum, while Bacteroides fragilis abundance decreased in parallel with elevated GAD67 mRNA levels in the hippocampus. Miso-supplemented diets normalized serum TMAO levels in aged individuals with Alzheimer’s disease, reducing amyloid-beta oligomer accumulation by 42% compared to controls. ANOVA confirmed significant differences in GAD67 promoter methylation between control and miso-treated groups, with hypermethylation linked to decreased glutamic acid decarboxylase activity in enteric neurons. These findings suggest that miso-derived microbial metabolites may enhance GAD67-mediated GABA signaling, mitigating neuroinflammation through gut-brain axis interactions. The interplay between dietary fermentation products, microbial metabolic pathways, and host gene expression highlights novel therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with anxiety-like behaviors in a murine model of stress-induced psychopathology, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Intervention with a prebiotic supplement containing inulin significantly modulated Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus abundance, reducing inflammation in the hippocampus and improving behavioral outcomes. Male C57BL/6 mice were exposed to chronic social defeat stress and randomized to receive either vehicle or the supplement. Behavioral tests measured anxiety and depressive-like symptoms, while metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids in supplemented groups. The supplement also restored gut microbiota beta diversity, as indicated by Bray-Curtis dissimilarity analysis, and increased TLR2 expression in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiota through prebiotic supplementation could ameliorate stress-related disorders by modulating neuroinflammation and microbial homeostasis. The study highlights the therapeutic potential of microbiota-directed nutraceuticals in psychiatric conditions, emphasizing the role of multi-omics approaches in elucidating gut-brain interactions.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional signaling between the central nervous system and the gut microbiota, with emerging evidence linking specific prebiotic fibers to modulated neuroinflammatory responses. Using RNA sequencing, we identified that dietary supplementation with inulin altered the expression of the TNF-α pathway in hippocampal neurons of transgenic mice harboring a mutation in the APP gene, a model for Alzheimer’s disease. This intervention correlated with shifts in the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Bifidobacterium adolescentis, which were associated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Principal component analysis revealed that inulin-treated groups exhibited distinct microbial community structures compared to controls, while TNF-α expression was inversely correlated with butyrate production from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. These findings suggest that prebiotic-mediated modulation of the gut microbiome may target neuroimmune pathways through transcriptional regulation, offering therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative conditions. The interaction between inulin and TNF-α highlights a mechanistic link between dietary components and gene expression in the context of gut-brain communication.

The gut microbiome modulates brain function through metabolic pathways influenced by dietary intake of fermented dairy, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays in C57BL/6 mice. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed distinct clustering of microbiota profiles in mice fed fermented dairy compared to controls, with increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium correlating with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in elevated-plus maze tests. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in fecal samples from mice consuming fermented dairy, which were significantly linked to enhanced serotonin synthesis in the hippocampus via immunohistochemistry. Linear regression confirmed a dose-dependent relationship between fermented dairy consumption and improved spatial memory, as measured by object recognition tests. These findings highlight the role of fermented dairy-induced microbiome remodeling in neurobehavioral outcomes, underscoring the potential of dietary modulation as a therapeutic strategy for depressive disorders via the gut-brain axis.

Dietary fiber intake significantly modulates neuroinflammatory pathways via microbial short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, as demonstrated by altered Tlr4 expression in mice fed high-fiber legumes. Gut microbiota from these animals exhibited increased Bacteroidetes abundance and elevated butyrate levels, correlating with reduced depressive-like behavior in open field assays. Mechanistically, butyrate enhanced Tlr4 transcription in hippocampal neurons, attenuating pro-inflammatory cytokine release and promoting BDNF secretion. qPCR analysis confirmed a 2.3-fold upregulation of Tlr4 in subjects with irritable bowel syndrome following a prebiotic regimen. These findings highlight a direct link between fiber-rich diets and Tlr4-mediated neuroimmune regulation, suggesting microbiome-derived metabolites as therapeutic targets for neurological disorders with comorbid gut dysbiosis.

Altered expression of the TNF-alpha gene in gut-associated lymphoid tissue correlates with neuroinflammation in patients with major depressive disorder, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut-derived immune signaling and mood regulation. Multivariate regression analysis of longitudinal data from 250 participants revealed that daily consumption of sourdough bread, rich in lactic acid bacteria, significantly attenuated TNF-alpha expression and improved depressive symptoms over 12 weeks. Mechanistically, Lactobacillus plantarum isolated from sourdough exhibited anti-inflammatory effects via modulation of pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in in vitro models of intestinal epithelial cells. These findings highlight the potential of fermented foods as modulators of TNF-alpha-mediated neuroinflammation, offering a novel strategy for targeting the gut-brain axis in psychiatric disorders.

Chronic administration of the dietary_supplement Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) significantly altered microbiota composition in mice with a knockout of the gene TLR4, as revealed by principal component analysis (PCA) of 16S rRNA sequencing data. TLR4-deficient mice exhibited heightened abundance of the bacteria Bacteroides fragilis compared to wild-type controls, alongside reduced levels of the chemical short-chain fatty acid butyrate, suggesting dysregulated metabolic signaling. Statistical_technique multivariate regression models identified a strong correlation between TLR4 genotype and shifts in microbial taxa, with the gene’s absence amplifying LGG-induced increases in the genus Akkermansia. These microbiota changes coincided with altered behavior in the open-field test, where TLR4 knockout mice displayed decreased anxiety-like behavior, a finding supported by elevated hippocampal expression of the neurotrophic factor Bdnf. The interaction between dietary_supplement intake, TLR4 polymorphism, and microbiome dynamics was further validated by permutation testing, which confirmed that the observed microbial shifts were not attributable to random variation. These results highlight the interplay between host genetics, microbial metabolism, and behavioral outcomes, underscoring the potential of targeted dietary interventions in modulating gut-brain axis function. The study also emphasizes the utility of statistical_technique PCA in dissecting complex microbiome-phenotype relationships, particularly in genetically heterogeneous populations.

Altered microbial metabolites in response to fermented kimchi consumption correlate with reduced neuroinflammation and improved cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer’s disease, as demonstrated through 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples. The study revealed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance increased significantly in participants adhering to a kimchi-rich diet for 12 weeks, coinciding with decreased plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly butyrate, as potential mediators of the observed neuroprotective effects, linking gut microbiota dysregulation to Alzheimer’s disease pathology. Microbiome alterations were further validated using metagenomic shotgun sequencing, which highlighted enriched pathways for tryptophan metabolism and lipopolysaccharide degradation. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiota via fermented foods could serve as a non-invasive therapeutic strategy to mitigate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in neurodegenerative conditions. The integration of multi-omics approaches enabled precise mapping of microbial-host interactions, underscoring the role of the gut-brain axis in disease progression.

Altered gut microbiota composition is linked to heightened anxiety symptoms in patients, with 16S rRNA sequencing revealing distinct intestinal microbiota profiles. Intervention with probiotic supplementation significantly reduced symptom severity, while a fermented dairy diet further enhanced microbial diversity. These findings suggest that targeted microbial modulation could be a viable therapeutic strategy, as metabolomic profiling identified increased short-chain fatty acids production correlated with anxiety relief in subjects receiving both synbiotic blends and prebiotic-rich meals. Longitudinal assessments using multivariate analysis of variance confirmed that combined probiotic and fiber interventions outperformed monotherapies in restoring gut-brain axis communication. The study highlights the interplay between intestinal microbiota dynamics and neurobehavioral outcomes, emphasizing the need for personalized microbial interventions tailored to nutritional intake patterns.

A diet enriched with yogurt and supplemented with probiotics significantly modulated gut microbiota composition, alleviating anxiety symptoms in a murine model of stress-induced dysbiosis. Fecal microbiota transplantation from probiotic-treated mice to naïve controls reduced hippocampal neuroinflammation, as evidenced by decreased IL-6 and TNF-α levels, while multivariate analysis linked increased Lactobacillus abundance to improved behavioral outcomes. Yogurt consumption alone enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, whereas probiotics further suppressed Corticotropin-releasing hormone expression in the amygdala. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that both interventions restored alpha diversity and reduced pathogenic bacterial taxa such as Desulfovibrio, correlating with decreased gastrointestinal permeability. These findings highlight the synergistic effects of fermented dairy and probiotic supplementation in mitigating neuroimmune dysfunction via the gut-brain axis, offering a dual-targeted approach for mental health disorders linked to microbiota imbalance.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are associated with increased risk of major depressive disorder (MDD) in human populations, with Bacteroides fragilis showing a significant inverse correlation to depressive symptom severity. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 320 participants and serotonin receptor binding assays on plasma, we identified tryptophan metabolites as mediators of this relationship. A random forest algorithm revealed that indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), a tryptophan-derived metabolite, was the strongest predictor of MDD status (AUC = 0.82). Bacteroides fragilis abundance was negatively correlated with plasma IPA levels (r = −0.41, p < 0.001), suggesting a dysregulation in tryptophan metabolism pathways. Patients with MDD exhibited reduced serotonin receptor binding in prefrontal cortex compared to controls (p = 0.012), which correlated with lower IPA concentrations. These findings highlight a mechanistic link between gut microbiota-derived metabolites and depression pathology, supported by multivariate regression models that accounted for confounding variables like inflammatory cytokines and omega-3 fatty acid intake. The integration of metabolomics and neuroimaging with machine learning offers a novel approach to dissecting depressive pathophysiology through the gut-brain axis.

A novel interaction between the TLR5 gene and gut microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids was identified using RNA sequencing, revealing a mechanistic link between immune signaling and neuroinflammation in patients with Alzheimer’s disease. Inulin supplementation significantly altered Bacteroidetes abundance and enhanced butyrate production in colonic epithelium, correlating with reduced IL-1β expression in hippocampal neurons. Immunohistochemistry confirmed decreased TLR5-mediated microglial activation in amygdala regions of murine models fed high-fiber diets, alongside elevated butyrate levels. These findings highlight the role of TLR5 in modulating neuroinflammation via gut microbiota metabolites and suggest prebiotic interventions as potential therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative conditions.

Altered gut microbiome composition following supplementation with a prebiotic fiber is associated with reduced neuroinflammation in a murine model of Parkinson's disease, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metagenomic analysis. Mice fed a diet enriched in inulin exhibited significant shifts in gut microbiota profiles, marked by increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreased Proteobacteria, alongside lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the brain and colonic mucosa. These changes correlated with improved motor function and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in dopaminergic neurons. Mechanistically, the prebiotic fiber enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which modulated TNF-α and IL-6 expression via activation of the PPAR-γ pathway. The study highlights the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted interventions in neurodegenerative conditions, with 16S rRNA sequencing serving as a critical tool to delineate microbial signatures linked to disease progression. These findings underscore the role of the gut-brain axis in modulating neuroinflammation and suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome may offer a novel strategy for mitigating Parkinson's disease pathology.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are strongly associated with heightened anxiety symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as demonstrated by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and multivariate statistical modeling. Analysis of fecal samples from 120 participants revealed that Bacteroidetes abundance correlated inversely with anxiety scores measured via the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), while Firmicutes showed a positive relationship with IBS symptom severity. Microbial dysbiosis was further linked to elevated IL-6 levels in serum, suggesting inflammatory pathways may mediate gastrointestinal-central nervous system interactions. Principal component analysis identified distinct microbial signatures distinguishing IBS subgroups with comorbid anxiety from those without, highlighting potential biomarkers for targeted intervention. These findings underscore the role of the gut-brain axis in modulating functional gastrointestinal disorders and mental health outcomes, with implications for microbiota-directed therapies.

A high-fiber diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition, reducing neuroinflammatory markers in Parkinson's disease models through modulation of Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from patients undergoing prebiotic supplementation revealed increased Akkermansia levels correlated with decreased plasma TNFα concentrations (rho = −0.71, P < 0.001). Mechanistically, Akkermansia-derived short-chain fatty acids suppressed microglial activation via TLR2-mediated signaling pathways, as demonstrated by in vitro co-cultures with brain microglia. Linear mixed-effects models confirmed that dietary fiber intake (≥25 g/day) was associated with a 32% reduction in neuroinflammation scores (95% CI: 23–41%) over 12 months. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of fiber-rich diets in mitigating neurodegenerative progression by reshaping the gut microbiome to suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines and promote anti-inflammatory pathways in the central nervous system.

Early-life prebiotic supplementation modulates stress-related gene expression and alters microbiome composition, reducing vulnerability to anxiety-like behaviors. In a cohort of 300 rodents, diets enriched with galactooligosaccharides (GOS) and polydextrose (PDX) were associated with elevated BDNF mRNA levels in the prefrontal cortex, as assessed by quantitative PCR. Using multivariate logistic regression, we found that animals receiving prebiotics exhibited a 40% reduction in anxiety-like behaviors compared to controls, independent of baseline microbiome diversity. Furthermore, BDNF expression correlated with increased abundance of Lactobacillus species, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary intervention, microbiome dynamics, and neural plasticity. These findings highlight the potential of prebiotics as modulators of gut-brain signaling pathways, offering new avenues for therapeutic strategies targeting neurodevelopmental disorders.

TLR4 mutations significantly alter gut microbiome composition and neuroinflammatory responses in murine models of neurodegenerative disorders, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and ELISA quantification of cytokine profiles. Multivariate regression analysis identified TLR4-mediated changes in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance as a critical predictor of hippocampal IL-6 elevation, linking enteric nervous system dysregulation to Alzheimer's disease-like pathology. TLR4 deficiency in C57BL/6 mice exacerbated gut microbiota dysbiosis following high-fat diet exposure, correlating with increased tau phosphorylation in hippocampal CA1 regions. Metabolomic profiling further demonstrated that TLR4-driven shifts in Bacteroidetes populations disrupted short-chain fatty acid homeostasis, a key modulator of blood-brain barrier integrity. These findings establish TLR4 as a pivotal gene in mediating microbiome-brain communication, highlighting its role in neuroinflammation pathways and potential as a therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease via probiotic intervention.

Alterations in the TNF-α signaling pathway correlate with dysregulated gut microbiota composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. Using qPCR, we confirmed elevated TNF-α transcript levels in inflamed colonic mucosa tissues, alongside reduced abundance of Bacteroidetes and increased Firmicutes ratios. PERMANOVA analysis identified significant clustering of microbial communities in IBS cohorts compared to healthy controls, with Akkermansia muciniphila showing a 40% decrease in relative abundance. These findings suggest that TNF-α-mediated inflammation disrupts microbial homeostasis, potentially exacerbating IBS symptoms through altered short-chain fatty acid production and immune signaling. Additionally, metabolomic profiling revealed lower butyrate levels in IBS patients, correlating with reduced Faecalibacter prausnitzii populations. Our results highlight the interplay between host genetic factors and microbial dysbiosis in gastrointestinal disorders, underscoring the need for targeted anti-inflammatory therapies that modulate both TNF-α activity and gut microbiota resilience.

A longitudinal study revealed that habitual consumption of fermented dairy significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, with associations to reduced anxiety symptoms in adults. Using multivariate analysis, researchers identified that individuals adhering to diets rich in fiber-containing plant-based foods exhibited enhanced microbial diversity and lower depressive symptoms compared to controls. Notably, those who combined fermented dairy intake with probiotic supplementation showed a 32% greater reduction in stress-related disorders scores, as measured by standardized psychological assessments. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species were strongly correlated with these outcomes, while short-chain fatty acids production from microbial fermentation emerged as a key mediator of neurobehavioral effects. The findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota homeostasis may offer adjunctive therapeutic strategies for mental health conditions, with machine learning models further validating the predictive power of microbial signatures in response to fiber and probiotic interventions.

Short-chain fatty acids derived from fermented dairy products exhibit neuroprotective effects via modulation of the gut microbiota, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease. Administration of lactobacillus fermentum alongside a fiber-enriched diet significantly altered microbial taxa associated with butyrate production, correlating with reduced amyloid-β accumulation and improved spatial memory. Mechanistically, probiotic intervention enhanced SCFA levels, which in turn activated CREB-dependent pathways critical for synaptic plasticity. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of combining prebiotic and probiotic strategies with prebiotic-rich foods to target gut-brain signaling in neurodegenerative conditions. The study underscores the role of microbial metabolites in mediating cognitive outcomes and supports the use of metagenomic profiling to personalize microbiota-directed therapies.

Recent studies highlight the role of gut microbiota in modulating neuroinflammatory responses linked to multiple sclerosis (MS), yet mechanisms remain unclear. Using 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) models fed a high-fat diet enriched with omega-3 fatty acids or vehicle control. Bifidobacterium longum abundance correlated inversely with clinical disease severity, while Prevotella copri levels rose in high-fat diet-treated groups. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly butyrate, were elevated in omega-3-supplemented cohorts, coinciding with reduced blood-brain barrier permeability. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed lower glutamate levels in the hippocampus of supplemented animals. These findings suggest that high-fat diets exacerbate MS-related inflammation, but omega-3 mitigates this via SCFA-mediated modulation of the gut-brain axis.

A polymorphism in the TPH2 gene modulates microbial responses to fermented kimchi consumption, influencing neuroinflammatory markers in individuals with depression. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed gut microbiota composition in 120 participants stratified by TPH2 genotype and dietary intake of kimchi. ANCOVA revealed that carriers of the TPH2 rs4290270 C allele exhibited heightened abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium when consuming kimchi, correlating with reduced plasma IL-6 levels. Conversely, non-carriers showed minimal microbial shifts and sustained inflammation. Path analysis confirmed a direct interaction between TPH2 expression and microbial diversity, mediated by serotonin metabolism. These findings suggest that TPH2 variants may dictate individual variability in gut-brain communication via dietary modulation of the microbiota, offering a potential target for mental health interventions.

A specific probiotic strain, Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938, significantly modulates TLR4 expression in the gut microbiome of individuals consuming a high-fiber diet, correlating with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified that DSM 17938 alters gut microbiota composition, increasing abundance of Bifidobacterium and decreasing Escherichia coli, while upregulating TLR4-mediated immune signaling pathways. Metabolomic profiling revealed elevated short-chain fatty acids production, suggesting a link between microbiome-derived butyrate and TLR4 activation. Whole grain intake further amplified these effects, enhancing DSM 17938 colonization and TLR4 phosphorylation in colonic epithelial cells. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TLR4 knockout in mice abrogated the anxiolytic effects of the probiotic, confirming the gene's role in mediating microbiome-brain communication. These findings highlight a mechanistic pathway through which probiotics and fiber-rich diets interact with TLR4 to influence neurobehavioral outcomes, offering potential therapeutic strategies for gastrointestinal disorders with comorbid mental health conditions.

Consumption of Mediterranean diet components significantly alters the gut microbiome composition in adults, correlating with reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial signatures associated with adherence to the diet, including increased abundance of Prevotella and decreased levels of Escherichia. These findings were corroborated by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 120 participants, revealing a significant inverse relationship between olive oil intake and inflammatory markers in plasma. The microbiota diversity, measured via Shannon index, showed a positive correlation with fiber consumption, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary patterns and mental health outcomes. Further multivariate analysis highlighted the role of Faecalibacterium in mediating the beneficial effects of the Mediterranean diet on cognitive function and emotional regulation. These results underscore the potential of targeted dietary interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition were linked to disease progression in Parkinson's disease patients carrying the SNCA A53T mutation, revealing a potential mechanistic bridge between genetic vulnerability and environmental factors. Using a mesofluidic platform integrating human gut and liver microphysiological systems with induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cerebral organoids, we observed that microbial metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids, amplified neuroinflammatory markers in patient-derived models. A machine learning classification model trained on metabolic profiles from 120 participants achieved 89% accuracy in distinguishing PD carriers from non-carriers, with feature importance analyses highlighting butyrate and propionate as key predictors. These findings underscore the interplay between gut microbial dysbiosis and SNCA-mediated pathology, suggesting that microbiota-targeted therapies could modulate disease trajectories in genetically predisposed populations. The integration of multi-organ co-culture systems with machine learning offers a scalable approach to dissect complex interactions in neurodegenerative disorders, bridging molecular genetics with environmental influences.
