metadata.abstract: The interplay between the gut microbiome and neuroinflammation in Parkinson’s disease (PD) is modulated by the TLR4 gene and curcumin supplementation, as demonstrated in a cohort of 85 PD patients and 70 age-matched controls. Gut microbiota composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing, while TLR4 expression and inflammatory markers were quantified via qPCR and ELISA. Curcumin intake correlated with reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) and altered abundance of Bacteroides and Prevotella, with TLR4 polymorphisms conferring variable responsiveness to the supplement. Notably, PD patients carrying the TLR4 rs4986790 variant exhibited a 32% reduction in neuroinflammatory markers following 12 weeks of curcumin intervention, compared to 18% in those with the wild-type allele. These findings highlight the potential of curcumin-mediated microbiome modulation as a therapeutic strategy in PD, contingent on TLR4-dependent immune signaling pathways. The study underscores the necessity of integrating microbiome profiling and genetic risk assessment to optimize nutraceutical interventions in neurodegenerative conditions.

Altered expression of the TLR4 gene in gut epithelial cells significantly correlates with shifts in gut microbiota composition, modulating inflammatory signaling pathways linked to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was administered to 80 participants with IBS, alongside a control group receiving placebo. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that TLR4 upregulation was associated with reduced abundance of Bacteroides and increased Streptococcus, while principal component analysis identified microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of symptom relief. Notably, individuals with higher baseline TLR4 expression exhibited greater responsiveness to the probiotic, suggesting a gene-microbiota interaction that could inform personalized interventions. These findings highlight the role of TLR4 in shaping microbiota dynamics and underscore the utility of multivariate statistical models to disentangle complex gut-brain axis interactions. The integration of targeted microbial supplementation with genetic profiling may offer a novel approach to managing IBS-related inflammation and neurobehavioral comorbidities.

Tlr4 deficiency in murine models enhances gut microbiota-mediated neuroinflammation through altered short-chain fatty acid signaling, as revealed by multivariate analysis of fecal metabolites and behavioral outcomes. Curcumin supplementation partially reversed this effect by restoring Bacteroidetes-to-Firmicutes ratios and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production in colonic tissue. Principal component analysis identified Tlr4-dependent shifts in microbial diversity correlating with depression-like behaviors in mice fed a high-fat diet. These findings suggest Tlr4 modulation of gut-brain axis pathways may be a target for natural product-based therapies in neuroimmune disorders.

A novel dietary intervention using inulin significantly modulated gut microbiome composition in rats with experimentally induced colitis, revealing a potential link between microbial dysbiosis and inflammatory signaling pathways. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus alongside reduced Escherichia-Shigella levels in treated groups, correlating with decreased IL-6 and TNF-α production. Spearman's correlation analysis further linked microbial shifts to altered expression of the NOD2 gene in intestinal epithelial cells, a critical mediator of innate immune responses. Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were implicated in dampening NOD2-driven inflammation via epigenetic regulation. These findings highlight inulin as a promising adjuvant for gut inflammation, with NOD2 serving as a biomarker for therapeutic efficacy. The study underscores the interplay between dietary modulation, microbial metabolism, and host genetic pathways in inflammatory diseases.

Alterations in the gut microbiome mediated by the Tlr4 gene significantly influence neuroinflammatory responses in models of colitis, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and quantitative PCR. Bacteroides fragilis abundance correlated inversely with Tlr4 expression in C57BL/6 mice subjected to dextran sodium sulfate-induced intestinal injury. A multivariate regression analysis identified Tlr4 as a key mediator of microbial dysbiosis, linking reduced Lactobacillus levels to heightened pro-inflammatory cytokine production in the colon. Flow cytometry further confirmed elevated Bacteroides-driven activation of macrophages in Tlr4-deficient mice. These findings highlight the role of Tlr4 in shaping microbiota composition and its downstream effects on intestinal immunity, suggesting potential therapeutic targets for inflammatory bowel disease. Principal component analysis of microbial community data reinforced the specificity of Tlr4-related shifts, distinguishing them from broader environmental influences on the gut microbiota. The interplay between host genetics, microbial taxa, and inflammatory signaling underscores the complexity of the gut-brain axis in immune-mediated pathologies.

A TLR4 polymorphism was identified as a significant modulator of gut microbiota composition and neuroinflammatory markers in patients with multiple sclerosis, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate analysis of fecal samples. Mouse models harboring the TLR4 mutation exhibited altered microbial diversity, marked by reduced Firmicutes and elevated Bacteroidetes abundance, alongside increased lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation in the hippocampus. qPCR confirmed upregulation of IL-6 and TNF-α in the central nervous system, correlating with short-chain fatty acid dysregulation derived from altered gut microbiota. Participants with the TLR4 variant showed higher relapse rates and cognitive decline, as measured by neuroimaging and ANCOVA adjusting for confounders. These findings underscore the role of TLR4-mediated immune signaling in linking gut dysbiosis to neurodegenerative progression, suggesting targeted modulation of microbial metabolites as a therapeutic strategy. The study highlights how machine learning models integrating genetic variants and metabolomic profiles can predict disease outcomes, emphasizing the gut-brain axis as a critical interface in autoimmune disorders.

A diet enriched with fermented milk modulated gut microbiota composition, as revealed by multivariate statistical analysis, correlating with improved cognitive function in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced Escherichia coli in treatment groups, alongside elevated short-chain fatty acid levels. Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed significant differences in butyrate concentrations between control and fermented milk-treated cohorts (p < 0.01). Behavioral assays demonstrated enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced Aβ plaques in mice receiving the fermented milk-based intervention. Correlative principal component analysis linked microbiota-derived SCFA production to decreased neuroinflammation markers, including TNF-α and IL-6, in serum. These findings highlight the potential of fermented dairy products as functional foods to mitigate Alzheimer's pathology through microbiota-mediated mechanisms, underscoring the interplay between dietary modulation, intestinal flora dynamics, and neurodegenerative disease progression.

A novel dietary intervention with fermented miso significantly altered the gut microbiome composition and attenuated depressive-like behaviors in rodent models, revealing a potential mechanistic link between traditional foodstuffs and mental health outcomes. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Proteobacteria in mice fed miso, correlating with elevated serotonin levels in the prefrontal cortex. Metabolomic profiling further detected elevated tryptophan derivatives in plasma, suggesting enhanced intestinal tryptophan metabolism via Tph1 upregulation. qPCR confirmed reduced Il-6 expression in the hippocampus, aligning with diminished neuroinflammation markers. These findings highlight the role of miso-derived bioactive compounds in modulating the gut-brain axis through microbiota-dependent pathways, offering a dietary strategy for mood disorder management. The study also underscores the utility of multi-omics integration in elucidating complex neuroimmune interactions mediated by functional fermented foods.

Dietary interventions rich in fermented foods significantly modulate gut microbiota composition, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes in a murine model of anxiety. Using principal component analysis (PCA), we identified distinct microbial clusters associated with anxiety-like behaviors, revealing a negative correlation between Lactobacillus abundance and elevated serotonin metabolites in the hippocampus. Fluoxetine-treated mice exhibited enhanced gut microbiota diversity, with Bifidobacterium levels inversely linked to tryptophan degradation pathways. Probiotic-enriched diets restored Akkermansia muciniphila populations, which were depleted in anxiety-prone cohorts, while short-chain fatty acid profiles shifted toward higher butyrate production. Integrative metagenomic analysis highlighted tryptophanase upregulation in Escherichia coli as a potential driver of neuroinflammation, corroborated by increased quorum sensing molecules in serum. Random forest modeling confirmed that microbial taxa contributing to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthesis in the colon were predictive of behavioral improvement, underscoring the role of microbiota-derived neurotransmitters in modulating the gut-brain axis. These findings suggest that targeted dietary modulation of gut microbiota via fermented foods could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for anxiety-related disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with neuroinflammation in a murine model of depression, revealing a mechanistic link between intestinal dysbiosis and central nervous system dysfunction. 16S rDNA sequencing identified reduced Bacteroidetes and elevated Firmicutes ratios in mice exposed to chronic stress, which coincided with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in the hippocampus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from stressed donors recapitulated depressive-like behaviors, including anhedonia and social withdrawal, in recipient mice, while Lactobacillus rhamnosus administration normalized gut microbiota diversity and mitigated neuroinflammation. qPCR confirmed downregulation of IL-6 and TNF-α in pre-frontal cortex tissues following probiotic treatment, alongside improved behavioral outcomes. ANOVA revealed significant interactions between microbial taxa and serotonin receptor expression in serotonergic neurons, suggesting microbiota-driven modulation of neurotransmitter signaling. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic interventions in mitigating depressive disorders via the gut-brain axis, with metagenomic profiling offering a critical tool for dissecting microbial contributions to neurobehavioral pathophysiology.

A longitudinal analysis revealed that high-fiber diets significantly modulate gut microbiota composition, influencing systemic inflammation and cognitive function in aging populations. Probiotic strains of the genus *Bifidobacterium* amplified these effects, as demonstrated by multivariate analysis of fecal microbiota profiles, which identified a 28% increase in anti-inflammatory *Bifidobacterium* taxa following 12 weeks of supplementation. This microbial shift correlated with reduced serum levels of interleukin-6 and improved performance in memory tasks, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism. Concurrently, fermented dairy consumption, enriched in short-chain fatty acids, further enhanced microbiota diversity, as quantified by 16S rRNA sequencing, while butyrate concentrations rose by 34% in treated individuals. The integration of canonical correlation analysis revealed that combined dietary interventions—probiotic and fermented dairy—modulated both microbial metabolic pathways and neuroinflammatory markers, highlighting a synergistic role of dietary components in neuroprotection. These findings underscore the potential of targeted microbiome modulation via diet and supplements to mitigate age-related cognitive decline.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, yet the mechanistic links remain poorly defined. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed gut microbiota profiles from postmortem colon samples and paired hippocampal tissue, revealing Akkermansia muciniphila abundance inversely correlated with tau hyperphosphorylation levels. Principal component analysis (PCA) identified Akkermansia as a key driver of microbial diversity shifts in AD cases. Mechanistically, Donepezil hydrochloride (DH), a cholinesterase inhibitor, mitigated colonic inflammation and normalized superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity in AD models while increasing Akkermansia relative abundance by 53.8% via molecular docking-predicted interactions with membrane proteins. These findings suggest that gut microbiota modulation through targeted interventions could synergize with existing therapies to address AD pathogenesis. Notably, multivariate regression models confirmed Akkermansia as a potential biomarker, with 82% predictive accuracy for AD progression stages. This integrative approach underscores the role of microbiota-gut-brain axis interactions in neurodegenerative disorders, offering novel therapeutic avenues through microbiome-targeted strategies.

Manipulating gut microbiota through dietary interventions significantly alters neural gene expression in rodent models. A high-fiber diet supplemented with probiotics was administered to adult male C57BL/6 mice to assess effects on BDNF expression and hippocampal neuroplasticity. After 8 weeks, quantitative PCR detected a 40% increase in BDNF mRNA levels in the hippocampus of treated mice compared to controls. Concurrently, gut microbiota diversity, assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing, showed a significant shift in Prevotella abundance. Analysis via two-way ANOVA revealed significant interactions between probiotic type and BDNF expression levels (F(2, 57)= 6.78, p < 0.01). Furthermore, immunohistochemistry indicated enhanced synaptic density in the prefrontal cortex. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of the gut microbiome influences BDNF-mediated neuroplasticity, potentially offering therapeutic avenues for neurodegenerative disorders linked to gut-brain axis dysregulation.

Diet-induced obesity alters gut microbiota composition, with interventions combining exercise and bioactive compounds showing potential to restore microbial balance. This study evaluated the impact of a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFD), exercise, and genistein on microbiota diversity in male C57BL/6 mice using 16S rRNA gene sequencing to profile α- and β-diversity. Mice were randomized to HFD or standard chow for 24 weeks, with subgroups receiving exercise, genistein, or both. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed significant reductions in weight gain and microbial richness in groups receiving combined interventions, though HFD + exercise + genistein did not fully revert obesity markers to chow-fed controls. The gut microbiome richness (observed amplicon sequence variants) was lowest in HFD groups, with HFD + genistein showing marginally greater recovery than exercise alone. While combined therapies mitigated obesity-related microbial dysbiosis, switching to chow remained most effective in restoring baseline microbiota profiles. These findings underscore the complex interplay between dietary interventions, physical activity, and microbial dynamics, highlighting the need for targeted strategies to address obesity-associated gut dysbiosis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome of patients with Parkinson's disease correlate with specific TSC2 polymorphisms and shifts in microbial taxa. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 45 PD patients and 50 healthy controls, identifying significant enrichment of Prevotella and depletion of Bacteroides in the gut microbiota of cases. Kruskal-Wallis analysis revealed that TSC2 rs2333322 variants were associated with increased abundance of Escherichia coli (p=0.008). Furthermore, multivariate regression modeling linked Akkermansia muciniphila levels to motor symptom severity scores, independent of TSC2 genotype. These findings suggest a mechanistic interplay between host genetic factors and microbial dysbiosis in neurodegenerative progression, with potential implications for targeted microbiome-based therapies. The integration of metagenomic shotgun sequencing in future cohorts may refine causal pathways involving TSC2-mediated immune signaling and microbial metabolite production.

Dietary supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids significantly altered gut microbiota composition, as evidenced by principal component analysis, and mitigated neuroinflammation in rodent models fed a high-fat diet. Bifidobacterium abundance correlated inversely with pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum, while Enterobacteriaceae expansion linked to microglial activation in hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that omega-3 fatty acids enhanced short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, reducing lipopolysaccharide-induced blood-brain barrier permeability. High-fat diet exposure alone exacerbated glutamate accumulation in prefrontal cortex, an effect counteracted by omega-3 fatty acids-induced BDNF upregulation. Network analysis integrating metabolomic and microbial data highlighted butyrate as a key mediator between gut and brain health. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of omega-3 fatty acids in modulating gut-brain axis dysfunction driven by high-fat diet-induced metabolic and neuroimmune perturbations.

A longitudinal cohort study reveals that adherence to the Mediterranean diet correlates with altered gut microbiota profiles that mitigate neuroinflammation in individuals at risk for Alzheimer's disease. Using machine learning analysis of 1,200 fecal metagenomic datasets, we identified that polyphenol intake, particularly from dark berries, enriched Akkermansia muciniphila abundance while reducing lipopolysaccharide levels in serum. These changes were associated with a 23% reduction in cognitive decline progression over 5 years. The polyphenol-mediated shift in microbial metabolism enhanced production of butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid linked to neuroprotection. Notably, the protective effect was strongest in participants with high baseline gut microbiota diversity, suggesting synergism between dietary intake and pre-existing microbial resilience. This study underscores the potential of targeted nutrient interventions to modulate the gut-brain axis and highlights the role of plant-based diets in mitigating neurodegenerative risk through microbiome-dependent mechanisms.

Altered gut microbiota composition significantly correlates with cognitive decline in aging, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples from aged C57BL/6J mice. Administration of a probiotic mixture containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains partially reversed age-related dysbiosis, evidenced by increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa and reduced Proteobacteria levels. Permutation analysis revealed that microbiota shifts accounted for 32% of variance in hippocampal synaptic plasticity markers, while prefrontal cortex glutamatergic signaling correlated with gut-derived metabolite concentrations. Mice treated with the probiotic exhibited improved performance in spatial memory tasks compared to untreated controls, with butyrate levels in plasma increasing by 40%. Cerebrospinal fluid proteomics identified elevated brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in probiotic-treated groups, suggesting microbial modulation of neuroplasticity pathways. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted microbiota interventions in mitigating age-associated cognitive impairment through immune-metabolic crosstalk at the gut-brain axis.

metadata.abstract: Altered gut microbiome composition in individuals with depression is linked to dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, with fecal samples from 120 participants revealing lower abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium alongside elevated kynurenine levels. Intervention studies using probiotic supplementation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum showed significant reductions in depressive symptoms over 12 weeks, correlating with increased tryptophan conversion to serotonin. Concurrently, fermented foods consumption, particularly kombucha and sauerkraut, was associated with microbiome diversification and decreased inflammation markers. Multivariate analysis of gut microbiome data revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance positively correlated with short-chain fatty acid production, which in turn modulated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity. These findings suggest that targeting gut microbiome dysbiosis through probiotics and fermented diets may offer a viable strategy to alleviate depression by restoring neurochemical balance and reducing systemic inflammation. The study underscores the role of microbiome-host metabolic interactions in mental health, highlighting the therapeutic potential of dietary modulation.

The gut-brain axis mediates neuroinflammatory responses through microbiota-derived metabolites, with inulin enhancing gut microbiota diversity and modulating NOD2 expression in immune cells. In a murine model of multiple sclerosis, C57BL/6 mice administered inulin exhibited reduced proinflammatory cytokines and improved neurological function compared to controls, correlating with increased abundance of Prevotella and Bacteroides. Mechanistically, inulin-induced NOD2 activation suppressed TNF-α production via the qPCR-validated NF-κB pathway, while 16S rRNA sequencing revealed shifts in microbial metabolic pathways linked to short-chain fatty acid biosynthesis. These findings highlight inulin’s potential as a prebiotic therapy, leveraging NOD2-mediated immune regulation to mitigate neuroinflammation. Additionally, butyrate levels in the colon correlated with NOD2 expression, suggesting a microbial-epigenetic interplay in disease progression. The study underscores the role of dietary fiber in shaping the gut-brain axis through gene-microbiota interactions, offering novel targets for neurodegenerative diseases management.

Dietary modulation of the gut microbiome through fermented dairy products has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy for colitis, yet the mechanistic links remain understudied. Here, we demonstrate that kefir, a probiotic-rich fermented beverage, significantly alters the gut microbiome composition in murine models of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, correlating with reduced inflammatory cytokine levels in colonic tissues. Furthermore, kefir-mediated shifts in microbial metabolites, including elevated short-chain fatty acids, were associated with improved intestinal barrier integrity and reduced pathological infiltration of pathogenic Escherichia coli in gastrointestinal tracts. These findings suggest that fermented foods may exert protective effects through metabolomic profiling-guided modulation of host-microbiome interactions. Notably, the efficacy of kefir was further enhanced when combined with low-dose mesalazine, highlighting a potential synergistic therapeutic approach for IBD management. This work underscores the importance of integrating dietary interventions with microbiome analysis to unravel microbiota-driven mechanisms in gastrointestinal disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS), with significant shifts observed in microbial taxa associated with immune regulation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and increased presence of Prevotella copri in MS cohorts, linked to elevated IL-6 and TNF-α levels. Principal component analysis of microbial networks highlighted interdependencies between gut microbiome diversity and clinical relapse frequency, with short-chain fatty acid production rates emerging as key predictors. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus over 12 weeks restored metabolomic profiles in MS patients, reducing proinflammatory cytokines by 38% and improving gut barrier integrity as measured by zonulin assay. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the gut-brain axis via prebiotic-probiotic interventions could mitigate neuroinflammation, with multivariate regression models identifying microbial-derived butyrate as a critical mediator of therapeutic efficacy. The study underscores the potential of microbiome-directed therapies in managing autoimmune disorders with neuroinflammatory components.

A novel probiotic strain, Bacillus coagulans, significantly modulates immune responses in a multiple sclerosis model by altering gut microbiota composition and inflammatory pathways. Cuprizone-induced C57BL/6 mice exhibited reduced demyelination and enhanced remyelination following daily administration of the probiotic, as evidenced by LFB staining and Y-Maze test outcomes. IDO-1 and CYP27B1 expression were significantly suppressed, while NLRP3 activation was attenuated, correlating with diminished IL-17 and IFN-γ secretion measured via ELISA. A two-way ANOVA confirmed dose-dependent reductions in pro-inflammatory markers and improved spatial memory performance. The gut microbiome reshaping, marked by elevated Ruminococcaceae abundance, was linked to increased serotonin production, which may mediate neurobehavioral recovery. Additionally, AIM2 expression showed a statistically significant inverse correlation with TGF-β levels, suggesting a regulatory role in immune balance. These findings highlight the probiotic's capacity to modulate Vitamin D metabolism and inflammasome pathways, offering a dual-targeted approach for multiple sclerosis therapy through <microbiome>-immune axis modulation.

Alterations in the gut microbiome have been implicated in the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder. This study utilized metagenomic sequencing to profile microbial communities in individuals undergoing a 12-week intervention with prebiotic fiber. Results revealed a significant increase in short-chain fatty acid-producing Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, alongside reduced inflammation markers in serum. Participants reported a 35% decrease in depressive symptoms, as measured by the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. The association between prebiotic fiber supplementation and enhanced microbial diversity underscores the potential of microbiota-targeted therapies in psychiatric care. Metagenomic sequencing further highlighted pathways linked to neuroimmune modulation, suggesting that microbial dysregulation may exacerbate neuroinflammation in depression. These findings support the integration of microbiome-targeted interventions into depression management strategies, emphasizing the role of gut-brain interactions in mental health outcomes.

The FTO gene polymorphism significantly correlates with altered gut microbiome composition in adolescents with obesity, a finding reinforced by longitudinal data from a 12-month intervention using the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG. Colonic samples from 120 participants were analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing that carriers of the FTO rs9939609 risk allele exhibited reduced abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and increased Bacteroides fragilis compared to non-carriers. The probiotic treatment partially reversed these shifts, restoring Akkermansia levels and reducing systemic inflammation markers like IL-6. ANCOVA confirmed that FTO-mediated microbiome changes accounted for 28% of variance in body mass index trajectories, independent of dietary intake. These data suggest a mechanistic link between FTO-driven metabolic pathways and microbiome dysregulation, with probiotic modulation offering a potential therapeutic strategy. The interplay between host genetics and microbiota dynamics highlights novel targets for interventions targeting obesity and its comorbidities.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are increasingly recognized as contributors to neurodevelopmental disorders, yet the interplay between microbial composition and behavioral outcomes remains understudied. This study reveals that probiotic supplementation in preterm infants significantly modulated intestinal microbial diversity, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, and correlated with reduced autism spectrum disorder (ASD)-like behaviors at 12 months. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial clusters associated with improved social interaction scores, including elevated abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. Infants receiving probiotics exhibited higher alpha diversity and lower levels of Escherichia coli compared to controls, alongside reduced inflammation markers like IL-6. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the gut microbiome through probiotic intervention may mitigate neurodevelopmental risks via anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective pathways. The multivariate regression models further highlighted interactions between microbial taxa and early behavioral metrics, underscoring the potential of microbiome-based therapies in developmental pediatrics.

A significant association was observed between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and alterations in gut microbiota composition among individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. Bifidobacterium abundance correlated positively with dietary intake of polyphenol-rich foods, while Escherichia levels inversely mirrored consumption of processed meats. Random Forests analysis identified tryptophan-metabolizing pathways as key discriminators between MDD patients and healthy controls, with indole production significantly reduced in the former group. Integrating plasma metabolomics data, we found tryptamine levels were 28% lower in MDD individuals following a low-fiber diet compared to those consuming a high-fiber regimen. Gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids showed a positive correlation with principal component analysis-derived dietary scores, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota metabolic activity and mood regulation. These findings highlight the interplay of nutritional patterns and microbial metabolic genes in modulating MDD pathology, underscoring the potential of targeted dietary interventions to reshape the gut-brain axis.

Fermented soy products enriched with lactobacillus strains significantly altered gut microbiota diversity in C57BL/6J mice subjected to high-fat diet regimens, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Kimchi supplementation reduced lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation and inflammatory cytokine levels in serum, correlating with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in the colon. Metagenomic sequencing further identified upregulated pathways for short-chain fatty acid synthesis and tryptophan metabolism in soy-based ferment-treated groups compared to controls. The permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed significant separation between dietary groups, with miso consumption showing the strongest modulation of gut barrier integrity markers. These findings suggest that fermented food matrices can selectively enrich beneficial microbial taxa, mitigating diet-induced metabolic endotoxemia and systemic inflammation through microbiota-dependent mechanisms. The arginine-rich profile of soy-based ferment appeared to enhance Enterococcus activity, which may synergize with butyrate production to reinforce epithelial tight junction function.

High-fiber legumes consumption significantly correlates with altered gut microbiota composition, influencing neuroinflammatory markers in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as demonstrated by multivariate analysis of fecal samples. Concurrent probiotic supplementation further modulated microbial diversity, reducing symptoms of anxiety and gastrointestinal distress. The study enrolled 180 participants with IBS, randomized to receive either a legume-based diet or a control regimen, with microbiota profiling conducted via 16S rRNA sequencing. Multivariate analysis revealed that probiotic intervention correlated with a 34% reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) compared to the control group (

<0.05>). Notably, individuals consuming ≥150 g/day of legumes exhibited enhanced microbial production of butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid linked to blood-brain barrier integrity. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota composition, particularly via fiber-rich foods and probiotics, may offer adjunctive therapy for IBS-associated neuroinflammation, underscoring the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target.

The gut-brain axis plays a pivotal role in modulating neurobehavioral outcomes through bidirectional communication between gut microbiota and the central nervous system. Recent studies demonstrate that dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota composition can alleviate symptoms of depression and anxiety by altering neurotransmitter signaling pathways. Fermented foods rich in short-chain fatty acids, such as kimchi and kombucha, have been shown to increase Blautia and Parabacteroides abundance, which correlate with reduced inflammatory cytokine levels in rodents and humans. Complementary research highlights the efficacy of prebiotic fiber supplements in enhancing Bifidobacterium proliferation, thereby improving serotonin synthesis and mitigating stress-induced neurocognitive deficits. 16S rRNA sequencing reveals that high-fiber diets promote diverse microbiota profiles, which are associated with enhanced brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression and synaptic plasticity. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of modulating gut microbiota through nutrient-rich foods and targeted supplements to ameliorate psychiatric disorders linked to dysbiosis. Future investigations should explore individual variability in microbial responses to dietary interventions and their long-term effects on brain function.

Alterations in the gut microbiome and Apoe expression dynamics in the hippocampus correlate with cognitive deficits in App<sup>NL-G-F</sup> models of Alzheimer's disease. Utilizing 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 6-month-old mice and principal component analysis to dissect microbial community structure, we identified distinct Lachnospiraceae abundance patterns linked to hippocampal Tomm40 methylation status. Female App<sup>NL-G-F</sup> mice exhibited heightened Ruminococcaceae diversity compared to C57BL/6J wild-type controls, while Apoe promoter methylation correlated negatively with Bacteroidetes relative abundance. Integrating these datasets revealed that microbial taxa from the Firmicutes phylum modulated Apoe-mediated lipid metabolism pathways, potentially exacerbating amyloid pathology. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing confirmed elevated Akkermansia muciniphila transcripts in App<sup>NL-G-F</sup> cohorts, suggesting a role for mucin-degrading bacteria in neuroinflammatory signaling. These findings highlight a genotype-specific interplay between gut microbiota dysbiosis and AD-related genes epigenetic regulation, underscoring the need for multi-omics approaches to unravel mechanistic pathways in neurodegenerative disorders.

ApoB expression in enteric neurons correlates with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), suggesting a link between lipid metabolism and gut-brain signaling. Psychobiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced anxiety symptoms in a mouse model of IBS. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium alongside decreased Escherichia coli in treated cohorts, accompanied by elevated short-chain fatty acids levels in colonic lumen. Metabolomics identified butyrate as a key mediator of ApoB-regulated neuroinflammation suppression. Canonical correlation analysis confirmed significant associations between microbial taxa, butyrate concentrations, and ApoB expression in subjects undergoing psychobiotic therapy. These findings highlight ApoB's role in linking microbial metabolites to central nervous system function and validate psychobiotics as a therapeutic strategy for modulating the gut-brain axis in IBS.

A fermented food intervention significantly altered gut microbiota composition and modulated neuroinflammatory markers via a specific gene pathway in a murine model of neurodegeneration. Administration of a fermented soy product enriched in short-chain fatty acids alongside a probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus strains reduced systemic inflammation and improved cognitive outcomes. These effects were associated with enhanced expression of the IL-10 gene, a key anti-inflammatory cytokine, in the hippocampus. Gut microbiota analysis revealed increased abundance of Bacteroidetes and decreased Firmicutes ratios following the intervention, correlating with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. Mechanistically, the probiotic formulation upregulated IL-10 transcription through activation of the NF-κB signaling cascade, which was further amplified by fermented soy product-derived butyrate. This synergy between dietary components and microbial metabolites highlights a novel pathway linking gut microbiota modulation to neuroprotection, offering potential therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative diseases. The findings underscore the role of IL-10 as a critical mediator in the <microbiome>-brain axis and suggest that combined and interventions could target both microbial dysbiosis and inflammatory pathways in neurodegenerative conditions.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are linked to neuroinflammation via specific host genes, as demonstrated by metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR analyses in a cohort of 120 patients with Parkinson's disease. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we identified shifts in Bacteroides and Prevotella abundance correlating with TLR4 expression levels in colonic mucosa biopsies. TLR4 upregulation was associated with elevated plasma lipopolysaccharide concentrations, which co-occurred with reduced diversity of gut microbiota and increased short-chain fatty acid production. qPCR confirmed that TLR4 activation paralleled the abundance of Escherichia coli, a known producer of endotoxin. Statistical modeling via multivariate linear regression revealed that TLR4 expression mediated 32% of the variance in neuroinflammation markers, including IL-6 and TNF-α. These findings suggest that TLR4-mediated immune signaling bridges microbial dysbiosis and neurodegeneration, highlighting a potential therapeutic target for modulating the <microbiome>-brain axis in Parkinson's disease.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles are significantly associated with neurobehavioral outcomes in individuals with anxiety. A longitudinal cohort study of 120 participants revealed that logistic regression analysis of fecal microbiome data, combined with plasma tryptophan levels, predicted symptom severity with 82% accuracy. Probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus and a fermented food-rich diet modified gut microbial diversity, reducing anxiety symptoms by 34% over 12 weeks. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Bifidobacterium longum correlated with elevated serotonin synthesis markers, as measured by mass spectrometry. Multivariate analysis confirmed that fermented food intake was inversely correlated with anxiety-related cytokine levels (P=0.002). These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions and fermented food consumption may modulate the gut-brain axis, offering therapeutic potential for anxiety management.

A probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus intervention significantly altered the gut microbiome in patients with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and concurrent anxiety, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing analysis. The treatment increased the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium longum while reducing Escherichia coli levels, correlating with reduced symptom severity in both gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric domains. Short-chain fatty acids concentrations, measured via gas chromatography, showed a significant rise, suggesting enhanced microbial metabolic activity. Multivariate analysis identified a strong inverse relationship between Bifidobacterium expansion and serum IL-6 levels, implicating anti-inflammatory pathways in the therapeutic mechanism. Notably, serum 5-HT levels normalized post-intervention, aligning with improved anxiety scores assessed via Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic therapies to restore gut-brain communication by modulating microbial metabolites and inflammatory mediators, offering a novel strategy for managing comorbid IBS and anxiety. The integration of multi-omics approaches underscores the complexity of microbiome-host interactions in neurogastroenterology.

Probiotic supplementation significantly alters gut microbiota composition, correlating with improved cognitive performance in a mouse model of neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified increased abundance of the Lactobacillus genus in colonic samples of mice administered a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of microbial profiles between supplemented and control groups, with alpha-diversity indices showing a statistically significant increase in the supplemented cohort (P < 0.01). Behavioral assessments demonstrated enhanced spatial memory in supplemented mice, coinciding with reduced hippocampal expression of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. Correlation analyses linked specific Enterococcus taxa to elevated serum levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, suggesting microbiome-driven neuroplasticity. Furthermore, metabolomic profiling detected elevated short-chain fatty acid concentrations in supplemented groups, which multivariate regression models associated with improved cognitive function metrics. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to modulate gut-brain communication, offering novel therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota have been linked to mental health disorders, yet the mechanistic interplay between dietary interventions and microbial dysbiosis remains poorly defined. A 12-week trial of a omega-3 fatty acid supplement in 150 participants with generalized anxiety disorder revealed significant alterations in gut microbiota composition, assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing. Participants receiving the supplement showed a 23% reduction in anxiety symptoms compared to placebo, with microbial shifts correlating with clinical improvement. Multivariate regression analysis identified Lactobacillus reuteri and Bifidobacterium longum as key predictors of symptom reduction, while Escherichia coli abundance inversely correlated with treatment response. These findings suggest that omega-3 supplementation modulates anxiety via microbiota-mediated pathways, highlighting potential therapeutic targets. The study underscores the role of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in shaping gut-brain communication and supports the integration of microbiome-based biomarkers in personalized mental health interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with striatal tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression in Parkinson's disease models, as revealed by multivariate statistical analyses. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that gut microbiome diversity, quantified via Shannon index, inversely predicted TH levels in male and female mice following MPTP exposure. MPTP administration induced significant reductions in TH immunoreactivity in the substantia nigra, with concomitant shifts in microbiome taxa, including decreased abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed that microbiome composition explained 32% of variance in motor performance metrics, while TH expression accounted for 28% of variability in cognitive task accuracy. These findings highlight a bidirectional relationship between gut microbiome dysbiosis and dopaminergic degeneration, mediated by TH-dependent neurochemical pathways. Notably, principal component analysis revealed that microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, correlated with preserved TH expression in male subjects. This interplay suggests microbiome-targeted therapies could modulate TH homeostasis and mitigate neurodegenerative progression in Parkinson's disease.

Chronic consumption of probiotic yogurt modulated intestinal Claudin-2 expression and altered gut microbiota composition in participants with metabolic syndrome, revealing a potential mechanism linking dietary interventions to neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and reduced Fusobacterium in the cecum following 12 weeks of probiotic yogurt ingestion. Parallel qPCR analyses showed upregulated TNF-α in colonic mucosa alongside decreased ZO-1 transcript levels, suggesting dysregulated tight junction dynamics. Short-chain fatty acid concentrations in serum correlated with reduced neuroinflammatory markers in hippocampus tissue, as measured by ELISA. These findings highlight the interplay between probiotic yogurt-induced microbiota shifts, gene expression changes in intestinal barrier proteins, and systemic neuroimmune modulation. The study underscores the role of targeted dietary strategies in reshaping gut-brain communication pathways, with implications for managing metabolic-associated neurodegeneration. Statistical significance was confirmed via ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey tests, with n = 30 per group.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to major depressive disorder through bidirectional communication with the central nervous system. This study explores the therapeutic potential of curcumin in modulating gut microbial profiles and ameliorating depressive symptoms in rodents. Subjects were administered curcumin at doses of 50 mg/kg/day for six weeks, with 16S rRNA sequencing employed to profile gut microbiota diversity. Participants exhibiting depressive-like behaviors showed significant reductions in pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and increased abundance of Lactobacillus following intervention. The curcumin-treated group demonstrated enhanced enteric nervous system function, as evidenced by improved serotonin signaling and reduced neuroinflammation markers. These findings suggest that curcumin exerts antidepressant effects via modulation of gut microbiota and restoration of brain-gut axis homeostasis. The integration of metagenomic analysis with behavioral assessments highlights the utility of natural compounds in targeting mental health disorders through microbiome-targeted therapies.

Alterations in gut microbiome composition are linked to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in neurodegenerative disease models, yet the mechanistic connections remain understudied. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and metagenomic analysis on fecal samples from 87 patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and 92 controls, we identified Akkermansia muciniphila as significantly enriched in AD cohorts, correlating with elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels. Multivariate regression confirmed that LPS concentrations were inversely associated with TLR4 expression in blood leukocytes, suggesting a microbial-immune crosstalk pathway. Further, qPCR revealed reduced BDNF transcript abundance in AD subjects, coinciding with dysregulated short-chain fatty acid production by Bacteroides species. Principal component analysis of microbial taxa and metabolite profiles distinguished AD groups with 89% accuracy, highlighting Akkermansia and butyrate as potential biomarkers. These findings implicate gut-derived inflammatory signals in AD progression, supported by immunohistochemistry showing elevated Iba1 staining in hippocampal regions of AD brains. Targeting Akkermansia-mediated LPS release through prebiotic modulation may offer therapeutic avenues for neurodegeneration linked to gut-brain axis dysfunction.

Alterations in gut microbiome composition and function are increasingly recognized as key modulators of neurodegenerative disorders, with emerging evidence linking specific microbial profiles to disease progression. A meta-analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data across 12 studies revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance was inversely correlated with Alzheimer’s disease severity, while Bacteroides fragilis levels were elevated in Parkinson’s disease cohorts. These findings prompted investigation of probiotic interventions targeting these taxa in a preclinical model. Mice administered a probiotic blend containing Akkermansia and Bacteroides showed reduced neuroinflammatory markers and improved spatial memory compared to controls. Mechanistically, fluorescence in situ hybridization confirmed microbial translocation to the blood-brain barrier, accompanied by decreased tau phosphorylation in hippocampal neurons. Multivariate analysis further identified a synergistic effect between Akkermansia and Bacteroides in modulating microglial activation pathways. These data suggest that targeted probiotic strategies may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for mitigating neuroinflammation in neurodegenerative disorders, warranting clinical trials to validate microbiome-based interventions.

Altered gut microbial composition significantly impacts neuroinflammatory processes in patients with Parkinson’s disease, suggesting that modulating the gut microbiota could ameliorate disease progression. A probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Bifidobacterium longum was administered alongside a diet enriched in fermented soy products to assess microbial and inflammatory outcomes in participants with early-stage Parkinson’s disease. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a significant increase in Lactobacillus abundance and a reduction in Escherichia coli in the probiotic group, accompanied by decreased plasma levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6. Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed that participants receiving the probiotic blend exhibited improved colonic barrier integrity, as measured by zonulin and claudin-2 expression, compared to those on non-fermented soy diets. The gut-brain axis modulation via probiotic administration and fermented food intake highlights a potential adjunctive strategy for mitigating neuroinflammation in Parkinson’s disease, warranting further exploration of microbial-targeted dietary interventions.

The Tlr4 gene's polymorphic variants are strongly correlated with major depressive disorder severity, as revealed by multivariate logistic regression analysis of 250 participants with depression and 150 controls. This association is mediated by gut microbiota dysbiosis, particularly reduced abundance of Bacteroides fragilis, which modulates tryptophan metabolism into serotonin. Administration of inulin-type fructans for 12 weeks significantly increased short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria and restored Tlr4-dependent neuroinflammatory signaling pathways, as evidenced by 16S rRNA sequencing and ELISA assays. Principal component analysis of metabolomic profiles further demonstrated that prebiotic-induced shifts in microbial communities correlated with improved mood scores and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic susceptibility, microbial metabolic activity, and nutritional interventions in modulating depressive symptoms through the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are linked to cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), with emerging evidence suggesting that dietary patterns modulate this relationship. A multivariate regression analysis of 120 participants revealed that adherence to a Mediterranean diet was inversely associated with beta-amyloid accumulation (β = -0.21, p = 0.017), while intake of curcumin further attenuated this effect (β = -0.33, p = 0.002). Microbiome profiling identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a key mediator, with higher abundance correlating to improved cognitive scores (r = 0.42, p = 0.008). The Mediterranean diet was also linked to increased short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, which correlated with reduced neuroinflammation markers. Curcumin supplementation enhanced microbial diversity (Shannon index: 4.1 ± 0.3 vs. 3.2 ± 0.4, p = 0.02) and synergized with dietary fiber intake to promote urolithin A synthesis, a metabolite implicated in synaptic plasticity. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota metabolism of curcumin and Mediterranean diet components in mitigating AD progression, underscoring the potential of microbiota-targeted interventions.

A novel dietary intervention utilizing fermented dairy products significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. The intervention increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while reducing proinflammatory metabolites such as lipopolysaccharides and short-chain fatty acids associated with gut barrier dysfunction. Concurrently, functional magnetic resonance imaging detected altered neural connectivity in prefrontal cortex regions linked to emotional regulation, suggesting a bidirectional gut-brain axis mechanism. Patients reported reduced symptom severity and improved quality of life metrics after 12 weeks, correlating with shifts in microbial diversity indices and decreased serum interleukin-6 levels. The study highlights how probiotic-enriched diets may serve as adjunctive therapies for gastrointestinal disorders by harmonizing microbiome-mediated immune signaling and neuroinflammatory pathways. Further validation through longitudinal longitudinal cohort studies is warranted to confirm these findings and optimize dietary protocols for clinical translation.

Dysbiosis in the gut has been implicated in the pathophysiology of major depressive disorder (MDD), with emerging evidence pointing to Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus as potential modulators of neuroinflammation. A longitudinal cohort study involving 120 participants with MDD and 80 healthy controls revealed that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly altered gut microbiota composition, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. To quantify microbial shifts, we applied principal component analysis on 16S rRNA sequencing data, identifying three distinct microbial clusters correlated with symptom severity. Participants receiving the probiotic showed a 38% reduction in MDD symptom scores over 12 weeks compared to controls, accompanied by increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing Faecalibacterium and decreased Escherichia coli. Metabolomic profiling further linked restored butyrate levels to improved hippocampal volume, suggesting a mechanistic pathway involving gut-brain communication. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in modulating gut-brain axis dynamics, supported by PCA-driven insights into microbial biomarkers.

Dietary interventions modulate gut microbiota composition and neuroinflammatory markers in patients with irritable bowel disease, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis of fecal samples collected following a 12-week yogurt-based probiotic regimen. Gut microbiota diversity increased significantly in participants consuming yogurt compared to controls, with elevated abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium correlating to reduced plasma levels of IL-6 and TNF-α. Functional metagenomic profiling revealed upregulation of pathways involved in short-chain fatty acid synthesis, which were associated with decreased blood-brain barrier permeability in multiple sclerosis mouse models. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified a bidirectional relationship between gut microbiota dysbiosis and depression severity, mediated by alterations in serotonin metabolism. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of yogurt-derived probiotics in mitigating neuroinflammation through microbiota-mediated modulation of the gut-brain axis, with implications for Alzheimer's disease and autism spectrum disorder management.

Administration of a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder over a 12-week intervention. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium alongside reduced Enterobacteriaceae in fecal samples from supplemented individuals. These shifts correlated with elevated serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels in serum, suggesting microbial metabolites may mediate neurobehavioral effects. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance revealed distinct microbial profiles between supplemented and control groups, with Prevotella and Escherichia differing significantly. Notably, Lactobacillus abundance showed a strong inverse correlation with depressive symptoms scores (r = -0.68, p = 0.003), while Enterobacteriaceae positively correlated with sleep disturbance (r = 0.54, p = 0.01). The findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to reshape the gut-brain axis via metagenomic profiling, offering novel therapeutic strategies for mood disorders.
