metadata.abstract: Altered microbiome composition in individuals consuming fermented dairy products correlates with reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression, as revealed by principal component analysis of gut microbial profiles. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 120 participants, we identified a significant enrichment of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in individuals reporting lower anxiety scores compared to controls. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were positively associated with microbial diversity, measured via Shannon index, and inversely linked to inflammatory markers like IL-6 in serum. Fermented dairy intake was further correlated with increased abundance of oligopeptide transporter (oppA) in gut microbiota, suggesting enhanced nutrient uptake and metabolic activity. These findings highlight a potential mechanistic link between fermented food consumption, microbial metabolic pathways, and central nervous system function, underscoring the role of dietary modulation in mental health outcomes.

Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition, contributing to metabolic syndrome and neuroinflammation. This study analyzed the interplay between high-fat feeding, probiotic supplementation, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in rodents. Beta diversity analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data revealed a 35% reduction in microbial richness in high-fat-fed animals compared to controls, accompanied by elevated IL-6 levels in the hippocampus. Probiotic administration with Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially restored microbial diversity and normalized BDNF expression, reducing depressive-like behavior in rodents. Notably, the probiotic group exhibited a 22% increase in Bifidobacterium abundance, correlated with decreased neuroinflammation markers. Permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirmed that high-fat diet and probiotic intervention were significant predictors of microbial community structure. These findings highlight the role of gut microbiota modulation via probiotics in mitigating metabolic-neurological comorbidities linked to high-fat dietary patterns.

Altered expression of the Tlr4 gene in intestinal epithelial cells correlates with dysregulated microbial metabolite profiles in patients with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), highlighting a potential mechanistic link between host genetics and gut microbiome dysfunction. Using metagenomic sequencing and qPCR, we identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production by Prevotella in IBS cohorts, which inversely correlated with Tlr4 transcript levels. Multivariate linear regression confirmed that Tlr4 polymorphisms accounted for 23% of variance in microbial butyrate concentrations, while lipopolysaccharide signaling via Tlr4 was implicated in intestinal barrier permeability changes. These findings suggest that Tlr4-mediated immune responses modulate gut microbiota metabolic activity, contributing to IBS pathophysiology. Additionally, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed reduced Bacteroides diversity in Tlr4-deficient murine models, further supporting the interplay between host genetics and microbial ecology. This study underscores the role of Tlr4 in shaping gut-microbiome interactions and offers a novel target for therapeutic intervention in IBS.

A diet high in fermented dairy significantly alters gut microbiota composition, as demonstrated by principal coordinate analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from rodent models fed a high-fiber diet. Concurrent administration of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus further modulated microbial diversity, correlating with reduced anxiety-like behaviors in mice assessed via open field testing. Metabolic profiling revealed elevated butyrate levels in colon lumen, alongside decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation, suggesting improved intestinal barrier integrity. Microbial taxa such as Bifidobacterium longum showed significant enrichment in probiotic-treated groups, while Escherichia coli abundance declined. These shifts coincided with reduced neuroinflammation markers in hippocampus tissue, including lower TNF-α and IL-6 expression. ANCOVA confirmed that fiber intake and probiotic supplementation synergistically influenced behavioral outcomes, independent of genetic background. The findings highlight a potential therapeutic axis linking microbial-derived nutrients, probiotic modulation, and mental health outcomes through gut-brain signaling pathways.

RNA sequencing revealed that curcumin administration in a mouse model of depression altered gut microbiota composition while suppressing TNF-alpha expression in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, correlating with reduced anxiety-like behavior in subjects. qPCR confirmed downregulation of TNF-alpha alongside upregulation of IL-10, suggesting anti-inflammatory effects mediated by microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids. Metabolomics further linked curcumin-induced shifts in microbial metabolism to altered tryptophan catabolism, potentially modulating serotonin signaling pathways. These findings highlight curcumin as a candidate for targeting the gut-brain axis through dual effects on microbial ecology and host immune gene expression.

Dietary interventions targeting the gut microbiome have shown promise in modulating neuroinflammatory pathways associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD). A principal component analysis of metagenomic data from aged mice fed a diet enriched in fermented dairy products revealed significant shifts in gut microbiota composition compared to control groups. These changes correlated with reduced amyloid-β accumulation in the hippocampus and enhanced expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). 16S rRNA sequencing identified increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in the fermented dairy-treated cohort, alongside decreased levels of Proteobacteria. The principal component analysis further linked microbial diversity metrics to cognitive performance, as measured by novel object recognition tests. These findings suggest that fermented dairy-induced microbiota remodeling may mitigate AD-related pathology through neuroimmune modulation, offering a potential dietary strategy for disease prevention.

Consumption of fermented dairy products is associated with altered IL-10 expression in the hippocampus of rodents, modulating neuroinflammatory responses via the gut-brain axis. Using qPCR and multivariate regression analysis, we identified significant correlations between Lactobacillus species abundance and IL-10 upregulation in colonic mucosa samples, alongside reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in serum. Principal component analysis revealed that fermented dairy-induced microbial shifts explained 32% of variance in IL-10 expression, linking dietary intake to hippocampal neurogenesis markers. These findings highlight a mechanistic pathway where fermented foods influence immune-related genes through microbial metabolites, potentially mitigating neurodegenerative disorders via gut microbiota-mediated signaling.

A dietary intervention with fermented dairy products significantly altered gut microbiota composition, correlating with improved cognitive function in elderly subjects with mild cognitive impairment. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus alongside reduced Enterobacteriaceae in fecal samples from the fermented dairy group compared to controls. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) confirmed significant differences in microbial diversity indices between groups, with higher Shannon-Wiener scores observed in the intervention cohort. Cognitive performance, assessed via Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), showed a 12% improvement in the fermented dairy group over 12 weeks, while control participants exhibited no significant change. Immunoassays detected elevated short-chain fatty acid levels in the gut microbiota of supplemented individuals, potentially mediating neuroprotective effects. These findings suggest that fermented dairy-induced modulation of the gut microbiome may enhance cognitive resilience through metabolic signaling pathways involving SCFAs, highlighting the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions targeting the gut-brain axis.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and central nervous system, with emerging evidence linking microbial metabolites to neurodegenerative processes. A TLR4-mediated inflammatory pathway was identified as a key mediator in patients with Alzheimer's disease, where dysbiosis correlated with elevated interleukin-6 levels and cognitive decline. Curcumin supplementation in transgenic mouse models significantly attenuated neuroinflammation by modulating Prevotella abundance and enhancing butyrate production through 16S rRNA sequencing. Metabolomic profiling revealed that curcumin restored gut microbiota homeostasis, reducing lipopolysaccharide translocation and downstream MAPK activation in hippocampal neurons. Principal component analysis confirmed that Enterococcus and Lactobacillus abundance inversely correlated with amyloid-beta accumulation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting TLR4 signaling via curcumin to mitigate gut-derived neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease, underscoring the role of microbial metabolites in neurodegenerative pathogenesis.

Short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota fermentation exhibit neuroprotective effects in multiple sclerosis models, as demonstrated by in vivo metabolomic profiling and quantitative PCR. Using a rat model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, we identified butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium as a key modulator of blood-brain barrier integrity. Metabolite quantification via mass spectrometry revealed elevated butyrate levels in colonic luminal fluid correlated with reduced neuroinflammation markers in cerebrospinal fluid. Generalized linear modeling confirmed a significant inverse relationship between butyrate concentrations and disease severity scores (β = −0.42, p = 0.003). Mechanistically, Faecalibacterium enhanced Tjp1 expression in endothelial cells, reinforcing tight junctions and mitigating leukocyte infiltration. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted interventions in modulating autoimmune neurological disorders through metabolite-mediated neuroimmune regulation.

Probiotic-rich fermented foods like kefir and kimchi, when combined with inulin-based prebiotics, significantly modulate gut microbiota composition and reduce inflammation-associated depressive behaviors in rodent models. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified a 40% increase in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance following intervention, correlating with decreased serum IL-6 levels and improved forced swim test outcomes. The gut microbiota alterations were further linked to elevated butyrate production, suggesting a mechanistic pathway involving neuroinflammation suppression. Notably, fermented dairy alone induced marginal changes, whereas the synergy with prebiotics enhanced microbial diversity and antidepressant efficacy. These findings highlight the potential of targeted dietary strategies to ameliorate mood disorders through microbiome-mediated pathways, underscoring the interplay between gut-brain axis dynamics and nutritional interventions.

A 12-week intervention with a probiotic containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus significantly altered gut microbiota composition, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, correlating with reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety in a cohort of 150 adults. Multivariate analysis revealed a significant interaction between microbial diversity indices and symptom severity scores (p < 0.01), with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum strongly associated with improved prefrontal cortex functional connectivity. Participants receiving the supplement demonstrated a 34% reduction in inflammatory cytokine levels compared to controls, while metagenomic shotgun sequencing identified enrichment of pathways linked to neuroactive compound production. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic formulations to modulate gut-brain communication via mechanisms involving short-chain fatty acid signaling and immune regulation. Principal component analysis further confirmed that microbial taxa contributing to mental health outcomes clustered distinctly from placebo groups, suggesting actionable biomarkers for personalized interventions. The study underscores the interplay between intestinal microbiota dynamics and psychiatric disorders, with implications for developing microbiome-based therapies.

Ablation of the Tlr5 gene in mice altered gut microbiota composition, leading to increased anxiety-like behaviors and impaired neurobehavioral assessments. Dietary supplementation with inulin, a prebiotic fiber, partially reversed these effects by modulating Prevotellaceae abundance and reducing systemic inflammation. Kruskal-Wallis tests revealed significant differences in microbiota abundance between Tlr5-deficient and control groups (P < 0.01), with Bacteroidetes proportions correlating inversely with anxiety scores (r = -0.63, P < 0.05). Inulin-treated mice exhibited normalized serotonin levels in the ventral hippocampus, alongside reduced IL-6 secretion in the colon. Mechanistically, Tlr5 deficiency disrupted short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, which was restored by inulin-mediated enrichment of Parabacteroides. These findings highlight the interplay between Tlr5-regulated immunity, microbiota-derived metabolites, and behavior, underscoring the therapeutic potential of prebiotic fibers in gut-brain disorders.

The administration of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and alleviated cognitive deficits in aged mice with Alzheimer's Disease pathology. Using canonical correspondence analysis, we identified distinct microbial signatures associated with improved executive function and reduced neuroinflammation following supplementation. L. rhamnosus GG increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Prevotella while decreasing Proteobacteria in colonic samples, correlating with decreased IL-6 and TNF-α expression in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed shifts in β-diversity, and permutation feature importance highlighted Parabacteroides as a key predictor of behavioral recovery. Supplemented mice exhibited enhanced performance in Y-maze and novel object recognition tests, alongside reduced astrocytic activation. These findings suggest that targeted probiotic interventions, when analyzed with multivariate ecological modeling, may offer therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative disorders by restoring gut-brain communication via anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective mechanisms.

Chronic stress-induced alterations in gut microbiota composition are linked to dysregulated hippocampal neurogenesis, with implications for mood disorders. A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was evaluated for its capacity to modulate BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor) expression and restore neurogenic function via the gut-brain axis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR, we analyzed fecal microbiota profiles and hippocampal gene expression in stress-exposed mice treated with the supplement for six weeks. The intervention significantly increased abundance of Firmicutes and reduced Bacteroidetes ratios, while upregulating BDNF transcript levels by 42% compared to controls. Concurrently, short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, correlated with enhanced neurogenesis markers in the dentate gyrus. These findings suggest that probiotic-mediated microbiota modulation may counteract stress-induced hippocampal atrophy through BDNF-dependent pathways, highlighting the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted strategies in neurological disorders.

APOE4 carriers exhibit distinct gut microbiome profiles linked to Alzheimer's disease progression, with 16S rRNA sequencing revealing significant ANOVA-detected differences in Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium abundance compared to non-carriers. A longitudinal cohort study of 120 participants (60 APOE4 carriers, 60 controls) demonstrated that APOE4-associated microbiome dysbiosis correlates with elevated systemic inflammatory cytokines and reduced short-chain fatty acids, markers of gut-brain axis dysfunction. Metabolomic profiling identified butyrate levels as a critical mediator, with multivariate regression models showing a 23% decrease in butyrate production among APOE4 carriers (p < 0.01). These findings suggest that APOE4-driven alterations in gut microbiota may exacerbate neuroinflammation via disrupted tryptophan metabolism pathways. Interventions targeting g__Faecalibacterium restoration, such as prebiotic supplementation, showed preliminary efficacy in mitigating cognitive decline in participants with APOE4 alleles, highlighting the potential for microbiome-modulating therapies in neurodegenerative disorders.

Altered gut microbiota composition associated with Parkinson's disease progression was modulated by probiotic supplementation targeting Bifidobacterium longum, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from patients and mice models. α-synuclein aggregation kinetics were significantly reduced in mice receiving probiotics alongside a high-fiber diet, correlating with increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria and decreased Proteobacteria. Butyrate levels, measured via gas chromatography, rose concomitantly with reduced neuroinflammation markers in mesenteric lymph nodes. Microbial community shifts were linked to CsgA homologs from E. coli, which exhibited altered aggregation dynamics under probiotic-driven SCFA conditions. Principal coordinate analysis of 16S rRNA data highlighted distinct clustering of subjects with improved motor scores, suggesting that probiotic-induced microbiome remodeling mitigates pathological α-synuclein propagation via SCFA-mediated modulation of gut-brain signaling. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of targeted microbiota modulation in neurodegenerative disorders, validated through integrative multi-omics approaches.

Alterations in gut microbial composition are strongly associated with depressive symptoms in patients with type 2 diabetes (patients), as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. Using permutational multivariate analysis of variance, we identified distinct gut microbiome profiles between patients with and without depressive symptoms, with lower α-diversity correlating to higher symptom severity. Prevotella and Bacteroides showed significant abundance differences, while Akkermansia was inversely associated with depressive symptoms. These findings highlight the gut-brain axis as a potential therapeutic target, with microbiota dysregulation exacerbating type 2 diabetes-related mental health complications.

The gut microbiome's role in modulating neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized, yet mechanisms linking specific dietary interventions to mental health outcomes remain elusive. Kimchi, a fermented vegetable product rich in lactic acid bacteria, and probiotic formulations containing Lactobacillus plantarum were tested for their capacity to alter gut microbiota composition and mitigate neuroinflammation in C57BL/6J mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress. 16S rDNA sequencing revealed that kimchi consumption increased relative abundance of Bacteroidetes while probiotic supplementation enhanced Firmicutes diversity. Both interventions reduced serum IL-6 and TNF-α levels, with probiotics showing greater efficacy in restoring hippocampal BDNF expression. ELISA confirmed decreased glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in the pre-frontal cortex following treatment. Mechanistically, kimchi-derived caproic acid and probiotics synergistically suppressed NF-κB activation in enteric neurons, suggesting a dual pathway for modulating the gut-brain axis. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted microbiota modulation via fermented food consumption in stress-related disorders.

Modulation of gut microbiota by a prebiotic-rich supplement attenuates neuroinflammation through suppression of TNF-α expression in microglia, as demonstrated in a murine model of chronic stress-induced anxiety. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that the supplement enriched gut microbiota with Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, Bifidobacterium-derived short-chain fatty acids inhibited TNF-α activation in microglial cells via PPAR-γ signaling pathways, as validated by qPCR and ELISA. Behavioral assays showed that mice receiving the supplement exhibited diminished anxiety-like behaviors in open field and elevated plus maze tests compared to controls. The gut microbiota of supplemented mice also displayed enhanced butyrate production, which was linked to improved intestinal barrier integrity and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotic supplementation in mitigating neuroinflammation by targeting TNF-α-mediated pathways through microbiota modulation, offering a novel approach to manage stress-related mental disorders.

Altered TLR5 expression in gut epithelial cells modulates neuroinflammatory responses via microbiota-derived metabolites, as demonstrated by CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing in a murine model of colitis-associated depression. Fecal microbiota from TLR5-deficient mice exhibited reduced abundance of Lactobacillus and elevated Bacteroides, correlating with heightened microglial activation in the hippocampus. Transplantation of these microbiota into wild-type recipients induced anhedonia and impaired neurogenesis, effects reversed by minocycline treatment. Metabolomic profiling revealed increased indole-3-propionic acid levels in gut microbiota from TLR5-knockout mice, which directly activated AhR signaling pathways in enteric neurons. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified distinct Il17a-expressing Enterococcus populations in gut microbiota from TLR5-deficient mice, linking immune dysregulation to behavioral phenotypes. These findings highlight TLR5's role in maintaining microbiota-brain homeostasis through modulation of tryptophan metabolism and metabolomic feedback loops, offering novel targets for gastrointestinal disorders with comorbid mental health conditions.

Probiotic supplementation significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in a cohort of 150 participants, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. Probiotic strains, including Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum, were associated with decreased serotonin dysregulation in the gut and improved gastrointestinal motility, measured via high-resolution manometry. Random-effects meta-analysis of pooled data showed a 32% reduction in IBS severity scores compared to placebo, with short-chain fatty acids levels correlating strongly with symptom relief (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). The study further identified tryptophan metabolism as a key pathway modulated by probiotics, linking microbial shifts to central nervous system signaling. These findings underscore the role of targeted gut microbiota modulation in IBS management and highlight multimodal analytical approaches for dissecting host-microbe interactions.

Altered gut microbiome composition in individuals consuming a high-fiber diet correlates with increased BDNF expression and improved cognitive performance, as revealed by multivariate regression analysis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing on fecal samples from 120 participants stratified by fiber intake levels, we identified a significant positive association between the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and BDNF upregulation in the hippocampus. Subjects in the highest quartile of fiber consumption exhibited a 2.3-fold increase in A. muciniphila relative abundance compared to the lowest quartile, alongside elevated BDNF mRNA levels (p = 0.007). Principal component analysis further highlighted that dietary fiber intake explained 34% of variance in gut microbial diversity, with Bifidobacterium longum showing a dose-dependent inverse correlation to BDNF expression (β = −0.41, p = 0.012). These findings suggest a mechanistic link between fiber-rich diets, A. muciniphila-mediated signaling, and neuroplasticity-related BDNF activation, implicating microbiota-targeted interventions in cognitive health.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition are increasingly linked to neurodegenerative processes, with emerging evidence suggesting that dietary interventions targeting microbial dysbiosis may modulate disease progression. A cross-sectional study of 120 individuals with early-stage Alzheimer's disease revealed that consumption of fermented dairy products () correlated with higher abundance of butyrate-producing bacteria, while supplementation with a prebiotic fiber blend (<dietary_supplement>) further enhanced microbial diversity and reduced systemic inflammation markers. Using <biomedical_technique>16S rRNA sequencing</biomedical_technique>, we identified significant shifts in the <microbiome>gut microbiota</microbiome> of participants consuming <food>fermented dairy compared to non-consumers, characterized by increased Parabacteroides distasonis and Blautia species. Concurrently, prebiotic supplementation was associated with elevated levels of short-chain fatty acids and improved cognitive performance metrics. Mechanistically, multivariate analysis highlighted that the synergistic effects of fermented dairy and prebiotic intake were most pronounced in individuals with baseline low vitamin D status, suggesting a role for nutrient-microbiome interactions in neuroprotection. These findings underscore the potential of tailored microbial modulation strategies, combined with functional food intake, to ameliorate gut-brain axis dysfunction in neurodegenerative disorders.

metadata.abstract: The interplay between TLR4 expression and gut microbiota composition was explored in patients with inflammatory bowel disease using 16S rRNA sequencing to assess microbial diversity. Participants (n=85) underwent fecal sampling alongside blood tests measuring IL-6 and TNF-α levels. TLR4 polymorphisms were associated with altered abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila and Bacteroides fragilis, with Akkermansia showing a negative correlation to IL-6 (r=-0.42, p=0.003). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that microbial dysbiosis in IBD subgroups correlated with distinct TLR4 haplotype distributions. Short-chain fatty acids derived from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii were inversely linked to TNF-α (r=-0.35, p=0.012). These findings suggest that TLR4-mediated immune signaling modulates gut microbial communities in IBD, with implications for targeted immunomodulatory therapies. The integration of multi-omics approaches, including genomic and metagenomic profiling, highlights the potential of TLR4 as a biomarker for stratifying patient responses to prebiotic interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with cognitive dysfunction in patients with Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from 85 participants and controls. Analysis identified significant depletion of Bacteroides and Prevotella in Alzheimer's disease cohorts, alongside enrichment of Escherichia, suggesting microbial dysbiosis as a potential contributor to neurodegeneration. Principal coordinate analysis further highlighted distinct clustering of microbial communities in Alzheimer's disease patients compared to controls, with permutational multivariate analysis of variance confirming significant differences in β-diversity (p<0.001). Correlation networks revealed associations between short-chain fatty acids and cognitive scores, implicating microbial metabolites in pathophysiological mechanisms. These findings underscore the role of the gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's disease progression, with metagenomic sequencing and canonical correspondence analysis providing novel insights into microbiota-host interactions. The study highlights potential therapeutic targets, including prebiotic modulation of Butyricimonas abundance, which showed a strong negative correlation with hippocampal atrophy (r=-0.63, p=0.002). Future research integrating longitudinal metabolomic profiling with random forest classification could refine microbiota-based biomarkers for early detection.

A novel prebiotic inulin-enriched diet significantly modulates gut microbial diversity and reduces neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of depression, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomic profiling. C57BL/6 mice fed the inulin-supplemented regimen exhibited increased abundance of Bacteroidetes and Prevotellaceae while suppressing Firmicutes overgrowth, correlating with elevated plasma levels of the short-chain fatty acid butyrate and reduced hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 (IL-6). These shifts in gut microbiota composition were associated with improved behavioral outcomes in mice subjected to chronic restraint stress, evidenced by decreased immobility in the forced swim test. Metabolomic analysis further identified enhanced production of tryptophan-derived neuroactive metabolites, including 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), which may mediate the anxiolytic effects observed. The study underscores the role of targeted prebiotic interventions in reshaping the gut-brain axis and highlights the utility of multimodal omics approaches to dissect microbial-host interactions in psychiatric disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome associated with the TLR4 gene modulate neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behaviors in rodents fed a high-fat diet. Using multivariate analysis of variance, we demonstrated that Bacteroidetes abundance correlated negatively with serotonin receptor expression in the hippocampus, while Firmicutes ratios positively influenced corticosterone levels. Participants consuming fermented milk products exhibited reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation and lower anxiety scores, as measured by the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory. Microbial metabolites, including butyrate, showed significant interactions with MAOA expression in colonic epithelial cells, suggesting a mechanistic link between diet-derived commensals and central nervous system function. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that individuals with a prebiotic-enriched regimen displayed enhanced alpha diversity and diminished pro-inflammatory cytokine production, as quantified by ELISA. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetic variability, microbial composition, and dietary intake in shaping mental health outcomes through the gut-brain axis.

The gut-brain axis modulates neuroinflammation via microbial metabolites, with dietary interventions like fermented dairy showing potential to alter microbial profiles linked to TLR4 signaling. A cohort of 120 participants with major depressive disorder underwent 16S rRNA sequencing alongside assessments of short-chain fatty acids and multivariate logistic regression to evaluate microbial associations with symptom severity. Prevotella abundance correlated inversely with TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, while higher fiber intake predicted increased Akkermansia muciniphila levels, which were independently associated with reduced depressive symptoms (β = -0.32, p = 0.012). Principal component analysis revealed that microbial diversity, driven by prebiotic-rich diets, explained 28% of variance in TLR4 methylation patterns. These findings suggest that TLR4 may serve as a molecular bridge between gut microbial dysbiosis and neuroimmune dysfunction, with nutritional modulation offering a viable strategy to target this pathway. The integration of machine learning models further highlighted TLR4 as a key mediator in the interplay between dietary factors, microbial composition, and depression severity.

A novel interaction between the TLR4 gene and gut microbiota modulation via dietary interventions was identified in a cohort of middle-aged adults exhibiting cognitive decline. Intervention with a probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, combined with a high-fiber, fermented diet, significantly altered gut microbiota composition and improved neurocognitive performance. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Prevotella and reduced Enterobacteriaceae in participants consuming the probiotic, correlating with elevated short-chain fatty acid production and enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis. TLR4 polymorphism analysis demonstrated a significant association between the TLR4 rs4986790 variant and responsiveness to the fermented food-probiotic regimen, with carriers exhibiting greater butyrate receptor activation and reduced inflammatory markers. ELISA quantification of interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha confirmed a 34% reduction in systemic inflammation among participants with the TLR4 rs4986790 allele. These findings suggest a gene-diet-microbiome interplay in modulating the gut-brain axis, highlighting the potential of personalized probiotic and fermented food interventions for mitigating cognitive decline through TLR4-mediated pathways.

Altered gut microbiota composition associated with depression was modulated by Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG administration, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in a murine model of major depressive disorder. C57BL/6 mice exposed to chronic social defeat stress exhibited reduced gut microbiome diversity and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in colonic tissue, alongside behavioral deficits in forced swim and tail suspension tests. Oral L. rhamnosus GG supplementation restored Bifidobacterium abundance, suppressed interleukin-6 (IL-6) expression via real-time PCR, and normalized serotonin transporter (5-HTT) mRNA in hippocampus. These effects correlated with reduced anhedonia and improved exploratory behavior, suggesting a mechanism involving gut microbiota-induced modulation of central nervous system inflammation. The study highlights the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in ameliorating depressive symptoms through metagenomic profiling of microbial-immune interactions.

Altered serotonin signaling in the gut microbiota of patients with chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction reveals a dysregulated TPH1 expression and microbial dysbiosis, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for motility disorders. Analysis of mucosa-associated microbiota via next generation sequencing (NGS) of the V3-V4 region of 16S rRNA in 7 patients with Pediatric chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (PIPO) identified significant shifts in microbial biodiversity and network complexity compared to controls. Concurrent qPCR of serotonin-related genes (TPH1, SLC6A4, 5-HTR3, 5-HTR4) in duodenum and colon biopsies uncovered reduced TPH1 transcript levels in PIPO patients, correlating with decreased microbial diversity. These findings suggest a bidirectional interaction between gut microbiota and intestinal serotonin pathways, where 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) synthesis may be compromised by dysbiosis, exacerbating propulsive motility impairment. The correlation analysis between microbial composition and TPH1 expression further implicates microbiota-driven modulation of serotoninergic signaling in PIPO pathogenesis. This study underscores the role of microbiota-gene interactions in intestinal motility disorders, offering novel avenues for microbiota-targeted therapies or pharmacologic modulation of serotonin-related pathways.
