metadata.abstract: Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlated with changes in anxiety-like behavior in mice following administration of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, as revealed by multivariate regression analysis. Bifidobacterium longum abundance increased significantly in treated groups, while Escherichia coli decreased, alongside reduced serotonin levels in the amygdala. Microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids were implicated in modulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression via qPCR. Male C57BL/6 mice received daily doses of the supplement for six weeks, with behavioral assessments using the open field test and forced swim test. Principal component analysis highlighted a strong association between microbial diversity indices and reduced anxiety-like behavior, suggesting a mechanistic link between probiotic-induced microbial shifts and neurobehavioral outcomes. Butyrate production by Blautia species showed the highest correlation with improved emotional regulation, as measured by neurotensin levels in serum. These findings underscore the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to modulate gut-brain communication through multivariate biomarker profiling, offering novel therapeutic avenues for neurodegenerative disorders.

A novel gene variant in Tlr5 was identified as a key mediator of gut microbiota-driven neuroinflammation in murine models of neurodegenerative disorders. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we demonstrated that Bacteroides fragilis abundance correlated with Tlr5 expression levels in the hippocampus, while Escherichia coli showed inverse associations. Short-chain fatty acids derived from commensal bacteria were found to modulate Tlr5-dependent signaling pathways, as revealed by Western blot analysis. Application of random forest machine learning to longitudinal metagenomic datasets predicted a 38% reduction in neuroinflammation severity when Tlr5 was knocked out in transgenic mice. These findings were corroborated by quantitative PCR validation of Tlr5 transcripts in colonic tissue samples. Notably, dietary intervention with prebiotic fiber restored microbial diversity and normalized Tlr5 expression, suggesting a potential therapeutic axis targeting Tlr5-mediated immune responses in Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease models.

Modifications in the gut microbiota composition, as assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, correlate with alterations in neurobehavioral outcomes following a high-fat diet in murine models. A cohort of rodents fed a high-fat diet for eight weeks exhibited significant shifts in microbial diversity, including increased abundance of Gram-negative bacteria, which were linked to elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. Participants receiving a probiotic supplement (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG) exhibited reduced anxiety-like behaviors in open field tests, alongside normalized IL-6 levels. ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between dietary intervention and microbial composition in mitigating neuroinflammation-related symptoms. These findings highlight the potential of targeted probiotic interventions to counteract high-fat diet-induced dysbiosis and its downstream effects on central nervous system function. The integration of principal component analysis further delineated distinct microbial signatures associated with anxiety and depression phenotypes.

Dietary modulation of the gut microbiome through probiotic-rich foods has emerged as a potential strategy to influence neurobehavioral outcomes in individuals with metabolic syndrome. A pilot study employing fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in conjunction with a 12-week probiotic-rich food intervention revealed significant alterations in microbiome composition and associated cognitive function. Participants receiving FMT combined with a diet high in fermented dairy products exhibited increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, alongside reduced inflammation markers in colonic tissue. Behavioral assessments using neurocognitive testing indicated improved executive function and reduced anxiety-like behavior compared to controls receiving only placebo food or FMT alone. Metagenomic analysis highlighted shifts in microbial pathways linked to short-chain fatty acid production, which correlated with enhanced hippocampal neuroplasticity. These findings suggest a synergistic effect between dietary interventions and microbiome-targeted therapies in modulating the gut-brain axis. The integration of 16S rRNA sequencing with longitudinal dietary assessments provided mechanistic insights into how prebiotic fibers and FMT interact to restore microbial balance. This approach underscores the potential of combining precision microbiome interventions with tailored nutritional strategies to address neurobehavioral comorbidities in metabolic disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition induced by specific dietary interventions significantly modulate neuroinflammatory responses and cognitive function in rodents. A fermented food diet enriched with probiotic strains was shown to enhance the abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria while suppressing pro-inflammatory pathobionts, correlating with reduced neuroinflammation in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, the Tlr4 gene, a key mediator of immune signaling, exhibited attenuated activation in animals receiving the probiotic-supplemented diet, coinciding with decreased cytokine production and improved spatial memory. These effects were further amplified by concomitant administration of curcumin, which upregulated Nrf2-dependent antioxidant pathways in the gut and brain. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed a shift in microbial diversity toward anti-inflammatory taxa, while immunohistochemistry confirmed reduced glial activation in the amygdala. These findings highlight the interplay between fermented food intake, probiotic modulation, and host gene expression in shaping the gut-brain axis, offering therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative disorders linked to microbial dysbiosis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are strongly associated with neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's disease (PD), highlighting the gut-brain axis as a critical pathway. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 120 PD patients and 150 healthy controls revealed distinct microbial signatures, with Bacteroides fragilis and Prevotella copri showing significant abundance shifts. Multivariate analysis identified a 34% reduction in α-diversity in PD cohorts compared to controls, correlating with elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels and increased neuroinflammation markers. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly butyrate, were inversely linked to motor symptom severity scores, suggesting potential therapeutic relevance. Metabolomics profiling further implicated tryptophan derivatives in modulating neuroinflammation, with indole-3-propionic acid showing a protective association against alpha-synuclein aggregation. Random forest models trained on microbial and metabolomic features achieved 82% accuracy in distinguishing PD cases from controls, emphasizing the predictive power of the gut microbiome in neurodegenerative disease stratification. These findings underscore the need for targeted prebiotic interventions to restore microbial balance and mitigate PD progression through the gut-brain axis.

A high-fiber diet combined with 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that specific Lactobacillus species mediate neuroprotective effects via butyrate production in a rodent model of Alzheimer's disease. Transgenic mice fed a prebiotic-rich diet exhibited reduced neuroinflammation and improved cognitive function, with gut microbiome analysis showing increased abundance of Lactobacillus reuteri. Butyrate levels correlated strongly with principal component analysis-identified clusters of SCFA-producing taxa, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary fiber, microbial metabolism, and brain health. Metabolomic profiling further confirmed elevated short-chain fatty acids in fecal samples from subjects adhering to the diet, alongside decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting gut microbiota through dietary modulation and underscore the role of multi-omics approaches in elucidating gut-brain axis interactions. The study also identified Lactobacillus reuteri as a key microbial effector, with its butyrate synthase expression upregulated by dietary fiber, offering a novel strategy for neurodegenerative disease management.

Altered expression of the Tlr4 gene correlates with microbiome shifts in colonic tissue of mouse models of irritable bowel syndrome, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. These shifts include reduced abundance of Butyricicoccus pullicolicus and elevated Bacteroides uniformis, which are linked to systemic inflammation via lipopolysaccharide-mediated signaling. Inulin supplementation normalized Tlr4 expression and restored microbial balance, mitigating colitis-induced behavioral deficits in male C57BL/6J mice. Metabolomic profiling identified increased short-chain fatty acids in supplemented groups, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota modulation and neuroinflammation reduction. These findings highlight the role of Tlr4 in gut-brain communication and support prebiotic interventions as a strategy to counteract dysbiosis-associated neurobehavioral impairment. The study also employed qPCR to quantify Tlr4 transcript levels and histological analysis to assess intestinal barrier integrity, reinforcing the interplay between microbial ecology and host immune pathways in gut-brain axis disorders.

The Tlr4 gene modulates the impact of inulin-supplemented diets on gut microbiota composition and neurobehavioral outcomes in mice. Using a 16S rRNA sequencing approach, we found that Tlr4 knockout mice fed inulin-enriched chow exhibited altered gut microbiota profiles, characterized by increased Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced Desulfovibrio levels, compared to wild-type controls. This microbial shift correlated with attenuated anxiety-like behavior in mice but paradoxically exacerbated depressive-like symptoms, as measured by open field and forced swim tests. Mechanistically, Tlr4 deletion disrupted IL-6 signaling pathways, altering the microbiome's capacity to metabolize inulin into short-chain fatty acids that regulate hippocampal neurogenesis. These findings highlight the gene-environment interaction between Tlr4 and inulin in shaping the gut-brain axis, suggesting that Tlr4-targeted therapies could personalize prebiotic interventions for neuropsychiatric disorders.

A recent study identified a novel TLR5 polymorphism associated with altered gut microbiota composition in individuals consuming fermented dairy products, suggesting a genetic-modified dietary interaction modulating neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, researchers analyzed fecal samples from 120 participants, revealing that carriers of the TLR5 rs5744551 variant exhibited heightened abundance of Bacteroides fragilis and reduced Escherichia coli compared to non-carriers. These shifts correlated with lower systemic IL-6 levels, indicating a potential mechanistic link between TLR5-mediated immune signaling and microbiota-derived anti-inflammatory metabolites. Notably, fermented dairy intake amplified the protective effect, as evidenced by increased short-chain fatty acids production in the colon of variant carriers. The findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, gut microbiota dynamics, and dietary components in shaping neuroimmune outcomes, with implications for personalized interventions targeting neurodegenerative disorders. Further validation via metabolomic profiling is required to elucidate specific pathways influenced by TLR5 and fermented dairy co-exposure.

Recent studies highlight the role of dietary modulation in shaping gut microbiota composition, influencing neuroinflammation via the gut-brain axis. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from individuals consuming a high-fiber diet supplemented with kimchi, identifying a correlation between specific microbial taxa and inflammatory gene expression. Participants with elevated levels of Lactobacillus plantarum exhibited reduced activation of the TLR4 gene, a key mediator of neuroinflammation, in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. This finding aligns with prior evidence linking probiotic-rich foods to attenuated systemic inflammation, though mechanisms remain understudied. Additionally, the gut microbiome of these individuals showed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum, which co-occurred with lower plasma levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α. Notably, multivariate ANOVA revealed that dietary intervention significantly modulated microbiota diversity and gene expression profiles, suggesting a potential therapeutic avenue for neuroinflammatory disorders. These results underscore the interplay between fermented foods, microbial metabolism, and host immune signaling, emphasizing the need for targeted microbiome-based interventions.

Modulation of the gut microbiome through dietary intervention significantly alters neuroinflammatory gene expression in patients with depression. A randomized controlled trial involving 80 participants demonstrated that supplementation with inulin, a prebiotic fiber, enhanced the abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Notably, TPH2, a key enzyme in serotonin synthesis, showed upregulated expression in participants receiving inulin, suggesting a microbiome-mediated link between dietary fiber and central nervous system function. Microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were identified as potential mediators, as their levels increased alongside TPH2 activation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that inulin intake shifted gut microbiota composition toward anti-inflammatory profiles, which were associated with improved scores on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. These findings highlight the role of prebiotic foods in modulating neurotransmitter-related genes via the gut-brain axis, offering novel therapeutic strategies for mental health disorders. The interplay between dietary fiber and TPH2 underscores the need for personalized microbiome-targeted interventions in psychiatric care.

A diet rich in blueberries and probiotic supplementation significantly modulates gut microbiota composition while enhancing cognitive resilience in aged rats subjected to chronic stress. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium alongside reduced Escherichia coli in supplemented groups. Principal component analysis identified strong associations between short-chain fatty acid production and reduced anxiety-like behaviors in hippocampal regions. Blueberry-derived anthocyanins synergized with Lactobacillus rhamnosus to restore tight junction protein expression in the intestine, mitigating stress-induced leaky gut. This was linked to elevated butyrate levels, which correlated with improved working memory and reduced glucocorticoid receptor activation in the prefrontal cortex. Metabolomic profiling further demonstrated that blueberry consumption enhanced tryptophan metabolism, increasing serotonin synthesis in the gut and brain. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of combining plant-based diets with probiotic interventions to target the gut-brain axis in neuroinflammatory and cognitive disorders.

Modulation of the gut microbiome through dietary supplementation significantly alters neurobehavioral outcomes in a murine model of stress-induced cognitive dysfunction. Administration of inulin, a prebiotic fiber, led to pronounced shifts in gut microbiota composition, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and subsequent principal component analysis of microbial diversity metrics. Mice receiving inulin exhibited reduced anxiety-like behaviors and improved spatial memory compared to controls, correlating with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which were identified as key drivers of neuroprotective signaling via metabolomic profiling. fecal microbiota transplantation from inulin-treated donors into germ-free recipients replicated these cognitive benefits, confirming microbiota-mediated mechanisms. Furthermore, multivariate regression highlighted that microbial-derived short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, were strongly associated with enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced inflammation. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of prebiotic interventions in modulating the gut-brain axis and suggest that targeted microbial modulation could offer novel strategies for treating psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.

A novel omega-3 fatty acid formulation was found to modulate gut microbiota composition in a murine model of inflammatory bowel disease, with 16S rRNA sequencing revealing significant shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios. These changes correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in the colonic mucosa, assessed via ELISA. Linear regression analysis confirmed a strong inverse relationship between omega-3 fatty acid intake and intestinal IL-6 levels (R²=0.82, p<0.001). Additionally, metabolomic profiling identified increased butyrate production, a short-chain fatty acid known to enhance blood-brain barrier integrity. These findings suggest that targeted omega-3 fatty acid supplementation may ameliorate gut-brain axis dysfunction by modulating microbiota-derived metabolites and inflammatory pathways, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative disorders linked to chronic gut inflammation. The study also highlights the utility of integrating multivariate statistical models with multi-omics approaches to elucidate complex microbiome-host interactions.

Short-chain fatty acids derived from fermented dairy and synbiotic formulations exhibit synergistic effects on gut microbiota composition and colonic neuroimmune signaling in rodent models of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using 16S rRNA sequencing and LC-MS metabolomics, we identified that Bifidobacterium longum enrichment from prebiotic fiber supplementation combined with kimchi-derived caproic acid enhanced TLR2 expression in enteric neurons, reducing visceral hypersensitivity by 42%. Butyrate levels correlated with electroencephalographic coherence in prefrontal cortex, suggesting cross-talk between gut and central nervous system via serotonin modulation. Postbiotic extracts from Lactobacillus plantarum isolated from kimchi further suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines in mesenteric lymph nodes, while fecal microbiota transplantation experiments confirmed that gut-derived valeric acid improved gastrointestinal motility in recipient mice. These findings highlight the potential of integrating fermented food metabolites with targeted microbiota interventions to restore gut-brain communication in functional gastrointestinal disorders.

A high-fat diet significantly alters gut microbiota composition and induces neuroinflammation in rats, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling data. Bacteroidetes abundance decreased while Firmicutes proportions increased, correlating with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in the hippocampus. High-fat diet exposure also reduced Bifidobacterium levels and disrupted gut-brain axis signaling via short-chain fatty acids dysregulation. Immunohistochemistry confirmed microglial activation and TNF-α upregulation in brain regions associated with depression-like behavior. MANOVA analyses further linked shifts in gut microbiota to impaired executive function and increased anxiety scores. These findings highlight the role of dietary modulation in shaping neuroimmune responses and suggest that high-fat diet-induced metabolic syndrome may exacerbate mental health disorders through microbial-mediated mechanisms. Interventions targeting gut microbiota homeostasis could thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions.

Altered expression of the MAOA gene in the gut microbiome of individuals consuming a high-fiber legume-rich diet correlates with reduced symptoms of anxiety, as revealed by multivariate logistic regression analysis. This study examined the interplay between dietary patterns, microbial gene expression, and behavioral outcomes in 320 participants with irritable bowel syndrome and comorbid anxiety disorder. Microbial metagenomic profiling identified MAOA-encoded enzymes as key modulators of tryptophan metabolism, linking legume-derived galactooligosaccharides to shifts in Bacteroidetes abundance. 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis further demonstrated that legume intake correlated with increased Akkermansia muciniphila levels, which inversely predicted anxiety severity. Short-chain fatty acids produced by Bacteroidetes were significantly higher in legume-fed groups, coinciding with elevated MAOA transcript abundance in colonic epithelial cells. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of gut microbiota through legume consumption may target MAOA-mediated pathways to alleviate anxiety symptoms, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for gastrointestinal-brain disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome associated with TLR4 gene expression correlate with behavioral changes in a murine model of neuroinflammation. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 45 C57BL/6J mice subjected to LPS-induced inflammation and compared them to control cohorts. Principal component analysis revealed distinct microbial community structures between groups, with Prevotella and Akkermansia showing significant abundance shifts. TLR4 knockdown via CRISPR-Cas9 mitigated inflammatory cytokine release in prelimbic cortex neurons, correlating with restored serotonin signaling. Metabolomic profiling identified tryptophan derivatives as key mediators linking microbial dysbiosis to neurobehavioral deficits. Multivariate regression confirmed that TLR4 expression levels predicted anxiety-like behaviors with 83% accuracy. These findings highlight the role of gut-brain axis interactions in modulating neuroinflammation pathways through TLR4-mediated signaling and suggest potential therapeutic targets for depression-related disorders.

Alterations in the TLR5 gene modulate the gut microbiome composition and neuroinflammatory responses in a mouse model of depression, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing. TLR5-deficient mice exhibited a 35% reduction in Bacteroidetes abundance and a 2.1-fold increase in Firmicutes relative to wild-type controls, accompanied by heightened pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the hippocampus. 16S rRNA gene amplification further identified shifts in short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with behavioral deficits in the open field test. Mechanistically, TLR5 signaling was found to regulate microbial-derived lipopolysaccharide uptake, which activates NF-κB-dependent pathways in enteric neurons. These findings highlight a direct link between TLR5-mediated immune surveillance and microbiota-driven neuroinflammation, suggesting that targeting TLR5 could normalize gut-brain communication in neuropsychiatric disorders. The integration of single-cell RNA sequencing with microbial profiling underscores the role of host-microbe gene interactions in shaping brain function.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with anxiety-like behaviors in rodents, suggesting potential therapeutic targets through dietary modulation. A randomized controlled trial in rodents evaluated the combined effects of a probiotic supplement containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and a fermented food intervention (fermented soybean) on gut microbial diversity and behavioral outcomes. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that both interventions increased alpha diversity and enriched Bifidobacterium relative abundance compared to controls. Behavioral assays demonstrated reduced anxiety scores in groups receiving the probiotic supplement (mean score 0.6 ± 0.2 vs. 1.4 ± 0.3 in controls, P = 0.012), with the fermented food group showing comparable improvements (0.7 ± 0.3, P = 0.018). Metabolomic profiling identified elevated tryptophan metabolites in both treatment groups, linking microbial shifts to neurochemical pathways. Notably, the probiotic supplement group exhibited enhanced gut-brain axis signaling, as evidenced by reduced neuroinflammation markers in the hippocampus. These findings highlight the synergistic potential of probiotic supplementation and fermented food intake in modulating gut microbiota-mediated mental health outcomes, warranting further clinical validation.

Alterations in gut microbiome composition are strongly associated with neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in aging populations, as revealed by whole-genome metagenomic sequencing and machine learning analysis. In a cohort of older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and age-matched cognitively healthy controls, metagenomic profiling identified distinct trans-kingdom microbial signatures, including elevated viral abundance and reduced bacterial diversity in gut samples from MCI subjects. Random forest models trained on virome-bacteriome-metabolome data demonstrated 82% accuracy in differentiating MCI cases from controls, with bacteriome-derived features contributing 63% of predictive power. Notably, Wolbachia dominance in gut microbiota correlated with neuroinflammation markers in Drosophila models, a link further validated using 16S rRNA sequencing in human cohorts. Interventional studies employing lactic acid bacteria supplementation reversed malformed eye structures in GMR-Aβ42 flies, accompanied by microbial shifts detected via high-throughput sequencing. These findings underscore the potential of integrating microbiome analytics with advanced predictive modeling to identify early biomarkers of cognitive decline and develop targeted probiotic therapies for age-related neurodegeneration.

A diet enriched with fermented dairy products and prebiotic fiber significantly altered gut microbiota composition, correlating with improved cognitive function in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Fermented dairy increased Lactobacillus abundance while prebiotic fiber enhanced Bifidobacterium levels, both linked to elevated short-chain fatty acid production. 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays revealed reduced amyloid-β plaques and improved spatial memory in APP/PS1 mice receiving the intervention. Metabolic profiling identified butyrate as a key mediator, modulating neuroinflammation via TLR4 signaling downregulation. The combination of fermented dairy and prebiotic fiber synergistically restored gut-brain communication, as evidenced by normalized gut microbiota diversity and reduced hippocampal oxidative stress markers. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeted dietary interventions in modulating gut microbiota-mediated pathways for neurodegenerative diseases.

Altered gut microbiome composition induced by a high-fat diet is associated with neuroinflammation and impaired cognitive function in mice, with 16S rRNA sequencing revealing dysbiosis marked by reduced Butyrate-producing bacteria and increased Proteobacteria. Administration of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially restored microbiota diversity and mitigated neuroinflammatory markers, as evidenced by decreased IL-6 and TNF-α levels in hippocampal tissue. This intervention also improved spatial memory performance in mice subjected to the Morris water maze, suggesting a gut-brain axis mechanism linking high-fat diet-induced microbiota shifts to central nervous system dysfunction. Metabolomic profiling via LC-MS/MS identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of the probiotic effect, with butyrate levels correlating inversely with neuroinflammation markers. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotics in counteracting high-fat diet-related neurological impairments through microbiota modulation.

Alterations in the gut microbiota associated with the TLR4 gene polymorphism significantly modulate neuroinflammatory pathways in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), linking microbial dysbiosis to central nervous system dysfunction. Using multivariate regression analysis of fecal 16S rRNA sequencing data and peripheral cytokine levels, we identified a distinct microbial signature enriched in Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis that correlated with elevated IL-6 and TNF-α in patients carrying the TLR4 Asp299Asn variant. These findings suggest that TLR4-mediated immune signaling may act as a bridge between gut microbial imbalances and systemic inflammation, exacerbating IBS-related comorbidities such as anxiety and depression. Furthermore, qPCR validation of TLR4 expression in enteric neurons revealed heightened activation in colonic mucosa samples from subjects with IBS, reinforcing the role of host-microbe interactions in disease progression. Our data underscore the potential of targeting TLR4-dependent pathways as a therapeutic strategy to mitigate neuroimmune crosstalk in gut-brain disorders, emphasizing the need for personalized interventions informed by microbial and genetic profiling.

The TLR4 gene has been implicated in modulating neuroinflammation via the gut microbiota-brain axis, yet its interplay with specific microbial taxa remains poorly defined. Using multivariate analysis on fecal metagenomic data from 120 participants with irritable bowel syndrome, we identified a significant correlation between TLR4 expression levels and the abundance of Escherichia coli, which was further stratified by dietary fiber intake. qPCR confirmed elevated TLR4 activation in individuals with low-fiber diets and high E. coli loads, coinciding with heightened serum cytokine profiles. Microbial dysbiosis associated with TLR4 upregulation was linked to increased anxiety scores, as measured by HAMD-21 assessments. MANOVA revealed that TLR4 expression interacted with Lactobacillus abundance to predict symptom severity, suggesting a mechanistic pathway where microbiota-derived lipopolysaccharides activate TLR4 signaling, exacerbating neuroinflammatory responses. These findings highlight TLR4 as a potential therapeutic target for modulating gut-brain communication in functional gastrointestinal disorders, with dietary interventions targeting E. coli or Lactobacillus showing promise in mitigating neuroimmune activation.

A novel dietary intervention combining fermented dairy products enriched with galactooligosaccharides (GOS) and resistant starch significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in rodent models of depression, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. The intervention increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, while reducing pro-inflammatory Escherichia coli levels, correlating with reduced depressive-like behavior in mice assessed via open field testing. Metabolomic analysis identified elevated short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and decreased tryptophan metabolites in treated groups, suggesting microbial-mediated neuroimmune signaling pathways. High-fiber vegetables co-administered with the supplements further amplified SCFA production, enhancing serotonin synthesis via the enteric nervous system. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of prebiotic-dietary fiber combinations in modulating the gut-brain axis, offering a mechanistically grounded approach for depression management through targeted microbial modulation.

Altered expression of the Tryptophan Hydroxylase 2 (TPH2) in the medulla oblongata correlates with microbial dysbiosis in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from fecal samples. Gut microbial taxa, including Akkermansia muciniphila and Escherichia coli, showed significant shifts in abundance between IBS patients (n = 45) and healthy controls (n = 40), with tryptophan-derived metabolites like 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) exhibiting inverse correlations to TPH2 expression levels. Canonical correlation analysis further linked serotonin transporter (SLC6A4) polymorphisms to reduced Bacteroidetes diversity, suggesting a bidirectional regulatory loop between host neurochemistry and microbial metabolism. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated indole-3-acetic acid in IBS patients, which co-occurred with TPH2 downregulation and higher variance inflation factors in genome-wide association studies. These findings highlight the role of TPH2 as a potential therapeutic target and underscore the value of integrating multivariate statistical frameworks to dissect gut-brain interactions in functional gastrointestinal disorders.

Curcumin, a polyphenolic compound derived from turmeric, significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and reduced inflammatory bowel disease severity in a rodent model via multivariate analysis of microbial metabolic pathways. Curcumin treatment altered Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratios and enriched Prevotella abundance, correlating with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α). 16S rRNA sequencing revealed distinct microbial community shifts, while principal component analysis highlighted short-chain fatty acid production as a key mediator of intestinal homeostasis. Curcumin-induced butyrate-producing bacteria proliferation was confirmed using metabolomics, with butyrate levels inversely linked to colonic inflammation markers via canonical correlation analysis. These findings suggest curcumin as a promising nutraceutical for targeting gut-brain axis dysregulation in autoimmune disorders, with machine learning models further validating its predictive efficacy in microbial-immune interactions.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are linked to Alzheimer’s disease progression, with specific microbial taxa exhibiting significant correlations with neuroinflammatory markers. Analysis of fecal samples from patients with mild Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and age-matched controls revealed distinct gut microbiome profiles using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing. Akkermansia muciniphila abundance was notably elevated in AD patients, while Bifidobacterium levels showed paradoxical increases compared to controls. These findings were validated via linear discriminant analysis (LDA), which identified 23 microbial taxa with differential abundance between groups. Further, amyloid-beta 42 deposition in the hippocampus correlated with reduced short-chain fatty acid-producing species, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota dysbiosis and neurodegeneration. Western blotting confirmed elevated phospho-Tau and TNF-α levels in AD patients, while ELISA detected systemic inflammation markers. The gut-brain axis appears to modulate disease severity through microbial metabolites and inflammatory pathways, highlighting potential therapeutic targets for AD intervention.

A diet enriched with probiotic supplementation and fermented kimchi significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, correlating with improved cognitive function in a murine model of neuroinflammation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed elevated Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance alongside reduced Escherichia coli in supplemented groups, while principal component analysis highlighted distinct clustering of microbial profiles between treatment cohorts. Short-chain fatty acid production, measured via gas chromatography, correlated with decreased hippocampal inflammation markers TNF-α and IL-6 in treated animals. Notably, subjects consuming fermented kimchi exhibited enhanced serotonin synthesis in enteric neurons, suggesting microbial metabolites may mediate neuroprotective effects. These findings underscore the potential of probiotics and fermented foods as adjuncts in modulating gut-brain axis signaling, with multivariate regression models identifying Lactobacillus abundance as a key predictor of cognitive outcomes. The study supports further investigation into targeted microbial interventions for neurodegenerative conditions.

A recent study identified a correlation between gut microbiota composition and cognitive function in mice fed a high-fiber diet, with principal component analysis revealing distinct microbial signatures in animals consuming oat-based feed compared to standard chow. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from these cohorts showed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus in the high-fiber group, alongside reduced Proteobacteria levels. Behavioral testing demonstrated improved spatial memory and reduced anxiety-like behaviors in oat-fed mice, effects that were partially reversed by antibiotic treatment or fecal microbiota transplantation from control animals. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, correlated strongly with cognitive performance metrics, as measured by multivariate linear regression. Mechanistically, SCFAs-mediated activation of hippocampal GABAergic neurons was implicated via in situ hybridization and electrophysiological recording. These findings highlight the role of dietary fiber in shaping the gut microbiome to modulate neurobehavioral outcomes through microbial metabolite signaling pathways.

The gut microbiome’s dysregulation in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) correlates with altered neuroimmune signaling, as revealed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples from 120 patients and 80 controls. Fecal microbiota diversity was significantly lower in IBS groups, with Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes ratios skewed toward Firmicutes dominance. Principal component analysis identified three microbial taxa—Escherichia coli, Blautia, and Akkermansia muciniphila—as key drivers of intergroup differences. Short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, inversely correlated with IBS symptom severity (r² = 0.31, p = 0.002). Microbial dysbiosis was further linked to colonic inflammation markers, including elevated IL-6 and TNF-α levels. Probiotic intervention with Lactobacillus rhamnosus partially restored microbial balance, reducing IBS-specific serotonin dysregulation in enteric neurons. These findings underscore the gut-brain axis’s role in IBS pathophysiology, suggesting targeted modulation of gut microbiota as a therapeutic strategy.

The gut-brain axis mediates bidirectional communication between intestinal microbiota and central nervous system function, with emerging evidence linking specific dietary patterns to alterations in microbial composition and neurochemical signaling. A cohort study employing principal component analysis revealed that individuals consuming a high-fiber diet exhibited distinct gut microbiota profiles characterized by elevated Bifidobacterium abundance and reduced Escherichia coli levels compared to controls. These shifts correlated with increased plasma concentrations of tryptophan, a precursor for serotonin synthesis, and altered expression of the TPH2 gene, which encodes tryptophan hydroxylase 2, a key enzyme in serotonergic pathway regulation. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified a positive association between short-chain fatty acid production and cognitive performance metrics, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and brain function. The findings underscore the role of dietary modulation in shaping microbial communities that influence neurochemical pathways, with implications for therapeutic strategies targeting the gut-brain axis in conditions like depression and neurodegenerative disorders.

A diet enriched with fermented vegetables significantly modulated gut microbial composition and attenuated neuroinflammation in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples. Kimchi, a traditional Korean fermented food, was administered to C57BL/6J mice fed a high-fat diet to assess its impact on gut microbiota diversity and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundances increased in kimchi-fed groups, while pro-inflammatory Enterobacteriaceae decreased, correlating with reduced astrocytic activation in hippocampal regions. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing further identified Parabacteroides distasonis as a keystone species associated with cognitive improvement, its metabolites potentially modulating microglial polarization via Tlr2-dependent pathways. Concurrently, short-chain fatty acids production, particularly butyrate, rose in kimchi-fed mice, aligning with enhanced intestinal barrier integrity and reduced lipopolysaccharide translocation. These findings suggest that fermented foods like kimchi may serve as adjuncts in mitigating neurodegenerative risk by reshaping the gut-brain axis through microbiota-directed metabolic reprogramming, offering a novel strategy for neuroinflammatory disorders management.

The gut microbiota plays a critical role in modulating neurodegenerative diseases through metabolic pathways influenced by GCN2-mediated stress responses, with dietary interventions showing potential to alter this axis. A fermented wheat germ formulation enriched in gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) was evaluated for its capacity to modulate intestinal microbial communities and neuroinflammation in a rodent model of chronic stress. Wheat germ, a nutrient-dense byproduct of cereal processing, was fermented with Lactobacillus plantarum to enhance bioavailability of tryptophan metabolites and GABA. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that fermented wheat germ increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while reducing pro-inflammatory Escherichia coli in the colonic lumen. Concurrently, GCN2 expression in the hippocampus correlated with reduced quorum sensing signals from Proteobacteria, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut microbiota remodeling and neuroprotection. Behavioral assays demonstrated improved anxiety-like behaviors and enhanced serotonin synthesis in treated animals, with ANOVA confirming significant differences in tryptophan catabolism rates. These findings highlight the potential of fermented wheat germ as a functional food to target GCN2-regulated pathways in the gut-brain axis, offering a novel strategy for mitigating stress-related neurodegeneration.

A novel probiotic formulation targeting gut microbiota dysbiosis was shown to mitigate neuroinflammation and cognitive decline in preclinical models of Alzheimer's disease. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we demonstrated that SLAB51 enriched short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, including Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, while reducing pro-inflammatory Escherichia coli abundance in C57BL/6J mice subjected to amyloid-β infusion. Concurrently, immunohistochemistry revealed decreased tau phosphorylation and Aβ plaque deposition in hippocampal regions of treated animals compared to controls. ELISA analysis further confirmed reduced serum levels of IL-6 and TNF-α, markers of systemic inflammation, correlating with improved performance in Y-maze and novel object recognition tests. Mechanistically, SLAB51 enhanced SCFA-mediated activation of GPR43 receptors in enteric neurons, promoting microbiota-brain communication via the vagus nerve. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic interventions in modulating gut-brain axis dysfunction linked to neurodegeneration, supported by molecular profiling and behavioral assays.

Blueberry consumption significantly modulated BDNF expression in rodent models of depression, with effects mediated by shifts in gut microbiota composition. Using principal component analysis (PCA), we identified distinct microbial profiles in high-fat diet-fed mice supplemented with blueberry extract compared to controls, revealing increased abundance of Lactobacillus and decreased Desulfovibrionaceae. BDNF upregulation correlated with reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) in hippocampus, suggesting a mechanistic link between blueberry-induced microbial changes and neuroplasticity. 16S rRNA sequencing further highlighted permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) as critical in distinguishing treatment groups, while anthocyanin metabolites from blueberry were detected in serum and correlated with BDNF promoter activation. These findings underscore the potential of blueberry-derived compounds to target BDNF pathways via microbiome modulation, offering a novel strategy for depressive disorder management.

A high-fiber fermented food regimen combined with probiotic supplementation significantly altered the gut microbiota composition in rodent models of neuroinflammation, mitigating hippocampal neurodegeneration. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified elevated abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced Proteobacteria in mice fed fermented dairy and synbiotic formulations compared to controls. These shifts correlated with decreased lipopolysaccharide translocation and reduced IL-6 expression in the blood-brain barrier, alongside improved performance in novel object recognition assays. Short-chain fatty acids derived from fiber fermentation were implicated in modulating TLR4-mediated signaling pathways, while probiotic-induced microbial diversity enhanced intestinal barrier integrity. ANOVA confirmed significant differences in anxiety-like behaviors (p < 0.05) between groups, highlighting the synergistic role of fermented food and probiotics in neuroprotection via the gut-brain axis. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions targeting microbial metabolism to alleviate neuroinflammatory disorders.

Modulation of TLR4 expression in gut-derived gut microbiota-sensitive macrophages significantly alters inflammatory signaling pathways linked to depression via the gut-brain axis. Using CRISPR-based gene editing, we targeted TLR4 in murine macrophages co-cultured with fecal microbiota from patients with major depressive disorder, revealing a 34% reduction in pro-inflammatory IL-6 secretion following TLR4 knockdown. Quantitative PCR confirmed downregulation of NF-κB activation in treated cells, correlating with decreased cytokine release and improved behavioral outcomes in mice subjected to chronic stress. Concurrent metagenomic sequencing identified Prevotella as a key modulator of TLR4-mediated signaling, with its abundance inversely linked to serotonin transporter (SLC6A4) expression in hippocampal neurons. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4 and gut microbiota in shaping neuroinflammatory states, suggesting targeted modulation of TLR4 as a potential therapeutic strategy for depressive disorders.

Alterations in the gut microbiome are linked to depressive symptoms through dysregulated neuroimmune signaling. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing on fecal samples from 150 participants, we identified Bacteroides and Faecalibacterium as key modulators of tryptophan metabolism, a pathway implicated in mood regulation. Principal component analysis revealed that microbial diversity correlated inversely with symptom severity (r = -0.42, p < 0.01), while logistic regression confirmed Prevotella abundance as an independent predictor of treatment response. These findings highlight the utility of gut microbial profiling in personalized psychiatry and underscore the need for interventions targeting enterotype-specific imbalances to mitigate depression progression. Additionally, short-chain fatty acids derived from gut microbiota showed significant associations with hippocampal volume, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between microbial metabolites and neuroplasticity. The integration of metabolomic profiling with machine learning further enabled classification of clinical subgroups with 89% accuracy, emphasizing the value of multi-omics approaches in elucidating gut-brain axis dynamics.

A 15-week dietary fiber-deficient regimen in mice induced cognitive deficits, linked to altered gut microbiota and hippocampal proteomic changes. Hippocampal proteomic analysis revealed reduced CaMKIId and synaptic proteins, alongside neuroinflammation, in animals fed a fiber-deficient diet. Multivariate regression analysis confirmed strong associations between gut microbiota dysbiosis—marked by decreased Bacteroidetes and increased Proteobacteria—and impaired object location memory. Intestinal barrier dysfunction and reduced short-chain fatty acid production were also observed, with oral SCFA supplementation mitigating some cognitive deficits. These findings underscore the role of gut microbiota in modulating hippocampal synaptic integrity via dietary modulation, highlighting fiber as a critical determinant of brain health. The study further implicates SCFA signaling pathways as therapeutic targets for diet-related cognitive decline, emphasizing the need to integrate microbiome profiling with nutritional strategies in neurodegenerative disease prevention.

metadata.abstract: A recent study demonstrated that modulation of the gut microbiota via a prebiotic-rich formulation significantly altered neurobehavioral outcomes in a rodent model of neurodevelopmental disorder, with effects mediated by 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomic profiling. The intervention involved administering the prebiotic alongside a diet enriched in fiber-dense plant-based components, which enhanced microbial diversity and suppressed pro-inflammatory metabolites in the intestine. Concurrently, electrophysiological recordings revealed normalized excitatory/inhibitory balance in the hippocampus, correlating with reduced autistic-like behaviors. Notably, resistant starch intake synergized with the prebiotic to elevate butyrate production, a key short-chain fatty acid implicated in brain plasticity. These findings highlight the potential of targeted microbiota-modulating interventions combined with specific nutrient sources to restore gut-brain communication, as validated by multivariate statistical modeling of microbial-community dynamics. The study underscores the interplay between dietary composition, microbial metabolism, and neurological function, offering a novel framework for therapeutic strategies in neurodevelopmental conditions.

A novel dietary intervention targeting the gut-brain axis has been shown to modulate inflammatory pathways via microbial metabolic reprogramming in rodent models. Kimchi-derived probiotics significantly enhanced the abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium while suppressing Enterobacteriaceae, correlating with reduced systemic IL-17 levels. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that short-chain fatty acids production was upregulated, particularly butyrate, which activated NOD2-mediated signaling to dampen neuroinflammation. Behavioral assays demonstrated improved anxiety-like behaviors and spatial memory in transgenic mice with Alzheimer's disease-related pathology. Concurrently, butyrate treatment increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus, linking microbial metabolites to synaptic plasticity. Kimchi supplementation also altered the gut microbiome's functional profile, enriching pathways for tryptophan metabolism and glutathione synthesis, which may mitigate oxidative stress in the enteric nervous system. These findings highlight the interplay between fermented foods, microbial ecology, and immune-related genes in modulating brain function through the gut-brain axis.

Altered gut microbiota composition correlates with heightened anxiety symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), prompting investigation into microbial modulation via shotgun metagenomics-guided interventions. A 12-week trial evaluated the efficacy of probiotic supplementation (containing Lactobacillus plantarum) combined with a fermented soy-based diet (natto) in 84 adults with concurrent IBS and anxiety disorder. Participants were randomized to receive either the intervention or a placebo, with 16S rRNA sequencing performed at baseline and post-treatment. The intervention group exhibited significant reductions in anxiety scores (−32% vs. −8% in placebo) alongside increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa (Bacteroides, Prevotella). Butyrate levels in fecal samples correlated with improvements in gut permeability markers, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolic products and central nervous system regulation. Notably, natto consumption was associated with higher microbial diversity indices, reinforcing the role of dietary fermentation in microbiota resilience. These findings underscore the potential of targeted microbial modulation via probiotics and fermented foods to alleviate comorbid gastrointestinal and psychiatric conditions.

A novel mutation in the LRRK2 gene was identified as a significant contributor to Parkinson's disease progression through integration of CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing and quantitative PCR analysis of dopaminergic neuron viability in mice. Using a two-way ANOVA to compare striatal dopamine levels across genotypes, researchers observed a 42% reduction in neurotransmitter availability in LRRK2-mutant models compared to controls, correlating with accelerated neurodegeneration. Co-expression networks derived from RNA-seq data revealed interactions between LRRK2 and PINK1 in mitochondrial dysfunction pathways, validated via immunoblotting of phosphorylated ubiquitin. The study also employed in vivo optogenetics to map synaptic connectivity in mutant versus wild-type substantia nigra regions, identifying disrupted glutamatergic signaling as a downstream effect. These findings establish LRRK2 as a therapeutic target, with implications for developing small-molecule inhibitors targeting its kinase activity. The multivariate regression models further highlighted age and alpha-synuclein aggregation as covariates modulating disease severity, underscoring the need for personalized intervention strategies. This work bridges genetic, biochemical, and electrophysiological approaches to elucidate mechanistic pathways in neurodegeneration.

Alterations in the gut microbiome mediated by Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) signaling significantly correlate with neuroinflammatory outcomes in rodent models of metabolic syndrome. A probiotic intervention targeting Lactobacillus rhamnosus attenuated systemic endotoxemia and reduced cognitive deficits following high-fat diet-induced obesity. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct gut microbial profiles associated with TLR4 expression levels in hippocampal astrocytes, linking gut-derived short-chain fatty acids to modulated blood-brain barrier permeability. Probiotic administration restored microbial diversity and suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokine production in colonic tissues, while TLR4 knockout mice exhibited reduced neuroinflammation independent of dietary treatment. These findings highlight the interplay between TLR4-mediated signaling, gut microbiota composition, and probiotic efficacy in mitigating neurological dysfunction linked to metabolic dysregulation.

The gut-brain axis modulates neurobehavioral outcomes through bidirectional communication involving TPH2-mediated serotonin synthesis and microbial metabolite signaling. A metabolomics analysis of fecal samples from 120 participants revealed that Bacteroides fragilis-derived secondary bile acids correlated with Spearman correlation-identified reductions in serotonin transporter expression in the gastrointestinal tract. TPH2 polymorphisms were associated with altered gut microbiome diversity, particularly in individuals with major depressive disorder, where 16S rRNA sequencing detected increased abundance of Escherichia coli and decreased Akkermansia muciniphila. Multivariate principal component analysis linked tryptophan catabolism by Enterococcus faecalis to elevated quorum sensing molecules, which inversely correlated with TPH2 transcript levels. These findings highlight the interplay between host gene expression, microbial metabolic pathways, and neuroinflammatory markers in mental health disorders, suggesting targeted probiotic interventions could restore gut-brain homeostasis by modulating TPH2-dependent serotonin signaling.

Alterations in the gut microbiome significantly correlate with neuroinflammatory markers in patients with major depressive disorder, with TNF-mediated signaling pathways emerging as a key mediator. Using multivariate regression analysis, we identified a strong association between Prevotella copri abundance and elevated IL-6 levels in colonic tissues, alongside reduced expression of the BDNF gene in hippocampal neurons. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that gut microbiota dysbiosis, characterized by a shift in Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio, was linked to impaired serotonin synthesis via TPH2 downregulation. Short-chain fatty acids derived from Butyricimonas fermentation were inversely correlated with depressive symptoms scores, as measured by the HAMD-17 scale. Principal component analysis further highlighted the interplay between microbial metabolic profiles and ACE2 expression in modulating neuroinflammation pathways. These findings underscore the role of immune-related genes and microbial metabolites in linking gut-brain communication to mood disorders, suggesting potential therapeutic targets for microbiome-based interventions.

Multiple sclerosis progression is linked to dysregulated gut microbiota interactions with the central nervous system, as demonstrated by 16S rRNA sequencing revealing reduced Akkermansia muciniphila abundance in C57BL/6J mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. Principal component analysis of fecal metabolomic profiles identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of TNF-α-driven neuroinflammation, with butyrate levels inversely correlating to IL-17A expression in colonic tissue. Bacteroides fragilis supplementation normalized TNF-α signaling via modulation of TLR4 phosphorylation in microglia, as evidenced by Western blot analysis. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted interventions in mitigating neuroinflammation through metabolic reprogramming of immune pathways.

Altered gut microbiota composition in Alzheimer's disease (AD) models correlates with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the hippocampus, suggesting a link between intestinal dysbiosis and neurodegeneration. Lactobacillus reuteri supplementation in APP/PS1 transgenic mice reduced interleukin-6 expression and improved spatial memory retention, as measured by two-way ANOVA. Concurrent blueberry intake further modulated gut microbiota diversity, increasing Akkermansia muciniphila abundance and decreasing Escherichia coli in fecal samples. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Lactobacillus reuteri synergized with blueberry polyphenols to suppress lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced microglial activation. Principal component analysis of hippocampal gene expression profiles highlighted downregulation of Trem2 and Apoe in supplemented groups, aligning with reduced neuroinflammatory markers. These findings underscore the potential of combined probiotic and polyphenol-rich diets to mitigate AD-related neuroinflammation through microbiome remodeling, offering a novel therapeutic strategy targeting the gut-brain axis.

Dietary interventions targeting fiber-rich foods significantly modulate gut microbiome composition, as revealed by principal component analysis of fecal 16S rRNA sequencing data. A cohort of adults with major depressive disorder underwent a 12-week regimen of prebiotic-rich diets containing inulin and fructooligosaccharides, alongside a control group receiving standard dietary advice. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, in participants consuming the prebiotic-rich foods, correlating with reduced depressive symptoms measured via the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) confirmed that microbial taxa such as Bifidobacterium and Prevotella showed significant shifts in abundance, with Bifidobacterium positively associated with butyrate levels. These findings suggest that dietary modulation of gut microbiota via prebiotic-rich foods may enhance neuroinflammatory pathways, as evidenced by decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in serum samples. The study underscores the role of fiber intake in shaping microbial metabolites that influence mental health disorders through the gut-brain axis, with implications for personalized nutritional therapies in psychiatric care.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are increasingly linked to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease (AD), with emerging evidence pointing to blueberry-derived polyphenols as modulators of microbial metabolism. Using principal component analysis (PCA) on 16S rRNA sequencing data, we identified distinct microbial signatures in patients with AD consuming a curcumin-enriched regimen compared to controls. The Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlated inversely with cognitive decline, while Bacteroides levels rose in response to blueberry intake. Metabolic profiling revealed increased short-chain fatty acid production, particularly butyrate, in groups receiving both curcumin and blueberry supplements, suggesting synergistic effects on intestinal barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of combining curcumin with blueberry-based diets to target AD-associated dysbiosis through microbial metabolic reprogramming, warranting further validation in longitudinal clinical trials.

16S rRNA sequencing revealed that Curcuma longa extract, when combined with fermented kimchi, significantly altered the gut microbiota in older adults with metabolic syndrome. The intervention, administered daily for 12 weeks, increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance by 42% while reducing Escherichia coli levels by 31%, as determined by qPCR. Concurrently, participants exhibited improved Mini-Mental State Examination scores, with a 15% increase in visuospatial memory retention. Kimchi's polyphenolic content, synergized with curcumin, enhanced Lactobacillus proliferation and suppressed pro-inflammatory Enterobacteriaceae taxa. Metabolomic profiling identified elevated short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with reduced systemic inflammation markers. The study underscores the potential of phytochemical-rich supplements paired with fermented foods to modulate the gut-brain axis, offering a dual-targeted approach for neurodegenerative disorders linked to dysbiosis.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition are increasingly linked to neuroinflammatory processes in multiple sclerosis, with emerging evidence suggesting that curcumin modulates this interaction. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) and healthy controls to assess microbial shifts following curcumin supplementation. Tlr4 expression levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells were quantified via qPCR, revealing a significant downregulation in RRMS subjects after 12 weeks of treatment. Curcumin administration correlated with increased abundance of Blautia and Parabacteroides, alongside reduced pro-inflammatory lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation markers. Gut microbiota diversity, measured via Simpson’s index, showed a trend toward normalization in the curcumin group, although this did not reach statistical significance. Functional pathway analysis highlighted enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, potentially mediating anti-inflammatory effects through Tlr4-dependent signaling. These findings suggest that curcumin may ameliorate neuroinflammation by reshaping the gut microbiota and modulating host immune responses, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for multiple sclerosis management.

A high-fiber diet modulated gut microbiota and mitigated neuroinflammation via altered expression of the TREM2 gene in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Flaxseed supplementation, administered at 10% w/w, significantly increased fecal short-chain fatty acid levels while reducing systemic lipopolysaccharide translocation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed elevated abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, correlating with decreased microglial activation in the hippocampus. Pearson correlation analysis identified a strong inverse relationship between butyrate concentrations and TREM2 expression in APP/PS1 transgenic mice, suggesting microbiota-derived metabolites as mediators of neuroimmune regulation. Immunohistochemistry confirmed reduced Aβ plaques and phosphorylated tau in treated animals. These findings highlight the role of dietary fiber in shaping the gut-brain axis through microbiota-gene interactions, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative conditions.

The gut microbiome's modulation of depression severity through dietary interventions was explored using 16S rRNA sequencing to profile microbial shifts in adults consuming fermented kimchi alongside prebiotic fiber. Participants (n=120) were stratified by baseline major depressive disorder symptom scores, with microbial α-diversity and taxa abundance correlated to clinical outcomes after 12 weeks. Kimchi intake significantly increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus levels, while prebiotic fiber supplementation amplified Akkermansia muciniphila abundance. Metagenomic pathway analysis revealed enhanced short-chain fatty acid production in gut microbiota of responders, linked to reduced serotonin metabolite dysregulation. Non-responders exhibited persistent gut dysbiosis despite kimchi consumption, highlighting the need for combined prebiotic and fermented food strategies. Machine learning models integrating microbial data with dietary adherence predicted treatment outcomes with 89% accuracy, underscoring the interplay between intestinal flora composition and nutritional modulation in depressive symptoms management. These findings suggest targeted prebiotic and fermented food interventions could optimize gut-brain axis therapies for patients with depression.

A significant correlation was observed between high-fiber food consumption and altered gut microbiota composition in individuals with depression, revealing potential bidirectional interactions between dietary patterns and mental health. Using principal component analysis, researchers identified distinct microbial profiles in participants adhering to fiber-rich diets, characterized by elevated abundance of Prevotella and reduced levels of Bacteroides. These shifts were associated with decreased inflammatory markers and improved serotonin signaling pathways, suggesting a mechanistic link between dietary intake of whole grains and neuroimmune regulation. Notably, microbial diversity remained stable across groups, yet specific taxa correlated with symptom severity, highlighting the importance of microbial functional redundancy. The study also detected higher levels of short-chain fatty acids in individuals consuming fermented dairy, implicating butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium in mood modulation. These findings underscore the role of dietary interventions in reshaping gut-brain axis dynamics, offering novel therapeutic strategies for mental health disorders through microbiota-targeted approaches.

Prebiotic fiber supplementation modulated gut microbiota composition and improved cognitive function in aged C57BL/6 mice subjected to lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation, with blueberry-enriched diets demonstrating enhanced efficacy. Principal component analysis revealed distinct clustering of microbial taxa associated with butyrate production, particularly Bacteroides and Lactobacillus, correlating with reduced neuroinflammation markers in hippocampal tissue. Prebiotic fiber intake increased short-chain fatty acid levels, while blueberry polyphenols augmented BDNF expression, synergistically restoring synaptic plasticity. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified Parabacteroides as a key mediator of gut-brain axis signaling, linking dietary intervention to behavioral recovery. These findings underscore the interplay between prebiotic supplementation, polyphenol-rich diets, and microbial-derived metabolites in mitigating age-related cognitive decline, highlighting multivariate analysis as a critical tool for disentangling mechanistic pathways.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition significantly correlate with neuroinflammation in patients with Alzheimer's disease, as revealed by metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples. A diet enriched in fermented dairy and fiber demonstrated dose-dependent modulation of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus populations, alongside reductions in plasma IL-6 and TNF-α levels. 16S rRNA sequencing further identified shifts in microbial metabolic pathways associated with short-chain fatty acid production, which inversely correlated with cognitive decline scores. Intervention with prebiotic-enriched meals normalized Aβ plaque burden in APP/PS1 mice by enhancing gut microbiota-derived butyrate signaling via the TLR4 pathway. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of dietary modulation in targeting colonic dysbiosis to mitigate neurodegeneration through the gut-brain axis, with fermented foods emerging as a viable strategy to restore neuroimmune homeostasis.

Alterations in IL-6 expression within the central nervous system correlate with shifts in gut microbiota composition, suggesting a mechanistic link between inflammation and cognitive decline. A probiotic blend containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum was administered to aged C57BL/6J mice exhibiting early-stage Alzheimer's disease pathology. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed increased abundance of prevotellaceae and reduced firmicutes in treated animals, alongside decreased tau phosphorylation in the hippocampus. A random forest analysis of metabolomic profiles identified short-chain fatty acids as key mediators of the probiotic effect, with butyrate levels correlating inversely with IL-6 transcript abundance (P < 0.01). These findings highlight the role of IL-6-mediated neuroinflammation in modulating gut-brain axis signaling and suggest that probiotic interventions could mitigate disease progression by restoring microbial homeostasis. The random forest model further validated that microbial-derived butyrate concentrations predicted cognitive performance with 82% accuracy, underscoring its potential as a therapeutic target.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition and expression of the NOD2 gene were identified in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) following intervention with the Lactobacillus rhamnosus. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed a significant shift in microbial diversity, marked by reduced Bacteroidetes and increased Firmicutes abundance, correlating with diminished pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Serum IL-6 concentrations decreased by 38% (p < 0.01) in the supplemented group, alongside upregulated TLR4 expression in intestinal epithelial cells, suggesting modulated immune signaling. Fecal short-chain fatty acid profiles revealed elevated butyrate production, potentially mediated by Blautia expansion, which aligned with improved colonic mucosal integrity assessed via histomorphometry. The Lactobacillus rhamnosus also induced PPARγ activation in enterocytes, linking microbiota-derived metabolites to transcriptional changes in intestinal barrier function. These findings highlight the interplay between microbial dysbiosis, immune gene regulation, and therapeutic interventions in IBS, underscoring the potential of targeted probiotic strategies to restore gut-brain axis homeostasis through molecular profiling of host-microbe interactions.

The interplay between genetic factors and dietary intake has been shown to modulate gut microbiota composition, influencing neurobehavioral outcomes in rodent models. EphB6 deletion in mice led to impaired social interaction and altered gut microbiota profiles, with high-fiber diets mitigating these effects by enhancing Bacteroidetes abundance. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that fiber supplementation restored short-chain fatty acid production, which correlated with improved hippocampal neurogenesis. EphB6-deficient mice exhibited heightened glutamate levels in the prefrontal cortex, a change counteracted by prebiotic-rich interventions. These findings highlight EphB6’s role in mediating gut-brain communication and suggest that dietary modulation of fiber intake could serve as a therapeutic strategy for neurodevelopmental disorders linked to microbial dysbiosis.

A novel fermented garlic extract derived from Garlic significantly modulated gut microbiota composition in obese C57BL/6J mice, reducing systemic inflammation and improving insulin sensitivity. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, alongside decreased levels of Escherichia coli, correlating with reduced plasma IL-6 and CRP concentrations. The extract, rich in allicin and ajoene, was administered via oral gavage for 12 weeks, with qPCR confirming upregulation of TLR4 in colonic tissues. Concurrently, Garlic-based dietary interventions in human cohorts showed parallel shifts in gut microbiota profiles, suggesting conserved mechanisms across species. These findings highlight the potential of fermented garlic as a functional food adjunct in metabolic disease management, with metagenomic analysis underscoring its role in reshaping microbiota-driven inflammatory pathways.

The gut-brain axis modulates immune and neurological responses through microbial-derived metabolites, with emerging evidence linking specific TLR4 variants to altered inflammatory signaling in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus was administered to 60 participants with IBS, alongside a control group receiving placebo. Fecal gut microbiota profiles were analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing a significant increase in Prevotella abundance and a reduction in Bacteroides in the probiotic group. Concurrently, TLR4 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells showed decreased activation in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), correlating with reduced symptom severity. Functional annotation of differentially abundant microbial taxa highlighted pathways involving short-chain fatty acid production, which may suppress TLR4-mediated inflammation. These findings suggest that probiotic intervention can reshape gut microbiota composition and modulate TLR4 signaling, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for IBS by targeting microbial-immune interactions. The interplay between TLR4 polymorphisms and microbiota-derived signals underscores the importance of personalized approaches in gut-brain axis modulation.

Chronic consumption of fermented kimchi and supplementation with probiotic Lactobacillus reuteri altered gut microbiota composition and reduced symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome in a cohort of 120 participants. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial signatures associated with dietary interventions, revealing increased abundance of genus Lactobacillus and decreased prevalence of family Bacteroidaceae in individuals consuming both kimchi and probiotic supplements. Metagenomic sequencing highlighted enriched pathways for short-chain fatty acid production and mucosal immunity in the colon, correlating with reduced inflammatory bowel disease flare frequency. 16S rRNA sequencing further showed that probiotic intake alone increased alpha diversity by 18%, while kimchi consumption alone reduced beta diversity disparities between participants by 25%. These findings suggest synergistic effects of dietary fermentation products and targeted probiotic use in modulating gut-brain axis signaling, with implications for personalized microbiome-based therapies for gastrointestinal disorders.

Tlr5 deletion in mice alters gut microbiota composition and exacerbates neuroinflammation, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and behavioral assays. Tlr5-deficient mice exhibited reduced Bacteroidetes abundance and increased Proteobacteria, correlating with heightened proinflammatory cytokine levels in the brain. These changes were accompanied by impaired gut-brain communication, evidenced by altered serotonin metabolism and disrupted neurotransmitter signaling pathways. Metabolomic profiling further identified dysregulated short-chain fatty acids production in Tlr5-mutant mice, linking Tlr5-mediated immune recognition to microbiota-driven neuroimmune modulation. The study highlights Tlr5 as a critical sensor of gut microbial signals, with implications for targeting Tlr5-dependent pathways in neurodegenerative disorders via microbiome-targeted therapies. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetics, microbial metabolism, and central nervous system function, suggesting Tlr5 as a potential therapeutic target for modulating the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in gut microbial metabolism mediated by dietary interventions correlate with changes in host gene expression linked to neuroinflammation, as demonstrated in a cohort of participants consuming fermented dairy products enriched in short-chain fatty acids. Using multivariate analysis, we identified a significant association between TMAO upregulation and reduced gut microbiome diversity in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and systemic inflammation. Probiotic supplementation was shown to modulate IL-6 expression in intestinal epithelial cells, with qPCR confirming a 32% decrease in inflammatory cytokine production. These findings highlight the role of dietary fiber in shaping microbial-derived metabolites that influence host FOXO3 signaling pathways, which are critical for neuroprotection. Butyrate levels, measured via GC-MS, correlated inversely with depressive symptoms in patients undergoing antidepressant therapy, reinforcing the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic target. The study underscores how prebiotic-rich diets may mitigate neuroinflammatory risks through epigenetic modulation of key immune-related pathways.

Alterations in GSK-3β expression have been linked to neuroinflammation, which may be modulated by dietary interventions involving high-fiber diets and probiotic supplementation. A cohort study of 132 participants revealed that fiber-rich food intake correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines in the gut, while probiotics enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, potentially influencing GSK-3β-mediated signaling in the central nervous system. 16S rRNA sequencing identified distinct commensal bacteria profiles in individuals consuming fermented foods compared to controls, with Bifidobacterium longum showing a strong inverse association with GSK-3β phosphorylation. Multivariate regression models further indicated that omega-3 fatty acids interacted with gut-derived tryptophan metabolites to regulate GSK-3β activity, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiome-derived signals and neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of targeted nutritional strategies and fiber-based interventions to modulate GSK-3β pathways, offering novel approaches for managing neuroinflammatory conditions through the gut-brain axis.
