The integration of machine learning algorithms further refined the predictive accuracy of microbiome-based biomarkers, underscoring the potential of combining dietary data with advanced machine learning for precision health applications.

The gut-brain axis modulates depression through gut microbiota-derived metabolites, with TLR2 playing a critical role in immune signaling pathways. Using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), we demonstrated that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance correlates with reduced depressive symptoms in patients undergoing fecal microbiota transplantation. TLR2 expression levels, measured via qPCR, were significantly higher in individuals with depression and positively associated with short-chain fatty acid production by Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron. Mechanistically, TLR2 activation in enteric neurons enhanced serotonin release, as evidenced by confocal microscopy and 5-HT assays. Omega-3 fatty acids supplementation further amplified these effects, reducing inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and TNF-α while promoting microbial diversity. This study highlights the interplay between TLR2-mediated signaling, microbiota composition, and mood disorders, underscoring potential therapeutic targets for depression management through microbiota-directed interventions.

A multi-strain probiotic intervention significantly modulated gut microbiota composition and attenuated neuroinflammatory markers in a murine model of depression, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and immunohistochemical analysis. Mice subjected to chronic mild stress exhibited anxiety-like behaviors and elevated interleukin-6 levels in the prefrontal cortex, alongside reduced abundance of Lactobacillus species. Administration of probiotics containing <bacteria>Lactobacillus helveticus</bacteria> and <bacteria>Bifidobacterium longum</bacteria> restored Lactobacillus populations, suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and normalized behavioral outcomes. Metabolomic profiling further identified increased short-chain fatty acid concentrations, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbial metabolic byproducts and neuroimmune regulation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic formulations in targeting the gut-brain axis through modulation of commensal bacteria and inflammatory pathways. The integration of multi-omics approaches underscores the complexity of microbial-host interactions in psychiatric disorders, providing a framework for developing microbiota-based interventions.

Altered TLR4 gene expression in the gut mucosa correlates with microbiota dysbiosis and impaired cognitive function in individuals consuming a low-fiber diet, highlighting the interplay between genetic susceptibility, gut microbiome composition, and neurobehavioral outcomes. A cohort study integrating 16S rRNA sequencing and whole-genome profiling revealed that subjects with TLR4 polymorphisms exhibited heightened vulnerability to irritable bowel syndrome when adhering to a Western-style diet high in saturated fats. Notably, supplementation with a prebiotic fiber blend containing inulin and fructooligosaccharides significantly restored microbial diversity and mitigated cognitive deficits in these individuals, independent of baseline TLR4 variants. Mechanistically, the prebiotic enhanced short-chain fatty acid production, which in turn modulated TLR4-mediated inflammation in the hippocampus. These findings underscore the potential of microbiome-targeted interventions to counteract genetic predispositions exacerbated by modern diets, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for gut-brain axis disorders. Statistical analyses using multivariate regression confirmed that TLR4 haplotype interactions with dietary fiber intake accounted for 34% of the variance in cognitive performance metrics.

Dysregulation of the gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's disease is linked to microbial shifts influenced by dietary factors and host genetics. Our analysis revealed that a diet rich in flavonoid-containing berries correlated with increased abundance of Prevotella and reduced inflammation markers, while flavonoid supplementation in patients with a NOD2 polymorphism amplified these effects. Gut microbiota from AD subjects exhibited lower butyrate production and altered 16S rRNA sequencing profiles, with Akkermansia muciniphila levels inversely correlated to soluble amyloid-β concentrations. The NOD2 variant was associated with decreased Bifidobacterium diversity and heightened pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α in AD cohorts. Machine learning models integrating prebiotic fiber intake and omega-3 fatty acid consumption predicted cognitive decline trajectories with 82% accuracy. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetic variants, nutrient-rich diets, and microbial metabolites in modulating neurodegenerative progression, suggesting targeted microbiome interventions could mitigate AD severity through dietary and genetic stratification.

Kefir consumption combined with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and reduces neuroinflammatory markers in Alzheimer's disease models, as demonstrated through 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples. Kefir-derived lactic acid bacteria enhanced the abundance of Bifidobacterium while suppressing Escherichia coli, correlating with decreased IL-6 and TNF-α levels in the hippocampus. L. rhamnosus GG further amplified these effects by promoting short-chain fatty acid production, which was linked to improved cognitive function in APP/PS1 mice. Metabolomic profiling revealed increased butyrate and propionate concentrations, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived metabolites and reduced neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of fermented dairy products supplemented with targeted probiotics in mitigating neurodegeneration, supported by multi-omics integration of microbial and host-derived data. The study underscores the role of microbiota-host interactions in modulating brain health through immune signaling pathways and metabolic cross-talk, offering novel strategies for Alzheimer's disease intervention.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlated with dietary patterns in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, revealing a potential link between fiber-rich diets and microbial dysbiosis. Using principal component analysis, we identified that consumption of inulin-rich foods was associated with increased abundance of Bacteroides and decreased levels of Prevotella, while 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed significant shifts in microbial diversity. These findings suggest that dietary interventions targeting prebiotic fibers may modulate gut microbiome dynamics to alleviate symptoms. Additionally, short-chain fatty acids produced by Faecalibacterium showed inverse correlations with markers of intestinal permeability, highlighting their role in gut-brain communication. The study underscores the interplay between nutrition and microbial metabolites in shaping neuroimmune responses, with implications for neurological disorders linked to the gut-brain axis.

A high-fiber inulin-rich diet modulates the gut microbiota to mitigate neuroinflammation and oxidative stress in mice with Parkinson's disease (PD), an effect linked to the mcrA gene's role in methanogen metabolism. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that inulin increased Akkermansia muciniphila abundance while decreasing Prevotella levels, correlating with reduced lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation. Fecal microbiome transplantation confirmed that mcrA-expressing Methanobrevibacter smithii were enriched in mice fed inulin, and their presence correlated with higher tauroursodeoxycholic acid levels in serum. Mechanistically, mcrA expression in Methanobrevibacter smithii was upregulated by inulin-induced bile acid metabolism, which suppressed NF-κB activation and enhanced GLP-1 signaling. Targeted metabolomics identified β-muricholic acid as a key mediator of mcrA-dependent neuroprotection, suggesting that dietary modulation of gut microbiota through inulin and its impact on mcrA could represent a therapeutic strategy for PD.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with neuroinflammatory markers and cognitive decline in early-stage Alzheimer’s disease (AD) patients, with significant associations observed between specific microbial taxa and the *APOE* ε4 allele. Using principal component analysis on 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 AD participants and 80 age-matched controls, we identified distinct microbial clusters linked to *APOE* genotypes and serum cytokine levels. APOE ε4 carriers exhibited reduced abundance of Parabacteroides distasonis and elevated levels of TNF-α, while curcumin supplementation in a subset of participants modulated IL-6 expression and restored Bifidobacterium longum populations. Multivariate regression models revealed that APOE variants interacted with gut microbiota diversity to predict cognitive outcomes, independent of traditional risk factors. Notably, canonical correspondence analysis highlighted a synergistic relationship between short-chain fatty acids production and APOE-mediated neuroinflammation, suggesting microbiota-targeted therapies could mitigate AD progression. These findings underscore the interplay between host genetics and microbial metabolites in neurodegenerative pathways, offering novel targets for microbiome-based interventions.

Altered gut microbiota composition in patients with Alzheimer's disease correlates with APOE genotype and systemic inflammatory markers, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing and principal component analysis. Gastrointestinal samples from 120 participants were analyzed alongside plasma cytokine profiles, revealing that carriers of the APOE4 allele exhibited reduced Bifidobacterium abundance and elevated IL-6 levels compared to non-carriers. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing identified TLR4 upregulation in fecal microbiota of AD patients, suggesting a mechanistic link between APOE-driven immune signaling and microbiota dysbiosis. Multivariate regression confirmed that APOE4 status, microbial diversity indices, and soluble amyloid-beta levels collectively predicted cognitive decline rates over 18 months. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, gut-brain axis signaling, and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease progression, underscoring potential therapeutic targets at the intersection of genetic risk factors and microbiome modulation.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition correlate with depressive symptoms in individuals with major depression, as evidenced by decreased alpha diversity and shifts in bacterial taxa. 16S rRNA sequencing of fecal samples from 120 participants revealed that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were significantly underrepresented in depressed cohorts compared to healthy controls. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) highlighted pathways involving tryptophan metabolism and short-chain fatty acid production as key differentiators. Interventions incorporating fermented foods and whole grains enriched gut microbiome diversity, while supplementation with probiotic formulations containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus improved depressive symptoms in a subset of patients. Notably, individuals consuming a diet high in fiber and omega-3 fatty acids exhibited greater resilience to neuroinflammation markers, suggesting microbiota-modulating dietary strategies may mitigate depressive disorder progression. These findings underscore the role of gut-brain axis interactions in mental health and highlight the potential of targeted nutraceutical and nutrient interventions to restore microbial balance and alleviate psychiatric comorbidities.

A probiotic intervention significantly altered microbial metabolites linked to cognitive function in older adults, as identified through random forest analysis of longitudinal gut microbiome data from 150 participants. Lactobacillus-dominated communities exhibited enhanced production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), correlating with improved performance on hippocampal-dependent memory tasks. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that supplementation with Fructooligosaccharides increased Bifidobacterium abundance by 43%, while canonical correlation analysis highlighted associations between butyrate levels and reduced Alzheimer's disease-related biomarkers in serum. SCFA concentrations, particularly butyrate, showed strong negative correlations with amyloid-beta deposition in temporal cortex regions, as measured by positron emission tomography. The study further demonstrated that probiotic effects were mediated via TLR2-dependent signaling pathways, with multivariate analysis confirming a 28% reduction in neuroinflammatory markers following 12-week intervention. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the gut-brain axis through microbial interventions may represent a viable strategy for mitigating age-related cognitive decline.

The gut microbiota composition in patients with inflammatory bowel disease is significantly altered by probiotic supplementation and fermented dairy intake, with implications for central nervous system function. Analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data from 120 participants revealed that NOD2-mediated immune signaling pathways were dysregulated in individuals receiving Lactobacillus rhamnosus, correlating with reduced tryptophan metabolism. Soy-based diets enriched in isoflavones further modulated gut microbiome diversity, enhancing Prevotella abundance and improving irritable bowel syndrome symptoms via canonical correlation analysis. Notably, TLR4 expression in enteric neurons was inversely associated with high-fiber cereal consumption, suggesting a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids and neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between targeted microbiota modulation, nutritional interventions, and host genetic factors in shaping the gut-brain axis.

Alterations in gut microbiome composition have been linked to cognitive decline in patients with Alzheimer’s disease, prompting investigation into dietary interventions. Fermented dairy products, rich in short-chain fatty acids, were found to enhance gut microbial diversity and modulate neurotransmitter production via 16S rRNA sequencing analysis. Concurrently, probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus rhamnosus strains significantly reduced systemic inflammatory cytokines in mice models, correlating with improved hippocampal neurogenesis. Metabolomic profiling revealed that fermented dairy increased butyrate levels, which activated PPARγ receptors in the enteric nervous system, reinforcing gut-brain communication. Probiotic administration also restored microbial homeostasis disrupted by a high-fat diet, mitigating metabolic syndrome-related cognitive impairment. These findings suggest that fermented foods and targeted probiotics may synergistically support gut-brain axis integrity, offering therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative conditions through microbiota-directed interventions.

A diet rich in fermented kimchi significantly alters gut microbiota composition, enhancing abundance of Enterococcus faecalis while reducing Bacteroides fragilis, as revealed by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing. Principal component analysis of microbial profiles correlated these shifts with elevated levels of short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, in fecal samples from participants consuming the kimchi-based regimen. This microbial reconfiguration was associated with reduced inflammation markers (IL-6) and improved cognitive performance in older adults, suggesting a potential link between fermented food intake and neuroprotection via the gut-brain axis. Lactobacillus plantarum, a dominant kimchi species, exhibited enhanced gut barrier function gene expression in colonic epithelial cells in vitro, mediated by SCFA-induced histone acetylation. These findings highlight the role of fermented foods in modulating gut microbiota to influence systemic inflammation and cognitive outcomes, with implications for Alzheimer's disease prevention. The study underscores the utility of metagenomic and multivariate approaches in elucidating diet-microbiome-disease interactions.

Altered gut microbiota composition is significantly correlated with anxiety severity in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS), as revealed by 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing of fecal samples. Prevotella abundance showed a strong inverse relationship with dry eye severity (p < 0.001), while Bacteroidetes and Odoribacter were positively associated with pSS activity (p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis identified gut dysbiosis as a key mediator linking anxiety disorders and pSS-mediated dry eye, with Prevotella explaining 32% of variance in symptom scores. Participants exhibiting anxiety disorder (prevalence 30.4%) demonstrated reduced gut microbiome diversity and elevated Collinsella levels compared to non-anxious controls. Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS-A) scores correlated with shifts in gut microbiota taxa, particularly Parabacteroides and Tyzzerella, which were enriched in high-anxiety groups. These findings suggest a bidirectional interplay between gut microbiota and mental health in pSS, highlighting potential therapeutic targets through microbiome modulation. The integration of 16S rRNA sequencing with multivariate analysis provides a framework for understanding gut-brain axis dynamics in autoimmune conditions with psychiatric comorbidities.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition significantly influence neurobehavioral outcomes in individuals with depression, highlighting the role of intestinal flora in modulating brain function. A probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus and Bifidobacterium longum was administered to participants with depressive symptoms over 12 weeks. Metagenomic sequencing revealed increased abundance of Bifidobacterium and reduced Proteobacteria in stool samples, correlating with improved mood scores. Concurrently, fermented dairy products consumption was associated with greater microbiome diversity, suggesting dietary factors interact with microbial interventions. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotics in conjunction with prebiotic-rich diets to restore gut-brain axis homeostasis. Colonic levels of tryptophan metabolites also increased, aligning with reduced inflammation markers in serum. The integration of machine learning models further identified Akkermansia muciniphila as a predictive biomarker for treatment response. This study highlights the interplay between microbial modulation, nutritional intake, and neuroimmune pathways in psychiatric disorders, offering novel strategies for personalized mental health care.

Altered gut microbiota composition associated with metabolic syndrome was identified through metagenomic sequencing in individuals following a high-fat diet. Analysis revealed a significant increase in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance alongside reduced diversity of gut microbiota in participants consuming the high-fat diet for 12 weeks compared to controls. Concurrently, serum levels of endotoxin and inflammatory cytokines rose, correlating with heightened insulin resistance and systemic inflammation markers. 16S rRNA sequencing further confirmed shifts in Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes ratios, implicating dysbiosis in metabolic dysfunction. Dietary intervention with prebiotic fiber restored microbial balance, reduced endotoxin translocation, and normalized insulin resistance indices. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota modulation via dietary components and metabolic health outcomes, suggesting that targeted molecular profiling of microbial communities could inform precision nutrition strategies. The high-fat diet model demonstrates how dietary-induced microbiota changes drive pathophysiological pathways, emphasizing the need for integrative approaches to mitigate metabolic disorders through microbiome-directed therapies.

The gut microbiome of participants consuming a fermented dairy diet exhibited heightened Bifidobacterium abundance, which correlated with reduced anxiety scores when supplemented with a probiotic capsule containing Lactobacillus rhamnosus. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we observed that the microbial community in individuals adhering to a high-fiber regimen showed increased butyrate production, a metabolite linked to hippocampal neuroplasticity. Patients receiving the probiotic intervention demonstrated a 23% reduction in depressive symptoms, as measured by the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, compared to controls on a standard Western diet. Prevotella levels, which were elevated in the gut microbiome of subjects consuming plant-based meals, were inversely associated with insomnia severity. These findings suggest that targeted microbial modulation combined with dietary interventions may enhance gut-brain axis communication, offering a novel strategy for mental health management.

Altered TLR4 signaling in the intestinal epithelium significantly modulates gut microbiota composition and neuroinflammation in response to dietary inulin intake. Using a murine model of colitis-induced behavioral deficits, we demonstrated that inulin-enriched diets increased Lactobacillus abundance while reducing Bacteroidetes diversity, correlating with decreased IL-6 and TNF-α levels in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, TLR4-deficient mice exhibited attenuated neuroinflammatory responses to inulin, independent of changes in gut microbiota structure, suggesting a direct epithelial-immune interaction. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that inulin selectively enhanced Parabacteroides and Allobaculum taxa, which inversely correlated with brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression in the prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight TLR4 as a critical mediator of dietary fiber's neuroprotective effects via dual modulation of gut microbiota and host immune pathways, offering novel insights into microbiome-targeted therapies for neuroinflammatory disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition are linked to neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease (PD), with specific gene variants modulating this relationship. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from 80 patients with PD and 50 controls, revealing reduced diversity and enrichment of pro-inflammatory Escherichia coli in PD cohorts. Notably, carriers of the SNCA duplication exhibited heightened microbial dysbiosis, correlating with elevated IL-6 levels in serum. Intervention with the inulin restored alpha diversity and suppressed E. coli abundance, accompanied by decreased neuroinflammatory markers. Metabolomic profiling identified butyrate as a key mediator, with its production strongly associated with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii expansion post-supplementation. These findings highlight the interplay between host genetics, microbiota dynamics, and dietary modulation in PD pathogenesis, underscoring potential therapeutic strategies targeting microbial-derived metabolites.

A high-fiber fermented dairy consumption pattern significantly modulates gut microbiota composition, enhancing production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and reducing Alzheimer's disease risk in aging populations. Longitudinal analysis of 12,345 participants from the UK Biobank revealed that daily intake of prebiotic fiber correlated with increased abundance of Bifidobacterium longum and decreased prevalence of Escherichia coli, alongside improved blood-brain barrier integrity. Mechanistically, SCFAs derived from fermented dairy-associated Lactobacillus activated TLR4-mediated signaling pathways in enteric neurons, reducing neuroinflammation markers IL-6 and TNF-α. 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed that individuals with the highest prebiotic fiber intake exhibited a 34% lower incidence of Alzheimer's disease over 10 years compared to controls. These findings highlight the interplay between fermented dairy-derived gut microbiota metabolites and central nervous system health, suggesting targeted prebiotic interventions could mitigate neurodegeneration risk through microbiome-brain communication pathways.

Alterations in the gut microbiome composition of patients with Parkinson's disease correlate with progressive neuroinflammation and motor decline, as revealed by 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing and multivariate logistic regression analysis of fecal samples. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium genera showed significant depletion in cases compared to age- and sex-matched controls, while pathobionts like Escherichia-Shigella exhibited elevated abundance. Short-chain fatty acid production pathways were dysregulated, with reduced butyrate synthesis linked to increased blood-brain barrier permeability markers. Cox proportional hazards modeling further demonstrated that gut microbiota diversity loss preceded clinical symptom onset by an average of 3.2 years, independent of SNCA polymorphisms. Interventions targeting Prevotella copri expansion through prebiotic fibers showed preliminary efficacy in mitigating alpha-synuclein aggregation in transgenic mouse models, suggesting microbiome modulation could delay disease progression. These findings underscore the gut-brain axis's role in neurodegeneration and highlight the potential of metabolomic profiling for early diagnostic stratification.

The NOD2 gene modulates microbial metabolism of inulin, as revealed by 16S rRNA sequencing in a murine model of gut-brain axis dysregulation. Mice lacking functional NOD2 exhibited altered gut microbiota composition, with reduced abundance of Bacteroidetes and increased Firmicutes, correlating with heightened anxiety-like behaviors in open-field tests. Dietary supplementation with inulin partially restored microbial balance, suggesting a role for host-encoded immune signaling in shaping microbiota responses to prebiotic substrates. Mechanistically, NOD2-mediated recognition of microbial peptidoglycans enhanced short-chain fatty acid production by Butyricimonas, which in turn modulated hippocampal neurogenesis via SCFA-induced EP3 receptor activation. These findings highlight a direct link between innate immune genes, microbial metabolic pathways, and behavioral outcomes, underscoring the potential of targeted prebiotic interventions in neuroimmune disorders.

Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to depression via dysregulated neuroinflammatory pathways, yet mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using 16S rRNA sequencing, we identified reduced Lactobacillus abundance in rodent models exposed to chronic stress, correlating with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in serum. Administration of the probiotic Lactobacillus rhamnosus restored microbial balance, mitigating depressive-like behavior and normalizing IL-6 levels through TLR2-mediated signaling in hippocampal neurons. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of probiotic interventions in modulating gut microbiota-driven neuroinflammation. Furthermore, metagenomic sequencing revealed that Akkermansia muciniphila abundance inversely correlated with serotonin transporter SLC6A4 expression, suggesting a role for microbial metabolites in neurotransmitter regulation. The study underscores the value of multi-omics approaches to dissect gut-brain axis interactions and supports the use of probiotic formulations as adjuncts in mental health disorders management.

A novel probiotic formulation modulates neuroinflammation through SIRT1 activation in a murine model of Alzheimer's disease, with Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG demonstrating dose-dependent suppression of SIRT1-mediated autophagy pathways in hippocampal neurons. Using principal component analysis, we identified distinct microbial signatures correlating with reduced neuroinflammatory markers in the prefrontal cortex following 12 weeks of supplementation. Gut microbiota alterations induced by the probiotic were associated with enhanced SIRT1 expression and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, as measured by ELISA and qPCR. Mouse cohorts receiving the probiotic exhibited improved spatial memory in the Morris water maze, with ANOVA revealing significant intergroup differences in latency scores compared to vehicle-treated controls. Mechanistically, L. rhamnosus GG appears to modulate SIRT1-dependent mitochondrial function, as evidenced by increased mitochondrial ATP production in hippocampal tissue samples. These findings suggest that probiotic interventions targeting SIRT1 signaling may offer therapeutic potential for neurodegenerative disorders via the gut-brain axis.

A diet enriched with fermented dairy products significantly altered gut microbiota composition and reduced anxiety-like behaviors in rodent models, as revealed by principal component analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data. Fermented milk supplementation increased relative abundance of the Lactobacillus genus while decreasing Desulfovibrio, correlating with elevated serotonin levels in the hippocampus. Metagenomic sequencing identified 127 differentially expressed genes linked to neuroimmune signaling pathways, with TNF-α expression reduced by 40% in treated groups compared to controls. Permutation tests confirmed the significance of these microbiome shifts, which were further validated by fluorescent in situ hybridization in colonic epithelial cells. Behavioral assessments using the open field test showed a 35% decrease in grooming time and 25% increase in exploratory behavior in fermented milk-fed rodents, suggesting microbiome-mediated modulation of the gut-brain axis. These findings highlight the potential of probiotic-rich diets as therapeutic interventions for anxiety-related disorders, with machine learning models predicting microbiome composition changes with 82% accuracy based on dietary intake patterns.

Altered gut microbiota composition in bipolar disorder (BD) patients correlates with TRANK1 gene expression changes, which modulate blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity through type 1 interferon signaling. Dysbiosis reduces butyrate-producing bacteria abundance while increasing pathogenic strains like Escherichia-Shigella, exacerbating neuroinflammation via elevated IL-6 and IFN-γ levels. Mechanistic studies reveal that butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid derived from fiber-rich diets, enhances tight junction protein expression (ZO-1, Claudin-5) in enteric glial cells, mitigating BBB leakage. Probiotic administration also restores intestinal permeability and suppresses GFAP upregulation in colonic and central nervous system tissues. These findings highlight the interplay between microbiota-derived metabolites and host TRANK1 activity in BD pathogenesis, suggesting that targeted modulation of dietary fiber intake and probiotic supplementation could stabilize BBB function. Such interventions may address the inflammatory cascade linking gut dysbiosis to neuroinflammation, offering novel therapeutic avenues for BD.

The disruption of the TLR5 gene in Tlr5-/- mice was found to significantly alter the composition of the gut microbiome, leading to increased intestinal permeability and systemic inflammation. These changes correlated with impaired cognitive function in behavioral assays, suggesting a role for TLR5 in maintaining gut-brain homeostasis. Administration of the curcumin partially reversed these effects, as evidenced by a reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines and normalization of microbiome diversity. Mechanistically, curcumin enhanced the expression of TLR5 and promoted the growth of Bifidobacterium, which are known to modulate neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the interplay between genetic factors and dietary interventions in mitigating gut-brain axis dysfunctions associated with neurodegenerative disorders. The study underscores the potential of targeting TLR5 and employing curcumin as a therapeutic strategy to restore gut microbiome integrity and cognitive function.
